books.name: Genesis
books.intro: Moses opens the history of creation and the fall, then follows God's covenant dealings with Abraham's family. Chapters 1 to 11 set the world's condition before us. Chapters 12 to 50 follow the family through whom the promised blessing will come.
books.introText: Moses opens the history of creation and the fall, then follows God's covenant dealings with Abraham's family. Chapters 1 to 11 set the world's condition before us. Chapters 12 to 50 follow the family through whom the promised blessing will come.

helps.text: Stories are told tightly and often without comment. Don't assume that what the text reports it endorses.
helps.html: Stories are told tightly and often without comment. Don't assume that what the text reports it endorses.

helps.text: God created all things out of nothing by His word in the space of six days, and all very good. This is the doctrine of creation, confessed in WCF 4.1. Read Genesis 1 and 2 together. The second chapter attends more closely to the creation of man, his calling, and the marriage covenant. It doesn't describe a second creation.
helps.html: God created all things out of nothing by His word in the space of six days, and all very good. This is the doctrine of creation, confessed in WCF 4.1. Read Genesis 1 and 2 together. The second chapter attends more closely to the creation of man, his calling, and the marriage covenant. It doesn't describe a second creation.

helps.text: Genesis 2.1 to 3 records God’s rest on the seventh day. This is the pattern for the Sabbath, set into the creation order before sin and before Sinai. The fourth commandment will draw on this pattern. Under the new covenant the day moves from the seventh to the first, kept by the church as the Lord’s Day in honor of the risen Christ.
helps.html: Genesis 2.1 to 3 records God’s rest on the seventh day. This is the pattern for the Sabbath, set into the creation order before sin and before Sinai. The fourth commandment will draw on this pattern. Under the new covenant the day moves from the seventh to the first, kept by the church as the Lord’s Day in honor of the risen Christ.

helps.text: The covenant of works was made with Adam in the garden. Life was promised on condition of perfect, personal, and perpetual obedience. Death was threatened upon breach. WCF 7.2. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was the appointed test. Without this covenant, you can't rightly read Romans 5 or the active obedience of Christ.
helps.html: The covenant of works was made with Adam in the garden. Life was promised on condition of perfect, personal, and perpetual obedience. Death was threatened upon breach. WCF 7.2. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was the appointed test. Without this covenant, you can't rightly read Romans 5 or the active obedience of Christ.

helps.text: The fall in Genesis 3 is real history with cosmic consequences. The serpent was real. The fruit was real. Sin and death entered the human race through Adam, as Romans 5 confirms. The covenant of works was broken in the fall.
helps.html: The fall in Genesis 3 is real history with cosmic consequences. The serpent was real. The fruit was real. Sin and death entered the human race through Adam, as Romans 5 confirms. The covenant of works was broken in the fall.

helps.text: Genesis 3.15 is the first preaching of the gospel and the first announcement of the covenant of grace. The seed of the woman who crushes the serpent’s head is Christ. From this verse forward the whole Bible runs toward His cross and resurrection.
helps.html: Genesis 3.15 is the first preaching of the gospel and the first announcement of the covenant of grace. The seed of the woman who crushes the serpent’s head is Christ. From this verse forward the whole Bible runs toward His cross and resurrection.

helps.text: The flood in Genesis 6 to 9 is a real global judgment. Noah’s ark is a type of salvation in Christ. The covenant with Noah preserves the world for the unfolding of redemption.
helps.html: The flood in Genesis 6 to 9 is a real global judgment. Noah’s ark is a type of salvation in Christ. The covenant with Noah preserves the world for the unfolding of redemption.

helps.text: The genealogies trace real descent through the early generations. Their age notices contribute to the chronology. Don't assume either gaps or an exhaustive modern timetable without examining how each genealogy is written.
helps.html: The genealogies trace real descent through the early generations. Their age notices contribute to the chronology. Don't assume either gaps or an exhaustive modern timetable without examining how each genealogy is written.

helps.text: The Abrahamic covenant in chapters 12, 15, and 17 is the foundation of all later covenants. The promises of seed, land, and blessing to the nations are fulfilled in Christ and the church.
helps.html: The Abrahamic covenant in chapters 12, 15, and 17 is the foundation of all later covenants. The promises of seed, land, and blessing to the nations are fulfilled in Christ and the church.

helps.text: Patriarchal narratives often report sin without comment. Jacob’s deceit, Judah’s sin with Tamar, Abraham’s lies about Sarah are reported but not endorsed. The text is teaching by displaying real men, not always by approving their acts.
helps.html: Patriarchal narratives often report sin without comment. Jacob’s deceit, Judah’s sin with Tamar, Abraham’s lies about Sarah are reported but not endorsed. The text is teaching by displaying real men, not always by approving their acts.

helps.text: Joseph's rejection, suffering, and later exaltation provide fruitful comparisons with Christ. Unlike Adam or the Passover, Joseph isn't explicitly identified as a type in the New Testament. Use the comparison without giving every detail a hidden meaning.
helps.html: Joseph's rejection, suffering, and later exaltation provide fruitful comparisons with Christ. Unlike Adam or the Passover, Joseph isn't explicitly identified as a type in the New Testament. Use the comparison without giving every detail a hidden meaning.

helps.text: The book closes pointing forward. Joseph dies in Egypt looking for the promised land. The reader is meant to feel that the story isn't finished.
helps.html: The book closes pointing forward. Joseph dies in Egypt looking for the promised land. The reader is meant to feel that the story isn't finished.

helps.text: Read Genesis as the seedbed of the whole Bible. Themes that begin here run through every later book. The two Adams. The two seeds. The covenants. The promised land. The blood of the lamb. All begin here.
helps.html: Read Genesis as the seedbed of the whole Bible. Themes that begin here run through every later book. The two Adams. The two seeds. The covenants. The promised land. The blood of the lamb. All begin here.

studies.title: Adam acts as a covenant head
studies.html: The command concerning the tree is given to an upright man who owes God obedience. Genesis 3 then records the breach, judgment, and promised victory over the serpent. Romans 5.12 to 19 explains the representative relation that makes Adam’s act consequential for his descendants. This is why the account is more than a lesson about making poor choices. Christ’s obedience answers the ruin brought by the first head of mankind.
studies.distinction: Adam’s original obligation and a fallen sinner’s way of salvation mustn’t be treated as the same covenant arrangement.
studies.question: Compare Genesis 2.17 with Romans 5.18 to 19. What depends upon the act of each representative?

studies.title: The promise develops without changing its Savior
studies.html: Abraham believes God’s promise, and righteousness is counted to him. Romans 4 uses this account to explain justification apart from works. Galatians 3 traces the blessing to Christ and includes Gentile believers as Abraham’s children through faith. The later fulfillment doesn’t make Abraham’s household or Israel’s history unreal. It reveals how God brings the promised blessing to the nations through the one Redeemer.
studies.distinction: The historical forms of the promise and its saving substance are related, but they aren’t interchangeable in every detail.
studies.question: How does Romans 4 use the timing of Abraham’s faith and circumcision to explain justification?

books.name: Exodus
books.intro: God brings Israel out of slavery and establishes His covenant at Sinai. The book moves from deliverance in Egypt to God's dwelling among His people in the tabernacle. Redemption precedes the giving of the law.
books.introText: God brings Israel out of slavery and establishes His covenant at Sinai. The book moves from deliverance in Egypt to God's dwelling among His people in the tabernacle. Redemption precedes the giving of the law.

helps.text: Worship is regulated by the Word. The pattern of the tabernacle was given by God, not invented by Moses. This pattern shapes how God is to be worshiped under both testaments.
helps.html: Worship is regulated by the Word. The pattern of the tabernacle was given by God, not invented by Moses. This pattern shapes how God is to be worshiped under both testaments.

helps.text: The exodus is the central act of redemption in the Old Testament and is the pattern for the greater redemption Christ accomplishes. Luke calls Christ’s death His exodus in Luke 9.31.
helps.html: The exodus is the central act of redemption in the Old Testament and is the pattern for the greater redemption Christ accomplishes. Luke calls Christ’s death His exodus in Luke 9.31.

helps.text: Pharaoh hardening his heart and God hardening his heart are both said in the text. Both are true. God is sovereign over the heart of the king and the king is responsible for his rebellion. This is the same pattern as Romans 9.
helps.html: Pharaoh hardening his heart and God hardening his heart are both said in the text. Both are true. God is sovereign over the heart of the king and the king is responsible for his rebellion. This is the same pattern as Romans 9.

helps.text: The Passover in Exodus 12 establishes substitution. The lamb dies in place of the firstborn. The blood on the doorpost protects those inside. Christ is our Passover.
helps.html: The Passover in Exodus 12 establishes substitution. The lamb dies in place of the firstborn. The blood on the doorpost protects those inside. Christ is our Passover.

helps.text: The crossing of the Red Sea is a real event and is also a picture of baptism (1 Corinthians 10.2) and of deliverance from the power of the world.
helps.html: The crossing of the Red Sea is a real event and is also a picture of baptism (1 Corinthians 10.2) and of deliverance from the power of the world.

helps.text: Manna from heaven (chapter 16) and water from the rock (chapter 17) are real provisions and also point to Christ as bread of life and source of living water (John 6, 1 Corinthians 10.4).
helps.html: Manna from heaven (chapter 16) and water from the rock (chapter 17) are real provisions and also point to Christ as bread of life and source of living water (John 6, 1 Corinthians 10.4).

helps.text: Distinguish the moral, ceremonial, and judicial law in Exodus 19 to 24. The moral law binds everyone. Christ has fulfilled the ceremonial law, which is abrogated under the New Testament. Israel's judicial laws expired with that nation, except for the general equity that remains obligatory. WCF 19.3 and WCF 19.4 make these distinctions. General equity is the abiding moral justice of those laws, not permission to discard their instruction or to restore Israel's national constitution wholesale.
helps.html: Distinguish the moral, ceremonial, and judicial law in Exodus 19 to 24. The moral law binds everyone. Christ has fulfilled the ceremonial law, which is abrogated under the New Testament. Israel's judicial laws expired with that nation, except for the general equity that remains obligatory. WCF 19.3 and WCF 19.4 make these distinctions. General equity is the abiding moral justice of those laws, not permission to discard their instruction or to restore Israel's national constitution wholesale.

helps.text: The fourth commandment (20.8 to 11) commands a Sabbath rest, grounded in the creation pattern of Genesis 2. The moral substance of the commandment continues. The day moves under the new covenant from the seventh to the first, kept by the church as the Lord’s Day in honor of the risen Christ. WCF 21.7 to 8.
helps.html: The fourth commandment (20.8 to 11) commands a Sabbath rest, grounded in the creation pattern of Genesis 2. The moral substance of the commandment continues. The day moves under the new covenant from the seventh to the first, kept by the church as the Lord’s Day in honor of the risen Christ. WCF 21.7 to 8.

helps.text: The tabernacle in chapters 25 to 40 is a portable sanctuary patterned after a heavenly reality (Hebrews 8). The ark, the table, the lampstand, the altar, the laver, the veil, the holy place, and the most holy place all teach truth about access to God through Christ.
helps.html: The tabernacle in chapters 25 to 40 is a portable sanctuary patterned after a heavenly reality (Hebrews 8). The ark, the table, the lampstand, the altar, the laver, the veil, the holy place, and the most holy place all teach truth about access to God through Christ.

helps.text: The golden calf in chapter 32 shows how quickly the human heart turns to idolatry, even after great deliverance. It also shows that men who try to worship the true God by their own devised means fall under judgment. This is a warning to every reader.
helps.html: The golden calf in chapter 32 shows how quickly the human heart turns to idolatry, even after great deliverance. It also shows that men who try to worship the true God by their own devised means fall under judgment. This is a warning to every reader.

helps.text: The book ends with the glory of the Lord filling the tabernacle. God dwells with His people, but Moses can't enter. A greater mediator is needed.
helps.html: The book ends with the glory of the Lord filling the tabernacle. God dwells with His people, but Moses can't enter. A greater mediator is needed.

studies.title: Deliverance comes before Sinai
studies.html: The commandments begin by identifying the Lord who brought Israel out of bondage. They are spoken within a history of redemption, not offered to enslaved sinners as a ladder by which they can first earn God’s rescue. Their moral demands nevertheless remain serious. Reading the order carefully guards the gospel while preserving the law’s use in directing a redeemed people’s life.
studies.distinction: A law’s place after deliverance doesn’t make obedience optional, and the presence of commands doesn’t make redemption earned.
studies.question: What does Exodus 20.2 contribute to the way the following commandments should be received?

studies.title: The calf and the worship of the true God
studies.html: Aaron announces a feast to the Lord, but the calf doesn’t become acceptable because His name is invoked. Israel corrupts worship by making an image and approaching God through a device He hasn’t appointed. The narrative therefore reaches beyond the worship of a different deity. Read it with the second commandment and the tabernacle instructions that precede it.
studies.distinction: Sincerity and a religious label cannot supply God’s authorization for an invented act of worship.
studies.question: How do Aaron’s announcement and God’s verdict show the difference between intended worship and acceptable worship?

books.name: Leviticus
books.intro: The Lord teaches a redeemed people how sinful men may approach a holy God. Sacrifice and priesthood stand at the center of the book. Read these ordinances with Hebrews beside you to see their fulfillment in Christ.
books.introText: The Lord teaches a redeemed people how sinful men may approach a holy God. Sacrifice and priesthood stand at the center of the book. Read these ordinances with Hebrews beside you to see their fulfillment in Christ.

helps.text: The book divides roughly into laws of sacrifice (1 to 7), laws of priesthood (8 to 10), laws of clean and unclean (11 to 15), the day of atonement (16), and the holiness code (17 to 27). Hold this map in mind.
helps.html: The book divides roughly into laws of sacrifice (1 to 7), laws of priesthood (8 to 10), laws of clean and unclean (11 to 15), the day of atonement (16), and the holiness code (17 to 27). Hold this map in mind.

helps.text: The five offerings (burnt, grain, peace, sin, guilt) each teach part of the picture of Christ’s work. The burnt offering is total devotion. The sin offering is atonement for offense. The peace offering is fellowship. The guilt offering is restitution.
helps.html: The five offerings (burnt, grain, peace, sin, guilt) each teach part of the picture of Christ’s work. The burnt offering is total devotion. The sin offering is atonement for offense. The peace offering is fellowship. The guilt offering is restitution.

helps.text: The priesthood of Aaron is real and also typological. Christ is the greater priest who fulfills and replaces the Aaronic line.
helps.html: The priesthood of Aaron is real and also typological. Christ is the greater priest who fulfills and replaces the Aaronic line.

helps.text: The death of Nadab and Abihu in chapter 10 stands as one of the great warnings of the Old Testament about worship. They offered strange fire that the Lord had not commanded them. Fire from the Lord consumed them. Worship not commanded by God isn't safer than worship forbidden by God. The regulative principle finds one of its sharpest illustrations here.
helps.html: The death of Nadab and Abihu in chapter 10 stands as one of the great warnings of the Old Testament about worship. They offered strange fire that the Lord had not commanded them. Fire from the Lord consumed them. Worship not commanded by God isn't safer than worship forbidden by God. The regulative principle finds one of its sharpest illustrations here.

helps.text: The laws of clean and unclean aren't arbitrary. They teach Israel that holiness touches every area of life and that sin defiles. Many of these laws are fulfilled in Christ, as Mark 7 makes clear.
helps.html: The laws of clean and unclean aren't arbitrary. They teach Israel that holiness touches every area of life and that sin defiles. Many of these laws are fulfilled in Christ, as Mark 7 makes clear.

helps.text: The day of atonement in chapter 16 is the high point of the book. The two goats together (one slain, one driven out) picture both the satisfying of God’s wrath and the carrying away of sin. Christ fulfills both.
helps.html: The day of atonement in chapter 16 is the high point of the book. The two goats together (one slain, one driven out) picture both the satisfying of God’s wrath and the carrying away of sin. Christ fulfills both.

helps.text: The holiness code (17 to 27) covers sexual ethics, social ethics, and worship. The moral teaching continues to apply. The ceremonial framing is fulfilled in Christ.
helps.html: The holiness code (17 to 27) covers sexual ethics, social ethics, and worship. The moral teaching continues to apply. The ceremonial framing is fulfilled in Christ.

helps.text: The sexual laws of chapter 18 and 20 are moral, not merely ceremonial, and remain binding. They're reaffirmed in the New Testament.
helps.html: The sexual laws of chapter 18 and 20 are moral, not merely ceremonial, and remain binding. They're reaffirmed in the New Testament.

helps.text: The laws of the festival calendar in chapter 23 (Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Pentecost, Trumpets, Atonement, Booths) all find their meaning in Christ and the gospel age. They're no longer binding as feasts but they teach the shape of redemption.
helps.html: The laws of the festival calendar in chapter 23 (Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Pentecost, Trumpets, Atonement, Booths) all find their meaning in Christ and the gospel age. They're no longer binding as feasts but they teach the shape of redemption.

helps.text: The blessings and curses of the law come into view late in the book (chapter 26) and prepare the reader for the long history that follows. Israel’s exile and return work out the patterns named here.
helps.html: The blessings and curses of the law come into view late in the book (chapter 26) and prepare the reader for the long history that follows. Israel’s exile and return work out the patterns named here.

studies.title: Ceremonial uncleanness is not identical with personal guilt
studies.html: Some conditions that bring ceremonial uncleanness arise through ordinary bodily life. Their ritual consequences teach Israel about holiness, access, and the need for cleansing. They don’t mean that childbirth or every bodily condition is itself a moral transgression. Distinguish the ordinance’s covenant function from the moral character of the event it regulates, then trace ceremonial fulfillment through Christ.
studies.distinction: Ritual classification mustn’t be turned into a moral accusation against a person whom the passage doesn’t accuse.
studies.question: What does Leviticus 12 require, and which moral accusation would go beyond its words?

studies.title: One atonement portrayed through distinct actions
studies.html: On the day of atonement, blood is brought into the sanctuary and the live goat bears the confessed iniquities away. The actions together portray cleansing and the removal of sin. Hebrews 9 to 10 explains why repeated animal offerings cannot accomplish the final reality. Christ enters by His own blood and obtains redemption that doesn’t need to be renewed by another sacrifice.
studies.distinction: The two goats don’t establish two saving mediators or two independent ways of dealing with guilt.
studies.question: How does Hebrews distinguish the ceremony’s repetition from the sufficiency of Christ’s offering?

books.name: Numbers
books.intro: Israel travels from Sinai toward the promised land, but unbelief keeps a generation in the wilderness. The two censuses distinguish the generation that came out of Egypt from the generation preparing to enter Canaan.
books.introText: Israel travels from Sinai toward the promised land, but unbelief keeps a generation in the wilderness. The two censuses distinguish the generation that came out of Egypt from the generation preparing to enter Canaan.

helps.text: The censuses in chapters 1 and 26 mark two generations. Read the intervening accounts of unbelief and death with that contrast in mind. The book continues after the second census with instructions for life in the land.
helps.html: The censuses in chapters 1 and 26 mark two generations. Read the intervening accounts of unbelief and death with that contrast in mind. The book continues after the second census with instructions for life in the land.

helps.text: The complaints and rebellions of Israel aren't minor incidents. They're the pattern of unbelief that the rest of Scripture warns against. Each one shows the human heart in the absence of faith.
helps.html: The complaints and rebellions of Israel aren't minor incidents. They're the pattern of unbelief that the rest of Scripture warns against. Each one shows the human heart in the absence of faith.

helps.text: Korah’s rebellion (chapter 16) attacks Moses and Aaron’s appointed authority. God vindicates His mediators. The lesson carries forward to Christ as the appointed mediator who must not be despised.
helps.html: Korah’s rebellion (chapter 16) attacks Moses and Aaron’s appointed authority. God vindicates His mediators. The lesson carries forward to Christ as the appointed mediator who must not be despised.

helps.text: The bronze serpent in chapter 21 is the clearest typological link Christ Himself draws to His own crucifixion (John 3.14 to 15). Look on Him and live.
helps.html: The bronze serpent in chapter 21 is the clearest typological link Christ Himself draws to His own crucifixion (John 3.14 to 15). Look on Him and live.

helps.text: Balaam in chapters 22 to 24 is a strange episode. A pagan prophet pronounces blessings on Israel he could not change. The prophecies in chapter 24 reach all the way to Christ. "there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel" (Numbers 24.17).
helps.html: Balaam in chapters 22 to 24 is a strange episode. A pagan prophet pronounces blessings on Israel he could not change. The prophecies in chapter 24 reach all the way to Christ. "there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel" (Numbers 24.17).

helps.text: The story of the daughters of Zelophehad (chapter 27, 36) shows that God’s law honors justice toward those without standing in their society.
helps.html: The story of the daughters of Zelophehad (chapter 27, 36) shows that God’s law honors justice toward those without standing in their society.

helps.text: The cities of refuge in chapter 35 protect a person accused of manslaughter until the case is judged. Begin with their role in preserving justice. A comparison with refuge in Christ is an application, not a license to turn every legal detail into a type.
helps.html: The cities of refuge in chapter 35 protect a person accused of manslaughter until the case is judged. Begin with their role in preserving justice. A comparison with refuge in Christ is an application, not a license to turn every legal detail into a type.

helps.text: Numbers shows that being delivered from Egypt isn't the same as entering the rest. A whole generation perished in between. Hebrews 3 and 4 use this exactly to warn against falling away.
helps.html: Numbers shows that being delivered from Egypt isn't the same as entering the rest. A whole generation perished in between. Hebrews 3 and 4 use this exactly to warn against falling away.

helps.text: The book records both judgment and grace. God judges sin severely. He also remains faithful to His covenant and brings a new generation through.
helps.html: The book records both judgment and grace. God judges sin severely. He also remains faithful to His covenant and brings a new generation through.

studies.title: Covenant privileges do not make unbelief harmless
studies.html: The wilderness generation has witnessed deliverance and received God’s ordinances, yet many perish under judgment. First Corinthians 10 deliberately uses their shared privileges to warn the church. Outward participation is real and significant, but it isn’t identical with saving faith. The warning should produce watchfulness rather than either sacramental presumption or contempt for the privileges themselves.
studies.distinction: A distinction between outward and inward grace doesn’t reduce the visible covenant community to a meaningless fiction.
studies.question: What shared privileges does 1 Corinthians 10 name, and why doesn’t Paul treat them as a guarantee against judgment?

studies.title: The bronze serpent and its appointed use
studies.html: The Lord appoints the bronze serpent as the means through which the afflicted Israelites are to look and live. Jesus identifies this event with the lifting up of the Son of man in John 3.14 to 15. The connection is authoritative because Christ supplies it. Later, the object becomes an occasion of idolatry and is destroyed in 2 Kings 18.4. An appointed sign cannot be used faithfully apart from God’s appointed purpose.
studies.distinction: A biblical type doesn’t authorize later religious veneration of its physical object.
studies.question: What does Jesus identify as the correspondence, and what later use of the object does Scripture condemn?

books.name: Deuteronomy
books.intro: Moses addresses Israel before his death and their entry into Canaan. He recounts God's dealings with them and urges covenant faithfulness. Read the commands within this sustained appeal to love and obey the Lord.
books.introText: Moses addresses Israel before his death and their entry into Canaan. He recounts God's dealings with them and urges covenant faithfulness. Read the commands within this sustained appeal to love and obey the Lord.

helps.text: Deuteronomy is structured like an ancient suzerain treaty between a great king and his vassal people. There's a historical prologue (1 to 4), the stipulations of the law (5 to 26), the blessings and curses (27 to 28), and the covenant ratification with witnesses (29 to 30). This treaty form was well known in the ancient Near East and marks the book as a formal covenant renewal document, the renewal of the Sinai covenant with the second generation before they entered the land.
helps.html: Deuteronomy is structured like an ancient suzerain treaty between a great king and his vassal people. There's a historical prologue (1 to 4), the stipulations of the law (5 to 26), the blessings and curses (27 to 28), and the covenant ratification with witnesses (29 to 30). This treaty form was well known in the ancient Near East and marks the book as a formal covenant renewal document, the renewal of the Sinai covenant with the second generation before they entered the land.

helps.text: The law restated here isn't new. It's the Sinai law preached again to the new generation. Many specifics are repeated and applied to settled life in the land.
helps.html: The law restated here isn't new. It's the Sinai law preached again to the new generation. Many specifics are repeated and applied to settled life in the land.

helps.text: The Shema (6.4) is one of the most important verses in the Old Testament. It declares the unity of God and grounds the call to love Him with all you're.
helps.html: The Shema (6.4) is one of the most important verses in the Old Testament. It declares the unity of God and grounds the call to love Him with all you're.

helps.text: The promise of a prophet like Moses (18.15) is fulfilled in Christ, as Peter says in Acts 3 and Stephen says in Acts 7.
helps.html: The promise of a prophet like Moses (18.15) is fulfilled in Christ, as Peter says in Acts 3 and Stephen says in Acts 7.

helps.text: The commands for kings in Deuteronomy 17.14 to 20 forbid multiplying horses, wives, and wealth, and require attention to God's law. Compare Solomon's later conduct with these warnings.
helps.html: The commands for kings in Deuteronomy 17.14 to 20 forbid multiplying horses, wives, and wealth, and require attention to God's law. Compare Solomon's later conduct with these warnings.

helps.text: Cities of refuge are reaffirmed (chapter 19). Justice and mercy meet in the law’s provisions for the accused.
helps.html: Cities of refuge are reaffirmed (chapter 19). Justice and mercy meet in the law’s provisions for the accused.

helps.text: The blessings and curses (chapters 27 to 28) aren't threats in passing. They become the framework for understanding the entire later history of Israel and the prophetic witness against her sin.
helps.html: The blessings and curses (chapters 27 to 28) aren't threats in passing. They become the framework for understanding the entire later history of Israel and the prophetic witness against her sin.

helps.text: The covenant in 29 to 30 calls for circumcision of the heart (30.6). Paul picks this up in Romans 2 and Colossians 2 to apply it to every believer.
helps.html: The covenant in 29 to 30 calls for circumcision of the heart (30.6). Paul picks this up in Romans 2 and Colossians 2 to apply it to every believer.

helps.text: The Song of Moses (chapter 32) is a prophetic poem that sees Israel’s future apostasy and God’s faithfulness despite it. It's quoted often in the New Testament.
helps.html: The Song of Moses (chapter 32) is a prophetic poem that sees Israel’s future apostasy and God’s faithfulness despite it. It's quoted often in the New Testament.

helps.text: The book ends with Moses’s death. The mediator of the old covenant can't bring the people fully home. The reader is left waiting for a greater Moses.
helps.html: The book ends with Moses’s death. The mediator of the old covenant can't bring the people fully home. The reader is left waiting for a greater Moses.

studies.title: The commanded heart and the heart God gives
studies.html: Moses calls Israel to turn to the Lord and also promises that the Lord will circumcise their hearts so that they love Him. The command establishes real duty. The promise reveals the divine work needed for a fallen people to fulfill that duty from the heart. Don’t reason from a command alone that fallen man possesses the saving ability to obey it apart from grace.
studies.distinction: Moral responsibility and dependence upon regenerating grace are not competing explanations of conversion.
studies.question: How does Deuteronomy 30.6 relate God’s action to the love He requires?

studies.title: The prophet like Moses
studies.html: Moses promises a prophet whom the people must hear. Acts 3.19 to 26 identifies Jesus as the fulfillment. The wider passage also supplies a test for false claims to speak in God’s name. Christ is more than a useful teacher within a continuing line of equally authoritative revelations. His coming brings the climactic revelation to which the prophets bore witness.
studies.distinction: A prophetic fulfillment in Christ doesn’t erase the original command to reject false prophecy.
studies.question: How do Acts 3 and Hebrews 1 together clarify the authority of the promised Prophet?

books.name: Joshua
books.intro: The Lord brings Israel into Canaan under Joshua and gives the tribes their inheritance. His promises are fulfilled, yet the remaining enemies and the people's weakness show that the final rest still lies ahead.
books.introText: The Lord brings Israel into Canaan under Joshua and gives the tribes their inheritance. His promises are fulfilled, yet the remaining enemies and the people's weakness show that the final rest still lies ahead.

helps.text: The crossing of the Jordan in chapter 3 mirrors the crossing of the Red Sea. A new generation enters under a new leader. Both are real events with theological weight.
helps.html: The crossing of the Jordan in chapter 3 mirrors the crossing of the Red Sea. A new generation enters under a new leader. Both are real events with theological weight.

helps.text: The fall of Jericho in chapter 6 shows that the conquest is the Lord’s work. Israel marches and shouts. God brings down the wall.
helps.html: The fall of Jericho in chapter 6 shows that the conquest is the Lord’s work. Israel marches and shouts. God brings down the wall.

helps.text: Achan’s sin in chapter 7 shows that one man’s sin can defile the whole camp. The seriousness of sin under the covenant is real and present.
helps.html: Achan’s sin in chapter 7 shows that one man’s sin can defile the whole camp. The seriousness of sin under the covenant is real and present.

helps.text: The Gibeonite deception in chapter 9 shows the danger of acting without inquiring of the Lord. Israel makes a treaty without prayer and is bound by it.
helps.html: The Gibeonite deception in chapter 9 shows the danger of acting without inquiring of the Lord. Israel makes a treaty without prayer and is bound by it.

helps.text: The destruction of the Canaanites was a specific judicial act of God, given to one people at one time, against nations whose iniquity had reached its full measure (Genesis 15.16). It isn't a pattern for any later war.
helps.html: The destruction of the Canaanites was a specific judicial act of God, given to one people at one time, against nations whose iniquity had reached its full measure (Genesis 15.16). It isn't a pattern for any later war.

helps.text: The land was distributed by lot among the tribes (chapters 13 to 21). The boundaries are real and were known. Cities of refuge and Levitical cities were set apart for justice and worship.
helps.html: The land was distributed by lot among the tribes (chapters 13 to 21). The boundaries are real and were known. Cities of refuge and Levitical cities were set apart for justice and worship.

helps.text: Joshua’s farewell address (chapter 23 to 24) calls Israel to choose whom they will serve. The covenant renewal at Shechem is one of the great moments of the book.
helps.html: Joshua’s farewell address (chapter 23 to 24) calls Israel to choose whom they will serve. The covenant renewal at Shechem is one of the great moments of the book.

helps.text: The book reports that the Lord gave Israel rest (21.43 to 45) and yet Hebrews 4 says the rest of God remains for the people of God. Both are true. The land was a real foretaste. The full rest is in Christ.
helps.html: The book reports that the Lord gave Israel rest (21.43 to 45) and yet Hebrews 4 says the rest of God remains for the people of God. Both are true. The land was a real foretaste. The full rest is in Christ.

studies.title: The conquest is a judicial commission
studies.html: The fall of Jericho occurs within Israel’s specific commission concerning Canaan. Genesis 15.16 places the coming judgment within God’s patience toward the inhabitants. The event displays His justice and His freedom to judge through appointed agents. It doesn’t authorize the church to seize land or destroy unbelievers. The church receives a commission to preach and a spiritual discipline appropriate to its nature.
studies.distinction: Receiving a historical judgment as righteous doesn’t make its particular commission transferable to every later community.
studies.question: What divine authorization distinguishes the conquest from an ordinary claim that a religious cause justifies violence?

studies.title: A real rest that does not exhaust the promise
studies.html: Joshua says that the Lord fulfilled His good promises and gave Israel rest. Hebrews 4 nevertheless teaches that a rest remains for God’s people. These statements agree because the land’s rest is a real historical gift without being the final completion of God’s saving purpose. The later promise doesn’t require us to deny what Joshua says was actually accomplished.
studies.distinction: A preliminary fulfillment can be genuine without being exhaustive.
studies.question: Why does Hebrews appeal to a later word through David when explaining the rest that remains?

books.name: Judges
books.intro: Israel repeatedly turns from the Lord, suffers oppression, and receives deliverance. The judges themselves are deeply flawed. The closing accounts expose the misery of a people doing what is right in their own eyes.
books.introText: Israel repeatedly turns from the Lord, suffers oppression, and receives deliverance. The judges themselves are deeply flawed. The closing accounts expose the misery of a people doing what is right in their own eyes.

helps.text: The book moves through cycles of apostasy, oppression, repentance, and deliverance. Each cycle is worse than the last. The trajectory is downward.
helps.html: The book moves through cycles of apostasy, oppression, repentance, and deliverance. Each cycle is worse than the last. The trajectory is downward.

helps.text: The judges aren't always godly examples. Samson is gifted by God but ruled by lust. Jephthah makes a rash vow with terrible results. Gideon ends his life setting up an idol. The text reports without endorsing.
helps.html: The judges aren't always godly examples. Samson is gifted by God but ruled by lust. Jephthah makes a rash vow with terrible results. Gideon ends his life setting up an idol. The text reports without endorsing.

helps.text: The deliverers point forward to Christ as the true Deliverer, who is fully righteous and fully able to save.
helps.html: The deliverers point forward to Christ as the true Deliverer, who is fully righteous and fully able to save.

helps.text: Israel’s failure to drive out the Canaanites (chapter 1 to 3) leads to compromise and idolatry throughout the book. The lesson is that sin tolerated becomes sin committed.
helps.html: Israel’s failure to drive out the Canaanites (chapter 1 to 3) leads to compromise and idolatry throughout the book. The lesson is that sin tolerated becomes sin committed.

helps.text: The story of Deborah and Barak (chapter 4 to 5) celebrates God’s deliverance through unexpected means. The song of Deborah is one of the oldest poems in Scripture.
helps.html: The story of Deborah and Barak (chapter 4 to 5) celebrates God’s deliverance through unexpected means. The song of Deborah is one of the oldest poems in Scripture.

helps.text: The story of Gideon (chapter 6 to 8) shows how God strengthens faith over time but also how a deliverer can become a snare.
helps.html: The story of Gideon (chapter 6 to 8) shows how God strengthens faith over time but also how a deliverer can become a snare.

helps.text: Jephthah's vow in chapter 11 has divided interpreters. Some understand a human sacrifice. Others understand a dedication to lifelong virginity. The text records mourning for his daughter and her virginity, but doesn't explicitly describe a tabernacle office for her. Neither interpretation makes a rash vow a model of faithfulness.
helps.html: Jephthah's vow in chapter 11 has divided interpreters. Some understand a human sacrifice. Others understand a dedication to lifelong virginity. The text records mourning for his daughter and her virginity, but doesn't explicitly describe a tabernacle office for her. Neither interpretation makes a rash vow a model of faithfulness.

helps.text: The story of Samson (chapter 13 to 16) is a lesson in gifts without character. He is used by God in spite of himself.
helps.html: The story of Samson (chapter 13 to 16) is a lesson in gifts without character. He is used by God in spite of himself.

helps.text: The closing chapters (17 to 21) are appalling. Idolatry, civil war, sexual atrocity. The book ends in chaos to drive home that without a king Israel can't live.
helps.html: The closing chapters (17 to 21) are appalling. Idolatry, civil war, sexual atrocity. The book ends in chaos to drive home that without a king Israel can't live.

studies.title: An instrument of deliverance can still sin grievously
studies.html: Gideon’s deliverance is God’s mercy to Israel, but the ephod he makes becomes a snare. The narrator doesn’t require us to choose between acknowledging God’s use of Gideon and condemning Gideon’s corrupt act. Hebrews 11 commends faith in particular acts without declaring every act of the named person righteous. Read commendation according to its stated scope.
studies.distinction: An example of faith isn’t a blanket endorsement of a person’s character or every decision.
studies.question: What does the narrator explicitly say about the ephod after recounting Gideon’s victory?

studies.title: The need for a king reaches beyond political order
studies.html: The closing refrain exposes a people whose self-directed conduct has produced appalling evil. Later history shows that merely acquiring a king won’t cure that rebellion. Saul and even David fail. The narrative prepares for righteous kingship while the whole canon directs that hope to Christ. Don’t reduce the book either to a slogan for monarchy or to a collection of private moral lessons.
studies.distinction: The failure of anarchy doesn’t establish that every exercise of royal power is righteous.
studies.question: How do the failures of later kings help you understand what kind of deliverer Israel ultimately needs?

books.name: Ruth
books.intro: During the days of the judges, the Lord preserves a grieving family through Ruth's faithfulness and Boaz's redemption. This small household history leads to David's family line and, in time, to Christ.
books.introText: During the days of the judges, the Lord preserves a grieving family through Ruth's faithfulness and Boaz's redemption. This small household history leads to David's family line and, in time, to Christ.

helps.text: The book opens with famine and emptiness. Naomi loses her husband and sons in Moab. The setting is grief.
helps.html: The book opens with famine and emptiness. Naomi loses her husband and sons in Moab. The setting is grief.

helps.text: Ruth’s confession in 1.16 to 17 is one of the most beautiful confessions in the Bible. She turns from her gods to the God of Israel and from her people to His people. Her conversion is the door by which she enters the covenant community.
helps.html: Ruth’s confession in 1.16 to 17 is one of the most beautiful confessions in the Bible. She turns from her gods to the God of Israel and from her people to His people. Her conversion is the door by which she enters the covenant community.

helps.text: Boaz acts as a family redeemer in a case involving land and the preservation of a family name. Read Ruth 4 alongside Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 25, while noticing that the case isn't identical to the levirate law for a deceased man's brother.
helps.html: Boaz acts as a family redeemer in a case involving land and the preservation of a family name. Read Ruth 4 alongside Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 25, while noticing that the case isn't identical to the levirate law for a deceased man's brother.

helps.text: The threshing floor scene in chapter 3 isn't a seduction. Ruth invokes the kinsman-redeemer law in a customary way. Boaz responds with honor.
helps.html: The threshing floor scene in chapter 3 isn't a seduction. Ruth invokes the kinsman-redeemer law in a customary way. Boaz responds with honor.

helps.text: The redemption at the gate in chapter 4 is a public legal act. The closer kinsman declines. Boaz redeems and takes Ruth as wife.
helps.html: The redemption at the gate in chapter 4 is a public legal act. The closer kinsman declines. Boaz redeems and takes Ruth as wife.

helps.text: The genealogy at the end (4.18 to 22) is the point of the book. The line runs from Perez through Boaz to David.
helps.html: The genealogy at the end (4.18 to 22) is the point of the book. The line runs from Perez through Boaz to David.

helps.text: Matthew 1 picks up the genealogy and places Ruth in the line of Christ. A converted Gentile woman in the family tree of the Messiah.
helps.html: Matthew 1 picks up the genealogy and places Ruth in the line of Christ. A converted Gentile woman in the family tree of the Messiah.

helps.text: The book teaches that God’s providence works in ordinary lives, ordinary fields, and ordinary marriages to accomplish redemptive history.
helps.html: The book teaches that God’s providence works in ordinary lives, ordinary fields, and ordinary marriages to accomplish redemptive history.

helps.text: Read Ruth as the bright candle in the dark night of the judges. The same Israel that's collapsing in Judges has Boaz and Ruth quietly faithful in Bethlehem.
helps.html: Read Ruth as the bright candle in the dark night of the judges. The same Israel that's collapsing in Judges has Boaz and Ruth quietly faithful in Bethlehem.

helps.text: The book is short. Read it through in one sitting at least once a year.
helps.html: The book is short. Read it through in one sitting at least once a year.

studies.title: Redemption proceeds through ordinary faithfulness
studies.html: Ruth goes to glean, Boaz notices her, and the narrator lets the apparent smallness of these events lead toward David’s family. God’s providence works through lawful labor and kindness. The account doesn’t require every participant to know the full significance of what is happening. Nor does it promise that every faithful act will produce a visible success comparable to Ruth’s.
studies.distinction: Providential importance isn’t the same as a guarantee that we can recognize God’s entire purpose in our circumstances.
studies.question: Which ordinary duties in this chapter become part of God’s larger preservation of a family?

studies.title: The family redeemer and the greater redemption
studies.html: Boaz’s action concerns property, kinship, and the continuation of a dead man’s name. Those legal details belong to the story’s literal sense. They also make redemption a concrete reality within the family line that leads to Christ. Comparisons with Christ’s willing, costly redemption are profitable when they preserve these facts rather than assigning a spiritual equivalent to every witness or object.
studies.distinction: A sound redemptive comparison must not replace the legal and family circumstances the text actually narrates.
studies.question: Which obligations does Boaz undertake publicly, and how does the genealogy connect this family event to redemptive history?

books.name: 1 Samuel
books.intro: Samuel's ministry leads into Israel's monarchy. Saul's failure and David's anointing show that outward stature cannot supply the faithful king God's people need. Watch how the Lord establishes His chosen servant through suffering.
books.introText: Samuel's ministry leads into Israel's monarchy. Saul's failure and David's anointing show that outward stature cannot supply the faithful king God's people need. Watch how the Lord establishes His chosen servant through suffering.

helps.text: Hannah’s prayer (chapter 2) opens the book with a song of God exalting the lowly. Mary’s Magnificat in Luke 1 echoes it deliberately.
helps.html: Hannah’s prayer (chapter 2) opens the book with a song of God exalting the lowly. Mary’s Magnificat in Luke 1 echoes it deliberately.

helps.text: Samuel’s call (chapter 3) shows the failure of the priesthood under Eli and the raising up of a faithful prophet. The word of God comes to a child while the established religion is dim.
helps.html: Samuel’s call (chapter 3) shows the failure of the priesthood under Eli and the raising up of a faithful prophet. The word of God comes to a child while the established religion is dim.

helps.text: The ark narrative (chapters 4 to 7) shows that God isn't bound by Israel’s idolatry. The ark goes into Philistine hands and returns on its own terms.
helps.html: The ark narrative (chapters 4 to 7) shows that God isn't bound by Israel’s idolatry. The ark goes into Philistine hands and returns on its own terms.

helps.text: The people demand a king like the nations (chapter 8). The Lord grants their request as judgment. Saul is the king they wanted.
helps.html: The people demand a king like the nations (chapter 8). The Lord grants their request as judgment. Saul is the king they wanted.

helps.text: Saul begins well but disobeys repeatedly (chapters 13, 15). His kingdom is taken from him because he refuses to obey the word of the Lord.
helps.html: Saul begins well but disobeys repeatedly (chapters 13, 15). His kingdom is taken from him because he refuses to obey the word of the Lord.

helps.text: David is anointed in secret (chapter 16). The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon him. Saul’s spirit grows tormented.
helps.html: David is anointed in secret (chapter 16). The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon him. Saul’s spirit grows tormented.

helps.text: The Spirit’s coming on a man in this period for empowering and gifting is one form of His work. The same Spirit also regenerated and indwelt Old Testament saints for sanctification, as WCF 7.5 to 6 affirms in teaching the unity of the covenant of grace. Don't read the Old Testament as if the Spirit was absent from saving work in the saints. Pentecost added measure and breadth, not the saving work itself.
helps.html: The Spirit’s coming on a man in this period for empowering and gifting is one form of His work. The same Spirit also regenerated and indwelt Old Testament saints for sanctification, as WCF 7.5 to 6 affirms in teaching the unity of the covenant of grace. Don't read the Old Testament as if the Spirit was absent from saving work in the saints. Pentecost added measure and breadth, not the saving work itself.

helps.text: David and Goliath (chapter 17) is a real event and is also a picture of God using the small and faithful to defeat the proud and large. Christ is the greater David who defeats the greater enemy.
helps.html: David and Goliath (chapter 17) is a real event and is also a picture of God using the small and faithful to defeat the proud and large. Christ is the greater David who defeats the greater enemy.

helps.text: The friendship of David and Jonathan (chapters 18 to 20) shows covenant loyalty across the line of Saul’s house.
helps.html: The friendship of David and Jonathan (chapters 18 to 20) shows covenant loyalty across the line of Saul’s house.

helps.text: David’s flight from Saul (chapters 21 to 30) takes years. He is anointed but not yet enthroned. The pattern foreshadows Christ as the rightful King who suffered before His glory.
helps.html: David’s flight from Saul (chapters 21 to 30) takes years. He is anointed but not yet enthroned. The pattern foreshadows Christ as the rightful King who suffered before His glory.

helps.text: The book ends with Saul’s death (chapter 31). The way is clear for David to rise. The Davidic line that leads to Christ is being prepared.
helps.html: The book ends with Saul’s death (chapter 31). The way is clear for David to rise. The Davidic line that leads to Christ is being prepared.

studies.title: God evaluates a king by His Word
studies.html: Saul tries to explain disobedience by appealing to intended sacrifice. Samuel answers that obedience is better than sacrifice. The rebuke doesn’t make God indifferent to worship. It exposes the attempt to use a religious act as compensation for refusing His command. Saul’s position and apparent success cannot overrule the Word by which his kingship is judged.
studies.distinction: A proposed religious benefit doesn’t excuse an action God forbids.
studies.question: How does Saul describe his intention, and how does Samuel expose the fault in that defense?

studies.title: The shepherd fights as Israel’s representative
studies.html: David’s victory is a real battle whose outcome delivers the people he represents. His confidence rests upon the Lord rather than comparative military strength. The pattern can direct us toward the greater deliverance accomplished by Christ, while the chapter also teaches courage grounded in God’s honor. Neither connection licenses us to rename each stone as a private spiritual technique.
studies.distinction: An illustrative application must remain subordinate to the narrated battle and its covenant setting.
studies.question: Who receives the benefit of David’s victory, and what reason does David give for expecting deliverance?

books.name: 2 Samuel
books.intro: David's kingdom is established, and the Lord promises an enduring throne to his house. David's grave sins bring lasting sorrow. The covenant promise directs our hope beyond David to his righteous Son.
books.introText: David's kingdom is established, and the Lord promises an enduring throne to his house. David's grave sins bring lasting sorrow. The covenant promise directs our hope beyond David to his righteous Son.

helps.text: David is anointed king in chapter 5 and brings the ark to Jerusalem in chapter 6. The city becomes the center of worship and rule.
helps.html: David is anointed king in chapter 5 and brings the ark to Jerusalem in chapter 6. The city becomes the center of worship and rule.

helps.text: The Davidic covenant in chapter 7 promises a son who will reign forever, a house that won't be cut off, a kingdom established forever. The prophecy reaches beyond Solomon to Christ. Hebrews 1 quotes it as fulfilled in Him.
helps.html: The Davidic covenant in chapter 7 promises a son who will reign forever, a house that won't be cut off, a kingdom established forever. The prophecy reaches beyond Solomon to Christ. Hebrews 1 quotes it as fulfilled in Him.

helps.text: David’s sin with Bathsheba and his murder of Uriah (chapter 11) is the dark center of the book. Nathan’s confrontation in chapter 12 is one of the great pastoral confrontations of Scripture.
helps.html: David’s sin with Bathsheba and his murder of Uriah (chapter 11) is the dark center of the book. Nathan’s confrontation in chapter 12 is one of the great pastoral confrontations of Scripture.

helps.text: The consequences of David’s sin work out through the rest of the book. The death of his son. The rape of Tamar. Absalom’s rebellion. The sword doesn't depart from his house.
helps.html: The consequences of David’s sin work out through the rest of the book. The death of his son. The rape of Tamar. Absalom’s rebellion. The sword doesn't depart from his house.

helps.text: Absalom’s revolt (chapters 15 to 18) drives David from Jerusalem and crosses the Jordan with him in flight. The pattern of an anointed king rejected by his own and crossing through suffering is one Christ will fulfill more deeply.
helps.html: Absalom’s revolt (chapters 15 to 18) drives David from Jerusalem and crosses the Jordan with him in flight. The pattern of an anointed king rejected by his own and crossing through suffering is one Christ will fulfill more deeply.

helps.text: David’s response to news of Absalom’s death (18.33) is one of the great laments of Scripture. He is broken not only as a king but as a father.
helps.html: David’s response to news of Absalom’s death (18.33) is one of the great laments of Scripture. He is broken not only as a king but as a father.

helps.text: The census of chapter 24 brings final judgment in the form of a plague. David buys the threshing floor of Araunah, which becomes the site of the temple. Even at the end, God is preparing the place where atonement will be made.
helps.html: The census of chapter 24 brings final judgment in the form of a plague. David buys the threshing floor of Araunah, which becomes the site of the temple. Even at the end, God is preparing the place where atonement will be made.

helps.text: Psalm 51 is David’s repentance after his sin with Bathsheba. Read it alongside 2 Samuel 11 and 12 to see the same heart.
helps.html: Psalm 51 is David’s repentance after his sin with Bathsheba. Read it alongside 2 Samuel 11 and 12 to see the same heart.

helps.text: David is presented as both a great king and a flawed man. Both are true. The Bible never airbrushes its heroes.
helps.html: David is presented as both a great king and a flawed man. Both are true. The Bible never airbrushes its heroes.

studies.title: The royal promise outlasts a sinful king
studies.html: The Lord promises David a house and an enduring throne. The near horizon includes David’s son, with discipline for iniquity. The final horizon is fulfilled in the sinless Son whose kingdom endures. Read the promises as a developing covenant rather than demanding that every clause apply identically to Solomon and Christ. Luke 1.32 to 33 identifies the enduring royal fulfillment.
studies.distinction: Fulfillment in Christ doesn’t make the disciplinary clauses a prediction that Christ Himself will commit sin.
studies.question: Which features concern David’s ordinary descendants, and which reach the everlasting reign announced in Luke 1?

studies.title: Pardon does not abolish fatherly discipline
studies.html: Nathan announces that the Lord has put away David’s sin, and also announces painful consequences. David isn’t earning pardon by enduring those consequences. The account distinguishes forgiveness from the removal of every temporal effect of wrongdoing. WCF 11.5 similarly distinguishes the justified person’s standing from the Father’s displeasure and corrective dealings when His children sin.
studies.distinction: Temporal suffering after sin isn’t proof that Christ’s satisfaction was insufficient or that punishment earns forgiveness.
studies.question: What does Nathan declare forgiven, and what consequences does he say will remain?

books.name: 1 Kings
books.intro: Solomon's reign begins in wisdom and ends in compromise. The kingdom divides, and the worship of the Lord is corrupted. The prophets confront kings with the covenant Word that measures every reign.
books.introText: Solomon's reign begins in wisdom and ends in compromise. The kingdom divides, and the worship of the Lord is corrupted. The prophets confront kings with the covenant Word that measures every reign.

helps.text: Solomon’s reign begins in wisdom (chapter 3) and prosperity (chapter 4) and reaches its height in the building and dedication of the temple (chapters 6 to 8).
helps.html: Solomon’s reign begins in wisdom (chapter 3) and prosperity (chapter 4) and reaches its height in the building and dedication of the temple (chapters 6 to 8).

helps.text: Solomon’s prayer at the dedication (chapter 8) is a model of covenant prayer. He asks God to hear from heaven when His people pray toward the temple.
helps.html: Solomon’s prayer at the dedication (chapter 8) is a model of covenant prayer. He asks God to hear from heaven when His people pray toward the temple.

helps.text: Solomon’s sin (chapter 11) comes through his many foreign wives who turn his heart to other gods. The wisest man in the world isn't safe from the lust that pulls every man.
helps.html: Solomon’s sin (chapter 11) comes through his many foreign wives who turn his heart to other gods. The wisest man in the world isn't safe from the lust that pulls every man.

helps.text: The kingdom divides under Rehoboam (chapter 12). The northern kingdom (Israel) under Jeroboam falls into immediate idolatry. The southern kingdom (Judah) keeps the Davidic line.
helps.html: The kingdom divides under Rehoboam (chapter 12). The northern kingdom (Israel) under Jeroboam falls into immediate idolatry. The southern kingdom (Judah) keeps the Davidic line.

helps.text: The northern kings are uniformly evil. Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Ahab, and the rest. The pattern is set by Jeroboam’s golden calves and continues.
helps.html: The northern kings are uniformly evil. Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Ahab, and the rest. The pattern is set by Jeroboam’s golden calves and continues.

helps.text: The southern kings are mixed. Some are godly, some are wicked. The Davidic line is preserved through them despite their failures.
helps.html: The southern kings are mixed. Some are godly, some are wicked. The Davidic line is preserved through them despite their failures.

helps.text: Elijah (chapter 17 to 19) is a turning point. He confronts Ahab and Jezebel, defeats the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and is shown by God in the still small voice that the Lord works not only in spectacle but in quiet faithfulness.
helps.html: Elijah (chapter 17 to 19) is a turning point. He confronts Ahab and Jezebel, defeats the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and is shown by God in the still small voice that the Lord works not only in spectacle but in quiet faithfulness.

helps.text: The narrative pattern is theological. Each king is evaluated by whether he walked in the way of David (good) or in the sins of Jeroboam (bad).
helps.html: The narrative pattern is theological. Each king is evaluated by whether he walked in the way of David (good) or in the sins of Jeroboam (bad).

helps.text: The book teaches that sin in leadership has long consequences for a people. Solomon’s compromise leads to centuries of disaster.
helps.html: The book teaches that sin in leadership has long consequences for a people. Solomon’s compromise leads to centuries of disaster.

studies.title: Wisdom without watchfulness does not prevent decline
studies.html: Solomon’s gifts and earlier prayers are real, yet the king later turns after other gods. Compare his conduct with Deuteronomy 17 rather than measuring him only by his achievements. The narrative exposes the insufficiency of gifts, wealth, and public accomplishment as guarantees of fidelity. It calls a reader to ongoing obedience without teaching that God has abandoned His promise to David.
studies.distinction: An impressive beginning doesn’t make later conduct immune from scriptural judgment.
studies.question: Which earlier royal warnings does Solomon’s conduct bring to mind?

studies.title: Invented worship can serve a political purpose
studies.html: Jeroboam designs calves, shrines, priests, and a festival to keep the people from returning to Jerusalem. The narrator identifies the feast as devised from his own heart. Convenience and political stability don’t authorize these changes. Read the account as a concrete instance of power attempting to reshape worship for human ends.
studies.distinction: A useful public outcome cannot turn an invented religious ordinance into God’s command.
studies.question: What motive drives Jeroboam’s arrangements, and how does the narrator identify their source?

books.name: 2 Kings
books.intro: Israel and Judah persist in covenant rebellion until exile comes. Faithful kings and prophetic deliverances show God's mercy, but neither kingdom can escape His announced judgment. A small closing mercy keeps hope alive for David's house.
books.introText: Israel and Judah persist in covenant rebellion until exile comes. Faithful kings and prophetic deliverances show God's mercy, but neither kingdom can escape His announced judgment. A small closing mercy keeps hope alive for David's house.

helps.text: Elijah’s translation in 2.11 and Elisha receiving a double portion of his spirit set up Elisha’s long ministry. The miracles of Elisha (chapters 2 to 8) are real and often picture aspects of Christ’s ministry.
helps.html: Elijah’s translation in 2.11 and Elisha receiving a double portion of his spirit set up Elisha’s long ministry. The miracles of Elisha (chapters 2 to 8) are real and often picture aspects of Christ’s ministry.

helps.text: The kings of Israel continue in the sins of Jeroboam. The northern kingdom is a steady downward slide.
helps.html: The kings of Israel continue in the sins of Jeroboam. The northern kingdom is a steady downward slide.

helps.text: The fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC (chapter 17) ends the northern kingdom. The text gives a long theological explanation for why it happened.
helps.html: The fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC (chapter 17) ends the northern kingdom. The text gives a long theological explanation for why it happened.

helps.text: Hezekiah of Judah (chapters 18 to 20) is a faithful king. His prayer in the face of Assyrian threat (19) is a model. The Lord delivers Jerusalem from Sennacherib.
helps.html: Hezekiah of Judah (chapters 18 to 20) is a faithful king. His prayer in the face of Assyrian threat (19) is a model. The Lord delivers Jerusalem from Sennacherib.

helps.text: Manasseh (chapter 21) is the most wicked king of Judah. His sin seals the coming exile. He is named as the reason God won't relent.
helps.html: Manasseh (chapter 21) is the most wicked king of Judah. His sin seals the coming exile. He is named as the reason God won't relent.

helps.text: Josiah (chapters 22 to 23) is the most faithful king after David. He rediscovers the law, leads a great reform, and celebrates the greatest Passover since the days of the judges. His reform doesn't avert the coming judgment but it does delay it.
helps.html: Josiah (chapters 22 to 23) is the most faithful king after David. He rediscovers the law, leads a great reform, and celebrates the greatest Passover since the days of the judges. His reform doesn't avert the coming judgment but it does delay it.

helps.text: The fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 BC (chapter 25) ends Judah’s monarchy. The temple is destroyed. The people are taken into exile.
helps.html: The fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 BC (chapter 25) ends Judah’s monarchy. The temple is destroyed. The people are taken into exile.

helps.text: The last paragraph of the book (25.27 to 30) is a hidden ray of hope. Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon. The Davidic line lives. The promise to David isn't finished.
helps.html: The last paragraph of the book (25.27 to 30) is a hidden ray of hope. Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon. The Davidic line lives. The promise to David isn't finished.

helps.text: The book teaches that God is patient but not endlessly so. After centuries of warning, judgment finally falls.
helps.html: The book teaches that God is patient but not endlessly so. After centuries of warning, judgment finally falls.

studies.title: Exile is interpreted by the covenant Word
studies.html: The account of Samaria’s fall interrupts political history with a sustained explanation of Israel’s sin. The writer isn’t merely reporting that Assyria had a stronger army. He interprets the defeat through God’s covenant warnings. Human causes remain real, while the text identifies the judicial purpose God accomplishes through them.
studies.distinction: Recognizing a revealed judgment in Israel’s history doesn’t authorize us to declare the hidden cause of every modern disaster.
studies.question: List the covenant offenses the chapter names before it explains the Lord’s removal of Israel.

studies.title: A faithful reform does not cancel every announced consequence
studies.html: Josiah humbles himself when the law is read, and the Lord receives that response. Yet the announced judgment upon Judah is not simply withdrawn. The account distinguishes the king’s personal reception of mercy from the accumulated public guilt of the people. Read both the promise to Josiah and the continuing judgment without collapsing them into a general formula about national revival.
studies.distinction: A genuine reform doesn’t provide a universal promise that every historical consequence will be reversed.
studies.question: How does the prophetic word distinguish what will happen to Judah from the mercy shown to Josiah?

books.name: 1 Chronicles
books.intro: Written for a community looking back from exile and restoration, Chronicles traces Israel's families and David's kingdom. Its attention to the temple and ordered worship reminds the returned people of their calling before God.
books.introText: Written for a community looking back from exile and restoration, Chronicles traces Israel's families and David's kingdom. Its attention to the temple and ordered worship reminds the returned people of their calling before God.

helps.text: The genealogies aren't optional. They establish the legal continuity of the people of God after the exile. They run from Adam to the post-exilic community.
helps.html: The genealogies aren't optional. They establish the legal continuity of the people of God after the exile. They run from Adam to the post-exilic community.

helps.text: Chronicles often passes over the worst sins of the kings (David’s sin with Bathsheba isn't retold). This isn't denial but selection. The chronicler is writing pastorally to encourage faith.
helps.html: Chronicles often passes over the worst sins of the kings (David’s sin with Bathsheba isn't retold). This isn't denial but selection. The chronicler is writing pastorally to encourage faith.

helps.text: David’s preparation for the temple is a major focus (chapters 22 to 29). Solomon will build it, but David gathers the materials and organizes the worship.
helps.html: David’s preparation for the temple is a major focus (chapters 22 to 29). Solomon will build it, but David gathers the materials and organizes the worship.

helps.text: The Levites and priests are organized in detail (chapters 23 to 27). Worship is to be ordered, not improvised.
helps.html: The Levites and priests are organized in detail (chapters 23 to 27). Worship is to be ordered, not improvised.

helps.text: David’s prayer in chapter 29 is a model of stewardship and praise. "Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty" (1 Chronicles 29.11).
helps.html: David’s prayer in chapter 29 is a model of stewardship and praise. "Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty" (1 Chronicles 29.11).

helps.text: The Davidic covenant is reaffirmed (chapter 17). The chronicler wants the post-exile community to know the promise still stands.
helps.html: The Davidic covenant is reaffirmed (chapter 17). The chronicler wants the post-exile community to know the promise still stands.

helps.text: The book lacks the details of the northern kingdom that Kings includes. Chronicles focuses on Judah and the temple.
helps.html: The book lacks the details of the northern kingdom that Kings includes. Chronicles focuses on Judah and the temple.

helps.text: The hand of God in history is visible throughout. Battles are won by prayer. Defeats follow disobedience.
helps.html: The hand of God in history is visible throughout. Battles are won by prayer. Defeats follow disobedience.

helps.text: Read Chronicles as a sermon to people who are tempted to think the promises have failed. The chronicler’s answer is that the line and the worship are preserved.
helps.html: Read Chronicles as a sermon to people who are tempted to think the promises have failed. The chronicler’s answer is that the line and the worship are preserved.

helps.text: Christ comes from the line traced here. The genealogies aren't dead history. They're the family tree of the King.
helps.html: Christ comes from the line traced here. The genealogies aren't dead history. They're the family tree of the King.

studies.title: Genealogy teaches covenant continuity
studies.html: The long family records locate the returned community within God’s dealings with Israel. The renewed presentation of the promise to David explains why this history matters after the collapse of the monarchy. Read names and lineage as historical testimony serving a theological purpose. Their theological role doesn’t make them invented or unimportant to the writer’s claim.
studies.distinction: Theological selection is compatible with truthful history. It doesn’t mean the writer is free to manufacture ancestry.
studies.question: Why would the promise of an enduring house matter to a community living after the exile?

studies.title: Worship follows the Lord’s appointed order
studies.html: David explains the earlier failure concerning the ark by reference to the appointed order. The correction is not simply greater enthusiasm. The Levites carry the ark as Moses commanded according to the Lord’s word. The account joins careful obedience with joy rather than making reverence a rival to gladness.
studies.distinction: Religious zeal doesn’t make the manner of approaching God a matter of indifference.
studies.question: What changes between the earlier transport of the ark and its corrected transport in this chapter?

books.name: 2 Chronicles
books.intro: The history of Judah is told with particular attention to the temple and the people's response to God. Reform brings real relief, but exile finally comes. Cyrus's decree opens the prospect of return.
books.introText: The history of Judah is told with particular attention to the temple and the people's response to God. Reform brings real relief, but exile finally comes. Cyrus's decree opens the prospect of return.

helps.text: Solomon’s temple dedication (chapter 6 to 7) is the high point of the book. The promise of 7.14 is given to Israel in covenant context. Apply it carefully and not as an unconditional promise to any nation.
helps.html: Solomon’s temple dedication (chapter 6 to 7) is the high point of the book. The promise of 7.14 is given to Israel in covenant context. Apply it carefully and not as an unconditional promise to any nation.

helps.text: The book covers only the kings of Judah, not Israel. The chronicler is writing for the post-exile community whose identity is in the southern kingdom and the temple.
helps.html: The book covers only the kings of Judah, not Israel. The chronicler is writing for the post-exile community whose identity is in the southern kingdom and the temple.

helps.text: Faithful kings are highlighted. Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah. Their reforms and prayers are given more attention than in Kings.
helps.html: Faithful kings are highlighted. Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah. Their reforms and prayers are given more attention than in Kings.

helps.text: The chronicler often shows that immediate divine response follows faithfulness or unfaithfulness. This isn't a wooden formula but a real pattern under the covenant.
helps.html: The chronicler often shows that immediate divine response follows faithfulness or unfaithfulness. This isn't a wooden formula but a real pattern under the covenant.

helps.text: Manasseh’s repentance (33.10 to 13) is recorded only in Chronicles. Even the worst king can turn and find mercy. This is pastorally pointed.
helps.html: Manasseh’s repentance (33.10 to 13) is recorded only in Chronicles. Even the worst king can turn and find mercy. This is pastorally pointed.

helps.text: The fall of Jerusalem (chapter 36) is told briefly but with theological clarity. The exile is judgment for unfaithfulness.
helps.html: The fall of Jerusalem (chapter 36) is told briefly but with theological clarity. The exile is judgment for unfaithfulness.

helps.text: The book ends with the decree of Cyrus (36.22 to 23) calling for the rebuilding of the temple. This is the bridge to Ezra-Nehemiah.
helps.html: The book ends with the decree of Cyrus (36.22 to 23) calling for the rebuilding of the temple. This is the bridge to Ezra-Nehemiah.

helps.text: The shape of the book is hopeful. From Solomon to Cyrus, the temple is the thread.
helps.html: The shape of the book is hopeful. From Solomon to Cyrus, the temple is the thread.

helps.text: The chronicler’s selection of material is teaching theology, not hiding facts. He writes to encourage the post-exile remnant to faithfulness.
helps.html: The chronicler’s selection of material is teaching theology, not hiding facts. He writes to encourage the post-exile remnant to faithfulness.

studies.title: A promise to Israel is not a blank national charter
studies.html: The answer to Solomon concerns the temple, the land, and judgments named within Israel’s covenant life. The call to humility and repentance reveals enduring truth about approaching God. The particular promise of healing the land belongs to its addressed people and administration. Its use must retain that setting instead of guaranteeing the political recovery of whichever nation quotes it.
studies.distinction: An enduring moral application doesn’t transfer every temporal covenant provision without qualification.
studies.question: Which surrounding details identify the people and place addressed by the promise?

studies.title: Mercy to Manasseh does not make repentance trivial
studies.html: Manasseh’s extreme wickedness is followed by affliction, humiliation, prayer, and a measure of reform. The account magnifies God’s mercy without portraying sin as inexpensive or pardon as a reward earned by suffering. Notice that the king’s changed conduct accompanies his appeal to God. It is evidence of repentance rather than payment for it.
studies.distinction: Great mercy should encourage a sinner to return, not encourage postponing repentance in order to continue sinning.
studies.question: What conduct after Manasseh’s prayer shows that his humiliation was more than a passing fear of punishment?

books.name: Ezra
books.intro: Exiles return to Judah, rebuild the temple, and face the need for spiritual reform. The restored community encounters opposition from outside and unfaithfulness within. God's Word must govern its life after the return.
books.introText: Exiles return to Judah, rebuild the temple, and face the need for spiritual reform. The restored community encounters opposition from outside and unfaithfulness within. God's Word must govern its life after the return.

helps.text: The decree of Cyrus (chapter 1) fulfills the prophecies of Isaiah 44 and 45 and Jeremiah 25. God uses a pagan king to accomplish His purposes.
helps.html: The decree of Cyrus (chapter 1) fulfills the prophecies of Isaiah 44 and 45 and Jeremiah 25. God uses a pagan king to accomplish His purposes.

helps.text: The temple foundation is laid in chapter 3 with mixed weeping and joy. The old men who remembered the first temple wept while the young men shouted for joy.
