helps.html: The temple foundation is laid in chapter 3 with mixed weeping and joy. The old men who remembered the first temple wept while the young men shouted for joy.

helps.text: Opposition from the surrounding peoples halts the work for years (chapter 4). The work resumes under the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah (chapter 5 to 6).
helps.html: Opposition from the surrounding peoples halts the work for years (chapter 4). The work resumes under the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah (chapter 5 to 6).

helps.text: The temple is finished in 516 BC, seventy years after its destruction. The Passover is celebrated. The community is reestablished in worship.
helps.html: The temple is finished in 516 BC, seventy years after its destruction. The Passover is celebrated. The community is reestablished in worship.

helps.text: Ezra arrives in chapter 7, sixty years after the temple is finished. He is a priest and a scribe skilled in the law of Moses. His task is to teach and apply the law.
helps.html: Ezra arrives in chapter 7, sixty years after the temple is finished. He is a priest and a scribe skilled in the law of Moses. His task is to teach and apply the law.

helps.text: Ezra’s prayer of confession (chapter 9) is one of the great prayers of Scripture. He confesses the sin of the community as his own.
helps.html: Ezra’s prayer of confession (chapter 9) is one of the great prayers of Scripture. He confesses the sin of the community as his own.

helps.text: Ezra 9 to 10 addresses marriages that compromised the returned community's covenant faithfulness. Ethnic difference alone wasn't the issue, as Ruth's reception into Israel shows. Don't turn this exceptional reform into permission for Christians to divorce unbelieving spouses. Read 1 Corinthians 7.12 to 16.
helps.html: Ezra 9 to 10 addresses marriages that compromised the returned community's covenant faithfulness. Ethnic difference alone wasn't the issue, as Ruth's reception into Israel shows. Don't turn this exceptional reform into permission for Christians to divorce unbelieving spouses. Read 1 Corinthians 7.12 to 16.

helps.text: The book emphasizes the law of Moses as the standard for the post-exile community. Ezra is the great teacher.
helps.html: The book emphasizes the law of Moses as the standard for the post-exile community. Ezra is the great teacher.

helps.text: The book teaches that restoration takes work, opposition, prayer, and reform. Coming home from exile isn't the end of the story.
helps.html: The book teaches that restoration takes work, opposition, prayer, and reform. Coming home from exile isn't the end of the story.

studies.title: A historical remedy must not overrule later instruction
studies.html: The returned community faces a covenant crisis involving marriages forbidden under Israel’s law. Read the remedy with Ezra 9 and the danger of renewed apostasy. Then distinguish that circumstance from Paul’s explicit directions for a believer already married to a consenting unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7.12 to 16. The enduring requirement of faithfulness doesn’t make the two situations legally identical.
studies.distinction: A narrative of covenant reform cannot be made to cancel a direct apostolic instruction about a different marriage situation.
studies.question: What would be lost if Ezra 10 were used as a general command to divorce an unbelieving spouse?

studies.title: The Word orders restoration
studies.html: Ezra sets his heart to study the law, practice it, and teach it. The order keeps instruction connected to understanding and obedience. His office and commission concern a particular historical task, but the moral relation remains profitable for anyone who teaches. Knowledge used to direct others while refusing God’s claim upon oneself is a failure to receive the very Word being taught.
studies.distinction: A teacher’s skill doesn’t replace the duty to submit personally to what Scripture commands.
studies.question: What three commitments are joined in Ezra 7.10, and why should none be detached from the others?

books.name: Nehemiah
books.intro: Nehemiah leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and joins in the reform of the community. Prayer and careful planning work together throughout the book. The final chapter shows how quickly a people can drift after public commitments.
books.introText: Nehemiah leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and joins in the reform of the community. Prayer and careful planning work together throughout the book. The final chapter shows how quickly a people can drift after public commitments.

helps.text: Nehemiah’s prayer in chapter 1 is a model. He confesses sin, recalls God’s promises, and asks for help. He prays before he plans.
helps.html: Nehemiah’s prayer in chapter 1 is a model. He confesses sin, recalls God’s promises, and asks for help. He prays before he plans.

helps.text: He plans carefully (chapter 2) before he speaks. He surveys the walls by night before announcing the work. Wisdom is part of leadership.
helps.html: He plans carefully (chapter 2) before he speaks. He surveys the walls by night before announcing the work. Wisdom is part of leadership.

helps.text: The wall is built in fifty-two days (chapter 6.15) despite intense opposition. Each man works on the section near his own house.
helps.html: The wall is built in fifty-two days (chapter 6.15) despite intense opposition. Each man works on the section near his own house.

helps.text: Opposition is mocking, threatening, and political. Nehemiah counters with prayer, watchfulness, and steady work.
helps.html: Opposition is mocking, threatening, and political. Nehemiah counters with prayer, watchfulness, and steady work.

helps.text: The reading of the law in chapter 8 leads to repentance and joy. The Levites help the people understand. Application follows understanding.
helps.html: The reading of the law in chapter 8 leads to repentance and joy. The Levites help the people understand. Application follows understanding.

helps.text: The covenant renewal in chapter 9 to 10 is one of the great prayers of confession in the Bible. The people commit themselves in writing to obey.
helps.html: The covenant renewal in chapter 9 to 10 is one of the great prayers of confession in the Bible. The people commit themselves in writing to obey.

helps.text: The book ends with renewed reform (chapter 13). Nehemiah returns and finds the people slipping. He leads another round of reform.
helps.html: The book ends with renewed reform (chapter 13). Nehemiah returns and finds the people slipping. He leads another round of reform.

helps.text: The pattern is that even after great spiritual moments, the people drift. This is realistic and worth reading honestly.
helps.html: The pattern is that even after great spiritual moments, the people drift. This is realistic and worth reading honestly.

helps.text: Nehemiah’s brief prayers throughout (often called arrow prayers) are worth marking. He prays in real time, in conversation with God in the middle of his work.
helps.html: Nehemiah’s brief prayers throughout (often called arrow prayers) are worth marking. He prays in real time, in conversation with God in the middle of his work.

studies.title: Understanding is part of hearing faithfully
studies.html: The people hear the law read and explained so that they understand its sense. Their sorrow and joy arise from receiving the Word, not from being led around its meaning by a dramatic experience. The account supports careful explanation in public ministry. It doesn’t imply that emotional response is either the enemy of truth or a sufficient test of having understood it.
studies.distinction: A strong feeling cannot establish an interpretation, but genuine understanding needn’t be emotionally cold.
studies.question: How does the narrator connect explanation, understanding, and the people’s response?

studies.title: A public vow cannot supply a new heart
studies.html: Nehemiah returns to find failures after the community’s solemn covenant commitments. Reform needs continuing oversight because a moving public occasion doesn’t remove remaining corruption. Read the particular Sabbath measures within Israel’s civic setting while retaining the continuing moral duty of holy rest. The law’s form of enforcement and its abiding moral claim must be distinguished.
studies.distinction: Failure after a vow doesn’t make obedience unnecessary, and a forceful historical remedy isn’t automatically the church’s present method.
studies.question: What does the recurrence of the sin teach about relying upon one past moment of public commitment?

books.name: Esther
books.intro: A threat against the Jews unfolds in the Persian court. Although God isn't named in the book, the timing and reversals display His providential preservation of His people. Neither palace power nor human schemes control the outcome.
books.introText: A threat against the Jews unfolds in the Persian court. Although God isn't named in the book, the timing and reversals display His providential preservation of His people. Neither palace power nor human schemes control the outcome.

helps.text: The setting is the Persian empire under Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). The events take place between Ezra 6 and Ezra 7.
helps.html: The setting is the Persian empire under Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). The events take place between Ezra 6 and Ezra 7.

helps.text: The king’s banquets and the deposing of Vashti (chapter 1) set the stage. The court is ostentatious and dangerous.
helps.html: The king’s banquets and the deposing of Vashti (chapter 1) set the stage. The court is ostentatious and dangerous.

helps.text: Esther becomes queen (chapter 2) without revealing her Jewish identity. Her cousin Mordecai counsels her.
helps.html: Esther becomes queen (chapter 2) without revealing her Jewish identity. Her cousin Mordecai counsels her.

helps.text: Haman’s plot (chapter 3) is to destroy all the Jews because of his hatred of Mordecai. The royal decree goes out.
helps.html: Haman’s plot (chapter 3) is to destroy all the Jews because of his hatred of Mordecai. The royal decree goes out.

helps.text: Mordecai’s words to Esther in 4.14 are a hinge moment. "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (KJV). Read providence in this verse.
helps.html: Mordecai’s words to Esther in 4.14 are a hinge moment. "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (KJV). Read providence in this verse.

helps.text: Esther’s banquet strategy (chapters 5 to 7) is wise and patient. She doesn't rush.
helps.html: Esther’s banquet strategy (chapters 5 to 7) is wise and patient. She doesn't rush.

helps.text: The reversal of Haman’s plot (chapter 7) is sudden and complete. He is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
helps.html: The reversal of Haman’s plot (chapter 7) is sudden and complete. He is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

helps.text: The Jews defend themselves and are delivered (chapter 8 to 9). Purim is instituted as a permanent feast of remembrance.
helps.html: The Jews defend themselves and are delivered (chapter 8 to 9). Purim is instituted as a permanent feast of remembrance.

helps.text: God isn't named in Esther. Follow the timing of the king's sleeplessness and the reversals that defeat Haman's plan. The narrative shows providence through ordinary circumstances without telling us that we can decode every event in our own lives.
helps.html: God isn't named in Esther. Follow the timing of the king's sleeplessness and the reversals that defeat Haman's plan. The narrative shows providence through ordinary circumstances without telling us that we can decode every event in our own lives.

studies.title: Providence is not the same as interpreting every coincidence
studies.html: The king’s sleepless night becomes a turning point in the preservation of the Jews. The narrator supplies a historical connection the reader can follow. We rightly recognize the Lord’s government of these circumstances. We must not infer that every coincidence in our own lives discloses an equally readable message about a chosen course of action.
studies.distinction: God’s comprehensive government doesn’t give us comprehensive knowledge of His secret purpose.
studies.question: Which sequence of events does the narrator disclose, and which hidden motives or future outcomes remain undisclosed?

studies.title: Preservation includes responsible human action
studies.html: Mordecai’s expectation of deliverance doesn’t make Esther passive. He presses her to act, and she recognizes the danger of approaching the king. The account joins confidence in God’s preservation with costly responsibility. This is a useful correction to the assumption that a sovereign purpose removes the need for means.
studies.distinction: Trust in providence isn’t permission to abandon a duty because God could accomplish His will another way.
studies.question: How do Mordecai’s confidence and Esther’s chosen action belong together?

books.name: Job
books.intro: Job's severe suffering becomes the occasion for a long dispute about God's justice. The reader knows facts hidden from Job and his friends. The Lord finally answers Job without giving him the full explanation available to the reader.
books.introText: Job's severe suffering becomes the occasion for a long dispute about God's justice. The reader knows facts hidden from Job and his friends. The Lord finally answers Job without giving him the full explanation available to the reader.

helps.text: The speeches of Job’s three friends are quoted but not endorsed. They give wrong counsel, as God says at the end (42.7).
helps.html: The speeches of Job’s three friends are quoted but not endorsed. They give wrong counsel, as God says at the end (42.7).

helps.text: The prologue shows the heavenly council where Satan accuses Job. Job is afflicted with God’s permission and within His limits. Satan is on a leash.
helps.html: The prologue shows the heavenly council where Satan accuses Job. Job is afflicted with God’s permission and within His limits. Satan is on a leash.

helps.text: Job’s first response (chapter 1.20 to 22 and 2.10) is faithful. He worships in his loss. He doesn't curse God.
helps.html: Job’s first response (chapter 1.20 to 22 and 2.10) is faithful. He worships in his loss. He doesn't curse God.

helps.text: The dialogues with the three friends (chapters 3 to 31) are long and circular. The friends insist Job’s suffering must be punishment for sin. Job insists on his integrity.
helps.html: The dialogues with the three friends (chapters 3 to 31) are long and circular. The friends insist Job’s suffering must be punishment for sin. Job insists on his integrity.

helps.text: Job brings real grief and hard questions before God. The Lord also corrects words spoken without understanding. The book permits honest lament without endorsing every accusation Job makes.
helps.html: Job brings real grief and hard questions before God. The Lord also corrects words spoken without understanding. The book permits honest lament without endorsing every accusation Job makes.

helps.text: Elihu addresses Job in chapters 32 to 37. Reformed interpreters differ over the value of his speeches. Examine his claims in their context rather than deciding the question merely from his omission in the final rebuke.
helps.html: Elihu addresses Job in chapters 32 to 37. Reformed interpreters differ over the value of his speeches. Examine his claims in their context rather than deciding the question merely from his omission in the final rebuke.

helps.text: Job’s response (40.4 to 5 and 42.1 to 6) is humble repentance. He doesn't get the answer he demanded. He gets God Himself.
helps.html: Job’s response (40.4 to 5 and 42.1 to 6) is humble repentance. He doesn't get the answer he demanded. He gets God Himself.

helps.text: The epilogue (42) restores Job’s fortunes. The friends are rebuked. Job prays for them and is heard.
helps.html: The epilogue (42) restores Job’s fortunes. The friends are rebuked. Job prays for them and is heard.

helps.text: The book teaches that not all suffering is punishment for specific sin. The doctrine of retribution as a universal rule is wrong.
helps.html: The book teaches that not all suffering is punishment for specific sin. The doctrine of retribution as a universal rule is wrong.

studies.title: A truthful book can quote mistaken arguments
studies.html: Job’s friends speak at length about God, often using claims that resemble truths found elsewhere. Their error lies especially in the way they apply retribution to Job’s case. The Lord’s final rebuke governs our reading of their speeches. We can’t turn an isolated sentence into an endorsed explanation merely because it appears inside an inspired book.
studies.distinction: Inspiration guarantees a truthful record of a speaker’s words. It doesn’t guarantee that the recorded speaker reasons rightly.
studies.question: Choose one accusation by a friend. How does the prologue or final verdict expose the accusation’s faulty application?

studies.title: Lament is permitted, and the sufferer can still need correction
studies.html: The book vindicates Job against the charge that his suffering must prove a hidden wicked life. Yet God also corrects Job’s attempt to establish his own case at the expense of divine justice. These judgments are compatible. A sufferer may need comfort against false accusations and correction for words spoken in anguish. Neither ministry should erase the other.
studies.distinction: Rejecting the friends' cruelty doesn’t require endorsing every conclusion Job draws from his pain.
studies.question: What error does the Lord challenge in Job 40.8, and how does that differ from the friends' accusation?

books.name: Psalms
books.intro: These inspired songs teach God's people to praise Him and pray in every condition. Follow their poetic language and their place within the Psalter's five books. The New Testament shows how their promises and royal hopes are fulfilled in Christ.
books.introText: These inspired songs teach God's people to praise Him and pray in every condition. Follow their poetic language and their place within the Psalter's five books. The New Testament shows how their promises and royal hopes are fulfilled in Christ.

helps.text: The Psalms teach us to bring grief and praise before God. Their inspired speakers may also confess sin, speak as kings, or describe the Messiah. Identify the speaker and the situation before making every line your own.
helps.html: The Psalms teach us to bring grief and praise before God. Their inspired speakers may also confess sin, speak as kings, or describe the Messiah. Identify the speaker and the situation before making every line your own.

helps.text: The categories of Psalms are useful. Psalms of lament (more than any other type), praise, thanksgiving, royal, wisdom, imprecatory, and pilgrimage.
helps.html: The categories of Psalms are useful. Psalms of lament (more than any other type), praise, thanksgiving, royal, wisdom, imprecatory, and pilgrimage.

helps.text: Hebrew parallelism is the key to reading. The second line repeats, expands, contrasts, or completes the first. Look at the relationship between the lines.
helps.html: Hebrew parallelism is the key to reading. The second line repeats, expands, contrasts, or completes the first. Look at the relationship between the lines.

helps.text: Messianic Psalms are those quoted in the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ. Psalm 2, 8, 16, 22, 40, 45, 69, 72, 89, 110, 118, and others. Read them with Christ in view.
helps.html: Messianic Psalms are those quoted in the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ. Psalm 2, 8, 16, 22, 40, 45, 69, 72, 89, 110, 118, and others. Read them with Christ in view.

helps.text: The royal psalms are about the king. Many of them go beyond David to Christ in their full meaning.
helps.html: The royal psalms are about the king. Many of them go beyond David to Christ in their full meaning.

helps.text: The imprecatory psalms (like 35, 69, 109, 137) call down judgment on enemies. They aren't personal vengeance. They're appeals to God’s justice. Christ Himself echoes their themes. The Reformed Presbyterian tradition sings these psalms in worship as part of the whole counsel of God. They aren't embarrassing relics. They're inspired prayers Christ gave His church.
helps.html: The imprecatory psalms (like 35, 69, 109, 137) call down judgment on enemies. They aren't personal vengeance. They're appeals to God’s justice. Christ Himself echoes their themes. The Reformed Presbyterian tradition sings these psalms in worship as part of the whole counsel of God. They aren't embarrassing relics. They're inspired prayers Christ gave His church.

helps.text: Christ Himself prayed and sang the Psalms (Matthew 26.30, Matthew 27.46). He quoted them often. The Psalms are His own prayer book.
helps.html: Christ Himself prayed and sang the Psalms (Matthew 26.30, Matthew 27.46). He quoted them often. The Psalms are His own prayer book.

helps.text: The five books of the Psalter (1 to 41, 42 to 72, 73 to 89, 90 to 106, 107 to 150) are intentionally arranged. Each ends with a doxology.
helps.html: The five books of the Psalter (1 to 41, 42 to 72, 73 to 89, 90 to 106, 107 to 150) are intentionally arranged. Each ends with a doxology.

helps.text: Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 together open the book. The first sets the way of the righteous against the way of the wicked. The second declares the kingship of Christ.
helps.html: Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 together open the book. The first sets the way of the righteous against the way of the wicked. The second declares the kingship of Christ.

helps.text: Exclusive psalmody is the Reformed Presbyterian doctrine that the church's songs of praise in worship are the inspired Psalms. We sing them without instrumental accompaniment. This follows the regulative principle of worship and the sufficiency of God's appointed praise. WCF 21.1 and WCF 21.5 state the governing principle and include the singing of psalms. They don't expressly use the later label exclusive psalmody or explicitly state the exclusion of instruments. Read the Psalter as the church's songbook as well as her book of prayer.
helps.html: Exclusive psalmody is the Reformed Presbyterian doctrine that the church's songs of praise in worship are the inspired Psalms. We sing them without instrumental accompaniment. This follows the regulative principle of worship and the sufficiency of God's appointed praise. WCF 21.1 and WCF 21.5 state the governing principle and include the singing of psalms. They don't expressly use the later label exclusive psalmody or explicitly state the exclusion of instruments. Read the Psalter as the church's songbook as well as her book of prayer.

studies.title: Identify the speaker before making every line your own
studies.html: A Psalm may speak in the voice of a suffering believer, a king, or the Messiah. Acts 2.25 to 32 explains Psalm 16’s fulfillment in Christ, whose body did not see corruption. Believers share resurrection hope through Him, but we don’t make the same claim about our bodies before the resurrection. The inspired fulfillment preserves a distinction between Christ’s experience and ours.
studies.distinction: Union with Christ gives real participation in His benefits without making every messianic statement directly autobiographical for each believer.
studies.question: Why does Peter appeal to David’s tomb when explaining the Psalm?

studies.title: Judgment prayers belong to God’s justice
studies.html: Imprecatory prayers ask the righteous Judge to deal with evil. Their place in inspired worship mustn’t be erased because judgment is uncomfortable. Yet singing them doesn’t authorize private revenge or hatred of a personal rival as such. Read them with Christ’s suffering, God’s judicial office, and the command to love enemies. We can desire repentance while also appealing for evil to be restrained and finally judged.
studies.distinction: Leaving vengeance to God is different from pretending that God will never judge.
studies.question: Compare the prayer with Romans 12.19 to 21. What belongs to God, and what duty remains with us?

books.name: Proverbs
books.intro: Proverbs teaches wisdom grounded in the fear of the Lord. Its sayings include commands, warnings, general observations, and promises whose force must be read in context. The opening discourses prepare us to understand the shorter sayings that follow.
books.introText: Proverbs teaches wisdom grounded in the fear of the Lord. Its sayings include commands, warnings, general observations, and promises whose force must be read in context. The opening discourses prepare us to understand the shorter sayings that follow.

helps.text: Many proverbs describe the ordinary consequences of conduct. Their truth doesn't require that every diligent person become rich or that every wicked person suffer immediately. Other sayings contain commands or promises. Decide which kind of statement you're reading from its words and context.
helps.html: Many proverbs describe the ordinary consequences of conduct. Their truth doesn't require that every diligent person become rich or that every wicked person suffer immediately. Other sayings contain commands or promises. Decide which kind of statement you're reading from its words and context.

helps.text: Compare Proverbs 26.4 and 26.5. The commands sound opposite until you consider the different dangers they address. Wisdom includes discerning which response fits the circumstance.
helps.html: Compare Proverbs 26.4 and 26.5. The commands sound opposite until you consider the different dangers they address. Wisdom includes discerning which response fits the circumstance.

helps.text: Chapters 1 to 9 are extended discourses from a father to a son, contrasting Lady Wisdom and the adulteress. Read them as a unit before approaching the short sayings.
helps.html: Chapters 1 to 9 are extended discourses from a father to a son, contrasting Lady Wisdom and the adulteress. Read them as a unit before approaching the short sayings.

helps.text: The fear of the Lord is the foundation of wisdom. An unbeliever can recognize that honest work often benefits a household, but can't receive the book's wisdom rightly while rejecting the God who gives it.
helps.html: The fear of the Lord is the foundation of wisdom. An unbeliever can recognize that honest work often benefits a household, but can't receive the book's wisdom rightly while rejecting the God who gives it.

helps.text: Proverbs 8 personifies wisdom. Christ is the wisdom of God, as 1 Corinthians 1.24 teaches, but the poem must not be used to suggest that the eternal Son was created. Distinguish personification from a direct statement about His divine origin.
helps.html: Proverbs 8 personifies wisdom. Christ is the wisdom of God, as 1 Corinthians 1.24 teaches, but the poem must not be used to suggest that the eternal Son was created. Distinguish personification from a direct statement about His divine origin.

helps.text: The book teaches that there are basically two ways to live, the way of wisdom and the way of folly. The two paths lead to different ends.
helps.html: The book teaches that there are basically two ways to live, the way of wisdom and the way of folly. The two paths lead to different ends.

helps.text: Proverbs about the tongue, money, work, family, friendship, and the heart are scattered throughout. Use a thematic approach to study them together.
helps.html: Proverbs about the tongue, money, work, family, friendship, and the heart are scattered throughout. Use a thematic approach to study them together.

helps.text: The strange and adulterous woman of chapters 5 to 7 is both a real warning and a picture of folly itself. Avoiding sexual sin is part of the way of wisdom.
helps.html: The strange and adulterous woman of chapters 5 to 7 is both a real warning and a picture of folly itself. Avoiding sexual sin is part of the way of wisdom.

helps.text: Chapter 31’s portrait of the godly woman is the climax of the book. She is the embodiment of wisdom in everyday life.
helps.html: Chapter 31’s portrait of the godly woman is the climax of the book. She is the embodiment of wisdom in everyday life.

helps.text: Many proverbs are paired or grouped. Look for clusters of related sayings rather than reading each verse in isolation.
helps.html: Many proverbs are paired or grouped. Look for clusters of related sayings rather than reading each verse in isolation.

studies.title: Wisdom directs judgment, not a mechanical rule
studies.html: The neighboring commands identify two different dangers in answering a fool. One response can make us share his folly. Another can expose his conceit. The apparent tension trains discernment by requiring attention to circumstance and purpose. Neither command loses authority because its faithful application requires judgment.
studies.distinction: A context-sensitive command isn’t a mere suggestion, and a binding command needn’t specify one identical response to every situation.
studies.question: Describe a case where entering an argument would share its folly and a case where silence would leave error unchallenged.

studies.title: Personified wisdom does not make the Son a creature
studies.html: The chapter gives wisdom a poetic voice in relation to God’s creation. Christians rightly confess Christ as God’s wisdom, but the personification mustn’t be pressed into a literal account of the Son’s origin. John 1.1 to 3 expressly distinguishes the eternal Word from everything made through Him. Any application of Proverbs 8 to Christ must preserve that distinction.
studies.distinction: A canonical connection between Christ and wisdom doesn’t transfer every poetic expression into an account of His divine generation.
studies.question: What does John 1 say that prevents reading Proverbs 8 as proof that the Son was created?

books.name: Ecclesiastes
books.intro: The Preacher examines the brevity and frustrations of life under the sun. He exposes the failure of created things to bear the weight of ultimate hope while teaching us to receive ordinary gifts from God. The book concludes with the fear of God and coming judgment.
books.introText: The Preacher examines the brevity and frustrations of life under the sun. He exposes the failure of created things to bear the weight of ultimate hope while teaching us to receive ordinary gifts from God. The book concludes with the fear of God and coming judgment.

helps.text: The phrase under the sun locates the discussion in our earthly life. It doesn't automatically mean the speaker is reasoning as an atheist. The Preacher speaks repeatedly of God's gifts and judgments within that life.
helps.html: The phrase under the sun locates the discussion in our earthly life. It doesn't automatically mean the speaker is reasoning as an atheist. The Preacher speaks repeatedly of God's gifts and judgments within that life.

helps.text: The Preacher exposes the frustration of trying to master life or find lasting gain in what passes away. His calls to enjoy God's gifts belong to his wisdom, rather than to an unbelieving viewpoint that must all be discarded.
helps.html: The Preacher exposes the frustration of trying to master life or find lasting gain in what passes away. His calls to enjoy God's gifts belong to his wisdom, rather than to an unbelieving viewpoint that must all be discarded.

helps.text: "Vanity" (hebel in Hebrew) means breath or vapor. It's a metaphor for the fleeting, elusive nature of life. It doesn't mean meaningless in the modern sense.
helps.html: "Vanity" (hebel in Hebrew) means breath or vapor. It's a metaphor for the fleeting, elusive nature of life. It doesn't mean meaningless in the modern sense.

helps.text: The book observes that life under the sun has many puzzles. The wicked prosper. The righteous suffer. Death comes to all. Wisdom doesn't always pay.
helps.html: The book observes that life under the sun has many puzzles. The wicked prosper. The righteous suffer. Death comes to all. Wisdom doesn't always pay.

helps.text: The Preacher tests pleasure (chapter 2), work (chapter 2 and 4), wisdom (chapter 7), and wealth (chapter 5). All come up short as ultimate ends.
helps.html: The Preacher tests pleasure (chapter 2), work (chapter 2 and 4), wisdom (chapter 7), and wealth (chapter 5). All come up short as ultimate ends.

helps.text: The famous passage in chapter 3 ("To every thing there is a season") is part of the Preacher’s argument that times and seasons are fixed and a man can't find them out.
helps.html: The famous passage in chapter 3 ("To every thing there is a season") is part of the Preacher’s argument that times and seasons are fixed and a man can't find them out.

helps.text: The book repeatedly counsels enjoying the simple gifts of God in their proper place. Eat your bread. Drink your wine. Enjoy your wife. Work with your hands. Receive these as gifts.
helps.html: The book repeatedly counsels enjoying the simple gifts of God in their proper place. Eat your bread. Drink your wine. Enjoy your wife. Work with your hands. Receive these as gifts.

helps.text: The Preacher doesn't deny God’s order. He says it's largely beyond human searching out. Faith trusts what it can't fully see.
helps.html: The Preacher doesn't deny God’s order. He says it's largely beyond human searching out. Faith trusts what it can't fully see.

helps.text: The repeated attention to death makes us reckon with our limits. Read the passages together rather than treating an isolated statement about the dead as the Bible's complete teaching about life after death.
helps.html: The repeated attention to death makes us reckon with our limits. Read the passages together rather than treating an isolated statement about the dead as the Bible's complete teaching about life after death.

helps.text: Read Ecclesiastes in light of Christ. The vanity under the sun is real. But in Christ, all our labor isn't in vain (1 Corinthians 15.58).
helps.html: Read Ecclesiastes in light of Christ. The vanity under the sun is real. But in Christ, all our labor isn't in vain (1 Corinthians 15.58).

studies.title: Life under the sun is life we cannot master
studies.html: The Preacher acknowledges God’s ordering of time and our inability to search His work comprehensively. The phrase under the sun doesn’t by itself label every statement as an atheist’s error. Much of the book is wise reflection upon real limits in a fallen world. Its calls to enjoy God’s gifts must be heard as part of its instruction rather than automatically discarded as a false stage of thought.
studies.distinction: Human inability to comprehend providence isn’t evidence that providence lacks order.
studies.question: How does the passage join God’s work, human limits, and the duty to receive daily good?

studies.title: A limited observation is not a complete doctrine of death
studies.html: The passage confronts the ending of earthly activity and our shared approach to death. Read its statements in that argument, alongside the book’s teaching about judgment and the rest of Scripture’s clearer account of the soul. WCF 32 doesn’t deny the seriousness of death when it confesses conscious existence after it. It follows the fuller canonical witness.
studies.distinction: An observation about the dead no longer participating in earthly life doesn’t necessarily describe every aspect of their existence.
studies.question: Compare Ecclesiastes 9 with Luke 23.43 and Philippians 1.21 to 23. What question is each passage answering?

books.name: Song of Solomon
books.intro: The Song speaks in love poetry with shifting voices and vivid imagery. Christian interpreters have long connected its bride and bridegroom with Christ and His church. Reformed readers differ over how that spiritual reading relates to the poem's celebration of human marriage.
books.introText: The Song speaks in love poetry with shifting voices and vivid imagery. Christian interpreters have long connected its bride and bridegroom with Christ and His church. Reformed readers differ over how that spiritual reading relates to the poem's celebration of human marriage.

helps.text: The book is poetry. Read it as poetry, not as a moral code or as a doctrinal discourse.
helps.html: The book is poetry. Read it as poetry, not as a moral code or as a doctrinal discourse.

helps.text: Notice the shifts between the woman, the man, and the companions. Speaker assignments supplied in modern editions are editorial helps, not part of the inspired Hebrew text.
helps.html: Notice the shifts between the woman, the man, and the companions. Speaker assignments supplied in modern editions are editorial helps, not part of the inspired Hebrew text.

helps.text: This guide reads the poem as celebrating marital love within the larger biblical pattern of Christ and His bride. Older Reformed expositors often gave the spiritual reading a more direct and central place. Explain that difference rather than claiming historical unanimity.
helps.html: This guide reads the poem as celebrating marital love within the larger biblical pattern of Christ and His bride. Older Reformed expositors often gave the spiritual reading a more direct and central place. Explain that difference rather than claiming historical unanimity.

helps.text: Ephesians 5.25 to 33 establishes the relation between marriage and Christ's love for the church. It provides a sound canonical connection, but doesn't explain every image in the Song for us.
helps.html: Ephesians 5.25 to 33 establishes the relation between marriage and Christ's love for the church. It provides a sound canonical connection, but doesn't explain every image in the Song for us.

helps.text: Read the imagery as poetry before assigning spiritual correspondences. A detail about a garden or a jewel doesn't come with an automatic doctrinal equivalent.
helps.html: Read the imagery as poetry before assigning spiritual correspondences. A detail about a garden or a jewel doesn't come with an automatic doctrinal equivalent.

helps.text: The poetry uses imagery from nature, perfume, food, and the body. The imagery is strange to modern ears but expresses delight, longing, beauty, and union.
helps.html: The poetry uses imagery from nature, perfume, food, and the body. The imagery is strange to modern ears but expresses delight, longing, beauty, and union.

helps.text: The poem moves through longing and the delight of being together. Spiritual applications should rest on the Bible's teaching about Christ and His people, without turning every separation into a fixed stage of Christian experience.
helps.html: The poem moves through longing and the delight of being together. Spiritual applications should rest on the Bible's teaching about Christ and His people, without turning every separation into a fixed stage of Christian experience.

helps.text: The book teaches that desire isn't sin when it's rightly ordered. Sexual longing within marriage is approved by God.
helps.html: The book teaches that desire isn't sin when it's rightly ordered. Sexual longing within marriage is approved by God.

helps.text: The repeated charge about awakening love calls for restraint. Read Song of Solomon 2.7, 3.5, and 8.4 together and consider how the refrain functions within the poem.
helps.html: The repeated charge about awakening love calls for restraint. Read Song of Solomon 2.7, 3.5, and 8.4 together and consider how the refrain functions within the poem.

helps.text: When applying the bridegroom's love to Christ, remember that the application rests on the wider biblical marriage pattern. Don't assume that every action of a human lover can be transferred directly to the Savior.
helps.html: When applying the bridegroom's love to Christ, remember that the application rests on the wider biblical marriage pattern. Don't assume that every action of a human lover can be transferred directly to the Savior.

helps.text: Read the Song with reverence. Many of the most spiritually rich believers across the centuries have meditated long on this book. It isn't embarrassing. It's holy ground.
helps.html: Read the Song with reverence. Many of the most spiritually rich believers across the centuries have meditated long on this book. It isn't embarrassing. It's holy ground.

studies.title: A spiritual application needs a textual foundation
studies.html: The poem speaks through the lovers' voices and the imagery of spring. Older Reformed expositors commonly developed a direct spiritual reading concerning Christ and His people. Other Reformed readers begin with marital love and trace its canonical relation to Christ through Ephesians 5. Whichever relation is argued, the imagery’s literary function must govern the application rather than a fixed code invented for each flower or animal.
studies.distinction: Respect for historic interpretation requires understanding its argument, not treating every inherited detail as inspired commentary.
studies.question: Choose one image and explain its function in the poem before suggesting a spiritual application.

studies.title: Love’s goodness belongs within God’s moral order
studies.html: The Song treats love as powerful and worthy of delight while its refrains warn against awakening it improperly. Read that celebration within Scripture’s teaching about marriage and chastity. The book’s poetry doesn’t suspend the moral law, and the law doesn’t make marital affection impure. The literal sense calls for reverent attention to human love as God orders it.
studies.distinction: Celebrating created desire isn’t approval of every desire or every occasion for its expression.
studies.question: How do the Song’s delight and its repeated calls for restraint belong together?

books.name: Isaiah
books.intro: Isaiah proclaims judgment and salvation amid Judah's unfaithfulness and the threat of foreign empires. The book reaches from his own historical setting to the Servant's suffering and the new creation. Follow how the New Testament identifies these promises with Christ.
books.introText: Isaiah proclaims judgment and salvation amid Judah's unfaithfulness and the threat of foreign empires. The book reaches from his own historical setting to the Servant's suffering and the new creation. Follow how the New Testament identifies these promises with Christ.

helps.text: Isaiah ministered in Judah from roughly 740 to 680 BC. He saw four kings. The book reflects the Assyrian crisis (chapters 36 to 39) and looks forward to the Babylonian exile and return.
helps.html: Isaiah ministered in Judah from roughly 740 to 680 BC. He saw four kings. The book reflects the Assyrian crisis (chapters 36 to 39) and looks forward to the Babylonian exile and return.

helps.text: The vision in chapter 6 is foundational. Isaiah sees the Lord, is undone, is cleansed, and is sent. This pattern shapes the whole book.
helps.html: The vision in chapter 6 is foundational. Isaiah sees the Lord, is undone, is cleansed, and is sent. This pattern shapes the whole book.

helps.text: Chapters 1 to 12 contain great messianic passages. The virgin birth in 7.14. The child who is "The mighty God, The everlasting Father" in 9.6. The shoot from the stump of Jesse in 11.
helps.html: Chapters 1 to 12 contain great messianic passages. The virgin birth in 7.14. The child who is "The mighty God, The everlasting Father" in 9.6. The shoot from the stump of Jesse in 11.

helps.text: Chapters 13 to 23 contain oracles against the nations. God is sovereign over more than Israel.
helps.html: Chapters 13 to 23 contain oracles against the nations. God is sovereign over more than Israel.

helps.text: Chapters 24 to 27 are sometimes called Isaiah’s Apocalypse. They contain great visions of cosmic judgment and the swallowing up of death.
helps.html: Chapters 24 to 27 are sometimes called Isaiah’s Apocalypse. They contain great visions of cosmic judgment and the swallowing up of death.

helps.text: Chapters 36 to 39 are historical narrative about Hezekiah. They form a hinge between the first and second halves of the book.
helps.html: Chapters 36 to 39 are historical narrative about Hezekiah. They form a hinge between the first and second halves of the book.

helps.text: Chapters 40 to 55 are the great consolation. They open with "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" They contain the four Servant Songs that find their fulfillment in Christ.
helps.html: Chapters 40 to 55 are the great consolation. They open with "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" They contain the four Servant Songs that find their fulfillment in Christ.

helps.text: Isaiah 53 is the climax. The Servant suffers for the sins of His people, bearing their iniquity. The chapter is quoted in the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ.
helps.html: Isaiah 53 is the climax. The Servant suffers for the sins of His people, bearing their iniquity. The chapter is quoted in the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ.

helps.text: Chapters 56 to 66 look beyond the return from exile to the new heavens and new earth (65, 66). These chapters blend present and consummative realities.
helps.html: Chapters 56 to 66 look beyond the return from exile to the new heavens and new earth (65, 66). These chapters blend present and consummative realities.

studies.title: The Servant bears guilt without becoming morally sinful
studies.html: The Servant suffers for the transgressions of others while remaining righteous. Acts 8.30 to 35 identifies the passage’s fulfillment in Jesus. The transfer of guilt is judicial, not a corruption of Christ’s character. He bears the liability of His people’s sins and satisfies God’s justice. His innocence is essential to the passage’s account of substitution.
studies.distinction: Christ’s bearing sin doesn’t mean He personally commits it, becomes morally defiled, or ceases to be the righteous Son.
studies.question: Which statements distinguish the Servant’s righteousness from the iniquities He bears?

studies.title: The promised King and His divine titles
studies.html: The child born to reign on David’s throne is described with titles that reach beyond an ordinary king. Matthew 4.12 to 16 connects the preceding light in Galilee to Jesus' ministry, and Luke 1 connects His reign to David’s enduring throne. The title everlasting Father must be read consistently with the revealed distinction between the Father and the Son. It doesn’t identify Jesus as the Person who sends Him.
studies.distinction: A royal title expressing the Messiah’s enduring care mustn’t be used to collapse the Persons of the Trinity.
studies.question: How do the New Testament’s identification of the King and its personal distinctions guide this reading?

books.name: Jeremiah
books.intro: Jeremiah warns Judah before Jerusalem's fall and ministers through its devastation. His own sufferings accompany the message he bears. Amid judgment, the Lord promises a new covenant with forgiveness and a law written on the heart.
books.introText: Jeremiah warns Judah before Jerusalem's fall and ministers through its devastation. His own sufferings accompany the message he bears. Amid judgment, the Lord promises a new covenant with forgiveness and a law written on the heart.

helps.text: Jeremiah ministered from about 627 to after 586 BC. He saw the fall of Jerusalem and was taken to Egypt against his will.
helps.html: Jeremiah ministered from about 627 to after 586 BC. He saw the fall of Jerusalem and was taken to Egypt against his will.

helps.text: He is sometimes called the weeping prophet because of his laments and his suffering. He is a type of Christ in his rejection by his own people.
helps.html: He is sometimes called the weeping prophet because of his laments and his suffering. He is a type of Christ in his rejection by his own people.

helps.text: The book includes oracles, sermons, narratives, laments, and prophecies. The genre changes throughout. Read each section according to its kind.
helps.html: The book includes oracles, sermons, narratives, laments, and prophecies. The genre changes throughout. Read each section according to its kind.

helps.text: The temple sermon (chapter 7 and 26) confronts the false confidence that the temple itself protects Jerusalem. Without repentance, the temple won't save them.
helps.html: The temple sermon (chapter 7 and 26) confronts the false confidence that the temple itself protects Jerusalem. Without repentance, the temple won't save them.

helps.text: The seventy years of exile prophecy (25.11, 29.10) is a specific predictive prophecy fulfilled exactly. Daniel reads it (Daniel 9) and prays accordingly.
helps.html: The seventy years of exile prophecy (25.11, 29.10) is a specific predictive prophecy fulfilled exactly. Daniel reads it (Daniel 9) and prays accordingly.

helps.text: The new covenant promise (31.31 to 34) is the highest point of the book. The law written on the heart, sins forgiven, all knowing the Lord. Hebrews 8 quotes it as fulfilled in Christ.
helps.html: The new covenant promise (31.31 to 34) is the highest point of the book. The law written on the heart, sins forgiven, all knowing the Lord. Hebrews 8 quotes it as fulfilled in Christ.

helps.text: Symbolic actions include the linen sash (13), the smashed jar (19), the wooden and iron yokes (27 to 28), and the field at Anathoth (32). Each action is a prophecy in physical form.
helps.html: Symbolic actions include the linen sash (13), the smashed jar (19), the wooden and iron yokes (27 to 28), and the field at Anathoth (32). Each action is a prophecy in physical form.

helps.text: The fall of Jerusalem is recorded (chapter 39 and 52). The judgment promised across the book finally comes.
helps.html: The fall of Jerusalem is recorded (chapter 39 and 52). The judgment promised across the book finally comes.

helps.text: Jeremiah's removal to Egypt is narrated in chapters 42 to 44. The book itself ends in chapter 52 with Jerusalem's fall and a limited mercy shown to Jehoiachin. Don't confuse the order of the book with the sequence of Jeremiah's life.
helps.html: Jeremiah's removal to Egypt is narrated in chapters 42 to 44. The book itself ends in chapter 52 with Jerusalem's fall and a limited mercy shown to Jehoiachin. Don't confuse the order of the book with the sequence of Jeremiah's life.

studies.title: The new covenant promises an inward work
studies.html: The Lord promises forgiveness and His law written within His people. Hebrews 8 quotes this passage to explain the better covenant mediated by Christ. The contrast concerns the accomplishment and administration of God’s saving promise. It doesn’t mean Old Testament believers lacked all inward grace, or that New Testament believers have no remaining sin. Compare David’s faith and Paul’s account of continuing conflict.
studies.distinction: The promise’s fullness mustn’t be explained by denying the reality of grace before Christ or imagining perfection before glory.
studies.question: What defects of the former administration does Hebrews name, and what does Christ’s mediation accomplish?

studies.title: A restoration promise must retain its address
studies.html: The letter directs exiles to settle, seek the city’s welfare, and reject false promises of a quick return. The assurance of a future is tied to God’s announced seventy years and His purpose for the exiled people. A reader who removes those details can turn a call to patient fidelity into a promise of immediate personal success, nearly reversing Jeremiah’s pastoral purpose.
studies.distinction: God’s faithfulness comforts all His people, but the named timetable and historical return aren’t a private promise to each reader.
studies.question: How do the commands to build and plant challenge the false expectation Jeremiah opposes?

books.name: Lamentations
books.intro: Five poems mourn Jerusalem's destruction and confess the justice of God's judgment. Their grief isn't neatly resolved. In the middle of the ruin, the writer still appeals to the Lord's mercy and calls His people to return.
books.introText: Five poems mourn Jerusalem's destruction and confess the justice of God's judgment. Their grief isn't neatly resolved. In the middle of the ruin, the writer still appeals to the Lord's mercy and calls His people to return.

helps.text: Lamentations was written in the immediate aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction. The grief is fresh and the wounds are open.
helps.html: Lamentations was written in the immediate aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction. The grief is fresh and the wounds are open.

helps.text: Chapters 1, 2, and 4 follow the Hebrew alphabet with one stanza for each letter. Chapter 3 uses three successive lines for each letter. Chapter 5 has twenty-two verses but no alphabetic sequence. The forms differ while giving order to grief.
helps.html: Chapters 1, 2, and 4 follow the Hebrew alphabet with one stanza for each letter. Chapter 3 uses three successive lines for each letter. Chapter 5 has twenty-two verses but no alphabetic sequence. The forms differ while giving order to grief.

helps.text: Chapter 3 has the central hope. The famous lines about new mercies every morning come from a man whose city has been destroyed and whose people have been killed and exiled.
helps.html: Chapter 3 has the central hope. The famous lines about new mercies every morning come from a man whose city has been destroyed and whose people have been killed and exiled.

helps.text: The book doesn't deny that the destruction was deserved. Sin brought the judgment.
helps.html: The book doesn't deny that the destruction was deserved. Sin brought the judgment.

helps.text: Yet the book also pours out raw grief. It doesn't bottle the pain. Faith and sorrow live in the same poem.
helps.html: Yet the book also pours out raw grief. It doesn't bottle the pain. Faith and sorrow live in the same poem.

helps.text: The book teaches us to lament. There's a kind of prayer that's needed when life falls apart. This book gives us its words.
helps.html: The book teaches us to lament. There's a kind of prayer that's needed when life falls apart. This book gives us its words.

helps.text: The questions in Lamentations 5.20 lead into the plea for restoration in 5.21 and the dark closing words of 5.22. Read the whole conclusion. It leaves the grief unresolved rather than supplying an easy ending.
helps.html: The questions in Lamentations 5.20 lead into the plea for restoration in 5.21 and the dark closing words of 5.22. Read the whole conclusion. It leaves the grief unresolved rather than supplying an easy ending.

helps.text: Christ wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19.41 to 44) in language that echoes Lamentations. The same Lord who judges also weeps.
helps.html: Christ wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19.41 to 44) in language that echoes Lamentations. The same Lord who judges also weeps.

studies.title: Hope is spoken within grief rather than after its removal
studies.html: The confession of God’s mercy appears amid a sustained lament over destruction. The writer recalls what gives hope without pretending that the city is already restored. Read the surrounding sorrow along with the familiar words about morning mercies. Scripture can teach trust and patience while allowing grief to remain painful and unresolved.
studies.distinction: An expression of faith isn’t a report that the sufferer’s distress has immediately ended.
studies.question: What remains grievous before and after the confession of hope, and what truth changes the writer’s response?

studies.title: An acknowledged judgment does not explain every sufferer’s case
studies.html: Jerusalem’s lament confesses that the Lord is righteous and the city’s rebellion real. This historical judgment has been announced by the prophets. We may therefore identify its covenantal cause because Scripture does so. Job prevents us from turning that revealed explanation into a universal method for accusing anyone whose life has collapsed.
studies.distinction: A cause disclosed for Jerusalem cannot simply be presumed for every person experiencing loss.
studies.question: What evidence authorizes the confession of covenant judgment here that Job’s friends lacked in their accusations?

books.name: Ezekiel
books.intro: A priest among the Babylonian exiles receives visions of God's glory, Jerusalem's judgment, and future restoration. The Lord exposes false confidence in the temple and promises to cleanse His people, give them a new heart, and dwell among them.
books.introText: A priest among the Babylonian exiles receives visions of God's glory, Jerusalem's judgment, and future restoration. The Lord exposes false confidence in the temple and promises to cleanse His people, give them a new heart, and dwell among them.

helps.text: Ezekiel was a priest taken into exile in Babylon. He prophesied to fellow exiles from about 593 to 571 BC.
helps.html: Ezekiel was a priest taken into exile in Babylon. He prophesied to fellow exiles from about 593 to 571 BC.

helps.text: The opening vision (chapter 1) is overwhelming. Wheels within wheels, four living creatures, the throne above. The point is that God’s glory is mobile and is with His people in exile, not bound to the temple in Jerusalem.
helps.html: The opening vision (chapter 1) is overwhelming. Wheels within wheels, four living creatures, the throne above. The point is that God’s glory is mobile and is with His people in exile, not bound to the temple in Jerusalem.

helps.text: Ezekiel's enacted signs include lying on his side and shaving his head. In chapter 24, the Lord makes the death of Ezekiel's wife and his commanded response a sign to the exiles. He doesn't instruct Ezekiel to cause her death.
helps.html: Ezekiel's enacted signs include lying on his side and shaving his head. In chapter 24, the Lord makes the death of Ezekiel's wife and his commanded response a sign to the exiles. He doesn't instruct Ezekiel to cause her death.

helps.text: The departure of God’s glory from the temple (chapter 8 to 11) is one of the great moments of the Old Testament. The judgment is that the Lord no longer dwells with His sinful people.
helps.html: The departure of God’s glory from the temple (chapter 8 to 11) is one of the great moments of the Old Testament. The judgment is that the Lord no longer dwells with His sinful people.

helps.text: The watchman passages (chapter 3, 33) describe Ezekiel’s calling. He must warn the people. If he doesn't, their blood is on his hands. If he does, his soul is delivered.
helps.html: The watchman passages (chapter 3, 33) describe Ezekiel’s calling. He must warn the people. If he doesn't, their blood is on his hands. If he does, his soul is delivered.

helps.text: The shepherd chapter (34) judges the false shepherds of Israel and promises that the Lord Himself will shepherd His people. Christ takes this up in John 10.
helps.html: The shepherd chapter (34) judges the false shepherds of Israel and promises that the Lord Himself will shepherd His people. Christ takes this up in John 10.

helps.text: The new heart promise (36.26 to 27) anticipates regeneration by the Spirit. A heart of stone replaced with a heart of flesh.
helps.html: The new heart promise (36.26 to 27) anticipates regeneration by the Spirit. A heart of stone replaced with a heart of flesh.

helps.text: Ezekiel 37 identifies the dry bones with the house of Israel and promises restoration. Its imagery illuminates God's power to give life. Distinguish that stated interpretation from further applications to regeneration and bodily resurrection.
helps.html: Ezekiel 37 identifies the dry bones with the house of Israel and promises restoration. Its imagery illuminates God's power to give life. Distinguish that stated interpretation from further applications to regeneration and bodily resurrection.

helps.text: Gog and Magog (chapter 38 to 39) are visionary, not strictly literal, foes from the north. Revelation 20.7 to 8 picks up this language for the final battle.
helps.html: Gog and Magog (chapter 38 to 39) are visionary, not strictly literal, foes from the north. Revelation 20.7 to 8 picks up this language for the final battle.

helps.text: The temple vision in chapters 40 to 48 is read here in light of Christ and the final dwelling of God with His people. Reformed interpreters differ over its details. Its sacrificial imagery must be understood consistently with Christ's sufficient, unrepeatable sacrifice in Hebrews 10.
helps.html: The temple vision in chapters 40 to 48 is read here in light of Christ and the final dwelling of God with His people. Reformed interpreters differ over its details. Its sacrificial imagery must be understood consistently with Christ's sufficient, unrepeatable sacrifice in Hebrews 10.

studies.title: The new heart is God’s gift
studies.html: The Lord promises cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit, causing His people to walk in His statutes. His action answers their pollution rather than rewarding an independently achieved renewal. Notice also the stated concern for His holy name. The passage supplies a rich account of sovereign grace whose result is obedient life, not freedom to disregard God’s commands.
studies.distinction: The promised obedience is the effect of inward grace, not a prior payment that persuades God to give it.
studies.question: Identify the actions God promises to perform and the changes in conduct that follow them.

studies.title: Read the temple vision with the finished sacrifice
studies.html: The return of glory answers the earlier vision of departure. Chapters 40 to 48 portray restored holiness and God’s dwelling with His people through detailed sanctuary imagery. This guide reads the vision in relation to Christ and His covenant people. Its debated details must be handled under Hebrews' clear teaching that His sacrifice fully answers guilt and cannot be supplemented by renewed animal atonement.
studies.distinction: Difficulty in a vision doesn’t authorize contradicting the plain sufficiency of Christ’s offering.
studies.question: How does the return of glory connect this vision with Ezekiel 10 to 11 and the promise of dwelling in Revelation 21?

books.name: Daniel
books.intro: Daniel and his companions serve under foreign rulers without surrendering their allegiance to God. Court narratives are followed by visions of successive kingdoms and their judgment. Earthly empires pass, but the dominion given to the Son of man endures.
books.introText: Daniel and his companions serve under foreign rulers without surrendering their allegiance to God. Court narratives are followed by visions of successive kingdoms and their judgment. Earthly empires pass, but the dominion given to the Son of man endures.

helps.text: The book divides cleanly into chapters 1 to 6 (historical narratives) and chapters 7 to 12 (visions of Daniel).
helps.html: The book divides cleanly into chapters 1 to 6 (historical narratives) and chapters 7 to 12 (visions of Daniel).

helps.text: Daniel and his friends in Babylon (chapters 1 to 6) are models of faithfulness in a pagan setting. They serve a foreign king without compromising their God.
helps.html: Daniel and his friends in Babylon (chapters 1 to 6) are models of faithfulness in a pagan setting. They serve a foreign king without compromising their God.

helps.text: Nebuchadnezzar’s dream (chapter 2) and the four-kingdom vision are paralleled in Daniel’s vision (chapter 7). The kingdoms are most likely Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome.
helps.html: Nebuchadnezzar’s dream (chapter 2) and the four-kingdom vision are paralleled in Daniel’s vision (chapter 7). The kingdoms are most likely Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome.

helps.text: The fiery furnace (chapter 3) and the lions’ den (chapter 6) display real deliverances from God in the face of forced idolatry. They're also patterns of faithful witness for every age.
helps.html: The fiery furnace (chapter 3) and the lions’ den (chapter 6) display real deliverances from God in the face of forced idolatry. They're also patterns of faithful witness for every age.

helps.text: The Son of Man vision (chapter 7) is foundational. Christ takes the title for Himself. The everlasting kingdom is His.
helps.html: The Son of Man vision (chapter 7) is foundational. Christ takes the title for Himself. The everlasting kingdom is His.

helps.text: Daniel 9.24 to 27 connects the seventy weeks with atonement, righteousness, and the coming of the Messiah. Historic Christian readings differ over the chronology and the final week. Work through the clauses before assigning dates. The Westminster Standards don't settle a detailed timetable.
helps.html: Daniel 9.24 to 27 connects the seventy weeks with atonement, righteousness, and the coming of the Messiah. Historic Christian readings differ over the chronology and the final week. Work through the clauses before assigning dates. The Westminster Standards don't settle a detailed timetable.

helps.text: The visions of chapters 8 and 11 deal in detail with the rise and fall of empires, especially Persia, Greece, the wars of Alexander’s successors, and Antiochus Epiphanes. These prophecies are remarkably specific and were largely fulfilled before Christ.
helps.html: The visions of chapters 8 and 11 deal in detail with the rise and fall of empires, especially Persia, Greece, the wars of Alexander’s successors, and Antiochus Epiphanes. These prophecies are remarkably specific and were largely fulfilled before Christ.

helps.text: Some readings of chapter 11 see a transition at some point in the chapter from Antiochus to a more distant antichrist figure. This is debated.
helps.html: Some readings of chapter 11 see a transition at some point in the chapter from Antiochus to a more distant antichrist figure. This is debated.

helps.text: Chapter 12 promises the resurrection of the dead, both to everlasting life and to shame. This is one of the clearest Old Testament resurrection passages.
helps.html: Chapter 12 promises the resurrection of the dead, both to everlasting life and to shame. This is one of the clearest Old Testament resurrection passages.

studies.title: The Son of man comes to the Ancient of days
studies.html: Attend to the direction of the vision. The Son of man is brought before the Ancient of days and receives dominion. The passage doesn’t simply describe a descent from heaven to earth. Jesus takes this title and authority to Himself. His exaltation and final public vindication belong together, but the scene’s own movement must be understood before it is placed within an eschatological outline.
studies.distinction: The word coming doesn’t identify the direction or occasion of an event without its context.
studies.question: Who approaches whom, what is given, and how does that clarify the kingdom’s divine source?

studies.title: Resurrection language must not be dissolved into national recovery
studies.html: Daniel speaks of awakening from the dust to everlasting life or shame. John 5.28 to 29 gives a clearer New Testament account of bodily resurrection to life and judgment. Symbolism elsewhere in Daniel doesn’t permit us to turn this hope entirely into a metaphor for improved circumstances. Read the reality indicated by the language, with the canonical teaching that explains it.
studies.distinction: A book containing visions can still make definite assertions about bodily events.
studies.question: What shared features connect Daniel 12 with Christ’s teaching about the resurrection in John 5?

books.name: Hosea
books.intro: Hosea's marriage becomes a prophetic sign of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness. The Lord names His people's sins and announces judgment, yet promises restoration by His mercy. The marriage imagery must be read alongside the covenant charges that follow.
books.introText: Hosea's marriage becomes a prophetic sign of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness. The Lord names His people's sins and announces judgment, yet promises restoration by His mercy. The marriage imagery must be read alongside the covenant charges that follow.

helps.text: Hosea ministered roughly from 750 to 715 BC, mostly to the northern kingdom.
helps.html: Hosea ministered roughly from 750 to 715 BC, mostly to the northern kingdom.

helps.text: His marriage to Gomer is a real prophetic sign-act. Whether she was already a prostitute when he married her or became one later is debated. Either way the picture is clear.
helps.html: His marriage to Gomer is a real prophetic sign-act. Whether she was already a prostitute when he married her or became one later is debated. Either way the picture is clear.

helps.text: The names of his children (Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, Lo-Ammi) are prophetic names of judgment. They're reversed in chapter 2.
helps.html: The names of his children (Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, Lo-Ammi) are prophetic names of judgment. They're reversed in chapter 2.

helps.text: Chapters 1 to 3 are the marriage section. Chapters 4 to 14 are the long sermon of judgment and call to return.
helps.html: Chapters 1 to 3 are the marriage section. Chapters 4 to 14 are the long sermon of judgment and call to return.

helps.text: The dominant accusation is spiritual adultery. Israel has gone after Baal and the calves of Jeroboam.
helps.html: The dominant accusation is spiritual adultery. Israel has gone after Baal and the calves of Jeroboam.

helps.text: Yet the love of God remains. "How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?" (11.8) is one of the great expressions of divine compassion in all Scripture.
helps.html: Yet the love of God remains. "How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?" (11.8) is one of the great expressions of divine compassion in all Scripture.

helps.text: The covenant pattern of Deuteronomy is everywhere in Hosea. Israel has broken covenant. The curses are coming. But mercy still calls.
helps.html: The covenant pattern of Deuteronomy is everywhere in Hosea. Israel has broken covenant. The curses are coming. But mercy still calls.

helps.text: Matthew 2.15 quotes Hosea 11.1 as fulfilled in Christ ("Out of Egypt have I called my son"). The original referent is Israel. Christ fulfills the typology.
helps.html: Matthew 2.15 quotes Hosea 11.1 as fulfilled in Christ ("Out of Egypt have I called my son"). The original referent is Israel. Christ fulfills the typology.

helps.text: Hosea 6.6 ("For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice") is quoted by Christ in Matthew 9.13 and 12.7. God wants the heart, not just the ritual.
helps.html: Hosea 6.6 ("For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice") is quoted by Christ in Matthew 9.13 and 12.7. God wants the heart, not just the ritual.

studies.title: Israel’s history reaches its faithful Son
studies.html: Hosea recalls the Lord’s love for Israel and the exodus. Matthew 2.15 then identifies the return of Jesus from Egypt as fulfillment. The first passage isn’t a failed prediction if it refers historically to Israel. The faithful Son embodies and fulfills the history and calling of the people named as God’s son. The inspired connection is typological rather than a denial of Hosea’s original reference.
studies.distinction: Fulfillment needn’t mean that the earlier words were a bare forecast with no historical subject in their own setting.
studies.question: What does Hosea say about Israel’s response, and how does Christ’s faithfulness differ?

studies.title: Mercy and sacrifice are not simple rivals
studies.html: The Lord exposes loyalty that disappears like morning mist and rejects sacrifice used in place of covenant faithfulness. Jesus applies the passage against those who misunderstand mercy. Hosea isn’t independently abolishing the sacrifices the Lord then required. The prophetic comparison condemns outward observance detached from the knowledge of God.
studies.distinction: A rebuke of empty ritual mustn’t become an excuse to reject the worship God actually commands.
studies.question: Read Matthew 9.9 to 13. How does Jesus apply Hosea’s rebuke to the accusation being made?

books.name: Joel
books.intro: A devastating locust plague becomes the occasion for repentance and warning about the day of the Lord. The promise of the Spirit's outpouring reaches its fulfillment at Pentecost. Joel also looks toward judgment on the nations and the Lord's dwelling with His people.
books.introText: A devastating locust plague becomes the occasion for repentance and warning about the day of the Lord. The promise of the Spirit's outpouring reaches its fulfillment at Pentecost. Joel also looks toward judgment on the nations and the Lord's dwelling with His people.

helps.text: Joel’s date is debated. He may have ministered before, during, or after the exile. The text doesn't nail it down.
helps.html: Joel’s date is debated. He may have ministered before, during, or after the exile. The text doesn't nail it down.

helps.text: The locust plague (chapter 1) is real. The land has been devastated.
helps.html: The locust plague (chapter 1) is real. The land has been devastated.

helps.text: Joel uses the plague as a picture of the day of the LORD. The greater judgment is coming.
helps.html: Joel uses the plague as a picture of the day of the LORD. The greater judgment is coming.

helps.text: The call to repentance (chapter 2.12 to 17) is one of the great calls in the Old Testament. "And rend your heart, and not your garments" (2.13).
helps.html: The call to repentance (chapter 2.12 to 17) is one of the great calls in the Old Testament. "And rend your heart, and not your garments" (2.13).

helps.text: The promise of the Spirit’s outpouring (2.28 to 32) is fulfilled at Pentecost. Peter quotes it as fulfilled in Acts 2.
helps.html: The promise of the Spirit’s outpouring (2.28 to 32) is fulfilled at Pentecost. Peter quotes it as fulfilled in Acts 2.

helps.text: The day of the LORD includes the judgment of the nations (chapter 3). The Lord roars from Zion.
helps.html: The day of the LORD includes the judgment of the nations (chapter 3). The Lord roars from Zion.

helps.text: The valley of decision (3.14) is the place where the nations are gathered for judgment.
helps.html: The valley of decision (3.14) is the place where the nations are gathered for judgment.

helps.text: The book ends with the LORD dwelling in Zion and the land flowing with the goodness of His blessing.
helps.html: The book ends with the LORD dwelling in Zion and the land flowing with the goodness of His blessing.

studies.title: Pentecost belongs to the promised last days
studies.html: Peter quotes Joel to explain the Spirit’s outpouring in Acts 2. The connection is stated by an apostle rather than inferred from a vague resemblance. The whole prophetic horizon includes the day of the Lord and deliverance for those who call upon Him. Fulfillment can be inaugurated in an identifiable event without requiring every feature of final consummation to have occurred at once.
studies.distinction: Already begun and fully completed aren’t identical claims about a promise’s fulfillment.
studies.question: Which event does Peter explain, and how does his sermon call the hearers to respond?

studies.title: The valley of decision is a scene of judgment
studies.html: The nations are summoned to the Lord’s judgment. The valley’s decision concerns His decisive judicial action, not an invitation to imagine crowds deciding whether to accept Him at an altar call. Follow the surrounding summons, harvest imagery, and divine voice. A familiar religious phrase must be tested by its actual setting before it becomes a sermon theme.
studies.distinction: A useful phrase in a modern appeal doesn’t establish that the phrase has that meaning in Joel.
studies.question: Who assembles the nations, who sits to judge, and whose decision controls the scene?

books.name: Amos
books.intro: Amos confronts prosperous Israel with its oppression and corrupt worship. Covenant privilege will not shelter an unrepentant people from judgment. The book ends with a promise concerning David's fallen house that James applies to the gathering of the Gentiles.
books.introText: Amos confronts prosperous Israel with its oppression and corrupt worship. Covenant privilege will not shelter an unrepentant people from judgment. The book ends with a promise concerning David's fallen house that James applies to the gathering of the Gentiles.

helps.text: Amos ministered roughly from 760 to 750 BC, during the prosperity of Jeroboam II in the north.
helps.html: Amos ministered roughly from 760 to 750 BC, during the prosperity of Jeroboam II in the north.

helps.text: The opening judgments address the surrounding nations, then Judah, and finally Israel. Count the sequence in Amos 1 to 2. Israel is the eighth target, not the seventh.
helps.html: The opening judgments address the surrounding nations, then Judah, and finally Israel. Count the sequence in Amos 1 to 2. Israel is the eighth target, not the seventh.

helps.text: The accusations are against oppression of the poor, dishonest scales, lavish living at the expense of others, and worship that ignores justice.
helps.html: The accusations are against oppression of the poor, dishonest scales, lavish living at the expense of others, and worship that ignores justice.

helps.text: The famous line "But let judgment run down as waters" (5.24) is from Amos. It's set against ritual without justice.
helps.html: The famous line "But let judgment run down as waters" (5.24) is from Amos. It's set against ritual without justice.

helps.text: Amos 4 contains a series of judgments God has sent. Each ends with "yet have ye not returned unto me"
helps.html: Amos 4 contains a series of judgments God has sent. Each ends with "yet have ye not returned unto me"

helps.text: The visions of chapters 7 to 9 show coming judgment and the fall of the northern kingdom.
helps.html: The visions of chapters 7 to 9 show coming judgment and the fall of the northern kingdom.

helps.text: Amos 8.11 prophesies a famine of hearing the words of the LORD. The withdrawal of God’s word is the deepest judgment.
helps.html: Amos 8.11 prophesies a famine of hearing the words of the LORD. The withdrawal of God’s word is the deepest judgment.

helps.text: The closing promise (9.11 to 15) is the rebuilding of the booth of David. James quotes this in Acts 15 as fulfilled in the inclusion of the Gentiles in the church.
helps.html: The closing promise (9.11 to 15) is the rebuilding of the booth of David. James quotes this in Acts 15 as fulfilled in the inclusion of the Gentiles in the church.

helps.text: The book teaches that God hates worship divorced from justice. Religion without obedience isn't religion.
helps.html: The book teaches that God hates worship divorced from justice. Religion without obedience isn't religion.

studies.title: God rejects worship joined to oppression
studies.html: The people desire the day of the Lord while neglecting justice and offering worship He refuses. The rebuke concerns a covenant people whose public religion shelters their disobedience. It does not teach that worship is unnecessary or that justice can purchase acceptance. Read the two duties together. The Lord who appoints worship also forbids the exploitation of a neighbor.
studies.distinction: Neither correct ceremonies nor social usefulness can compensate for refusing God’s revealed will.
studies.question: How does the wider chapter identify the injustice that makes the people’s confidence presumptuous?

studies.title: David’s restored tent includes Gentile believers
studies.html: James quotes the restoration promise in Acts 15 while defending the reception of Gentiles without circumcision. The apostolic application establishes that the promise concerns the messianic gathering, not only a reconstructed political structure.
