The land and kingdom imagery must be received in light of the fulfillment the New Testament actually identifies.
studies.distinction: An inspired application to Gentile salvation cannot be dismissed because the earlier imagery is drawn from Israel’s national life.
studies.question: What dispute is James addressing, and how does Amos supply an answer?

books.name: Obadiah
books.intro: Edom is judged for pride and violence against Judah in its distress. The short prophecy moves from a particular enemy to the day of the Lord upon the nations. Its closing hope rests in the Lord's kingdom.
books.introText: Edom is judged for pride and violence against Judah in its distress. The short prophecy moves from a particular enemy to the day of the Lord upon the nations. Its closing hope rests in the Lord's kingdom.

helps.text: Obadiah likely prophesied after 586 BC, after Edom assisted in or rejoiced over Jerusalem’s fall.
helps.html: Obadiah likely prophesied after 586 BC, after Edom assisted in or rejoiced over Jerusalem’s fall.

helps.text: The accusation against Edom is clear. They stood aloof and even joined in plundering Judah on the day of her trouble.
helps.html: The accusation against Edom is clear. They stood aloof and even joined in plundering Judah on the day of her trouble.

helps.text: The pride of Edom (verses 3 to 4) is judged. Their high mountain refuge won't save them.
helps.html: The pride of Edom (verses 3 to 4) is judged. Their high mountain refuge won't save them.

helps.text: The day of the LORD is near upon all nations (verse 15). The judgment of Edom is part of that larger day.
helps.html: The day of the LORD is near upon all nations (verse 15). The judgment of Edom is part of that larger day.

helps.text: Verse 17 promises that on Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions.
helps.html: Verse 17 promises that on Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions.

helps.text: The book ends with "the kingdom shall be the LORD’s" This is the ultimate horizon.
helps.html: The book ends with "the kingdom shall be the LORD’s" This is the ultimate horizon.

helps.text: Edom is a long-running enemy in the Bible, going back to Esau’s hostility to Jacob. The book stands in that long line.
helps.html: Edom is a long-running enemy in the Bible, going back to Esau’s hostility to Jacob. The book stands in that long line.

helps.text: Edom historically was destroyed and never restored as a nation. The prophecy was fulfilled.
helps.html: Edom historically was destroyed and never restored as a nation. The prophecy was fulfilled.

helps.text: The book teaches that God notices how nations and individuals treat His people in their distress.
helps.html: The book teaches that God notices how nations and individuals treat His people in their distress.

studies.title: Edom’s guilt is specified, not merely assumed
studies.html: The oracle names Edom’s conduct during Judah’s distress, including standing aloof and participating in violence. The judgment isn’t presented as arbitrary hostility toward an ethnic label. Read the charges closely before applying the passage. The broader biblical history of Jacob and Esau contributes context without making every later conflict a direct reenactment of the oracle.
studies.distinction: A prophetic nation-name isn’t a free label for whichever present group a reader opposes.
studies.question: Which acts does the prophet forbid, and how do those acts explain the announced judgment?

studies.title: The Lord’s kingdom is the final horizon
studies.html: The prophecy moves from Edom to the day of the Lord upon the nations and concludes with the kingdom belonging to Him. Particular historical judgments therefore belong within His wider judicial rule. The full canonical hope includes the final triumph of Christ, but an application must follow that revealed line rather than assigning modern borders to every named place.
studies.distinction: A final kingdom horizon doesn’t erase the oracle’s historical judgment or authorize an unsupported political map.
studies.question: Where does the prophecy broaden beyond Edom, and how does its final assertion direct hope?

books.name: Jonah
books.intro: The Lord sends Jonah to Nineveh, and the prophet resists both his calling and God's mercy toward the city. The narrative exposes Jonah's heart as well as Nineveh's sin. Jesus later uses Jonah's experience as a sign of His own death and resurrection.
books.introText: The Lord sends Jonah to Nineveh, and the prophet resists both his calling and God's mercy toward the city. The narrative exposes Jonah's heart as well as Nineveh's sin. Jesus later uses Jonah's experience as a sign of His own death and resurrection.

helps.text: Jonah was a real prophet from the time of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14.25). The book records his real mission.
helps.html: Jonah was a real prophet from the time of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14.25). The book records his real mission.

helps.text: Jesus treats Jonah as historical (Matthew 12.40, Luke 11.29 to 32). The fish, the three days, and Jonah’s preaching are all referenced as real.
helps.html: Jesus treats Jonah as historical (Matthew 12.40, Luke 11.29 to 32). The fish, the three days, and Jonah’s preaching are all referenced as real.

helps.text: Jonah’s flight from God (chapter 1) is the heart of the human heart. He runs from his calling to a Gentile city.
helps.html: Jonah’s flight from God (chapter 1) is the heart of the human heart. He runs from his calling to a Gentile city.

helps.text: The pagan sailors fear God before Jonah does (chapter 1). The contrast is intentional.
helps.html: The pagan sailors fear God before Jonah does (chapter 1). The contrast is intentional.

helps.text: The Hebrew and Greek terms for the creature don't settle its modern zoological classification. The point is the Lord's real preservation of Jonah and the sign Jesus draws from it in Matthew 12.40.
helps.html: The Hebrew and Greek terms for the creature don't settle its modern zoological classification. The point is the Lord's real preservation of Jonah and the sign Jesus draws from it in Matthew 12.40.

helps.text: Jonah's prayer in chapter 2 expresses thanksgiving for deliverance. Chapter 4 later exposes his continued resistance to mercy for Nineveh. Don't assume one faithful prayer means every sinful attitude has been conquered.
helps.html: Jonah's prayer in chapter 2 expresses thanksgiving for deliverance. Chapter 4 later exposes his continued resistance to mercy for Nineveh. Don't assume one faithful prayer means every sinful attitude has been conquered.

helps.text: The preaching at Nineveh (chapter 3) is brief. "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" (3.4). The repentance is great. Even the king repents.
helps.html: The preaching at Nineveh (chapter 3) is brief. "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" (3.4). The repentance is great. Even the king repents.

helps.text: Jonah’s anger at God’s mercy (chapter 4) is the climax of the book. He is more concerned about the plant than about the city of 120,000 people.
helps.html: Jonah’s anger at God’s mercy (chapter 4) is the climax of the book. He is more concerned about the plant than about the city of 120,000 people.

helps.text: The book ends with a question from God. There's no record of Jonah’s answer. The reader is meant to face the question himself.
helps.html: The book ends with a question from God. There's no record of Jonah’s answer. The reader is meant to face the question himself.

studies.title: A threatened judgment can serve God’s purpose of mercy
studies.html: Nineveh responds to the warning, and the Lord withholds the announced destruction. Jeremiah 18.7 to 10 explains the relation between such warnings and repentance. God’s relenting doesn’t mean He learned an unknown fact or lost control of His plan. The warning itself is a means by which He brings the people to the response He receives.
studies.distinction: An unchanging purpose is compatible with genuinely different dealings toward the unrepentant and the repentant.
studies.question: How does Jeremiah 18 explain why an announcement of judgment mustn’t always be treated as an unconditional prediction?

studies.title: The historical sign points beyond the prophet’s character
studies.html: Jesus connects Jonah’s three days with His own burial and resurrection in Matthew 12.40. The correspondence doesn’t make Jonah morally equivalent to Christ. The greater One willingly fulfills His mission, while Jonah repeatedly resists his. A type or sign can concern a particular event without making all features of the earlier person’s life messianic.
studies.distinction: A divinely identified correspondence has a scope. It isn’t a declaration that every feature corresponds.
studies.question: Which part of Jonah’s experience does Jesus identify, and what contrast remains between the two servants?

books.name: Micah
books.intro: Micah confronts injustice and false worship in Israel and Judah. Judgment alternates with promises of restoration under the ruler from Bethlehem. The book closes by celebrating God's covenant mercy toward sinners.
books.introText: Micah confronts injustice and false worship in Israel and Judah. Judgment alternates with promises of restoration under the ruler from Bethlehem. The book closes by celebrating God's covenant mercy toward sinners.

helps.text: Micah ministered roughly from 740 to 700 BC, overlapping with Isaiah.
helps.html: Micah ministered roughly from 740 to 700 BC, overlapping with Isaiah.

helps.text: The book alternates between oracles of judgment and oracles of hope. The pattern is intentional.
helps.html: The book alternates between oracles of judgment and oracles of hope. The pattern is intentional.

helps.text: The judgment is for social injustice (oppressing the poor, false weights), false prophecy, and idolatry.
helps.html: The judgment is for social injustice (oppressing the poor, false weights), false prophecy, and idolatry.

helps.text: The promise of the ruler from Bethlehem (5.2) is quoted by the chief priests in Matthew 2.6 as fulfilled in Christ. The eternal pre-existence of the Messiah is implied.
helps.html: The promise of the ruler from Bethlehem (5.2) is quoted by the chief priests in Matthew 2.6 as fulfilled in Christ. The eternal pre-existence of the Messiah is implied.

helps.text: Micah 4.1 to 5 is closely parallel to Isaiah 2.2 to 5. Both prophets see nations flowing to Zion in the latter days.
helps.html: Micah 4.1 to 5 is closely parallel to Isaiah 2.2 to 5. Both prophets see nations flowing to Zion in the latter days.

helps.text: Micah 6.8 is one of the most famous summaries of covenant life. Do justice. Love kindness. Walk humbly with your God.
helps.html: Micah 6.8 is one of the most famous summaries of covenant life. Do justice. Love kindness. Walk humbly with your God.

helps.text: The lawsuit of God against His people (chapter 6) calls the mountains and hills as witnesses. Israel is on trial for breach of covenant.
helps.html: The lawsuit of God against His people (chapter 6) calls the mountains and hills as witnesses. Israel is on trial for breach of covenant.

helps.text: The book ends with one of the great expressions of divine forgiveness (7.18 to 19). "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." (KJV).
helps.html: The book ends with one of the great expressions of divine forgiveness (7.18 to 19). "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." (KJV).

helps.text: The shepherd-king imagery runs through the book. The bad shepherds will be judged. The good Shepherd will gather His people.
helps.html: The shepherd-king imagery runs through the book. The bad shepherds will be judged. The good Shepherd will gather His people.

studies.title: Covenant duty is not a substitute gospel
studies.html: The passage asks what the Lord requires after confronting His people’s unfaithfulness. Justice, mercy, and humble walking reject the attempt to substitute impressive offerings for genuine obedience. These duties cannot be used as a new scheme of justification by moral achievement. Read them alongside Scripture’s account of the pardon and renewal sinners need in order to walk with God.
studies.distinction: A summary of righteous conduct doesn’t explain how a guilty person earns a righteous verdict.
studies.question: What escalating offerings are rejected before the Lord’s required conduct is stated?

studies.title: The ruler from Bethlehem is the promised Shepherd
studies.html: Matthew 2 identifies Bethlehem as the birthplace of the promised ruler. Micah’s description joins humble origins, ancient goings forth, and shepherding strength. The New Testament’s clear confession of the Son’s eternity governs our reading of His person. The promise concerns the one Messiah rather than every leader who comes from a small place.
studies.distinction: An application about humble service mustn’t displace the passage’s particular messianic reference.
studies.question: Which elements of Micah’s promise explain the chief priests' answer in Matthew 2.4 to 6?

books.name: Nahum
books.intro: Nahum announces Nineveh's fall and the end of Assyrian oppression. Its forceful poetry declares that the Lord will judge cruelty. The same divine justice that terrifies His enemies comforts those who take refuge in Him.
books.introText: Nahum announces Nineveh's fall and the end of Assyrian oppression. Its forceful poetry declares that the Lord will judge cruelty. The same divine justice that terrifies His enemies comforts those who take refuge in Him.

helps.text: Nahum’s date is between the fall of Thebes (663 BC), which he mentions, and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC), which he prophesies.
helps.html: Nahum’s date is between the fall of Thebes (663 BC), which he mentions, and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC), which he prophesies.

helps.text: Nineveh repented under Jonah’s preaching but later returned to its violence. Nahum announces the end of God’s patience.
helps.html: Nineveh repented under Jonah’s preaching but later returned to its violence. Nahum announces the end of God’s patience.

helps.text: The book opens (chapter 1) with a description of God as both jealous and slow to anger. Both are true. He had been slow with Nineveh for a long time.
helps.html: The book opens (chapter 1) with a description of God as both jealous and slow to anger. Both are true. He had been slow with Nineveh for a long time.

helps.text: The vivid descriptions of the siege (chapter 2 to 3) show actual battle scenes that came to pass.
helps.html: The vivid descriptions of the siege (chapter 2 to 3) show actual battle scenes that came to pass.

helps.text: The fall of Nineveh in 612 BC fulfilled the prophecy. The city was buried for centuries before being rediscovered in modern times.
helps.html: The fall of Nineveh in 612 BC fulfilled the prophecy. The city was buried for centuries before being rediscovered in modern times.

helps.text: Nahum 1.7 sits in the middle of judgment passages. The same God who judges is the refuge of those who trust Him.
helps.html: Nahum 1.7 sits in the middle of judgment passages. The same God who judges is the refuge of those who trust Him.

helps.text: The book teaches that God’s patience has limits. A century after Jonah, Nineveh is judged.
helps.html: The book teaches that God’s patience has limits. A century after Jonah, Nineveh is judged.

helps.text: The book also teaches that great empires aren't eternal. Assyria was the dominant power of its day. It fell.
helps.html: The book also teaches that great empires aren't eternal. Assyria was the dominant power of its day. It fell.

helps.text: Nahum’s name means "comfort." The fall of Assyria was comfort to the people Assyria had oppressed for generations.
helps.html: Nahum’s name means "comfort." The fall of Assyria was comfort to the people Assyria had oppressed for generations.

studies.title: Patience does not mean the absence of judgment
studies.html: Nahum describes the Lord as slow to anger and also as One who will not acquit wickedness. These are joined assertions about the same holy God. His earlier mercy to Nineveh in Jonah doesn’t obligate Him to approve later cruelty. Read the history of Assyrian oppression with the oracle’s declaration of justice.
studies.distinction: Divine patience gives space for repentance. It doesn’t transform persistent evil into innocence.
studies.question: How does the opening distinguish the Lord’s patience, power, and care for those who trust Him?

studies.title: God’s vengeance does not authorize private revenge
studies.html: The prophet indicts a bloody city for actual violence and deceit. The oracle belongs to God’s judicial word against an oppressive power. A Christian receives its comfort while remaining bound by the command against private vengeance. The church proclaims judgment and prays for deliverance, but doesn’t take every divine judicial prerogative into its own hands.
studies.distinction: A righteous sentence from God isn’t a personal commission for any reader to execute it.
studies.question: Compare Nahum’s oracle with Romans 12.19. Who possesses the right of vengeance, and what response is commanded of believers?

books.name: Habakkuk
books.intro: Habakkuk asks why God tolerates violence and then questions His use of Babylon as an instrument of judgment. The Lord answers, and the prophet learns to wait in faith. The final prayer expresses trust even when earthly supports fail.
books.introText: Habakkuk asks why God tolerates violence and then questions His use of Babylon as an instrument of judgment. The Lord answers, and the prophet learns to wait in faith. The final prayer expresses trust even when earthly supports fail.

helps.text: Habakkuk likely ministered around 605 to 600 BC, just before the Babylonian invasion.
helps.html: Habakkuk likely ministered around 605 to 600 BC, just before the Babylonian invasion.

helps.text: His first complaint (1.2 to 4) is about violence and injustice in Judah. How long will God let evil flourish?
helps.html: His first complaint (1.2 to 4) is about violence and injustice in Judah. How long will God let evil flourish?

helps.text: The Lord’s answer (1.5 to 11) is shocking. He is raising up the Babylonians to judge Judah. Habakkuk didn't see that coming.
helps.html: The Lord’s answer (1.5 to 11) is shocking. He is raising up the Babylonians to judge Judah. Habakkuk didn't see that coming.

helps.text: His second complaint (1.12 to 2.1) is even harder. How can a holy God use such a wicked nation as His instrument?
helps.html: His second complaint (1.12 to 2.1) is even harder. How can a holy God use such a wicked nation as His instrument?

helps.text: The Lord’s answer (2.2 to 20) includes the great line, "the just shall live by his faith" Trust in God when His ways are beyond our seeing.
helps.html: The Lord’s answer (2.2 to 20) includes the great line, "the just shall live by his faith" Trust in God when His ways are beyond our seeing.

helps.text: The five woes (2.6 to 20) are pronounced against Babylon. Their day will come. God’s instruments aren't exempt from God’s judgment.
helps.html: The five woes (2.6 to 20) are pronounced against Babylon. Their day will come. God’s instruments aren't exempt from God’s judgment.

helps.text: The closing prayer (chapter 3) is a hymn. It recounts God’s mighty acts in history and ends with one of the great expressions of trust in Scripture.
helps.html: The closing prayer (chapter 3) is a hymn. It recounts God’s mighty acts in history and ends with one of the great expressions of trust in Scripture.

helps.text: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom" (3.17 to 18) is the high point of trust in the Old Testament. Worship God when the harvest fails.
helps.html: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom" (3.17 to 18) is the high point of trust in the Old Testament. Worship God when the harvest fails.

helps.text: Paul quotes "The just shall live by faith" in Romans 1.17, Galatians 3.11, and the writer of Hebrews uses it in Hebrews 10.38. The verse becomes foundational for the doctrine of justification by faith.
helps.html: Paul quotes "The just shall live by faith" in Romans 1.17, Galatians 3.11, and the writer of Hebrews uses it in Hebrews 10.38. The verse becomes foundational for the doctrine of justification by faith.

studies.title: Living by faith answers the proud heart
studies.html: The contrast is between the proud soul and the righteous person who lives by faith. Paul draws upon this sentence in Romans 1.16 to 17 and Galatians 3.11 when explaining righteousness through faith. The original setting calls for trust while judgment and deliverance unfold. The apostolic use discloses its saving significance without severing faith from patient reliance upon God’s word.
studies.distinction: Faith’s persevering character doesn’t make our constancy the righteousness that merits justification.
studies.question: How does Paul’s use of the verse clarify the ground of a sinner’s standing before God?

studies.title: Joy can survive the loss of ordinary provision
studies.html: The prophet names the failure of crops and herds, then resolves to rejoice in the God of his salvation. The confession doesn’t deny that these losses are severe. It locates hope beyond the continuation of material support. This is trust exercised under threat, not a promise that correct faith will prevent economic deprivation.
studies.distinction: Spiritual joy doesn’t require calling loss pleasant or predicting immediate recovery.
studies.question: What circumstances are allowed to remain in the prophet’s confession, and what remains his reason for hope?

books.name: Zephaniah
books.intro: The day of the Lord brings judgment upon Judah and the nations. Zephaniah confronts complacency and calls the humble to seek the Lord. The prophecy ends with a purified people rejoicing in God's presence.
books.introText: The day of the Lord brings judgment upon Judah and the nations. Zephaniah confronts complacency and calls the humble to seek the Lord. The prophecy ends with a purified people rejoicing in God's presence.

helps.text: Zephaniah likely ministered in the early days of Josiah’s reign, before the great reform of 622 BC.
helps.html: Zephaniah likely ministered in the early days of Josiah’s reign, before the great reform of 622 BC.

helps.text: The day of the LORD is the central theme. It opens the book like a hammer.
helps.html: The day of the LORD is the central theme. It opens the book like a hammer.

helps.text: The judgment falls on Judah for syncretism, complacency, and idolatry, then on the surrounding nations, then on Jerusalem again.
helps.html: The judgment falls on Judah for syncretism, complacency, and idolatry, then on the surrounding nations, then on Jerusalem again.

helps.text: The remnant theme is strong. A humble and lowly people will be left who take refuge in the name of the LORD (3.12).
helps.html: The remnant theme is strong. A humble and lowly people will be left who take refuge in the name of the LORD (3.12).

helps.text: The book ends with one of the most stunning passages in the prophets (3.14 to 20). The LORD is in the midst of His people. He sings over them with joy.
helps.html: The book ends with one of the most stunning passages in the prophets (3.14 to 20). The LORD is in the midst of His people. He sings over them with joy.

helps.text: Zephaniah 3.17 ("he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing") is a verse worth memorizing.
helps.html: Zephaniah 3.17 ("he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing") is a verse worth memorizing.

helps.text: The seek-the-LORD passage (2.3) calls for righteousness and humility before the day of the LORD breaks.
helps.html: The seek-the-LORD passage (2.3) calls for righteousness and humility before the day of the LORD breaks.

helps.text: The book pulls together threads from earlier prophets and points forward to the gospel age and the consummation.
helps.html: The book pulls together threads from earlier prophets and points forward to the gospel age and the consummation.

helps.text: The day of the LORD is paired with the gathering of the nations to call upon the name of the LORD (3.9). The judgment serves the salvation.
helps.html: The day of the LORD is paired with the gathering of the nations to call upon the name of the LORD (3.9). The judgment serves the salvation.

studies.title: The day of the Lord overturns complacent religion
studies.html: Zephaniah addresses people who presume that the Lord will neither do good nor evil. Judgment answers that practical denial of His government. Their outward association with Judah doesn’t protect them from the covenant charge. Read the announced day first in the prophecy’s setting, then within the wider biblical certainty of final judgment.
studies.distinction: Covenant membership cannot be used to make God’s warnings irrelevant to a visibly religious community.
studies.question: What belief about the Lord’s action does Zephaniah 1.12 expose?

studies.title: God rejoices over a people He has purified
studies.html: The promised joy belongs within restoration that includes purified speech, humble refuge in the Lord, and the removal of deceit. God’s delight isn’t permission for His people to remain content in evil. Nor are their changed ways presented as a price that independently purchases His favor. Read the Lord’s gracious restoration and its moral result together.
studies.distinction: A comforting sentence must retain the identity and condition of the people described around it.
studies.question: What changes precede the declaration that the Lord rejoices over His people?

books.name: Haggai
books.intro: The returned exiles have neglected the temple while attending to their own homes. Haggai calls them to consider their ways and resume the work God appointed. Their small beginnings are set within His larger promise for His house and kingdom.
books.introText: The returned exiles have neglected the temple while attending to their own homes. Haggai calls them to consider their ways and resume the work God appointed. Their small beginnings are set within His larger promise for His house and kingdom.

helps.text: The setting is the post-exile community sixteen years after the return. The temple foundation has been laid but the work has stopped.
helps.html: The setting is the post-exile community sixteen years after the return. The temple foundation has been laid but the work has stopped.

helps.text: The first message (1.1 to 11) confronts the people for living in paneled houses while the temple lies in ruins.
helps.html: The first message (1.1 to 11) confronts the people for living in paneled houses while the temple lies in ruins.

helps.text: The Lord declares the cause of their economic frustration. They're seeking comfort while neglecting His house.
helps.html: The Lord declares the cause of their economic frustration. They're seeking comfort while neglecting His house.

helps.text: The work begins again in 1.12 to 15. The Lord stirs up the spirits of the leaders and the people.
helps.html: The work begins again in 1.12 to 15. The Lord stirs up the spirits of the leaders and the people.

helps.text: The second message (2.1 to 9) encourages those who remember the first temple. The glory of the latter house will be greater than the former. This is fulfilled when Christ Himself enters this temple.
helps.html: The second message (2.1 to 9) encourages those who remember the first temple. The glory of the latter house will be greater than the former. This is fulfilled when Christ Himself enters this temple.

helps.text: The third message (2.10 to 19) deals with holiness. Holiness isn't transferred by contact, but defilement is. The lesson is applied to their work.
helps.html: The third message (2.10 to 19) deals with holiness. Holiness isn't transferred by contact, but defilement is. The lesson is applied to their work.

helps.text: The fourth message (2.20 to 23) is to Zerubbabel personally. He is named as a signet ring, a chosen servant. The Davidic line is preserved through him.
helps.html: The fourth message (2.20 to 23) is to Zerubbabel personally. He is named as a signet ring, a chosen servant. The Davidic line is preserved through him.

helps.text: The book is intensely practical. It deals with houses, harvests, paneling, and storehouses. God’s prophets speak to ordinary life.
helps.html: The book is intensely practical. It deals with houses, harvests, paneling, and storehouses. God’s prophets speak to ordinary life.

helps.text: The temple Haggai helped build stood until Herod refurbished it. Christ entered it in His earthly ministry. It was destroyed in AD 70.
helps.html: The temple Haggai helped build stood until Herod refurbished it. Christ entered it in His earthly ministry. It was destroyed in AD 70.

studies.title: Providence can correct a disordered priority
studies.html: The Lord Himself interprets the people’s frustration as discipline connected with neglect of His house. We know the connection because His prophet declares it. The duty to attend to His appointed work is enduring, but this historical explanation doesn’t equip every teacher to diagnose poor harvests or low income as proof of a particular person’s disobedience.
studies.distinction: A revealed explanation of one community’s hardship is not a universal prosperity formula.
studies.question: What specific neglected duty does the prophet name, and where does he identify the connection with hardship?

studies.title: A small restored house belongs to a larger promise
studies.html: The visible smallness of the rebuilt temple discourages those who remember the former house. The Lord answers with His presence and His purpose for greater glory and peace. Hebrews 12.26 to 28 draws upon the shaking language as it directs believers to the unshakable kingdom. Follow that canonical connection rather than measuring fulfillment only by architecture or wealth.
studies.distinction: A prophetic promise of glory mustn’t be reduced to a guarantee that a present religious building will become impressive.
studies.question: How does Hebrews use the promised shaking to direct the church’s worship and confidence?

books.name: Zechariah
books.intro: Zechariah encourages the restored community through visions and promises concerning Jerusalem, priesthood, and kingship. The book reaches beyond the rebuilding of the temple to the coming Shepherd and King. Later Scripture helps explain its dense prophetic imagery.
books.introText: Zechariah encourages the restored community through visions and promises concerning Jerusalem, priesthood, and kingship. The book reaches beyond the rebuilding of the temple to the coming Shepherd and King. Later Scripture helps explain its dense prophetic imagery.

helps.text: Zechariah ministered in the post-exile community, encouraging the rebuilding of the temple. He was a contemporary of Haggai.
helps.html: Zechariah ministered in the post-exile community, encouraging the rebuilding of the temple. He was a contemporary of Haggai.

helps.text: The eight visions of chapters 1 to 6 are apocalyptic. Each has its meaning given in the chapter, often through the angel.
helps.html: The eight visions of chapters 1 to 6 are apocalyptic. Each has its meaning given in the chapter, often through the angel.

helps.text: The crowning of Joshua the priest (6.9 to 15) is striking. A priest is crowned as king. He is named as the Branch. This points to Christ as priest-king.
helps.html: The crowning of Joshua the priest (6.9 to 15) is striking. A priest is crowned as king. He is named as the Branch. This points to Christ as priest-king.

helps.text: The questions about fasting (chapters 7 to 8) move from external ritual to the heart of true worship. Justice, mercy, kindness.
helps.html: The questions about fasting (chapters 7 to 8) move from external ritual to the heart of true worship. Justice, mercy, kindness.

helps.text: Chapter 9.9 prophesies the king coming on a donkey. Matthew 21.5 quotes it as fulfilled at the triumphal entry.
helps.html: Chapter 9.9 prophesies the king coming on a donkey. Matthew 21.5 quotes it as fulfilled at the triumphal entry.

helps.text: Chapter 11.12 to 13 prophesies the thirty pieces of silver. Matthew 27.9 to 10 quotes it as fulfilled in Judas’s betrayal money.
helps.html: Chapter 11.12 to 13 prophesies the thirty pieces of silver. Matthew 27.9 to 10 quotes it as fulfilled in Judas’s betrayal money.

helps.text: Chapter 12.10 prophesies the pierced one whom they will mourn. John 19.37 quotes it as fulfilled at the cross. Revelation 1.7 picks it up for the second coming.
helps.html: Chapter 12.10 prophesies the pierced one whom they will mourn. John 19.37 quotes it as fulfilled at the cross. Revelation 1.7 picks it up for the second coming.

helps.text: Chapter 13.7 prophesies the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered. Christ quotes it of Himself in Matthew 26.31.
helps.html: Chapter 13.7 prophesies the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered. Christ quotes it of Himself in Matthew 26.31.

helps.text: Read Zechariah 14 in the prophetic setting of the Lord's kingship, His deliverance of Jerusalem, and the nations' worship. This guide understands its imagery through Christ's victory and the final holiness of His people. Its amillennial reading doesn't require the restoration of the ceremonial feasts after Christ has fulfilled them. Compare John 4:21-24 and Hebrews 10:1-18. WCF 33 confesses the final judgment, but doesn't settle every image or a particular millennial scheme.
helps.html: Read Zechariah 14 in the prophetic setting of the Lord's kingship, His deliverance of Jerusalem, and the nations' worship. This guide understands its imagery through Christ's victory and the final holiness of His people. Its amillennial reading doesn't require the restoration of the ceremonial feasts after Christ has fulfilled them. Compare John 4:21-24 and Hebrews 10:1-18. WCF 33 confesses the final judgment, but doesn't settle every image or a particular millennial scheme.

studies.title: Cleansing comes before the charge to serve
studies.html: Joshua stands in filthy garments while Satan accuses him. The Lord rebukes the accuser and commands a change of clothing as a sign of removed iniquity. The vision joins gracious cleansing with a charge to faithful service and the promise of the Branch. Don’t make Joshua’s obedience the cause of the pardon the vision first displays.
studies.distinction: A command following forgiveness states the pardoned person’s duty, not the merit by which pardon was secured.
studies.question: What is done for Joshua before the instruction concerning his walk is given?

studies.title: The pierced Shepherd and the fountain for sin
studies.html: The promise of mourning over the pierced one is followed in chapter 13 by cleansing and the striking of the shepherd. John 19.37 and Matthew 26.31 identify Christ’s suffering within these prophecies. The connection rests upon inspired interpretation. Read the surrounding promise of grace rather than turning the images into detached clues for a modern prediction scheme.
studies.distinction: Prophetic imagery finds its governing reference in Christ’s identified work before any proposed contemporary resemblance.
studies.question: How do the Gospel citations connect piercing and the scattered sheep to Jesus' passion?

books.name: Malachi
books.intro: The Lord confronts the restored community's corrupt worship and covenant unfaithfulness. The people's questions expose their resistance to His charges. The closing promise prepares for a messenger who will announce the Lord's coming.
books.introText: The Lord confronts the restored community's corrupt worship and covenant unfaithfulness. The people's questions expose their resistance to His charges. The closing promise prepares for a messenger who will announce the Lord's coming.

helps.text: Malachi likely ministered in the mid-fifth century BC, perhaps a contemporary of Nehemiah or shortly after.
helps.html: Malachi likely ministered in the mid-fifth century BC, perhaps a contemporary of Nehemiah or shortly after.

helps.text: The disputes structure the book. Each begins with a divine accusation, the people’s objection ("how have we...?"), and the Lord’s specific answer.
helps.html: The disputes structure the book. Each begins with a divine accusation, the people’s objection ("how have we...?"), and the Lord’s specific answer.

helps.text: The first dispute is over God’s love (1.2 to 5). The people doubt it. The Lord points to His electing love for Jacob over Esau.
helps.html: The first dispute is over God’s love (1.2 to 5). The people doubt it. The Lord points to His electing love for Jacob over Esau.

helps.text: The priests are rebuked for offering polluted sacrifices (1.6 to 2.9). They're bored with worship.
helps.html: The priests are rebuked for offering polluted sacrifices (1.6 to 2.9). They're bored with worship.

helps.text: The men are rebuked for divorcing their wives (2.10 to 16). "For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away" (2.16).
helps.html: The men are rebuked for divorcing their wives (2.10 to 16). "For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away" (2.16).

helps.text: The people are rebuked for robbing God in tithes and offerings (3.8 to 12). The exhortation to test the Lord in giving is given here.
helps.html: The people are rebuked for robbing God in tithes and offerings (3.8 to 12). The exhortation to test the Lord in giving is given here.

helps.text: The promise of the messenger to prepare the way (3.1) is fulfilled in John the Baptist (Mark 1.2).
helps.html: The promise of the messenger to prepare the way (3.1) is fulfilled in John the Baptist (Mark 1.2).

helps.text: The promise of Elijah (4.5) is fulfilled in John the Baptist as Christ identifies him in Matthew 11.14 and 17.10 to 13.
helps.html: The promise of Elijah (4.5) is fulfilled in John the Baptist as Christ identifies him in Matthew 11.14 and 17.10 to 13.

helps.text: Malachi 3.16 is the bright note. Those who fear the LORD speak with one another. A book of remembrance is kept before Him.
helps.html: Malachi 3.16 is the bright note. Those who fear the LORD speak with one another. A book of remembrance is kept before Him.

helps.text: The Old Testament closes with the threat of curse (4.6) and the promise of Elijah. The next voice in Scripture is John the Baptist crying in the wilderness.
helps.html: The Old Testament closes with the threat of curse (4.6) and the promise of Elijah. The next voice in Scripture is John the Baptist crying in the wilderness.

studies.title: The covenant Lord exposes contemptuous worship
studies.html: The priests bring defective offerings while questioning the charge against them. The Lord measures their conduct against the honor due His name. Their contempt isn’t corrected merely by retaining sacrificial activity. It calls for the faithful worship He has appointed. Under the new covenant, Christ fulfills the sacrifices, but approaching God carelessly remains incompatible with reverent service.
studies.distinction: A change in covenant administration doesn’t make the Lord’s holiness or the duty of reverence obsolete.
studies.question: How do the offered animals reveal an attitude the priests refuse to acknowledge?

studies.title: The coming messenger is identified by later revelation
studies.html: The prophecy closes with Moses' law and the coming of Elijah before the Lord’s day. Luke 1.16 to 17 explains John’s ministry in Elijah’s spirit and power. Jesus also relates the promise to John in Matthew 11.14. The fulfillment doesn’t require John to be Elijah reincarnated. Its sense is established by the inspired explanation of his calling.
studies.distinction: A prophetic personal identification must be read through the nature of the correspondence Scripture itself supplies.
studies.question: What features of John’s ministry does Luke connect with the promised work of Elijah?

books.name: Matthew
books.intro: Matthew presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, fulfilling Israel's Scriptures. His narrative is arranged around substantial blocks of teaching. Follow both the fulfillment quotations and the growing conflict that leads to the cross.
books.introText: Matthew presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, fulfilling Israel's Scriptures. His narrative is arranged around substantial blocks of teaching. Follow both the fulfillment quotations and the growing conflict that leads to the cross.

helps.text: The genealogy (chapter 1) is structured around Abraham, David, and the exile. It establishes Jesus as the legal heir of David.
helps.html: The genealogy (chapter 1) is structured around Abraham, David, and the exile. It establishes Jesus as the legal heir of David.

helps.text: The infancy narratives (chapters 1 to 2) emphasize Old Testament fulfillment. Five fulfillment quotations in the first two chapters.
helps.html: The infancy narratives (chapters 1 to 2) emphasize Old Testament fulfillment. Five fulfillment quotations in the first two chapters.

helps.text: The five discourses are the Sermon on the Mount (5 to 7), the missionary discourse (10), the parables of the kingdom (13), the church discourse (18), and the Olivet discourse (24 to 25).
helps.html: The five discourses are the Sermon on the Mount (5 to 7), the missionary discourse (10), the parables of the kingdom (13), the church discourse (18), and the Olivet discourse (24 to 25).

helps.text: The Sermon on the Mount describes the character and conduct of the citizens of the kingdom. It isn't a soteriology but an ethic for the redeemed.
helps.html: The Sermon on the Mount describes the character and conduct of the citizens of the kingdom. It isn't a soteriology but an ethic for the redeemed.

helps.text: The kingdom of heaven is Matthew’s preferred phrase. It's the same as the kingdom of God in the other gospels but adapted to Jewish reverence for the divine name.
helps.html: The kingdom of heaven is Matthew’s preferred phrase. It's the same as the kingdom of God in the other gospels but adapted to Jewish reverence for the divine name.

helps.text: The parables of chapter 13 teach the nature of the kingdom in this age. Mixed growth. Hidden treasure. Wheat and tares. Mustard seed and leaven. Read them as a unit.
helps.html: The parables of chapter 13 teach the nature of the kingdom in this age. Mixed growth. Hidden treasure. Wheat and tares. Mustard seed and leaven. Read them as a unit.

helps.text: The church discourse (chapter 18) gives Christ’s pattern for restoring an erring brother. Go privately. Take one or two. Tell it to the church. This is the foundational text on church discipline, ordained by Christ Himself.
helps.html: The church discourse (chapter 18) gives Christ’s pattern for restoring an erring brother. Go privately. Take one or two. Tell it to the church. This is the foundational text on church discipline, ordained by Christ Himself.

helps.text: The Last Supper (chapter 26) is Christ’s institution of the Lord’s Supper. The bread is His body. The cup is the new covenant in His blood. The supper is now the meal of the church, given by Christ to feed His people on Himself by faith until He comes.
helps.html: The Last Supper (chapter 26) is Christ’s institution of the Lord’s Supper. The bread is His body. The cup is the new covenant in His blood. The supper is now the meal of the church, given by Christ to feed His people on Himself by faith until He comes.

helps.text: The Great Commission (28.18 to 20) closes the book. Christ has all authority. The disciples are to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Baptism here, and the Lord’s Supper instituted in chapter 26, are the two sacraments given by Christ to His church.
helps.html: The Great Commission (28.18 to 20) closes the book. Christ has all authority. The disciples are to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Baptism here, and the Lord’s Supper instituted in chapter 26, are the two sacraments given by Christ to His church.

helps.text: Matthew presents Jesus as the new Moses. The mountain. The five discourses. The deliverance.
helps.html: Matthew presents Jesus as the new Moses. The mountain. The five discourses. The deliverance.

helps.text: He also presents Him as the new Israel. Out of Egypt called. Tested in the wilderness. Faithful where Israel failed.
helps.html: He also presents Him as the new Israel. Out of Egypt called. Tested in the wilderness. Faithful where Israel failed.

studies.title: Fulfillment preserves the law’s truth and distinguishes its forms
studies.html: Jesus denies that He came to destroy the law or the prophets. Their fulfillment in Him includes the accomplishment of promises and the completion of the ceremonial shadows. It doesn’t follow that every Mosaic ordinance remains unchanged, or that the moral law becomes disposable. Read the statement alongside Hebrews' account of fulfilled sacrifice and Christ’s own authoritative teaching about righteousness.
studies.distinction: Fulfillment isn’t either wholesale abolition or the unchanged continuation of every covenant ordinance.
studies.question: How would a reading of Matthew 5 that requires continuing animal sacrifice conflict with Hebrews 10?

studies.title: A discourse about judgment needs its own time markers
studies.html: Jesus speaks after the prediction concerning the temple, and the disciples ask about what is coming. The discourse includes warnings with historical reference and teaching about His coming. Reformed interpreters differ over the precise relation of its horizons. Read the questions, audience instructions, and later comparisons before deciding that every sentence refers only to AD 70 or only to a distant future.
studies.distinction: A difficult timetable mustn’t be settled by ignoring either the temple setting or the wider canonical teaching of Christ’s return.
studies.question: Which question prompts the discourse, and which instructions require attention to the first hearers' circumstances?

books.name: Mark
books.intro: Mark follows Jesus' ministry with a brisk narrative and particular attention to His authority and suffering. The disciples struggle to understand what His messiahship requires. The road to Jerusalem teaches them that His kingdom comes through the cross.
books.introText: Mark follows Jesus' ministry with a brisk narrative and particular attention to His authority and suffering. The disciples struggle to understand what His messiahship requires. The road to Jerusalem teaches them that His kingdom comes through the cross.

helps.text: Mark is the shortest gospel. Tradition says it reflects Peter’s preaching, with John Mark as the writer.
helps.html: Mark is the shortest gospel. Tradition says it reflects Peter’s preaching, with John Mark as the writer.

helps.text: The book opens with no genealogy. It launches into John the Baptist and Jesus’ baptism. The pace is set.
helps.html: The book opens with no genealogy. It launches into John the Baptist and Jesus’ baptism. The pace is set.

helps.text: The first half (1 to 8) shows the authority of Jesus. Authority over disease, demons, nature, sin, the Sabbath.
helps.html: The first half (1 to 8) shows the authority of Jesus. Authority over disease, demons, nature, sin, the Sabbath.

helps.text: The hinge is Peter’s confession (8.27 to 30). "Thou art the Christ." Immediately Jesus begins to teach the cross (8.31).
helps.html: The hinge is Peter’s confession (8.27 to 30). "Thou art the Christ." Immediately Jesus begins to teach the cross (8.31).

helps.text: The second half (Mark 8:31 to 16:20) is the journey to Jerusalem and the passion. Three predictions of the cross structure the journey.
helps.html: The second half (Mark 8:31 to 16:20) is the journey to Jerusalem and the passion. Three predictions of the cross structure the journey.

helps.text: The disciples are slow to understand. Their failure is honestly reported. This is comforting to every reader who feels slow.
helps.html: The disciples are slow to understand. Their failure is honestly reported. This is comforting to every reader who feels slow.

helps.text: The Olivet discourse (chapter 13) is briefer than Matthew’s version but covers the same ground.
helps.html: The Olivet discourse (chapter 13) is briefer than Matthew’s version but covers the same ground.

helps.text: The passion narrative (chapters 14 to 15) is told without sentimentality. The horror of the cross is preserved.
helps.html: The passion narrative (chapters 14 to 15) is told without sentimentality. The horror of the cross is preserved.

helps.text: The empty tomb (chapter 16) is described. The women find Him risen.
helps.html: The empty tomb (chapter 16) is described. The women find Him risen.

helps.text: The longer ending of Mark (16.9 to 20) is a real textual question among Reformed scholars. The two earliest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) end at 16.8. The vast majority of Greek manuscripts include the longer ending. The Westminster divines received the longer ending as Scripture, and the historic Reformed and confessional bibliology streams hold it as canonical. Modern textual criticism doubts it. Both views exist within the Reformed tradition. The doctrines taught in 16.9 to 20 are taught elsewhere in the canon, so the gospel doesn't stand or fall on this text.
helps.html: The longer ending of Mark (16.9 to 20) is a real textual question among Reformed scholars. The two earliest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) end at 16.8. The vast majority of Greek manuscripts include the longer ending. The Westminster divines received the longer ending as Scripture, and the historic Reformed and confessional bibliology streams hold it as canonical. Modern textual criticism doubts it. Both views exist within the Reformed tradition. The doctrines taught in 16.9 to 20 are taught elsewhere in the canon, so the gospel doesn't stand or fall on this text.

studies.title: A ransom is more than an example of courage
studies.html: Jesus answers a dispute about greatness by describing His service and the giving of His life as a ransom for many. His death supplies the pattern for humble service because it first accomplishes a redemption His disciples cannot perform. The ethical application depends upon His saving work rather than replacing it. Read the call to imitate Him without reducing the cross to a demonstration of selflessness.
studies.distinction: Christ is both our example and our Redeemer, but our imitation doesn’t accomplish the ransom He gives.
studies.question: How does the final verse establish a unique saving act while answering the disciples' desire for prominence?

studies.title: The cross defines the Messiah’s mission
studies.html: Peter confesses Christ and then resists the announcement of His suffering. Jesus rebukes that resistance before calling the disciples to take up the cross. The account distinguishes the saving necessity of His death from the self-denial required of His followers. A correct title for Jesus must be joined to receiving the mission He declares.
studies.distinction: The disciple’s cross isn’t a second atoning sacrifice, and messianic glory cannot be separated from the Savior’s suffering.
studies.question: What does Peter affirm correctly, and what announced necessity does he then oppose?

books.name: Luke
books.intro: Luke gives an orderly account of Jesus' life and ministry, continuing the story in Acts. He draws attention to God's mercy toward the poor and the outcast. Jesus' journey to Jerusalem leads to His death, resurrection, and commission to the nations.
books.introText: Luke gives an orderly account of Jesus' life and ministry, continuing the story in Acts. He draws attention to God's mercy toward the poor and the outcast. Jesus' journey to Jerusalem leads to His death, resurrection, and commission to the nations.

helps.text: Luke addresses Theophilus (1.3) as the named recipient. He writes carefully and chronologically.
helps.html: Luke addresses Theophilus (1.3) as the named recipient. He writes carefully and chronologically.

helps.text: The infancy narratives (chapters 1 to 2) are unique to Luke. They include the songs of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon.
helps.html: The infancy narratives (chapters 1 to 2) are unique to Luke. They include the songs of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon.

helps.text: The genealogy (3.23 to 38) runs from Jesus back to Adam, emphasizing His connection to all humanity.
helps.html: The genealogy (3.23 to 38) runs from Jesus back to Adam, emphasizing His connection to all humanity.

helps.text: The early ministry (chapters 4 to 9) opens with the Nazareth sermon (chapter 4) where Jesus identifies Himself with Isaiah 61.
helps.html: The early ministry (chapters 4 to 9) opens with the Nazareth sermon (chapter 4) where Jesus identifies Himself with Isaiah 61.

helps.text: The travel narrative (9.51 to 19.27) is the long journey toward Jerusalem. Many parables are placed here.
helps.html: The travel narrative (9.51 to 19.27) is the long journey toward Jerusalem. Many parables are placed here.

helps.text: Unique parables in Luke include the good Samaritan (10), the prodigal son (15), the rich man and Lazarus (16), and the Pharisee and the tax collector (18).
helps.html: Unique parables in Luke include the good Samaritan (10), the prodigal son (15), the rich man and Lazarus (16), and the Pharisee and the tax collector (18).

helps.text: Luke pays special attention to women. Mary, Elizabeth, Anna, the widow of Nain, the sinful woman, Mary and Martha, the women who supported Jesus, the women at the cross.
helps.html: Luke pays special attention to women. Mary, Elizabeth, Anna, the widow of Nain, the sinful woman, Mary and Martha, the women who supported Jesus, the women at the cross.

helps.text: Luke also pays attention to the poor and the outsider. The shepherds. The tax collectors. The Samaritans. The Gentile soldier whose servant was healed.
helps.html: Luke also pays attention to the poor and the outsider. The shepherds. The tax collectors. The Samaritans. The Gentile soldier whose servant was healed.

helps.text: The road to Emmaus account (24.13 to 35) is unique to Luke. Christ opens the Old Testament to two disciples and shows it's all about Him.
helps.html: The road to Emmaus account (24.13 to 35) is unique to Luke. Christ opens the Old Testament to two disciples and shows it's all about Him.

helps.text: The Great Commission in Luke is paired with the promise of the Spirit (24.49). This sets up the book of Acts.
helps.html: The Great Commission in Luke is paired with the promise of the Spirit (24.49). This sets up the book of Acts.

studies.title: The justified man brings no merit to his plea
studies.html: Luke identifies the audience as people who trust in their own righteousness and despise others. The Pharisee’s prayer inventories his achievements. The publican appeals for mercy. Jesus declares the latter justified. The parable doesn’t commend ignorance or indifference to conduct. It exposes the attempt to present religious performance as the reason God should accept a sinner.
studies.distinction: Humility is the posture of receiving mercy, not a new meritorious achievement that earns justification.
studies.question: How does Luke’s opening description determine the issue the parable resolves?

studies.title: The risen Christ corrects a merely spiritual explanation
studies.html: The disciples' fear leads them to suppose they see a spirit. Jesus directs attention to His hands and feet, invites touch, and eats before them. Those details are interpretive evidence within the narrative. A claim that resurrection means only the survival of His influence contradicts the account’s own distinction. His body is glorified, but the One who stands before them is the crucified Jesus truly raised.
studies.distinction: A glorified body is not the absence of a body.
studies.question: Which narrated actions specifically answer the disciples' mistaken explanation?

books.name: John
books.intro: John selects signs and extended teaching to show that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. His stated purpose is that readers believe and have life in His name. The opening account of the eternal Word governs the whole Gospel.
books.introText: John selects signs and extended teaching to show that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. His stated purpose is that readers believe and have life in His name. The opening account of the eternal Word governs the whole Gospel.

helps.text: A common outline identifies seven major signs before the passion. This is a useful arrangement, not John's claim that Jesus performed only seven miracles. Read John 20.30 to 31 and the further sign in chapter 21.
helps.html: A common outline identifies seven major signs before the passion. This is a useful arrangement, not John's claim that Jesus performed only seven miracles. Read John 20.30 to 31 and the further sign in chapter 21.

helps.text: The seven "I am" sayings (bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way truth and life, true vine) reveal His deity and mission.
helps.html: The seven "I am" sayings (bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way truth and life, true vine) reveal His deity and mission.

helps.text: The "I am" without predicate (8.58, 13.19, 18.5 to 6) takes up the divine name from Exodus 3.14. Jesus is YHWH.
helps.html: The "I am" without predicate (8.58, 13.19, 18.5 to 6) takes up the divine name from Exodus 3.14. Jesus is YHWH.

helps.text: The discourses are longer than in the synoptics. Nicodemus (chapter 3). The Samaritan woman (chapter 4). The bread of life (chapter 6). The good shepherd (chapter 10). The Upper Room (chapters 13 to 17).
helps.html: The discourses are longer than in the synoptics. Nicodemus (chapter 3). The Samaritan woman (chapter 4). The bread of life (chapter 6). The good shepherd (chapter 10). The Upper Room (chapters 13 to 17).

helps.text: The High Priestly Prayer (chapter 17) is one of the most precious passages in the Bible. Read it slowly.
helps.html: The High Priestly Prayer (chapter 17) is one of the most precious passages in the Bible. Read it slowly.

helps.text: The cross is presented as the lifting up and the glory. John uses the language of glorification for the crucifixion. The cross is the throne.
helps.html: The cross is presented as the lifting up and the glory. John uses the language of glorification for the crucifixion. The cross is the throne.

helps.text: The resurrection accounts (chapter 20 to 21) are intimate. Mary in the garden. Thomas’s doubt and confession.
helps.html: The resurrection accounts (chapter 20 to 21) are intimate. Mary in the garden. Thomas’s doubt and confession.

helps.text: Chapter 21 is an epilogue. The restoration of Peter is one of the great pastoral scenes in Scripture.
helps.html: Chapter 21 is an epilogue. The restoration of Peter is one of the great pastoral scenes in Scripture.

studies.title: The Word is God and is with God
studies.html: John asserts the Word’s deity and His personal relation to God before declaring that the Word became flesh. The passage doesn’t identify the Father and Son as one Person, nor describe the Son as a creature promoted to divine rank. Everything made is made through Him. His incarnation adds a true human nature without removing His eternal deity.
studies.distinction: Personal distinction doesn’t imply a lesser divine being, and incarnation doesn’t imply a change of deity into flesh.
studies.question: How do verses 1 to 3 and 14 together guard the identity of the incarnate Son?

studies.title: Coming to Christ is commanded and graciously secured
studies.html: Jesus calls hearers to believe while explaining that those given by the Father will come and that no one can come unless drawn by Him. The promise to raise the drawn person anchors the passage in effective grace, not merely the possibility of a better choice. Human unbelief remains culpable. Divine enabling supplies the explanation of faith without removing the duty to believe.
studies.distinction: A command to come doesn’t prove independent saving ability, and election doesn’t remove the gospel warrant to come.
studies.question: Trace the relation between being given, coming, being received, and being raised in these verses.

books.name: Acts
books.intro: Luke traces the risen Christ's work through the Spirit and the apostles. The witness moves from Jerusalem toward the nations, as Jesus promised. Read its events as the foundational history of the church while distinguishing apostolic signs from commands for every congregation.
books.introText: Luke traces the risen Christ's work through the Spirit and the apostles. The witness moves from Jerusalem toward the nations, as Jesus promised. Read its events as the foundational history of the church while distinguishing apostolic signs from commands for every congregation.

helps.text: Acts continues from Luke. The same author. The ascension of Christ closes Luke and opens Acts.
helps.html: Acts continues from Luke. The same author. The ascension of Christ closes Luke and opens Acts.

helps.text: The promise of the Spirit (1.8) gives the geographical outline of the book. Jerusalem (1 to 7), Judea and Samaria (8 to 12), the ends of the earth (13 to 28).
helps.html: The promise of the Spirit (1.8) gives the geographical outline of the book. Jerusalem (1 to 7), Judea and Samaria (8 to 12), the ends of the earth (13 to 28).

helps.text: Pentecost (chapter 2) is the founding event of the church age. The Spirit comes on all flesh as Joel prophesied. Peter’s sermon is a model of apostolic preaching.
helps.html: Pentecost (chapter 2) is the founding event of the church age. The Spirit comes on all flesh as Joel prophesied. Peter’s sermon is a model of apostolic preaching.

helps.text: The early Jerusalem church (chapters 2 to 7) shows the patterns of teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer.
helps.html: The early Jerusalem church (chapters 2 to 7) shows the patterns of teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer.

helps.text: Baptism is the entry sign of the new covenant church and is administered freely throughout Acts. Three thousand are baptized at Pentecost (2.41). The Ethiopian eunuch (8), Saul (9), Cornelius and his household (10), Lydia and her household (16), the Philippian jailer and his household (16), Crispus and his household (18). Watch the household pattern. The covenant sign is given not only to the believing head but to those of his house.
helps.html: Baptism is the entry sign of the new covenant church and is administered freely throughout Acts. Three thousand are baptized at Pentecost (2.41). The Ethiopian eunuch (8), Saul (9), Cornelius and his household (10), Lydia and her household (16), the Philippian jailer and his household (16), Crispus and his household (18). Watch the household pattern. The covenant sign is given not only to the believing head but to those of his house.

helps.text: Stephen’s sermon (chapter 7) is a sweeping summary of redemptive history that ends in his martyrdom. His death triggers the scattering of the church.
helps.html: Stephen’s sermon (chapter 7) is a sweeping summary of redemptive history that ends in his martyrdom. His death triggers the scattering of the church.

helps.text: Philip’s mission to Samaria (chapter 8) and the conversion of the Ethiopian eunuch open the door beyond Judaism.
helps.html: Philip’s mission to Samaria (chapter 8) and the conversion of the Ethiopian eunuch open the door beyond Judaism.

helps.text: The conversion of Saul (chapter 9, recounted in 22 and 26) is one of the great events of Christian history. The persecutor becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.
helps.html: The conversion of Saul (chapter 9, recounted in 22 and 26) is one of the great events of Christian history. The persecutor becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.

helps.text: The Jerusalem council (chapter 15) decides that Gentile believers don't have to keep the ceremonial law. This is the practical death of the Mosaic ceremonial system in the church.
helps.html: The Jerusalem council (chapter 15) decides that Gentile believers don't have to keep the ceremonial law. This is the practical death of the Mosaic ceremonial system in the church.

helps.text: Paul’s three missionary journeys (chapters 13 to 21) plant churches across the Roman world. His epistles fit into this narrative.
helps.html: Paul’s three missionary journeys (chapters 13 to 21) plant churches across the Roman world. His epistles fit into this narrative.

helps.text: The miraculous gifts in Acts (tongues, healings, prophecy) are foundational to the apostolic age. The historic Reformed position, in line with WCF 1.1, holds that these revelatory and sign gifts have ceased with the closing of the canon. Acts records the founding of the church, not the ongoing pattern of every age. Read the miracles as God’s authentication of the apostolic message in the foundational era.
helps.html: The miraculous gifts in Acts (tongues, healings, prophecy) are foundational to the apostolic age. The historic Reformed position, in line with WCF 1.1, holds that these revelatory and sign gifts have ceased with the closing of the canon. Acts records the founding of the church, not the ongoing pattern of every age. Read the miracles as God’s authentication of the apostolic message in the foundational era.

helps.text: The book ends with Paul in Rome preaching boldly (28.31). The geographical outline is complete. The gospel has reached the heart of the empire.
helps.html: The book ends with Paul in Rome preaching boldly (28.31). The geographical outline is complete. The gospel has reached the heart of the empire.

studies.title: The apostolic decision rejects another way of salvation
studies.html: The dispute begins with the claim that circumcision is necessary for salvation. Peter answers by pointing to God’s work among the Gentiles and salvation through the grace of the Lord Jesus. The council’s later practical directions must be read within that settled gospel claim. They cannot be turned back into conditions by which ritual obedience purchases acceptance.
studies.distinction: Apostolic instructions for holy fellowship aren’t an alternative ground of justification.
studies.question: What claim in verse 1 creates the dispute, and how does Peter’s conclusion answer it?

studies.title: Shared possessions are voluntary generosity
studies.html: The congregation’s care for need is displayed through willing gifts. Acts 5.4 expressly recognizes that Ananias’s property remained his and that its proceeds were at his disposal. His sin is deceit, not failure to surrender property under a universal rule abolishing ownership. WCF 26 preserves both communion in material help and each person’s title to his possessions.
studies.distinction: A demanding duty of generosity isn’t identical with compulsory elimination of private property.
studies.question: How does Peter’s statement in Acts 5.4 explain the sharing described at the end of Acts 4?

books.name: Romans
books.intro: Paul explains the righteousness God gives through faith in Christ and the life that follows from His mercy. The argument moves from universal guilt to justification, union with Christ, and the life of the church. Read each section within that sustained argument.
books.introText: Paul explains the righteousness God gives through faith in Christ and the life that follows from His mercy. The argument moves from universal guilt to justification, union with Christ, and the life of the church. Read each section within that sustained argument.

helps.text: Paul wrote Romans to a church he had not yet visited, probably from Corinth around AD 57. He sets out the gospel in full because he is preparing to come.
helps.html: Paul wrote Romans to a church he had not yet visited, probably from Corinth around AD 57. He sets out the gospel in full because he is preparing to come.

helps.text: The introduction (1.1 to 17) lands the thesis. The gospel is the power of God for salvation. Habakkuk 2.4 is the foundational text.
helps.html: The introduction (1.1 to 17) lands the thesis. The gospel is the power of God for salvation. Habakkuk 2.4 is the foundational text.

helps.text: The wrath of God (1.18 to 3.20) is set out comprehensively. The Gentile under nature, the Jew under the law, all the world stopped before God.
helps.html: The wrath of God (1.18 to 3.20) is set out comprehensively. The Gentile under nature, the Jew under the law, all the world stopped before God.

helps.text: Justification by faith (3.21 to 5.21) is the heart of the doctrine. Christ propitiates the wrath of God by His blood. Abraham is the model believer. Adam and Christ are the two heads.
helps.html: Justification by faith (3.21 to 5.21) is the heart of the doctrine. Christ propitiates the wrath of God by His blood. Abraham is the model believer. Adam and Christ are the two heads.

helps.text: The Adam-Christ parallel in Romans 5 can't be rightly read without the covenant of works. Adam acted as the federal head of the human race in the covenant of works. Christ acts as the federal head of His people in the covenant of grace. The first Adam’s disobedience brought condemnation. The last Adam’s obedience brings justification.
helps.html: The Adam-Christ parallel in Romans 5 can't be rightly read without the covenant of works. Adam acted as the federal head of the human race in the covenant of works. Christ acts as the federal head of His people in the covenant of grace. The first Adam’s disobedience brought condemnation. The last Adam’s obedience brings justification.

helps.text: Sanctification in chapters 6 to 8 covers union with Christ in His death and resurrection (6), the law and the inner conflict (7), and life in the Spirit (8). Romans 8 is one of the highest peaks of the Bible.
helps.html: Sanctification in chapters 6 to 8 covers union with Christ in His death and resurrection (6), the law and the inner conflict (7), and life in the Spirit (8). Romans 8 is one of the highest peaks of the Bible.

helps.text: Election and Israel (9 to 11) handles the hard question of why most Jews have not believed. Paul defends the freedom of God in election (9), the responsibility of unbelief (10), and the future of Israel and the Gentiles (11).
helps.html: Election and Israel (9 to 11) handles the hard question of why most Jews have not believed. Paul defends the freedom of God in election (9), the responsibility of unbelief (10), and the future of Israel and the Gentiles (11).

helps.text: Application (12 to 16) covers life in the body of Christ, life under the state, conscience and the weaker brother, and Paul’s plans.
helps.html: Application (12 to 16) covers life in the body of Christ, life under the state, conscience and the weaker brother, and Paul’s plans.

helps.text: Romans 9 answers the charge that God's promise has failed. Follow Paul's distinction between physical descent and God's electing purpose, and his use of Jacob and Esau. The argument supports unconditional election without excusing human unbelief.
helps.html: Romans 9 answers the charge that God's promise has failed. Follow Paul's distinction between physical descent and God's electing purpose, and his use of Jacob and Esau. The argument supports unconditional election without excusing human unbelief.

helps.text: Romans 11 forbids Gentile boasting and holds out hope concerning Israel. Some Reformed interpreters expect a future widespread conversion of ethnic Jews. Others understand the passage as describing their ingathering throughout this age. John Murray, an amillennialist, held the former view, so don't equate the alternatives with a simple division between millennial positions.
helps.html: Romans 11 forbids Gentile boasting and holds out hope concerning Israel. Some Reformed interpreters expect a future widespread conversion of ethnic Jews. Others understand the passage as describing their ingathering throughout this age. John Murray, an amillennialist, held the former view, so don't equate the alternatives with a simple division between millennial positions.

studies.title: The second Adam answers the first Adam’s condemnation
studies.html: Paul explains condemnation and justification through two representative men. The contrast concerns the judicial effect of their acts upon those represented. Christ’s obedience supplies the righteousness His people lack. Don’t turn the passage into an account only of bad and good examples. The language of condemnation and justification requires a legal and covenantal relation, while the surrounding chapters also teach real renewal.
studies.distinction: Imputed righteousness and inward sanctification belong together without being the same benefit.
studies.question: What does Paul attribute to the one man’s disobedience and to the other’s obedience?

studies.title: Election answers the charge that God’s promise failed
studies.html: Paul distinguishes natural descent from the children of promise and grounds election in God’s purpose rather than foreseen works. He also answers an objection concerning God’s justice. Follow that sequence rather than treating the chapter as an isolated puzzle about power. God’s sovereign mercy doesn’t make Him the author of sin, and the following discussion continues to hold unbelief responsible.
studies.distinction: Sovereignty and culpability are both asserted. Neither may be erased to make the other easier to explain.
studies.question: Why does Paul begin by distinguishing Israel according to the flesh from the children of promise?

books.name: 1 Corinthians
books.intro: Paul addresses a divided church whose conduct contradicts its profession. Questions about wisdom, sexual conduct, worship, and resurrection are brought under Christ's lordship. His corrections show how the gospel orders a congregation's life.
books.introText: Paul addresses a divided church whose conduct contradicts its profession. Questions about wisdom, sexual conduct, worship, and resurrection are brought under Christ's lordship. His corrections show how the gospel orders a congregation's life.

helps.text: Paul writes from Ephesus around AD 55, having received reports about the church and a letter from them.
helps.html: Paul writes from Ephesus around AD 55, having received reports about the church and a letter from them.

helps.text: The divisions over teachers (chapters 1 to 4) are dealt with by lifting up the cross as the wisdom of God against the world’s wisdom.
helps.html: The divisions over teachers (chapters 1 to 4) are dealt with by lifting up the cross as the wisdom of God against the world’s wisdom.

helps.text: The case of the immoral man (chapter 5) requires church discipline. Paul tells the church to put the unrepentant man out of the fellowship for the sake of his soul and the purity of the body. This is the same discipline Christ ordained in Matthew 18.
helps.html: The case of the immoral man (chapter 5) requires church discipline. Paul tells the church to put the unrepentant man out of the fellowship for the sake of his soul and the purity of the body. This is the same discipline Christ ordained in Matthew 18.

helps.text: First Corinthians 6 rebukes believers for pursuing grievances against one another before unbelieving courts. Read the argument about wronging a brother and receiving wrong. It doesn't abolish the magistrate's duty to judge crimes.
helps.html: First Corinthians 6 rebukes believers for pursuing grievances against one another before unbelieving courts. Read the argument about wronging a brother and receiving wrong. It doesn't abolish the magistrate's duty to judge crimes.

helps.text: Sexual immorality (chapter 6) is set against the believer’s union with Christ. The body matters.
helps.html: Sexual immorality (chapter 6) is set against the believer’s union with Christ. The body matters.

helps.text: Marriage and singleness (chapter 7) are both honored. The principles given are situational and need careful reading.
helps.html: Marriage and singleness (chapter 7) are both honored. The principles given are situational and need careful reading.

helps.text: Idol meat (chapters 8 to 10) is handled with the principle of love. The strong defer to the weak.
helps.html: Idol meat (chapters 8 to 10) is handled with the principle of love. The strong defer to the weak.

helps.text: Worship in the church (chapters 11 to 14) covers head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, and order in worship. The regulative principle (WCF 21.1) is the lens. Worship isn't a free creative space. It's governed by what God has commanded.
helps.html: Worship in the church (chapters 11 to 14) covers head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, and order in worship. The regulative principle (WCF 21.1) is the lens. Worship isn't a free creative space. It's governed by what God has commanded.

helps.text: The Lord’s Supper (11.17 to 34) is treated at length. Paul rebukes the abuses in Corinth and gives the apostolic instruction Christ Himself delivered. The bread and the cup are a participation in the body and blood of Christ. The supper is to be received with self-examination, with discernment of the body, and with reverence. Believers feed on Christ by faith and are knit together as one body. WCF 29.
helps.html: The Lord’s Supper (11.17 to 34) is treated at length. Paul rebukes the abuses in Corinth and gives the apostolic instruction Christ Himself delivered. The bread and the cup are a participation in the body and blood of Christ. The supper is to be received with self-examination, with discernment of the body, and with reverence. Believers feed on Christ by faith and are knit together as one body. WCF 29.

helps.text: Chapters 12 to 14 concern the use of spiritual gifts for the church's edification. This guide follows cessationism, distinguishing the extraordinary revelatory gifts of the apostolic foundation from continuing gifts of service and teaching. WCF 1.1 affirms the cessation of former ways of revelation. It doesn't teach that God has stopped healing or answering prayer.
helps.html: Chapters 12 to 14 concern the use of spiritual gifts for the church's edification. This guide follows cessationism, distinguishing the extraordinary revelatory gifts of the apostolic foundation from continuing gifts of service and teaching. WCF 1.1 affirms the cessation of former ways of revelation. It doesn't teach that God has stopped healing or answering prayer.

helps.text: The resurrection chapter (15) is foundational. If Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain. Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who sleep.
helps.html: The resurrection chapter (15) is foundational. If Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain. Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who sleep.

studies.title: The Supper gives communion without repeating the sacrifice
studies.html: Paul treats the cup and bread as communion in Christ’s blood and body and uses that relation to forbid fellowship with idols.
