This is more than an indifferent reminder, but it isn’t a change of the elements into Christ’s bodily substance. Read chapter 11’s institution and warnings with the teaching of His once-for-all offering. Believers truly receive Christ spiritually through faith.
studies.distinction: Real spiritual participation doesn’t require a repeated sacrifice or physical identity between the sign and Christ’s body.
studies.question: How does the reality of communion strengthen Paul’s warning against participation in idolatry?

studies.title: Spiritual body does not mean an immaterial body
studies.html: Paul contrasts the body’s present weakness and corruption with its risen glory and power. His comparison of seed and growth preserves continuity through transformation. The spiritual body is suited to the life of the resurrection, not a denial of bodily existence. Read the adjective within Paul’s contrast rather than importing the assumption that spiritual must mean nonphysical.
studies.distinction: A changed condition of bodily life is different from replacement of the body with an immaterial idea.
studies.question: Which contrasts describe the change, and how does the seed illustration preserve identity through it?

books.name: 2 Corinthians
books.intro: Paul defends his ministry and explains how Christ's strength is displayed through weakness. The letter also urges reconciliation and generous support for suffering saints. Read its personal passages as part of Paul's defense of genuine apostolic ministry.
books.introText: Paul defends his ministry and explains how Christ's strength is displayed through weakness. The letter also urges reconciliation and generous support for suffering saints. Read its personal passages as part of Paul's defense of genuine apostolic ministry.

helps.text: Paul writes between 1 Corinthians and his next visit, around AD 56. He has had a difficult relationship with this church.
helps.html: Paul writes between 1 Corinthians and his next visit, around AD 56. He has had a difficult relationship with this church.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) introduces the theme of comfort in affliction. The God of all comfort.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) introduces the theme of comfort in affliction. The God of all comfort.

helps.text: Paul’s defense of his integrity (chapters 1 to 2) reflects accusations against him. He answers with transparency.
helps.html: Paul’s defense of his integrity (chapters 1 to 2) reflects accusations against him. He answers with transparency.

helps.text: The new covenant ministry (chapter 3) contrasts the old and new covenants. The veil over Moses’s face is lifted in Christ.
helps.html: The new covenant ministry (chapter 3) contrasts the old and new covenants. The veil over Moses’s face is lifted in Christ.

helps.text: The treasure in jars of clay (chapter 4) is one of the great passages on Christian ministry. The light shines from broken vessels.
helps.html: The treasure in jars of clay (chapter 4) is one of the great passages on Christian ministry. The light shines from broken vessels.

helps.text: The eternal weight of glory (4.16 to 18) sets the present momentary affliction in its proper proportion.
helps.html: The eternal weight of glory (4.16 to 18) sets the present momentary affliction in its proper proportion.

helps.text: The ministry of reconciliation (chapter 5) presents the believer as Christ’s ambassador with the message that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ.
helps.html: The ministry of reconciliation (chapter 5) presents the believer as Christ’s ambassador with the message that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ.

helps.text: The collection for the Jerusalem saints (chapters 8 to 9) gives the principles of Christian giving. Cheerful, generous, sacrificial.
helps.html: The collection for the Jerusalem saints (chapters 8 to 9) gives the principles of Christian giving. Cheerful, generous, sacrificial.

helps.text: The defense of his apostleship (chapters 10 to 13) is sharp. Paul boasts in his weaknesses, his sufferings, and his thorn in the flesh. The strength of Christ rests on him.
helps.html: The defense of his apostleship (chapters 10 to 13) is sharp. Paul boasts in his weaknesses, his sufferings, and his thorn in the flesh. The strength of Christ rests on him.

studies.title: The letter and the Spirit are not text versus experience
studies.html: Paul contrasts covenant ministries and describes the Spirit’s life-giving work. He isn’t declaring that close attention to written words kills while private religious feeling saves. His own written instruction is authoritative apostolic ministry. Read the contrast with the stone tablets, the veil, and the surpassing glory of the new covenant rather than using a slogan to escape scriptural judgment.
studies.distinction: The Spirit who gives life doesn’t authorize meanings opposed to the Word He inspired.
studies.question: What features of Moses' ministry determine the contrast Paul is drawing?

studies.title: Sufficient grace is not a promise of removed affliction
studies.html: Paul asks repeatedly for the thorn to depart. The Lord’s answer supplies sufficient grace while leaving the affliction in place. The passage therefore contradicts the claim that faithful prayer must always secure the desired bodily or circumstantial relief. The exact identity of the thorn is uncertain, but its function in Paul’s account is clear.
studies.distinction: Knowing why an affliction is discussed here doesn’t give us certainty about its medical identity or every person’s suffering.
studies.question: How does the Lord answer the request without granting the removal Paul first sought?

books.name: Galatians
books.intro: Paul opposes teachers who require Gentile believers to receive circumcision and submit to the Mosaic order. Justification is through faith in Christ alone. Christian freedom therefore rules out both reliance on law-keeping for acceptance and indulgence of the flesh.
books.introText: Paul opposes teachers who require Gentile believers to receive circumcision and submit to the Mosaic order. Justification is through faith in Christ alone. Christian freedom therefore rules out both reliance on law-keeping for acceptance and indulgence of the flesh.

helps.text: Paul writes early, perhaps before the Jerusalem council, around AD 48 to 49 (or possibly later, around AD 55). The setting is the churches of Galatia, probably the southern Galatian region of Asia Minor.
helps.html: Paul writes early, perhaps before the Jerusalem council, around AD 48 to 49 (or possibly later, around AD 55). The setting is the churches of Galatia, probably the southern Galatian region of Asia Minor.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) skips the usual thanksgiving. Paul gets straight to the issue. There's no other gospel.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) skips the usual thanksgiving. Paul gets straight to the issue. There's no other gospel.

helps.text: Paul’s defense of his apostleship and the gospel he preaches (1.11 to 2.21) includes his confrontation with Peter at Antioch over hypocrisy.
helps.html: Paul’s defense of his apostleship and the gospel he preaches (1.11 to 2.21) includes his confrontation with Peter at Antioch over hypocrisy.

helps.text: The doctrinal heart (chapters 3 to 4) argues that justification is by faith from beginning to end. Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision. The law came later and could not annul the promise.
helps.html: The doctrinal heart (chapters 3 to 4) argues that justification is by faith from beginning to end. Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision. The law came later and could not annul the promise.

helps.text: Chapter 3 shows that the law was added because of transgressions until Christ came. The law is a guardian until faith.
helps.html: Chapter 3 shows that the law was added because of transgressions until Christ came. The law is a guardian until faith.

helps.text: In Galatians 4.21 to 31, Paul gives an inspired allegorical use of Sarah and Hagar to expose slavery under the law. He doesn't deny their historical existence. His apostolic interpretation gives no warrant for a reader to assign arbitrary hidden meanings to other narratives.
helps.html: In Galatians 4.21 to 31, Paul gives an inspired allegorical use of Sarah and Hagar to expose slavery under the law. He doesn't deny their historical existence. His apostolic interpretation gives no warrant for a reader to assign arbitrary hidden meanings to other narratives.

helps.text: The freedom in Christ (chapter 5) is freedom from the law’s curse and freedom for love. Freedom isn't lawlessness.
helps.html: The freedom in Christ (chapter 5) is freedom from the law’s curse and freedom for love. Freedom isn't lawlessness.

helps.text: The fruit of the Spirit (5.22 to 23) is contrasted with the works of the flesh (5.19 to 21). Both lists are illustrative, not exhaustive.
helps.html: The fruit of the Spirit (5.22 to 23) is contrasted with the works of the flesh (5.19 to 21). Both lists are illustrative, not exhaustive.

helps.text: The application (chapter 6) covers bearing one another’s burdens, sowing and reaping, and boasting only in the cross.
helps.html: The application (chapter 6) covers bearing one another’s burdens, sowing and reaping, and boasting only in the cross.

studies.title: The curse explains why law-keeping cannot justify sinners
studies.html: The law’s demand is comprehensive. A sinner cannot obtain a righteous verdict by selecting enough successful acts while ignoring the guilt of failure. Christ redeems His people from the curse by bearing it for them. The blessing received through faith therefore rests upon His accomplished work, not a reduced standard under which our imperfect obedience becomes sufficient merit.
studies.distinction: Grace doesn’t lower the law into an easier covenant of works. It supplies the Redeemer who fulfills and satisfies it.
studies.question: What relation does Paul establish between the law’s curse, Christ’s death, and the blessing of Abraham?

studies.title: Inspired allegory does not authorize arbitrary allegorizing
studies.html: Paul draws a divinely authorized correspondence between the two women, their sons, and two covenantal conditions. He doesn’t deny the narrated history. His argument rebukes reliance upon the law as a way of inheritance. The passage shows that a real history can bear an inspired figurative use, but it doesn’t make our own invented correspondences equally authoritative.
studies.distinction: Apostolic interpretation supplies warrant that an imaginative resemblance supplied only by the reader lacks.
studies.question: Which contrast between bondage and promise controls Paul’s use of the history?

books.name: Ephesians
books.intro: Paul describes God's saving purpose in Christ and the unity of His church. The second half teaches believers how to walk in keeping with that calling. Household duties and spiritual warfare belong to the same life of grace.
books.introText: Paul describes God's saving purpose in Christ and the unity of His church. The second half teaches believers how to walk in keeping with that calling. Household duties and spiritual warfare belong to the same life of grace.

helps.text: Paul writes from prison, probably from Rome around AD 60 to 62. The letter may have been a circular for the Asian churches with Ephesus as one stop.
helps.html: Paul writes from prison, probably from Rome around AD 60 to 62. The letter may have been a circular for the Asian churches with Ephesus as one stop.

helps.text: The opening doxology (1.3 to 14) is one of the highest theological passages in the New Testament. Election, redemption, sealing of the Spirit. All unto the praise of His glory.
helps.html: The opening doxology (1.3 to 14) is one of the highest theological passages in the New Testament. Election, redemption, sealing of the Spirit. All unto the praise of His glory.

helps.text: The prayer for spiritual sight (1.15 to 23) is one of the great prayers of Paul.
helps.html: The prayer for spiritual sight (1.15 to 23) is one of the great prayers of Paul.

helps.text: Salvation by grace through faith (2.1 to 10) is a foundational text. We were dead in sins. He made us alive together with Christ.
helps.html: Salvation by grace through faith (2.1 to 10) is a foundational text. We were dead in sins. He made us alive together with Christ.

helps.text: The unity of Jew and Gentile in one body (2.11 to 22) is the heart of the apostle’s ministry. The dividing wall has been broken.
helps.html: The unity of Jew and Gentile in one body (2.11 to 22) is the heart of the apostle’s ministry. The dividing wall has been broken.

helps.text: The mystery of the gospel (chapter 3) is now revealed. Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel through the gospel.
helps.html: The mystery of the gospel (chapter 3) is now revealed. Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel through the gospel.

helps.text: The application section opens with unity and gifts in the body (chapter 4).
helps.html: The application section opens with unity and gifts in the body (chapter 4).

helps.text: The new walk (4.17 to 5.21) covers honesty, hard work, pure speech, and Spirit-filled life.
helps.html: The new walk (4.17 to 5.21) covers honesty, hard work, pure speech, and Spirit-filled life.

helps.text: The household codes (5.22 to 6.9) cover marriage, parenting, and work. The marriage section presents marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.
helps.html: The household codes (5.22 to 6.9) cover marriage, parenting, and work. The marriage section presents marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.

helps.text: The armor of God (6.10 to 18) is the believer’s equipment for the spiritual battle. Each piece is identified with a doctrine or grace.
helps.html: The armor of God (6.10 to 18) is the believer’s equipment for the spiritual battle. Each piece is identified with a doctrine or grace.

studies.title: Election aims at holiness rather than indifference
studies.html: The Father chooses in Christ, the Son redeems through His blood, and believers are sealed with the Spirit. Paul’s praise relates the distinct works of the Persons within one gracious saving purpose. Holiness and adoption belong to the goal of election. A claim that election makes obedience unnecessary contradicts the purpose for which Paul says the blessing is given.
studies.distinction: The saving works of the Persons are distinct without being independent plans or competing divine wills.
studies.question: What purposes accompany God’s choosing, and how does the whole paragraph end in praise?

studies.title: New creation produces the works that cannot earn it
studies.html: Paul’s account begins with spiritual death and attributes life to God’s mercy. He then excludes boasting and identifies good works as the path prepared for those created in Christ. The argument gives works a necessary place without assigning them a justifying role. Salvation changes the person who walks, not merely the label placed upon an unchanged life.
studies.distinction: Good works are the appointed fruit and evidence of grace, not the contribution that completes an insufficient Savior.
studies.question: How do the order and connecting words of verses 8 to 10 establish the place of obedience?

books.name: Philippians
books.intro: Paul writes from prison to a church that has supported his ministry. He calls them to unity and steadfastness with Christ's humility before them. His own contentment shows what trust in Christ looks like amid changing circumstances.
books.introText: Paul writes from prison to a church that has supported his ministry. He calls them to unity and steadfastness with Christ's humility before them. His own contentment shows what trust in Christ looks like amid changing circumstances.

helps.text: Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 61. The Philippian church had sent him a gift through Epaphroditus.
helps.html: Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 61. The Philippian church had sent him a gift through Epaphroditus.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) is a thanksgiving. Paul recounts his confidence that God will complete the good work He began in them.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) is a thanksgiving. Paul recounts his confidence that God will complete the good work He began in them.

helps.text: Paul’s perspective on his imprisonment (1.12 to 26) is striking. The chains have advanced the gospel. To live is Christ. To die is gain.
helps.html: Paul’s perspective on his imprisonment (1.12 to 26) is striking. The chains have advanced the gospel. To live is Christ. To die is gain.

helps.text: Philippians 2.5 to 11 sets Christ's humility before the church. The Son didn't cease to be God when He took the form of a servant. His humiliation consists in taking our nature and obeying unto death, after which He is exalted as the incarnate Mediator.
helps.html: Philippians 2.5 to 11 sets Christ's humility before the church. The Son didn't cease to be God when He took the form of a servant. His humiliation consists in taking our nature and obeying unto death, after which He is exalted as the incarnate Mediator.

helps.text: The mind of Christ (2.5) is the application. The Philippians are to think and live like Him.
helps.html: The mind of Christ (2.5) is the application. The Philippians are to think and live like Him.

helps.text: Paul’s autobiography (chapter 3) recounts his old confidence and his new. He counts everything as loss compared to knowing Christ.
helps.html: Paul’s autobiography (chapter 3) recounts his old confidence and his new. He counts everything as loss compared to knowing Christ.

helps.text: Pressing on toward the prize (3.12 to 16) is one of the great athletic metaphors of the New Testament.
helps.html: Pressing on toward the prize (3.12 to 16) is one of the great athletic metaphors of the New Testament.

helps.text: Philippians 4.4 to 9 joins prayer and thanksgiving with disciplined attention to what is true and good. Bring anxiety to the Lord without treating the passage as a promise that a Christian will never feel distress.
helps.html: Philippians 4.4 to 9 joins prayer and thanksgiving with disciplined attention to what is true and good. Bring anxiety to the Lord without treating the passage as a promise that a Christian will never feel distress.

helps.text: Contentment in every circumstance (4.10 to 13) is learned, not natural. "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." is in this context.
helps.html: Contentment in every circumstance (4.10 to 13) is learned, not natural. "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." is in this context.

studies.title: The Son humbles Himself by taking, not by ceasing to be God
studies.html: The passage joins the form of God with the taking of the form of a servant. Christ’s humiliation includes incarnation and obedience to death. It doesn’t mean that His divine nature loses omniscience, holiness, or power. The one Person acts in genuine humanity, and the incarnate Mediator is exalted. Read the ethical call to humility through this true account of His person and work.
studies.distinction: Taking a human nature doesn’t change deity into humanity or subtract divine attributes from the eternal Son.
studies.question: Which actions explain His self-humbling, and which words preserve who He already is?

studies.title: A righteousness received through faith displaces self-confidence
studies.html: Paul sets his former religious advantages against the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. He rejects a righteousness of his own from the law and desires the righteousness received through faith. The following pursuit of resurrection life doesn’t reintroduce personal merit as a ground of acceptance. The believer presses on because he belongs to Christ, not to repair a defective justification.
studies.distinction: Striving in sanctification mustn’t be confused with earning the righteous standing Paul has just renounced achieving for himself.
studies.question: How does Paul’s account of being found in Christ govern the pursuit described in verses 12 to 14?

books.name: Colossians
books.intro: Paul sets forth Christ's supremacy against teaching that promises spiritual fullness elsewhere. Believers are complete in Him and must not return to human religious rules as a path to acceptance. Union with Christ also requires putting sinful conduct to death.
books.introText: Paul sets forth Christ's supremacy against teaching that promises spiritual fullness elsewhere. Believers are complete in Him and must not return to human religious rules as a path to acceptance. Union with Christ also requires putting sinful conduct to death.

helps.text: Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 60 to 61, to a church he had not personally founded. Epaphras had planted it.
helps.html: Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 60 to 61, to a church he had not personally founded. Epaphras had planted it.

helps.text: The false teaching at Colossae mixed Jewish ritual, asceticism, and angel-worship. Paul doesn't address each piece separately. He exalts Christ above them all.
helps.html: The false teaching at Colossae mixed Jewish ritual, asceticism, and angel-worship. Paul doesn't address each piece separately. He exalts Christ above them all.

helps.text: The opening prayer (1.9 to 14) is one of the great prayers of the apostle.
helps.html: The opening prayer (1.9 to 14) is one of the great prayers of the apostle.

helps.text: The Christ hymn (1.15 to 20) declares Him the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, the Creator, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, in whom all the fullness of God dwells.
helps.html: The Christ hymn (1.15 to 20) declares Him the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, the Creator, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, in whom all the fullness of God dwells.

helps.text: The reconciliation through His blood (1.20 to 23) applies the hymn to the believers.
helps.html: The reconciliation through His blood (1.20 to 23) applies the hymn to the believers.

helps.text: Paul’s ministry of the mystery (chapter 1.24 to 2.5) is the proclamation of Christ in you, the hope of glory.
helps.html: Paul’s ministry of the mystery (chapter 1.24 to 2.5) is the proclamation of Christ in you, the hope of glory.

helps.text: The warning against false teachers (2.6 to 23) is followed by the declaration that you've everything in Christ. He is the head. You're complete in Him.
helps.html: The warning against false teachers (2.6 to 23) is followed by the declaration that you've everything in Christ. He is the head. You're complete in Him.

helps.text: The new life (chapter 3) calls believers to set their minds on things above. The old man is put off. The new is put on.
helps.html: The new life (chapter 3) calls believers to set their minds on things above. The old man is put off. The new is put on.

helps.text: The household codes (3.18 to 4.1) cover marriage, children, and slaves. The principles apply broadly.
helps.html: The household codes (3.18 to 4.1) cover marriage, children, and slaves. The principles apply broadly.

studies.title: Firstborn is explained by Christ’s supremacy over creation
studies.html: The following clauses explain why Christ holds firstborn preeminence. All things were created by Him and for Him, and He is before all things. A reading that places Him among created things contradicts the reason Paul supplies. Don’t select one possible use of firstborn while ignoring the explanatory argument attached to it.
studies.distinction: A word’s possible reference to birth order doesn’t override the sense established by its present context.
studies.question: What reasons introduced in the paragraph establish Christ’s relation to everything created?

studies.title: Circumcision, baptism, and the inward reality
studies.html: Paul relates circumcision without hands, burial with Christ in baptism, and faith in God’s operation. The passage supports reading the covenant signs within union with Christ. The Westminster case for infant baptism also rests on the broader covenant pattern and the inclusion of believers' children, not on pretending these verses explicitly narrate an infant baptism. The inward grace must not be made automatic through outward administration.
studies.distinction: A theological connection between signs is significant without being, by itself, an explicit account of every recipient of baptism.
studies.question: What inward work and response does Paul name, and how do WCF 28.4 to 6 distinguish recipients from efficacy?

books.name: 1 Thessalonians
books.intro: Paul encourages a young church enduring opposition and answers questions about believers who have died. Christ's return grounds their hope and their present duties. Waiting for Him calls for faithful work and holiness.
books.introText: Paul encourages a young church enduring opposition and answers questions about believers who have died. Christ's return grounds their hope and their present duties. Waiting for Him calls for faithful work and holiness.

helps.text: Paul writes from Corinth around AD 50 to 51, shortly after planting the church (Acts 17). It's one of his earliest letters.
helps.html: Paul writes from Corinth around AD 50 to 51, shortly after planting the church (Acts 17). It's one of his earliest letters.

helps.text: The opening thanksgiving (chapter 1) celebrates their faith, love, and hope. The triad of Christian virtues.
helps.html: The opening thanksgiving (chapter 1) celebrates their faith, love, and hope. The triad of Christian virtues.

helps.text: Paul recounts his ministry among them (chapter 2). He defends his integrity against those who would slander him after his departure.
helps.html: Paul recounts his ministry among them (chapter 2). He defends his integrity against those who would slander him after his departure.

helps.text: The sending of Timothy and the news of their faith (chapter 3) is full of relief and joy.
helps.html: The sending of Timothy and the news of their faith (chapter 3) is full of relief and joy.

helps.text: The call to holiness (4.1 to 12) covers sexual purity, brotherly love, and orderly work.
helps.html: The call to holiness (4.1 to 12) covers sexual purity, brotherly love, and orderly work.

helps.text: The catching up of believers (4.13 to 18) is in answer to their question about those who had died. Paul says they won't miss the resurrection. They will rise first. The dead in Christ rise. The living are caught up to meet the Lord in the air. This passage describes the one second coming of Christ in glory, not a separate secret rapture before a tribulation. The Reformed tradition has consistently read 4.13 to 18 alongside 5.1 to 11 and Matthew 24 as one event. Christ comes once more in glory. The dead are raised. The judgment is held. The new heavens and new earth begin.
helps.html: The catching up of believers (4.13 to 18) is in answer to their question about those who had died. Paul says they won't miss the resurrection. They will rise first. The dead in Christ rise. The living are caught up to meet the Lord in the air. This passage describes the one second coming of Christ in glory, not a separate secret rapture before a tribulation. The Reformed tradition has consistently read 4.13 to 18 alongside 5.1 to 11 and Matthew 24 as one event. Christ comes once more in glory. The dead are raised. The judgment is held. The new heavens and new earth begin.

helps.text: The day of the Lord (chapter 5) comes like a thief. Believers aren't in darkness. Be alert and sober.
helps.html: The day of the Lord (chapter 5) comes like a thief. Believers aren't in darkness. Be alert and sober.

helps.text: The closing exhortations (5.12 to 22) are short and practical. Encourage the fainthearted. Pray without ceasing. Test everything.
helps.html: The closing exhortations (5.12 to 22) are short and practical. Encourage the fainthearted. Pray without ceasing. Test everything.

helps.text: The benediction (5.23) prays for the sanctification of the whole man, spirit and soul and body, blameless at the coming of the Lord.
helps.html: The benediction (5.23) prays for the sanctification of the whole man, spirit and soul and body, blameless at the coming of the Lord.

studies.title: The dead in Christ are not excluded from His coming
studies.html: Paul answers grief concerning believers who have died. Their death won’t deprive them of participation in Christ’s triumph. The dead rise and the living are gathered with them to meet the Lord. Read this as comfort grounded in one shared future with Christ, rather than beginning with a timetable whose divisions obscure the question Paul actually answers.
studies.distinction: The passage’s clear pastoral promise is stronger than a disputed reconstruction of every end-time sequence.
studies.question: What mistaken concern about the dead does Paul’s ordering of events directly correct?

studies.title: A prayer for the whole person is not a complete anatomy
studies.html: Paul prays that God sanctify the believers wholly and preserve them blameless at Christ’s coming. The mention of spirit, soul, and body emphasizes the comprehensiveness of that prayer. It mustn’t be made, without further argument, a proof that man consists of three separable substances. WCF 32 speaks of soul and body while confessing the complete salvation of the person.
studies.distinction: A rhetorical enumeration can be comprehensive without serving as a technical definition of every constituent part.
studies.question: What does the repeated emphasis on wholeness contribute to the prayer’s meaning?

books.name: 2 Thessalonians
books.intro: Paul corrects confusion about the day of the Lord and confronts disorderly idleness. The church must remain steadfast under persecution. Teaching about future events is joined to ordinary duties in the present.
books.introText: Paul corrects confusion about the day of the Lord and confronts disorderly idleness. The church must remain steadfast under persecution. Teaching about future events is joined to ordinary duties in the present.

helps.text: Paul writes shortly after 1 Thessalonians, perhaps a few months later, around AD 51 to 52.
helps.html: Paul writes shortly after 1 Thessalonians, perhaps a few months later, around AD 51 to 52.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) celebrates the church’s perseverance and lays out the comfort that Christ will be revealed from heaven with His mighty angels.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) celebrates the church’s perseverance and lays out the comfort that Christ will be revealed from heaven with His mighty angels.

helps.text: The day of the Lord (chapter 2) is the doctrinal center. Some had said the day was already present. Paul says no. Two things must come first.
helps.html: The day of the Lord (chapter 2) is the doctrinal center. Some had said the day was already present. Paul says no. Two things must come first.

helps.text: The rebellion (apostasy) and the man of lawlessness must be revealed before that day. The man of lawlessness sits in the temple of God claiming to be God.
helps.html: The rebellion (apostasy) and the man of lawlessness must be revealed before that day. The man of lawlessness sits in the temple of God claiming to be God.

helps.text: Something is restraining now. When the restrainer is removed, the man of lawlessness will be revealed.
helps.html: Something is restraining now. When the restrainer is removed, the man of lawlessness will be revealed.

helps.text: Christ will kill him by the breath of His mouth at His appearing. The lawless one comes by Satan’s power with all false signs and wonders.
helps.html: Christ will kill him by the breath of His mouth at His appearing. The lawless one comes by Satan’s power with all false signs and wonders.

helps.text: The chapter is one of the most important New Testament passages on end-time apostasy. It teaches that significant evil precedes Christ’s return. The church won't be removed before this happens. Christ’s coming, the destruction of the man of lawlessness, and the gathering of the saints are part of the one great day, not separate events.
helps.html: The chapter is one of the most important New Testament passages on end-time apostasy. It teaches that significant evil precedes Christ’s return. The church won't be removed before this happens. Christ’s coming, the destruction of the man of lawlessness, and the gathering of the saints are part of the one great day, not separate events.

helps.text: Chapter 3 confronts idleness. "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (3.10). The supposed nearness of the return doesn't excuse laziness.
helps.html: Chapter 3 confronts idleness. "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (3.10). The supposed nearness of the return doesn't excuse laziness.

helps.text: Paul’s command is to keep working, doing good, and waiting in steadiness.
helps.html: Paul’s command is to keep working, doing good, and waiting in steadiness.

studies.title: Read apostasy through doctrine, not a stream of headlines
studies.html: Paul corrects an alarming claim about the day of Christ by describing a rebellion and the man of sin. The original WCF 25.6 applies antichrist language to the papacy, a significant historic Reformed judgment that some later editions omit. Neither that confession nor the passage supplies a date calculation. The text directs attention to opposition against God and deception rather than a superficial resemblance to whichever public figure is currently feared.
studies.distinction: A confessional identification isn’t permission to invent a complete timetable or call every feared opponent the final fulfillment.
studies.question: Which claims and actions identify the opposition Paul describes, and which details remain unstated?

studies.title: Apostolic tradition is identified by its apostolic source
studies.html: Paul commands the church to hold what it received from him, whether orally or by letter. The authority is apostolic teaching, not the bare age or unwritten form of a later custom. Read the command with the completed apostolic witness. It doesn’t establish that any practice called tradition can be placed beyond examination by Scripture.
studies.distinction: The authority of a genuine apostle doesn’t pass automatically to every later claim of continuity with him.
studies.question: What identifies the teaching to be held, and how would you test a later claim to teach the same thing?

books.name: 1 Timothy
books.intro: Paul instructs Timothy about doctrine and conduct in the household of God. Qualifications for officers and directions for worship protect the church's witness. Read the practical instructions in light of the truth the church is called to uphold.
books.introText: Paul instructs Timothy about doctrine and conduct in the household of God. Qualifications for officers and directions for worship protect the church's witness. Read the practical instructions in light of the truth the church is called to uphold.

helps.text: Paul writes after his first Roman imprisonment, probably from Macedonia around AD 62 to 64. Timothy is in Ephesus.
helps.html: Paul writes after his first Roman imprisonment, probably from Macedonia around AD 62 to 64. Timothy is in Ephesus.

helps.text: The warning against false teachers (chapter 1) sets the tone. Some have departed from the faith and are teaching speculations.
helps.html: The warning against false teachers (chapter 1) sets the tone. Some have departed from the faith and are teaching speculations.

helps.text: Paul’s testimony of grace (1.12 to 17) is one of the moving passages of the letter.
helps.html: Paul’s testimony of grace (1.12 to 17) is one of the moving passages of the letter.

helps.text: The instructions on prayer (chapter 2) include praying for kings and for all to come to the truth. The truth is in Christ the one mediator.
helps.html: The instructions on prayer (chapter 2) include praying for kings and for all to come to the truth. The truth is in Christ the one mediator.

helps.text: The qualifications for overseers (3.1 to 7) and deacons (3.8 to 13) are detailed and serious. Reformed Presbyterians take these as binding for ordination.
helps.html: The qualifications for overseers (3.1 to 7) and deacons (3.8 to 13) are detailed and serious. Reformed Presbyterians take these as binding for ordination.

helps.text: The mystery of godliness (3.16) is a creedal statement about Christ.
helps.html: The mystery of godliness (3.16) is a creedal statement about Christ.

helps.text: The departure from the faith (chapter 4) is foretold for later times. Paul instructs Timothy to be nourished on the words of the faith.
helps.html: The departure from the faith (chapter 4) is foretold for later times. Paul instructs Timothy to be nourished on the words of the faith.

helps.text: First Timothy 5 addresses the care of widows and the treatment of elders. The directions concerning servants begin in chapter 6. Observe the conditions Paul places on congregational support rather than making the church responsible for every form of need indiscriminately.
helps.html: First Timothy 5 addresses the care of widows and the treatment of elders. The directions concerning servants begin in chapter 6. Observe the conditions Paul places on congregational support rather than making the church responsible for every form of need indiscriminately.

helps.text: The love of money (chapter 6) is a root of all kinds of evils. Godliness with contentment is great gain.
helps.html: The love of money (chapter 6) is a root of all kinds of evils. Godliness with contentment is great gain.

helps.text: The closing exhortation (6.11 to 16) is one of the great charges of the New Testament. Flee. Pursue. Fight. Take hold of eternal life.
helps.html: The closing exhortation (6.11 to 16) is one of the great charges of the New Testament. Flee. Pursue. Fight. Take hold of eternal life.

studies.title: The scope of prayer and the one Mediator
studies.html: Paul urges prayer extending even to rulers and grounds the appeal in the one God and one Mediator. Read comprehensive expressions within this argument rather than treating a single word as a complete theory of election. Scripture distinguishes God’s command to repent and the gospel’s indiscriminate call from His decree concerning whom He effectually brings to faith. None may be excluded from prayer or the gospel because of rank or background.
studies.distinction: The revealed duty to pray and evangelize widely doesn’t establish that every individual will be saved.
studies.question: Why are kings specifically named, and how does the one Mediator answer a narrow view of the gospel’s reach?

studies.title: Office qualifications concern stewardship, not superiority
studies.html: Paul requires a tested character and ability appropriate to office in God’s household. The qualifications aren’t merely an employment profile for an efficient organization. They serve the church’s spiritual care and witness. Read requirements about family conduct according to their purpose, and don’t assume that authority makes an officer immune from the discipline or accountability the same letter establishes.
studies.distinction: An appointed office is a ministry under Christ’s Word, not a claim that its holder is above that Word.
studies.question: How do the household comparisons explain the spiritual purpose of the qualifications?

books.name: 2 Timothy
books.intro: Near the end of his ministry, Paul urges Timothy to guard the gospel and endure suffering. Scripture equips God's servant, and faithful preaching remains his charge. Paul's hope rests in Christ rather than the apparent success of his circumstances.
books.introText: Near the end of his ministry, Paul urges Timothy to guard the gospel and endure suffering. Scripture equips God's servant, and faithful preaching remains his charge. Paul's hope rests in Christ rather than the apparent success of his circumstances.

helps.text: Paul writes from his second Roman imprisonment, probably around AD 67. He expects to die soon.
helps.html: Paul writes from his second Roman imprisonment, probably around AD 67. He expects to die soon.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) calls Timothy to fan into flame the gift God has given him. Don't be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) calls Timothy to fan into flame the gift God has given him. Don't be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul.

helps.text: The pattern of teaching is to be entrusted to faithful men who can teach others (2.2). Four generations of discipleship are in view.
helps.html: The pattern of teaching is to be entrusted to faithful men who can teach others (2.2). Four generations of discipleship are in view.

helps.text: Read all of the faithful saying in 2 Timothy 2.11 to 13. Christ's faithfulness includes keeping His promises and His warnings. Verse 13 can't be used to cancel the preceding warning about denying Him.
helps.html: Read all of the faithful saying in 2 Timothy 2.11 to 13. Christ's faithfulness includes keeping His promises and His warnings. Verse 13 can't be used to cancel the preceding warning about denying Him.

helps.text: The last days (chapter 3) are described as times of difficulty. Lovers of self, money, pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power.
helps.html: The last days (chapter 3) are described as times of difficulty. Lovers of self, money, pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power.

helps.text: The Scripture passage (3.14 to 17) declares that all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable. This is a foundational text for the Reformed doctrine of Scripture, undergirding both inspiration (WCF 1.2 to 3) and sufficiency (WCF 1.6).
helps.html: The Scripture passage (3.14 to 17) declares that all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable. This is a foundational text for the Reformed doctrine of Scripture, undergirding both inspiration (WCF 1.2 to 3) and sufficiency (WCF 1.6).

helps.text: The charge (4.1 to 5) is one of the strongest in the New Testament. Preach the word. Be ready in season and out of season.
helps.html: The charge (4.1 to 5) is one of the strongest in the New Testament. Preach the word. Be ready in season and out of season.

helps.text: The personal farewell (4.6 to 8) is moving. Paul has fought the good fight. He has finished the race. The crown of righteousness awaits.
helps.html: The personal farewell (4.6 to 8) is moving. Paul has fought the good fight. He has finished the race. The crown of righteousness awaits.

helps.text: Personal notes about coats and parchments (4.9 to 22) ground the letter in the real life of the apostle. He needed his cloak before winter.
helps.html: Personal notes about coats and parchments (4.9 to 22) ground the letter in the real life of the apostle. He needed his cloak before winter.

studies.title: Scripture equips the servant through its own teaching
studies.html: Timothy knows the sacred writings from childhood, and Paul declares Scripture to be God-breathed and profitable for the work of instruction and correction. The immediate reference includes the Old Testament. The wider apostolic witness also recognizes New Testament writings as Scripture. The doctrine concerns the divine source and authority of the writings, not merely the strength of a reader’s experience of them.
studies.distinction: Illumination helps us receive an already authoritative Word. It doesn’t turn an otherwise human text into God’s Word for one reader.
studies.question: What uses of Scripture follow from its divine origin, and what purpose do those uses serve?

studies.title: Christ’s faithfulness includes the truth of His warnings
studies.html: The faithful saying speaks of living with Christ, enduring, denying Him, and His enduring faithfulness. Verse 13 cannot be isolated to cancel verse 12. Christ doesn’t become false to His character or promises when a human profession fails. His faithfulness comforts His people and also establishes the seriousness of His judgment against denial.
studies.distinction: A promise of divine faithfulness isn’t a declaration that persistent unbelief has no consequence.
studies.question: What reading of verse 13 would directly contradict the preceding warning, and why must it be rejected?

books.name: Titus
books.intro: Paul charges Titus to appoint qualified elders and teach conduct that agrees with sound doctrine. God's grace saves His people and trains them to live godly lives. Good works follow mercy rather than earning it.
books.introText: Paul charges Titus to appoint qualified elders and teach conduct that agrees with sound doctrine. God's grace saves His people and trains them to live godly lives. Good works follow mercy rather than earning it.

helps.text: Paul writes between his Roman imprisonments, probably around AD 62 to 64, to Titus on Crete.
helps.html: Paul writes between his Roman imprisonments, probably around AD 62 to 64, to Titus on Crete.

helps.text: The opening (1.1 to 4) is unusually theological for a brief letter. Paul grounds his ministry in election and the hope of eternal life.
helps.html: The opening (1.1 to 4) is unusually theological for a brief letter. Paul grounds his ministry in election and the hope of eternal life.

helps.text: The qualifications for elders (1.5 to 9) are similar to 1 Timothy. They include character, family, and the ability to teach sound doctrine.
helps.html: The qualifications for elders (1.5 to 9) are similar to 1 Timothy. They include character, family, and the ability to teach sound doctrine.

helps.text: The condemnation of false teachers (1.10 to 16) names the Cretan tendency to lying. Even one of their own poets had said it.
helps.html: The condemnation of false teachers (1.10 to 16) names the Cretan tendency to lying. Even one of their own poets had said it.

helps.text: The household instructions (2.1 to 10) cover older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves. Each group has its own teaching, with the goal that the gospel be adorned.
helps.html: The household instructions (2.1 to 10) cover older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves. Each group has its own teaching, with the goal that the gospel be adorned.

helps.text: Titus 2.11 to 14 is one of the most beautiful summaries of the gospel. The grace of God has appeared, training us, while we wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.
helps.html: Titus 2.11 to 14 is one of the most beautiful summaries of the gospel. The grace of God has appeared, training us, while we wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

helps.text: Titus 3.1 to 7 moves from public conduct to God's saving mercy. The washing of regeneration describes the Spirit's renewing work. Read it with the sacramental distinctions in WCF 28 rather than inferring that the outward application of water automatically gives new life.
helps.html: Titus 3.1 to 7 moves from public conduct to God's saving mercy. The washing of regeneration describes the Spirit's renewing work. Read it with the sacramental distinctions in WCF 28 rather than inferring that the outward application of water automatically gives new life.

helps.text: The faithful saying (3.4 to 7) is a creedal summary. He saved us according to His mercy by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.
helps.html: The faithful saying (3.4 to 7) is a creedal summary. He saved us according to His mercy by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.

helps.text: Paul calls Titus to insist on these things so that those who believe will devote themselves to good works.
helps.html: Paul calls Titus to insist on these things so that those who believe will devote themselves to good works.

studies.title: Grace has a teaching purpose
studies.html: Paul moves from the appearing of saving grace to its instruction in godly life and the expectation of Christ’s glory. Christ gives Himself to redeem and purify a people zealous for good works. The purification is one purpose of redemption, not an optional improvement added by unusually serious Christians. Yet its position in the argument keeps obedience from becoming the purchase price of grace.
studies.distinction: The necessity of sanctification doesn’t make sanctification the ground of justification.
studies.question: Which purpose clauses explain what Christ intends His redeemed people to become?

studies.title: Renewal by the Spirit is not merit or automatic water efficacy
studies.html: The saving contrast is between former corruption and God’s mercy, expressly excluding works of righteousness as its cause. The washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost describe the divine renewal through which sinners receive life. Any sacramental connection must preserve that agency. WCF 28 refuses both contempt for baptism and the claim that everyone baptized is undoubtedly regenerate.
studies.distinction: A washing expression doesn’t authorize replacing the Spirit’s saving work with a mechanically effective outward act.
studies.question: What does Paul exclude as the cause of salvation, and to whom does he attribute renewal?

books.name: Philemon
books.intro: Paul appeals to Philemon concerning Onesimus, whom he has come to regard as a son in the faith. The details of Onesimus's departure aren't fully explained. The central request is that Philemon receive him as a beloved brother in Christ.
books.introText: Paul appeals to Philemon concerning Onesimus, whom he has come to regard as a son in the faith. The details of Onesimus's departure aren't fully explained. The central request is that Philemon receive him as a beloved brother in Christ.

helps.text: Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 60 to 62. The letter is brief and personal.
helps.html: Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 60 to 62. The letter is brief and personal.

helps.text: Onesimus was separated from Philemon and came to Paul. A flight from slavery is a common reconstruction, but the letter doesn't give all the circumstances. Build your interpretation on Paul's explicit appeal rather than an imagined backstory.
helps.html: Onesimus was separated from Philemon and came to Paul. A flight from slavery is a common reconstruction, but the letter doesn't give all the circumstances. Build your interpretation on Paul's explicit appeal rather than an imagined backstory.

helps.text: Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a beloved brother.
helps.html: Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a beloved brother.

helps.text: Paul doesn't command Philemon, though he could. He appeals on the basis of love.
helps.html: Paul doesn't command Philemon, though he could. He appeals on the basis of love.

helps.text: Paul offers to bear any debt Onesimus owes in verses 18 to 19. This can illustrate costly intercession, but Paul doesn't identify himself as a formal type of Christ.
helps.html: Paul offers to bear any debt Onesimus owes in verses 18 to 19. This can illustrate costly intercession, but Paul doesn't identify himself as a formal type of Christ.

helps.text: The principle in the letter is that the gospel transforms every human relationship. Master and slave become brothers in Christ.
helps.html: The principle in the letter is that the gospel transforms every human relationship. Master and slave become brothers in Christ.

helps.text: The letter requires Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother. It doesn't provide a full treatment of slavery as an institution. Follow the actual obligations Paul places upon a Christian master rather than making the letter endorse exploitation.
helps.html: The letter requires Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother. It doesn't provide a full treatment of slavery as an institution. Follow the actual obligations Paul places upon a Christian master rather than making the letter endorse exploitation.

helps.text: The personal greetings (verses 23 to 24) include several names familiar from Colossians. The two letters were sent together with Onesimus and Tychicus.
helps.html: The personal greetings (verses 23 to 24) include several names familiar from Colossians. The two letters were sent together with Onesimus and Tychicus.

helps.text: The letter shows Paul’s pastoral skill. He wins his case by appeal, not by command.
helps.html: The letter shows Paul’s pastoral skill. He wins his case by appeal, not by command.

studies.title: The appeal changes the relation between master and servant
studies.html: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother, and he makes the request in view of their fellowship in Christ. The letter doesn’t give a complete institutional treatment of slavery or explain every circumstance of Onesimus’s departure. Its explicit appeal nevertheless places a demanding claim upon how a Christian receives another believer. An incomplete treatment isn’t the same thing as permission for exploitation.
studies.distinction: Do not make a reconstruction of the missing history more authoritative than the obligations Paul actually states.
studies.question: Which requested change is explicit, and which details about the departure remain a reconstruction?

studies.title: An illustration of costly intercession is not a new proof of atonement
studies.html: Paul’s willingness to accept a debt can illustrate a mediator’s costly appeal. The literal claim concerns an actual possible obligation between these people. The doctrine of Christ’s satisfaction is established by passages that teach His saving work directly. The illustration may make that doctrine vivid, but it doesn’t establish every feature of penal substitution by itself.
studies.distinction: A moving analogy is subordinate to explicit biblical teaching and mustn’t be made to prove more than it can.
studies.question: State Paul’s actual offer, then distinguish it from the greater saving act taught in Isaiah 53.

books.name: Hebrews
books.intro: Hebrews calls its hearers to hold fast to Christ, the final revelation of God and the sufficient High Priest. Its human author isn't named. Its exposition and warnings show why returning to the shadows cannot supply what Christ alone has accomplished.
books.introText: Hebrews calls its hearers to hold fast to Christ, the final revelation of God and the sufficient High Priest. Its human author isn't named. Its exposition and warnings show why returning to the shadows cannot supply what Christ alone has accomplished.

helps.text: The warning passages (2.1 to 4, 3.7 to 4.13, 6.1 to 8, 10.26 to 31, 12.25 to 29) call hearers to persevere in the faith.
helps.html: The warning passages (2.1 to 4, 3.7 to 4.13, 6.1 to 8, 10.26 to 31, 12.25 to 29) call hearers to persevere in the faith.

helps.text: The author of Hebrews isn't named. John Owen defended Pauline authorship, while Calvin judged that the letter wasn't written by Paul. Historic Reformed interpreters were already divided. The book's authority rests on its inspiration, not on resolving that question.
helps.html: The author of Hebrews isn't named. John Owen defended Pauline authorship, while Calvin judged that the letter wasn't written by Paul. Historic Reformed interpreters were already divided. The book's authority rests on its inspiration, not on resolving that question.

helps.text: The hearers know the Old Testament deeply and face pressure to turn away from Christ. A predominantly Jewish-Christian audience is a reasonable inference. The precise location and circumstances aren't named.
helps.html: The hearers know the Old Testament deeply and face pressure to turn away from Christ. A predominantly Jewish-Christian audience is a reasonable inference. The precise location and circumstances aren't named.

helps.text: The opening (1.1 to 4) declares Christ to be the final Word of God, the radiance of the divine glory, and the heir of all things.
helps.html: The opening (1.1 to 4) declares Christ to be the final Word of God, the radiance of the divine glory, and the heir of all things.

helps.text: The supremacy of Christ over angels (1.5 to 2.18) and over Moses (3.1 to 6) sets up the case.
helps.html: The supremacy of Christ over angels (1.5 to 2.18) and over Moses (3.1 to 6) sets up the case.

helps.text: The rest passages (3.7 to 4.13) read Psalm 95 as still calling believers to enter God’s rest. The rest of God remains for the people of God. The Sabbath rest of Genesis 2 and the Lord’s Day of the new covenant are weekly anticipations of the eternal rest yet to come (4.9 to 10).
helps.html: The rest passages (3.7 to 4.13) read Psalm 95 as still calling believers to enter God’s rest. The rest of God remains for the people of God. The Sabbath rest of Genesis 2 and the Lord’s Day of the new covenant are weekly anticipations of the eternal rest yet to come (4.9 to 10).

helps.text: The high priesthood of Christ after the order of Melchizedek (4.14 to 7.28) is unique to Hebrews. Christ is a priest in a different line, eternal and effective. The threefold office of Christ as Prophet, Priest, and King is displayed especially here. As Priest, He intercedes for His people forever.
helps.html: The high priesthood of Christ after the order of Melchizedek (4.14 to 7.28) is unique to Hebrews. Christ is a priest in a different line, eternal and effective. The threefold office of Christ as Prophet, Priest, and King is displayed especially here. As Priest, He intercedes for His people forever.

helps.text: The new covenant (chapters 8 to 9) is better than the old. The blood of Christ obtains eternal redemption.
helps.html: The new covenant (chapters 8 to 9) is better than the old. The blood of Christ obtains eternal redemption.

helps.text: Hebrews 10 distinguishes Christ's sufficient sacrifice from the repeated offerings that could not remove sin. The warnings that follow expose the danger of rejecting the only Savior. They aren't teaching that an ordinary fall into sin makes repentance impossible.
helps.html: Hebrews 10 distinguishes Christ's sufficient sacrifice from the repeated offerings that could not remove sin. The warnings that follow expose the danger of rejecting the only Savior. They aren't teaching that an ordinary fall into sin makes repentance impossible.

helps.text: The race set before us (chapter 12) calls for endurance, looking to Jesus. The closing exhortations (chapter 13) are practical.
helps.html: The race set before us (chapter 12) calls for endurance, looking to Jesus. The closing exhortations (chapter 13) are practical.

helps.text: Warnings against apostasy are addressed to the visible congregation. God uses them to preserve His elect in faith. Distinguish a deliberate rejection of Christ from a believer who grieves over sin and seeks His mercy.
helps.html: Warnings against apostasy are addressed to the visible congregation. God uses them to preserve His elect in faith. Distinguish a deliberate rejection of Christ from a believer who grieves over sin and seeks His mercy.

studies.title: Perfected by one offering while being renewed in holiness
studies.html: The repeated sacrifices couldn’t remove guilt, but Christ’s one offering establishes a lasting acceptance for His people. The passage also identifies them in relation to sanctification. The finality of the sacrifice mustn’t be confused with completed moral perfection in this life. Nor may ongoing growth be used to make the sacrifice an unfinished transaction needing our merit to complete it.
studies.distinction: A sufficient atonement and incomplete present sanctification answer different questions and belong together in Christ.
studies.question: How do the repeated offerings, Christ’s seated position, and the covenant quotation establish the finality of His work?

studies.title: The severe warning protects the only refuge
studies.html: The warning describes grave apostasy after extensive participation in the privileges of the covenant community. The following words express confidence of better things accompanying salvation in the hearers. Read that distinction with the promise of God’s preserving grace and the repeated commands to draw near through Christ. The passage must neither be emptied of danger nor used to drive a repentant sinner away from the only Savior.
studies.distinction: A refusal of Christ after great privilege is not identical with every grievous fall of a believer who seeks His mercy.
studies.question: What distinction does verse 9 introduce, and how do the exhortations direct the congregation to perseverance?

books.name: James
books.intro: James addresses professing believers whose conduct must agree with their faith. His teaching echoes biblical wisdom and Christ's instruction about the heart. The letter exposes empty profession without making good works the ground of justification.
books.introText: James addresses professing believers whose conduct must agree with their faith. His teaching echoes biblical wisdom and Christ's instruction about the heart. The letter exposes empty profession without making good works the ground of justification.

helps.text: The famous "faith without works is dead" (2.17, 26) isn't a contradiction of Paul. Both apostles teach the same gospel from different angles.
helps.html: The famous "faith without works is dead" (2.17, 26) isn't a contradiction of Paul. Both apostles teach the same gospel from different angles.

helps.text: James, the half-brother of the Lord and the leader of the Jerusalem church, likely writes one of the earliest New Testament books, probably between AD 45 and 50.
helps.html: James, the half-brother of the Lord and the leader of the Jerusalem church, likely writes one of the earliest New Testament books, probably between AD 45 and 50.

helps.text: The audience is Jewish Christians scattered abroad, probably from the persecution after Stephen’s death.
helps.html: The audience is Jewish Christians scattered abroad, probably from the persecution after Stephen’s death.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) covers trials, asking for wisdom, and the danger of being a hearer only.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) covers trials, asking for wisdom, and the danger of being a hearer only.

helps.text: The royal law of love (chapter 2) is set against partiality. Treating the rich better than the poor breaks the law.
helps.html: The royal law of love (chapter 2) is set against partiality. Treating the rich better than the poor breaks the law.

helps.text: Faith and works (2.14 to 26) deals with the kind of faith that justifies. James and Paul aren't in conflict. Paul says works don't justify before God. James says faith without works isn't genuine faith.
helps.html: Faith and works (2.14 to 26) deals with the kind of faith that justifies. James and Paul aren't in conflict. Paul says works don't justify before God. James says faith without works isn't genuine faith.

helps.text: The tongue (chapter 3) is a small fire. The teacher is held to a higher standard. The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, and gentle.
helps.html: The tongue (chapter 3) is a small fire. The teacher is held to a higher standard. The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, and gentle.

helps.text: Quarrels and worldliness (chapter 4) come from desires within. Submit to God. Resist the devil.
helps.html: Quarrels and worldliness (chapter 4) come from desires within. Submit to God. Resist the devil.

helps.text: Warnings to the rich (chapter 5) echo the prophets. Their wealth is corroded as a witness against them.
helps.html: Warnings to the rich (chapter 5) echo the prophets. Their wealth is corroded as a witness against them.

helps.text: The closing chapter covers patience under suffering, prayer for the sick (anointing with oil and the prayer of faith), and the recovery of a wandering brother.
helps.html: The closing chapter covers patience under suffering, prayer for the sick (anointing with oil and the prayer of faith), and the recovery of a wandering brother.

studies.title: Living faith is vindicated by the works it produces
studies.html: James asks whether a claimed faith without deeds can save and illustrates its emptiness through neglected need. His appeal to Abraham’s offering of Isaac occurs after the righteousness credited in Genesis 15. Paul’s argument excludes works as the ground of God’s verdict. James exposes a profession whose fruit shows it isn’t living trust. Their different questions must be established from context, not resolved by making either apostle say less than he does.
studies.distinction: Faith alone receives Christ, but the faith that receives Him does not remain alone without its appointed fruit.
studies.question: How do the timing of Genesis 15 and Genesis 22 and James’s opening question clarify his argument?

studies.title: Temptation does not make God the author of sin
studies.html: James distinguishes enduring trial from being drawn into evil by one’s own lust. God’s good gifts and unchanging character rule out charging Him with moral enticement. Scripture elsewhere confesses His government over all events, including trials. The distinction concerns His holy agency and the creature’s sinful desire, not a region of life that has escaped His providence.
studies.distinction: God’s sovereign government doesn’t make Him morally culpable for the evil a creature desires and commits.
studies.question: Trace the sequence from desire to sin and death, then compare it with God’s described giving and begetting.

books.name: 1 Peter
books.intro: Peter writes to believers in Asia Minor who face hostility as strangers in the world. Their inheritance in Christ grounds a holy life under pressure. Christ's sufferings teach them both where salvation rests and how to endure wrong without retaliation.
books.introText: Peter writes to believers in Asia Minor who face hostility as strangers in the world. Their inheritance in Christ grounds a holy life under pressure. Christ's sufferings teach them both where salvation rests and how to endure wrong without retaliation.

helps.text: Peter writes from "Babylon" (likely Rome, code for the empire) around AD 62 to 64, before Nero’s persecution erupts.
helps.html: Peter writes from "Babylon" (likely Rome, code for the empire) around AD 62 to 64, before Nero’s persecution erupts.

helps.text: The audience is scattered believers in Asia Minor under social and possibly state pressure.
helps.html: The audience is scattered believers in Asia Minor under social and possibly state pressure.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) gives one of the great descriptions of the believer’s hope. Born again to a living hope. An inheritance kept for them.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) gives one of the great descriptions of the believer’s hope. Born again to a living hope. An inheritance kept for them.

helps.text: The call to holiness (1.13 to 25) flows from the redemption Christ has worked.
helps.html: The call to holiness (1.13 to 25) flows from the redemption Christ has worked.

helps.text: Believers are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation (2.9). The language is taken from Exodus and applied to the church.
helps.html: Believers are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation (2.9). The language is taken from Exodus and applied to the church.

helps.text: Submission to authorities (chapter 2) covers government, masters, and the example of Christ in His suffering.
helps.html: Submission to authorities (chapter 2) covers government, masters, and the example of Christ in His suffering.

helps.text: Marriage (chapter 3) addresses both wives and husbands, with special attention to wives whose husbands don't believe.
helps.html: Marriage (chapter 3) addresses both wives and husbands, with special attention to wives whose husbands don't believe.

helps.text: One longstanding interpretation of 1 Peter 3.18 to 20 understands Christ preaching by His Spirit through Noah to people now under judgment. Other interpretations exist, including among Reformed writers. The Westminster Standards don't settle every detail of this passage. Compare it with their teaching on Christ's death and the state of souls after death.
helps.html: One longstanding interpretation of 1 Peter 3.18 to 20 understands Christ preaching by His Spirit through Noah to people now under judgment. Other interpretations exist, including among Reformed writers. The Westminster Standards don't settle every detail of this passage. Compare it with their teaching on Christ's death and the state of souls after death.

helps.text: Chapter 4 calls for living for the will of God, not the passions of the flesh. Suffering for Christ should be expected.
helps.html: Chapter 4 calls for living for the will of God, not the passions of the flesh. Suffering for Christ should be expected.

helps.text: The closing (chapter 5) addresses elders and the whole church. Cast all your anxieties on Him. Resist the devil. The God of all grace will Himself restore you.
helps.html: The closing (chapter 5) addresses elders and the whole church. Cast all your anxieties on Him. Resist the devil. The God of all grace will Himself restore you.

studies.title: Baptism’s saving language is explained by Christ’s resurrection
studies.html: Peter connects Noah’s deliverance and baptism, then expressly distinguishes baptism from washing dirt off the body and relates it to a good conscience toward God through Christ’s resurrection. The inward reality and the risen Savior govern the passage. Its strong sacramental language mustn’t be reduced to an empty sign or expanded into automatic regeneration by water.
studies.distinction: The passage itself distinguishes outward washing from the saving reality to which baptism is joined.
studies.question: Which qualifying phrases prevent treating baptism here as merely a physical cleansing action?

studies.title: Christ’s suffering is both substitution and pattern
studies.html: Peter calls believers to endure wrong without retaliatory sin and grounds the instruction in Christ’s example. He also says Christ bore our sins and speaks of healing through His wounds. The same paragraph distinguishes His unique saving work from the conduct His followers imitate. Submission never changes a wrongdoer’s evil into righteousness or abolishes the magistrate’s duty to judge wrongdoing.
studies.distinction: Following the suffering Savior does not mean performing another atonement or declaring injustice morally acceptable.
studies.question: Which statements concern Christ’s unrepeatable work, and which direct the believer’s conduct?

books.name: 2 Peter
books.intro: Peter prepares believers to remain steadfast after his death. Apostolic testimony and the prophetic Word answer deceptive teachers and scoffers. The certainty of Christ's return calls the church to patient, holy living.
books.introText: Peter prepares believers to remain steadfast after his death. Apostolic testimony and the prophetic Word answer deceptive teachers and scoffers. The certainty of Christ's return calls the church to patient, holy living.

helps.text: Peter writes shortly before his death, probably around AD 65 to 67.
helps.html: Peter writes shortly before his death, probably around AD 65 to 67.

helps.text: The opening (chapter 1) calls believers to make their calling and election sure by adding virtue to faith and so on. The list builds the Christian character.
helps.html: The opening (chapter 1) calls believers to make their calling and election sure by adding virtue to faith and so on. The list builds the Christian character.

helps.text: The eyewitness testimony to Christ’s transfiguration (1.16 to 18) and the prophetic word (1.19 to 21) ground the apostle’s authority.
helps.html: The eyewitness testimony to Christ’s transfiguration (1.16 to 18) and the prophetic word (1.19 to 21) ground the apostle’s authority.

helps.text: The warning against false teachers (chapter 2) is severe. They will bring destructive heresies. Their judgment is sure.
helps.html: The warning against false teachers (chapter 2) is severe. They will bring destructive heresies. Their judgment is sure.

helps.text: The examples of judgment (the angels, the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah) show that God knows how to deliver the godly and judge the ungodly.
helps.html: The examples of judgment (the angels, the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah) show that God knows how to deliver the godly and judge the ungodly.

helps.text: The scoffers (3.3 to 4) say "Where is the promise of his coming?" Peter’s answer is that the Lord is patient, not slow.
helps.html: The scoffers (3.3 to 4) say "Where is the promise of his coming?" Peter’s answer is that the Lord is patient, not slow.

helps.text: Second Peter 3 describes the day of the Lord and the promised new heavens and new earth. Read it with Romans 8.18 to 23. The renewal of creation is a strong Reformed reading, but the precise nature of the fiery judgment should be argued from the passages. WLC 90 doesn't explicitly define that process.
helps.html: Second Peter 3 describes the day of the Lord and the promised new heavens and new earth. Read it with Romans 8.18 to 23. The renewal of creation is a strong Reformed reading, but the precise nature of the fiery judgment should be argued from the passages. WLC 90 doesn't explicitly define that process.

helps.text: The application (3.11 to 18) is moral. What kind of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness?
helps.html: The application (3.11 to 18) is moral. What kind of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness?

helps.text: Peter mentions Paul’s letters (3.15 to 16) as Scripture, alongside the other Scriptures. This is one of the early indicators of the canon forming.
helps.html: Peter mentions Paul’s letters (3.15 to 16) as Scripture, alongside the other Scriptures. This is one of the early indicators of the canon forming.

studies.title: Diligence confirms a calling it does not purchase
studies.html: Peter begins with divine provision and then urges growth in the graces of Christian life. Making calling and election sure concerns the confirmation of a gracious reality through its fruits. It doesn’t turn eternal election into a reward for later moral success. Read the exhortation as a serious means of assurance and perseverance, not a competing account of how grace originates.
studies.distinction: Evidence of election mustn’t be confused with its cause.
studies.question: What divine provision precedes the command to give diligence, and what does the resulting fruit confirm?

studies.title: Patience does not mean the promised day has failed
studies.html: Scoffers treat the apparent delay as evidence against Christ’s return. Peter answers with God’s different relation to time, His patience, and the certainty of judgment. The statement concerning a thousand years isn’t a formula for calculating the world’s final week. Its function is to rebuke measuring divine faithfulness by our timetable and to direct us toward repentance and holy conduct.
studies.distinction: An analogy about God’s relation to time cannot be turned into an inspired date-conversion chart.
studies.question: What objection does Peter answer, and what conduct does his answer require?

books.name: 1 John
books.intro: John gives assurance to believers while exposing false claims about Christ and the Christian life. His themes return throughout the letter. Read the tests of faith alongside his teaching about remaining sin and Christ's advocacy.
books.introText: John gives assurance to believers while exposing false claims about Christ and the Christian life. His themes return throughout the letter. Read the tests of faith alongside his teaching about remaining sin and Christ's advocacy.

helps.text: John writes late in the first century, probably in the 80s or 90s, from Ephesus to nearby churches.
helps.html: John writes late in the first century, probably in the 80s or 90s, from Ephesus to nearby churches.

helps.text: The false teachers had left the church (2.19) and were teaching that Christ wasn't truly in the flesh. John writes to root the church in the truth.
helps.html: The false teachers had left the church (2.19) and were teaching that Christ wasn't truly in the flesh. John writes to root the church in the truth.

helps.text: The opening (1.1 to 4) is a witness to the incarnation. We've heard, seen, looked upon, and touched.
helps.html: The opening (1.1 to 4) is a witness to the incarnation. We've heard, seen, looked upon, and touched.

helps.text: The light passages (1.5 to 2.2) call believers to walk in the light. If we say we've no sin we lie. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive.
helps.html: The light passages (1.5 to 2.2) call believers to walk in the light. If we say we've no sin we lie. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive.

helps.text: The tests of true profession run through the book. Right doctrine about Christ. Obedience to His commandments. Love for the brethren.
helps.html: The tests of true profession run through the book. Right doctrine about Christ. Obedience to His commandments. Love for the brethren.

helps.text: First John 2.15 to 17 forbids love for the world's sinful desires and pride. It doesn't forbid loving people or receiving created gifts with thanksgiving.
helps.html: First John 2.15 to 17 forbids love for the world's sinful desires and pride. It doesn't forbid loving people or receiving created gifts with thanksgiving.

helps.text: John speaks both of antichrist and of many antichrists in 1 John 2.18. Notice how he identifies the deceivers by their denial of the Father and the Son.
helps.html: John speaks both of antichrist and of many antichrists in 1 John 2.18. Notice how he identifies the deceivers by their denial of the Father and the Son.

helps.text: Read the strong statements about sin in chapter 3 alongside 1 John 1.8 to 2.2. New birth breaks sin's dominion without making a believer sinless in this life. John gives no permission to excuse a settled refusal to repent.
helps.html: Read the strong statements about sin in chapter 3 alongside 1 John 1.8 to 2.2. New birth breaks sin's dominion without making a believer sinless in this life. John gives no permission to excuse a settled refusal to repent.

helps.text: The love passages (chapter 4) climax in "God is love." Whoever doesn't love doesn't know God.
helps.html: The love passages (chapter 4) climax in "God is love." Whoever doesn't love doesn't know God.

helps.text: The assurance passages (chapter 5) close the book. We can know that we've eternal life. The book is written so that we may know.
helps.html: The assurance passages (chapter 5) close the book. We can know that we've eternal life. The book is written so that we may know.

studies.title: New birth breaks sin’s rule without producing present sinlessness
studies.html: John’s strong statements about sin must be read with 1 John 1.8 to 2.2, where believers acknowledge remaining sin and have an Advocate in Christ. The new life cannot make peace with sin as its governing pattern. Neither the letter’s warnings nor its provision for confession should be used to cancel the other.
studies.distinction: A settled refusal to repent and the grievous falls of a believer fighting sin are not the same condition.
studies.question: What would become contradictory if chapter 3 were taken to mean that a regenerate person never commits any sin?

studies.title: The tests confirm faith without replacing its object
