metadata.subtitle: A Layman’s Companion for Reading and Understanding Scripture

sources.title: Directory for the Publick Worship of God
Calvin on the authorship of Hebrews

examples.title: A metaphor that tells the truth
examples.question: Does calling Christ a door deny a real truth about Him?
steps: Read the words
Jesus is speaking about shepherds, sheep, and entry into safety. Calling Himself a door belongs to that sustained comparison.
Establish the meaning
A door is a figure for access. Christ is teaching that salvation and safety are found through Him. He is not describing His body as a wooden object.
Follow the consequence
Reading the figure as a figure receives the truth Christ intends. Figurative language does not mean an unreal Savior or an uncertain promise.
Apply it
Rest upon Christ as the only entrance to salvation. Do not turn the image into permission to invent additional ways of coming to God.

examples.title: Two commands that seem opposite
examples.question: Should you answer a fool or refuse to answer?
steps: Read both sayings
Verse 4 warns against becoming like a fool. Verse 5 warns against leaving him wise in his own conceit. The verses stand together intentionally.
Identify the distinction
Joining a foolish argument on its own terms can make you share its folly. A measured correction can expose the error. The dangers differ.
Avoid the misreading
Neither verse supplies a universal script for every conversation. Wisdom discerns which response the circumstance requires.
Apply it
Before replying, consider whether your answer will correct an error or simply draw you into sinful contention.

examples.title: A promise in its covenant setting
examples.question: Does this promise guarantee the recovery of any modern nation?
steps: Read the setting
The Lord answers Solomon after the dedication of the temple. The surrounding words concern Israel, the temple, and judgments upon its land.
Identify the recipients
The covenant people addressed are Israel under the Mosaic administration. A modern nation cannot simply put its own name in their place.
Trace the enduring truth
God requires repentance and hears His people. Those truths continue, but the particular covenant promise about the land must retain its setting.
Apply it
Pray for national repentance and confess the sins of the church. Do not claim that a particular political recovery is guaranteed by this passage.

examples.title: A narrative that reports wrongdoing
examples.question: Does Jacob receiving the blessing make his deception righteous?
steps: Observe what happens
Jacob lies to his father while seeking the blessing. The account records what he says without issuing a moral comment after every sentence.
Compare clearer teaching
God forbids false witness. His providential use of human actions does not make those actions innocent.
Follow the story
The family conflict and separation that follow are part of the narrative. Do not turn the successful deception into a technique for obtaining blessing.
Apply it
Trust God to keep His promises through faithful means. A desired result does not justify lying.

examples.title: A warning and the promise of preservation
examples.question: If God keeps His people, why warn them against falling away?
steps: Hear the warning
The congregation is told to beware of an evil heart of unbelief and to exhort one another. The danger is addressed seriously.
Read the promise too
John 10.27 to 29 teaches that Christ keeps His sheep. Scripture does not require us to discard either this promise or the warning in Hebrews.
Recognize the means
God preserves His people through means, including these warnings and the care of fellow believers. Perseverance is active faith sustained by grace.
Apply it
Listen when Scripture exposes unbelief. Seek help and turn to Christ. A believer grieved by sin should not mistake that grief for proof that repentance is impossible.

examples.title: A symbol and a real resurrection
examples.question: Does the Lamb mean Christ is only an idea?
steps: Observe the vision
John hears of the Lion and sees a Lamb standing as though slain. The images describe the same victorious Redeemer.
Use the Bible’s connections
The sacrificial lamb belongs to the Passover and the wider biblical teaching about sacrifice. John 1.29 identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God.
Name the reality
The vision portrays the crucified and risen Christ. The picture is symbolic. His death, resurrection, and authority are real.
Apply it
Worship the Savior whose sacrifice purchased His people. Do not confuse the visual form of a vision with a denial of the event it represents.

examples.title: God relents, yet does not change His mind like a man
examples.question: Does this chapter contradict itself about God?
steps: Read the two statements together
The chapter describes the Lord’s response to Saul’s rebellion and also denies that He repents as a man. The writer places both claims in the same account.
Identify what each statement teaches
The change in God’s dealings with Saul is real. The denial concerns creaturely instability or falsehood in God. His holy response to changed human conduct fulfills His righteous rule.
Compare clearer teaching
Numbers 23.19 and James 1.17 confirm God’s truthfulness and constancy. They do not make Him indifferent to Saul’s sin.
Apply the distinction
Trust God’s unchanging character while taking His warnings seriously. Do not imagine that He discovers facts late or that an earlier blessing makes rebellion safe.

examples.title: Faith alone and a faith that works
examples.question: Does James teach the opposite of Paul about justification?
steps: Identify James’s question
James examines a claim to faith that refuses practical help and produces no corresponding deeds. He asks whether that kind of profession can save.
Identify Paul’s question
Romans 4.1 to 8 asks about the basis on which God counts a sinner righteous. Paul excludes works as the ground and describes righteousness received through faith.
Follow Abraham’s history
Genesis 15 records righteousness counted through faith. Genesis 22 later displays Abraham’s faith in costly obedience. James uses the later act as the fulfillment and expression of living trust.
Confess both truths
Christ alone supplies justifying righteousness, received through faith alone. The faith that receives Him is living and produces obedience. Works neither purchase the verdict nor become irrelevant.

examples.title: A spiritual body is still a body
examples.question: Does spiritual mean that the resurrection is nonphysical?
steps: Follow the question
Paul is answering how the dead are raised and with what body they come. His answer concerns bodily resurrection, not whether bodies can be discarded.
Read the stated contrasts
He contrasts corruption with incorruption, dishonor with glory, and weakness with power. The transformed condition explains the difference.
Use the seed comparison
The seed and the resulting plant illustrate continuity through remarkable change. Luke 24.36 to 43 confirms the bodily reality of the risen Christ.
Apply the hope
Hope for actual resurrection and freedom from corruption. Do not make spiritual a dictionary shortcut that erases Paul’s subject.

examples.title: The water, the conscience, and the risen Savior
examples.question: Does Peter say that physical washing automatically regenerates?
steps: Read Peter’s own qualification
The statement concerning baptism is immediately distinguished from removing bodily dirt and related to a good conscience toward God.
Keep Christ’s work central
The saving reality is connected with the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has suffered for sins and is exalted. Water is not presented as an independent saving agent.
Use the sacramental distinction
WCF 27.2 explains the close relation between sign and thing signified. WCF 28.5 denies that everyone baptized is undoubtedly regenerate.
Receive the ordinance rightly
Honor Christ’s appointed sign without trusting an outward act in place of Christ. Keep the grace signified and the Spirit’s effective work distinct from mere physical administration.

examples.title: An inference supplied by Christ
examples.question: Can doctrine be biblical when it follows by inference?
steps: Hear the objection
The Sadducees offer a hypothetical case intended to make resurrection absurd. Jesus corrects their ignorance of Scripture and God’s power.
Trace Christ’s reasoning
He appeals to God’s declaration concerning the patriarchs and explains that God is not the God of the dead but of the living. The conclusion is reasoned from the revealed relation.
Distinguish deduction from invention
The reasoning depends on what God declares and what that declaration entails. It is not a hidden meaning supplied by a private impression.
Apply the method
When testing a doctrinal inference, state its premises and explain why its conclusion follows. A possible association carries less authority than a necessary consequence.

examples.title: A command does not establish independent ability
examples.question: How can Christ command faith while teaching that the Father must draw?
steps: Keep the whole discourse
Jesus calls for faith and exposes unbelief. He also explains that no one can come unless the Father draws him. Both claims belong to His teaching.
Distinguish duty from enabling
A command establishes what a hearer owes. It does not establish that a fallen heart can fulfill that duty apart from grace.
Follow the saving promise
Those given to the Son come to Him, are received, and are raised at the last day. God’s work is not described as a bare opportunity that leaves His purpose uncertain.
Apply both truths
Come to Christ on the warrant of His command and promise. Thank God for enabling faith rather than waiting to discover a secret decree before obeying the gospel call.

examples.title: A warning against sacrifice without mercy
examples.question: Did Hosea cancel the sacrificial worship God had commanded?
steps: Observe the accusation
The people’s goodness passes quickly, while their outward religion continues. The Lord exposes a failure of covenant faithfulness.
Read the comparison in its setting
The preference for mercy and the knowledge of God rebukes substituting ritual for obedience. It is not a denial that God had instituted sacrifices.
Watch Christ apply it
Matthew 9.9 to 13 uses the passage to answer an accusation against receiving sinners. The application preserves the priority of mercy over a self-justifying religious judgment.
Apply without abolishing duty
Worship as God commands and show the mercy He requires. Neither duty can be offered as compensation for refusing the other.

examples.title: The Spirit’s help is not a new meaning
examples.question: Does spiritual understanding let us bypass the words and their context?
steps: Identify what the Spirit reveals
Paul speaks of God’s wisdom made known through the Spirit, in contrast with the world’s inability to receive it. Apostolic revelation and the reception of its truth must be distinguished.
Read with the rest of Paul
The same apostle supplies sustained written arguments and commands that his teaching be received. He does not replace those words with each reader’s private impressions.
Distinguish revelation and illumination
The Spirit inspired the Word and enables its saving reception. Illumination gives understanding of what God has said rather than authority to add an unrelated message.
Apply it
Pray for a submissive heart and study the passage carefully. A strong spiritual feeling still needs to be tested by Scripture.

lessons.title: What rightly dividing requires
lessons.summary: Handle the Word faithfully by following its argument and teaching what it actually says.

sections.title: Begin where Paul begins
sections.html: In 2 Timothy 2.14 to 18, Paul contrasts approved labor with disputes about words and teaching that corrupts the faith. Hymenaeus and Philetus have gone wrong by saying the resurrection has already happened. Timothy must handle the Word truthfully before God. The charge concerns faithful teaching, not the clever arrangement of an interpretive system.

sections.title: Make distinctions the text makes
sections.html: Scripture distinguishes creation from redemption, Adam from Christ, and the old administration from the new. Those distinctions matter because the passages establish them. The expression rightly dividing doesn’t by itself prove that the Bible must be separated into dispensations with different saving gospels. Nor does covenant unity permit us to erase the changes Christ has brought.

sections.title: Let careful handling become a habit
sections.html: State the author’s claim before drawing a doctrine from it. Notice the reason he gives and the error he opposes. Then ask whether your conclusion follows from his words. A true doctrine can still be badly supported by a passage that teaches something else. Learning to reject an unsuitable proof text strengthens the truth rather than weakening it.

lessons.exercise: Read 2 Timothy 2.14 to 18. What specific error shows why sound handling of Scripture matters?
lessons.answer: The named teachers say the resurrection is already past and overthrow the faith of some. Paul treats their doctrinal claim as a departure from truth. His charge calls for accurate, faithful teaching rather than fruitless verbal conflict.

lessons.title: One true sense, many faithful applications
lessons.summary: The literal sense is the meaning conveyed by the words in their literary and historical setting.

sections.title: Read what the language is doing
sections.html: When Scripture says Christ is a door, the intended sense is a metaphor concerning access and salvation. Calling that reading literal doesn’t turn Christ into timber. When Luke narrates Christ’s bodily resurrection, the intended sense is a real event. Genre and context guide the distinction. They don’t give us permission to turn an unwelcome event into a metaphor.

sections.title: Distinguish fullness from invention
sections.html: WCF 1.9 teaches one true and full sense of Scripture. A promise may disclose more as God’s plan unfolds, and a divinely appointed type may reach its fulfillment in Christ. That fuller disclosure belongs to the intention of the divine Author. It doesn’t create a second, unrelated message hidden behind the first. Later revelation clarifies earlier revelation without making it false.

sections.title: Keep application accountable
sections.html: A passage can have many applications because the same truth bears upon different lives. Psalm 23 comforts a dying believer and also a believer facing ordinary fear. Their circumstances differ, but the Lord’s faithful shepherding remains the text’s subject. A private impression about a job offer isn’t another meaning of the Psalm. Personal usefulness must remain governed by what the passage teaches.

lessons.exercise: Explain why reading Christ as a figurative door and reading His resurrection as historical are consistent.
lessons.answer: The passages use different kinds of language. John 10 supplies a sustained shepherding comparison. Luke 24 expressly describes a risen body that can be touched and can eat. Faithful interpretation receives each passage according to its intended sense.

lessons.title: Follow the paragraph before using the verse
lessons.summary: Context includes the immediate sentence, the argument of the book, and its place within the canon.

sections.title: Find the main claim
sections.html: Read the paragraph and ask what assertion holds it together. Identify its reasons, examples, and consequences. In Ephesians 2.1 to 10, the movement is from death in sin to life by grace and then to the good works God prepares. Starting with verse 10 while ignoring verses 8 to 9 would reverse Paul’s explanation of salvation and obedience.

sections.title: Attend to connecting words
sections.html: Words such as therefore, because, if, and but show relationships between ideas. A therefore asks you to recover the preceding reason. An if may name a real condition without explaining whether the power to meet it comes from human nature or grace. Don’t make a grammatical observation carry a theological conclusion the rest of the passage doesn’t establish.

sections.title: Use wider context without losing the near
sections.html: The whole Bible helps us read a sentence, but the nearest context still matters. A collection of cross-references mustn’t replace the author’s actual argument. Begin with his own words, compare genuinely related passages, and return to the original paragraph to see whether your interpretation explains it. If your reading makes a sentence interrupt or contradict the argument, reconsider it.

lessons.exercise: In Ephesians 2.8 to 10, explain the relationship between works and salvation.
lessons.answer: Works are excluded as the ground of salvation and boasting. They are then identified as the appointed fruit of God’s new creation in Christ. The same paragraph rejects both self-justification and a Christian life indifferent to obedience.

lessons.title: Use words in sentences, not as secret codes
lessons.summary: A word can have several uses. The passage determines which use is present.

sections.title: Avoid importing every possible meaning
sections.html: The word world has different uses even within John’s writings. John 3.16 and 1 John 2.15 don’t command opposite attitudes toward the same thing in the same respect. One speaks of God’s saving love in sending His Son. The other forbids attachment to the sinful desires and pride described immediately afterward. A dictionary lists possibilities. Context selects the relevant use.

sections.title: Be modest about original languages
sections.html: A concordance can help locate passages, but a Strong’s number isn’t a complete grammar or a decision about meaning. A word’s origin doesn’t settle its present use, and a Greek tense doesn’t automatically prove a repeated act or an irreversible state. Compare careful translations and consult qualified explanations before building doctrine on a claim you can’t independently assess.

sections.title: Ask what the whole sentence affirms
sections.html: Pronouns, negatives, comparisons, and the scope of a statement matter. In 1 Corinthians 15.27, Paul expressly explains the exception within all things being subject to Christ. Scripture itself shows that apparently comprehensive words must be read with their stated subject and limits. Don’t narrow a word merely to protect a system, and don’t broaden it beyond the argument.

lessons.exercise: Why is finding a possible dictionary meaning insufficient to establish the meaning of a verse?
lessons.answer: A possible meaning must fit the author’s grammar, subject, and argument. Choosing a meaning because it supports a desired conclusion bypasses the evidence that determines which use the author intends.

lessons.title: How doctrine follows from Scripture
lessons.summary: A sound inference follows from what God has revealed. It does not fill a silence with our preferences.

sections.title: Distinguish statement from consequence
sections.html: Some doctrines appear in a direct statement. Others gather truths that Scripture teaches in several places. The church’s confession of the Trinity brings together the unity of God, the deity of each Person, and their personal distinctions. The absence of the word Trinity doesn’t make the doctrine unbiblical. The question is whether the teaching follows necessarily from the revealed facts.

sections.title: Observe Christ’s own reasoning
sections.html: In Matthew 22.31 to 32, Jesus reasons about the resurrection from God’s declaration concerning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The inference depends on what the living God says about His covenant relation to them. It isn’t a free association with a similar word. Follow the premises and ask why the conclusion must follow. A conclusion that merely could be true isn’t yet a necessary consequence.

sections.title: Test the proposed deduction
sections.html: State the biblical premises plainly, then state the conclusion. Ask whether another explanation could preserve all those premises without reaching that conclusion. Where an argument depends upon an uncertain reconstruction, acknowledge that weakness. The authority belongs to God’s truth, not to the confidence of our presentation. Confessional reasoning serves the Word by making its teaching explicit.

lessons.exercise: What distinguishes a necessary consequence from a plausible suggestion?
lessons.answer: A necessary consequence is required by the revealed premises. A plausible suggestion is compatible with them but not established by them. An illustration, a silence, or a possible historical reconstruction cannot alone bear the same weight as a necessary inference.

lessons.title: Read events and stories according to their purpose
lessons.summary: History teaches through real events. Parables teach through purposeful stories. Neither should be flattened into a list of isolated lessons.

sections.title: Ask how the narrator judges an event
sections.html: A narrative may approve conduct, condemn it, or report it without an immediate comment. David’s sin with Bathsheba isn’t justified because the narrator initially tells the story without inserting a moral verdict after each action. The wider narrative and God’s law make the judgment plain. Providence brings good out of evil without turning the evil into an example to imitate.

sections.title: Read parables as directed teaching
sections.html: Ask what question or conflict prompts a parable and how its conclusion answers it. The unjust steward in Luke 16 isn’t commended for dishonesty. The comparison concerns prudence in view of what is coming. Some details establish the story’s setting without supplying a separate doctrine. Yet don’t force every parable into a rigid rule that it can communicate only one simple idea.

sections.title: Distinguish apostolic foundations from ordinary patterns
sections.html: Acts records both continuing duties and unique events in the establishment of the church. Acts 2 describes the Spirit’s outpouring and the church’s continuing attention to apostolic teaching and prayer. Determine what later apostolic instruction makes normative. Neither copying every recorded circumstance nor dismissing all narrative as merely descriptive will rightly handle the book.

lessons.exercise: How would you test a claim that an action in Acts is required of every church?
lessons.answer: Examine the narrative’s purpose and any command it contains. Compare the apostles’ directions to churches elsewhere. Distinguish an enduring duty from a circumstance or an extraordinary sign associated with the apostolic foundation.

lessons.title: Let poetry teach with precision
lessons.summary: Poetic language is purposeful and true. Wisdom often teaches judgment rather than a mechanical formula.

sections.title: Follow the image and its boundaries
sections.html: Psalm 91 uses the image of shelter beneath God’s wings. The figure teaches His protection without describing a bodily feature in God. The same Psalm was misused when Satan detached its promise from a faithful relation to God’s will. Christ answered from Scripture that we must not tempt God. A true promise doesn’t authorize a reckless experiment.

sections.title: Attend to parallel lines
sections.html: Hebrew poetic lines may reinforce, contrast, or develop one another. Proverbs 15.1 contrasts a soft answer with grievous words. The parallel helps define the conduct being discussed. Don’t assume the second line introduces an unrelated subject, and don’t press the image beyond its function. Poetry requires close reasoning about the relationship between its words.

sections.title: Distinguish kinds of wisdom claim
sections.html: Some proverbs command conduct. Some describe ordinary consequences. Some proclaim settled truths about God. Job and Ecclesiastes show why diligence must not be turned into a guarantee of wealth or suffering into proof of a particular secret sin. Reading wisdom together lets the Bible qualify the assumptions we might otherwise impose on an isolated saying.

lessons.exercise: Why does Christ reject Satan’s proposed application of Psalm 91?
lessons.answer: The proposed action would tempt God. A promise of divine care cannot be detached from the duty to trust and obey Him. Christ reads Scripture consistently with Scripture rather than making one promise cancel a clear command.

lessons.title: Trace the fulfillment God reveals
lessons.summary: Prophecy speaks into real history and may look beyond its immediate setting to Christ and the consummation.

sections.title: Identify the historical concern
sections.html: The prophets address covenant rebellion, foreign powers, coming judgment, and promised restoration. Begin there rather than with a newspaper or a modern nation you think resembles an image. A later event may illustrate a prophetic pattern without being the fulfillment of that prophecy. Resemblance is a reason to examine a claim, not a proof that the claim is true.

sections.title: Keep near and final horizons connected
sections.html: Some promises have an initial historical realization and a greater fulfillment in Christ. David’s royal promise concerns his house and reaches the enduring reign of his Son. This fullness belongs to the development of God’s own promise. It isn’t permission to invent unlimited fulfillments. Let later inspired interpretation establish how the earlier passage reaches its goal.

sections.title: Respect prophetic form
sections.html: Mountain, temple, harvest, and cosmic imagery may convey realities in the forms familiar to the first hearers. Determine from the passage and later Scripture whether an image describes an earthly event, covenantal judgment, or final consummation. Symbolic language doesn’t cancel real fulfillment. A commitment to literal meaning requires us to receive the actual prophetic language, not replace it with a timetable we brought to the text.

lessons.exercise: How can you distinguish a greater fulfillment from an invented second meaning?
lessons.answer: Show the connection within the original promise and its inspired development. A greater fulfillment completes what God promised. An invented meaning assigns a new subject without textual or canonical warrant.

lessons.title: Read visions without surrendering certainty
lessons.summary: Apocalyptic visions disclose God’s rule through symbols. They call for faithfulness rather than speculative certainty.

sections.title: Begin with the book’s explanations
sections.html: Revelation identifies some symbols directly, including the lampstands in chapter 1. Other images draw upon Daniel, Ezekiel, and the Psalms. Follow those connections before constructing a meaning from the image’s modern appearance. A beast isn’t a visual prediction of a piece of technology merely because the technology frightens us or seems powerful.

sections.title: Distinguish image, referent, and event
sections.html: A symbolic description can portray a real historical power or a real future judgment. The Lamb is symbolic language for the actual incarnate Redeemer. The presence of imagery cannot be used to dissolve Christ’s bodily return or the resurrection of the dead. Equally, a real future fulfillment needn’t reproduce every feature of a vision as a physical object.

sections.title: Order your confidence
sections.html: The Westminster Standards confess a future return, resurrection, and judgment. The detailed arrangement of Revelation’s cycles and millennium is more disputed. This guide takes an amillennial reading and should explain its reasons. Don’t grant every proposed identification the certainty of the resurrection itself. Prophecy is meant to strengthen obedience and hope, not to make each generation announce that its calculations cannot fail.

lessons.exercise: When someone identifies a prophetic symbol with a current event, what evidence should you ask for?
lessons.answer: Ask for the symbol’s use in its passage, its Old Testament background, and the connection to the claimed event. Shared appearance or a suggestive number alone cannot establish the identification.

lessons.title: Read the Old Testament with the apostles
lessons.summary: Christ fulfills the earlier Scriptures without making their history unreal or their first meaning disposable.

sections.title: Recognize a divinely ordered pattern
sections.html: A type is grounded in God’s ordering of redemptive history. Adam’s representative role anticipates Christ, and the Passover sacrifice anticipates His saving death. The correspondence includes escalation. Christ is greater than the earlier person or institution. A type isn’t merely an interesting likeness that a reader discovers between two otherwise unrelated details.

sections.title: Let fulfillment preserve the history
sections.html: Matthew applies Hosea’s account of Israel’s exodus to Christ. Hosea truly spoke about Israel. Jesus fulfills Israel’s calling as God’s faithful Son, and Matthew identifies the connection under inspiration. The historical event and its fulfillment belong together. Treating the earlier account as imaginary would damage the pattern rather than protect its spiritual importance.

sections.title: Distinguish a type from an illustration
sections.html: A comparison between Joseph’s suffering and Christ’s suffering can be helpful. It doesn’t automatically establish a revealed equivalence for every feature of Joseph’s life. Apostolic allegory, as in Galatians 4, also has inspired authority that our imaginative applications lack. Explain whether you are tracing an identified biblical type or offering a subordinate illustration.

lessons.exercise: Why is the Passover’s connection to Christ stronger than a comparison between an incidental object and a spiritual experience?
lessons.answer: God instituted the Passover within redemption, and the New Testament expressly identifies Christ as our Passover. The connection is part of revealed history and interpretation rather than a resemblance supplied only by the reader.

lessons.title: Keep covenant unity and historical change together
lessons.summary: One saving Christ stands behind both Testaments. His coming changes the administration of God’s covenant, not the way sinners earn salvation.

sections.title: Distinguish works and grace
sections.html: Adam was obligated to perfect obedience under the covenant of works. After the fall, salvation is offered through Christ in the covenant of grace. Old Testament believers didn’t secure eternal life by performing ceremonies. Their faith rested upon the promised Redeemer, whose work was yet to be accomplished in history. Romans 4 makes Abraham’s justification by faith essential to Paul’s argument.

sections.title: Read Sinai in its setting
sections.html: God gives His law to a people He has delivered from Egypt. The Mosaic administration includes sacrifices that display the need for atonement as well as commands that expose sin. Reformed writers discuss how a works principle functions within that administration. Those debates mustn’t obscure the confessional truth that Old Testament saints were saved through the same Christ by grace.

sections.title: Ask how a command continues
sections.html: WCF 19 distinguishes moral, ceremonial, and judicial law. Christ fulfills the ceremonies, while God’s moral will continues to bind us. Israel’s judicial laws expire with its particular polity, except for the general equity that remains obligatory. Don’t classify a law merely by whether you like its application. Examine its subject, covenant function, and treatment elsewhere in Scripture.

lessons.exercise: Why doesn’t the presence of commands in the Old Testament prove that its saints earned salvation?
lessons.answer: Commands establish duty, not a sinner’s ability to merit life after the fall. The covenant’s promises and sacrifices directed believers to Christ. Paul explicitly argues that Abraham received righteousness through faith apart from works.

lessons.title: Distinguish God’s command from His saving promise
lessons.summary: The law reveals duty and sin. The gospel announces salvation accomplished by Christ and freely received through faith.

sections.title: Keep the ground of acceptance clear
sections.html: Christ’s obedience and satisfaction are the sole ground of justification. Faith receives Him rather than contributing a worthy performance. Repentance and obedience belong to Christian life, but they don’t supply part of the righteousness on which God’s verdict rests. A call to holiness becomes legalism when obedience is made the price of acceptance, not simply because it is seriously commanded.

sections.title: Keep the law’s good use
sections.html: Grace doesn’t turn the moral law into an enemy of the believer’s new life. The law exposes remaining sin and directs grateful obedience. Its condemning curse no longer rests upon those in Christ. Distinguishing these uses helps us read commands without trying to be justified by them, and receive pardon without treating disobedience as harmless.

sections.title: Don’t divide the Bible mechanically
sections.html: The Old Testament contains gospel promises, and the New Testament contains commands. Law and gospel aren’t labels for two different books or two kinds of salvation. Ask what a particular statement is doing. Is it revealing duty, exposing guilt, announcing Christ’s work, or directing those already redeemed? Often those functions appear together in one paragraph.

lessons.exercise: Explain why Titus 2.11 to 14 rules out both earning salvation and refusing obedience.
lessons.answer: Saving grace appears through Christ, who gives Himself to redeem His people. That same grace trains them to deny ungodliness and live faithfully. The training follows redemption and expresses its purpose. It does not purchase it.

lessons.title: Let clear doctrine govern difficult language about God
lessons.summary: Scripture speaks truly of the unchanging God and the incarnate Son in language suited to our understanding.

sections.title: Read divine accommodation carefully
sections.html: God speaks of His arm and His eyes so that we understand His power and knowledge. He isn’t a bodily creature. Passages describing His grief or relenting also teach real opposition to sin and real dealings with changing creatures. They don’t mean that He discovers facts late or revises an eternal purpose through ignorance. Read such language with His expressly revealed perfection and unchangeableness.

sections.title: Confess the Trinity without dividing God
sections.html: The Father sends the Son and the Spirit applies redemption. These personal distinctions don’t create three gods or three competing wills. The Persons share one divine being and will. Scripture’s personal language mustn’t be flattened into mere roles played by a single Person, and its unity mustn’t be broken into a society of separate divine beings.

sections.title: Distinguish Christ’s natures without dividing His Person
sections.html: The one Son is truly God and truly man. He can grow in wisdom and suffer according to His human nature without His deity becoming ignorant or mortal. Statements about the one Person are understood according to the nature involved. His humiliation doesn’t mean that He surrendered His divine attributes. He also possesses a true human will, obedient to the divine will He shares with the Father and the Spirit. His human obedience is real. This distinction guards both the reality of His suffering and His sufficiency as Savior.

lessons.exercise: How can Luke describe Christ growing in wisdom while John declares that the Word is God?
lessons.answer: The eternal Son has taken a genuine human nature. Human growth belongs to His humanity and does not cancel His divine perfection. There is one incarnate Person, not one human son beside a different divine Son.

lessons.title: Distinguish the blessings that belong together in Christ
lessons.summary: Union with Christ brings justification, adoption, and sanctification. Their inseparability does not make them interchangeable.

sections.title: Distinguish the verdict from the renewal
sections.html: Justification is God’s legal declaration that the believer is righteous on account of Christ. Sanctification is the Spirit’s work of renewing the believer in holiness. The renewal is real but incomplete in this life. If you make inward renewal the ground of the verdict, your acceptance rises and falls with your performance rather than resting upon the finished righteousness of Christ.

sections.title: Understand the source of faith
sections.html: In effectual calling the Spirit renews the sinner and brings him willingly to Christ. Faith is the means of receiving Christ, not the cause of new spiritual life. The logical relation matters even when we cannot identify separate moments in our experience. Don’t require a convert to discover a hidden experience of regeneration before he is warranted to believe the gospel.

sections.title: Read every grace within union
sections.html: Adoption gives the believer a Father’s welcome. Sanctification produces real conflict with remaining sin. Perseverance rests upon God’s preservation through appointed means. These aren’t separate salvation plans that can be chosen independently. Scripture directs us to the whole Christ, while distinguishing His benefits carefully enough to keep pardon, growth, and assurance in their proper relation.

lessons.exercise: Why is ongoing warfare with sin consistent with complete justification?
lessons.answer: Justification rests upon Christ’s perfect righteousness, not upon completed sanctification. The justified person is truly being renewed but still has remaining sin. The conflict calls for repentance and growth without reopening the ground of God’s accepting verdict.

lessons.title: Read covenant signs without confusing sign and thing signified
lessons.summary: Baptism and the Supper are real means of grace. Their outward administration does not automatically confer saving union with Christ.

sections.title: Distinguish visible membership and saving grace
sections.html: The visible church includes professing believers and their children. The invisible church is the whole number of the elect united to Christ. Scripture can address a visible congregation covenantally without declaring that every hearer is regenerate. That distinction helps explain both strong covenant language and the warnings against hypocrisy within the church.

sections.title: Understand sacramental language
sections.html: A passage can closely join a sign with the grace it represents. WCF 27 explains that the names and effects of one may be attributed to the other because of their sacramental relation. That relation isn’t a physical identity or an automatic result. Read baptismal passages alongside the explicit teaching that not everyone baptized is regenerate and that the Spirit gives grace in God’s appointed time.

sections.title: Receive what Christ actually gives
sections.html: At the Supper, believers truly feed upon Christ spiritually by faith. The bread and wine aren’t changed into His bodily substance, and the church doesn’t repeat His sacrifice. This is more than bare recollection, yet no bodily eating can substitute for faith. Read the institution with Paul’s warnings about reception and his teaching about the body’s communion.

lessons.exercise: Why can Paul speak of Israel’s common covenant privileges while warning that many were judged?
lessons.answer: Participation in outward covenant privileges did not guarantee saving faith. The warning calls the visible church to faithful reception of God’s gifts, not to confidence that an outward sign makes unbelief impossible.

lessons.title: Ask who receives a promise and on what terms
lessons.summary: Every promise is God’s true word. Its recipients and covenant setting determine how we may claim it.

sections.title: Name the original recipients
sections.html: A promise to an individual about a particular event doesn’t become a direct prediction about every reader. Jeremiah 29.10 to 14 addresses exiles and names a historical restoration. Its revelation of God’s faithfulness is profitable for us, but we aren’t authorized to claim its timetable as a guarantee that our personal plans will prosper.

sections.title: Attend to covenant conditions
sections.html: God’s promises may call for faith and repentance without making those responses the meritorious purchase of grace. Some temporal blessings concern Israel’s life in the land under the Mosaic covenant. Others concern the saving inheritance of those in Christ. Read the conditions and the covenant together rather than treating all promises as interchangeable statements about health, wealth, or national success.

sections.title: Receive fulfillment through Christ
sections.html: The New Testament directs believers to God’s faithfulness in Christ. This confirms the promises rather than erasing the historical shape in which they were first spoken. Trace how Scripture itself brings the promised blessing to the church. Sometimes the enduring application is trust in God’s character and duty to obey, not a claim that the original material circumstance will be repeated for you.

lessons.exercise: How is Jeremiah 29 profitable to a believer who is not among the Babylonian exiles?
lessons.answer: It reveals God’s faithfulness to His word and His government of His people’s trials. We learn to trust and seek Him. We do not acquire a promise that a chosen career, financial plan, or seventy-year timetable must be fulfilled for us.

lessons.title: Work patiently with texts that seem to disagree
lessons.summary: A difficulty deserves honest examination. Neither a hasty denial nor an invented harmonization does justice to Scripture.

sections.title: State the claims precisely
sections.html: A contradiction requires opposite claims about the same subject in the same respect. Paul excludes works as the ground of justification. James exposes a profession that lacks the fruit of living faith. Their arguments address different errors. Don’t announce agreement merely as a slogan. Show from each context why the supposed opposition has been misstated.

sections.title: Allow complementary selection
sections.html: Two historical accounts can select different details or summarize speeches differently without either being false. Distinguish a difference of emphasis from an incompatible assertion. Don’t fill every silence with a confident reconstruction. A proposed harmony should be labeled as a possible explanation unless the text itself establishes it.

sections.title: Let clearer teaching govern without silencing the hard text
sections.html: WCF 1.9 directs us to compare clearer passages. This doesn’t permit us to make the difficult words mean anything convenient. Account for their grammar and purpose as far as you can. Where a solution remains uncertain, confess the limit of your understanding while continuing to trust the God who cannot lie.

lessons.exercise: How would you distinguish a warranted interpretation from a merely possible reconciliation?
lessons.answer: A warranted interpretation is established by the passage’s words and relevant evidence. A possible reconciliation shows how accounts could agree without claiming to know an unstated circumstance. Possibility can answer an allegation of necessary contradiction, but it does not prove the reconstruction happened.

lessons.title: Hear warnings and promises without distorting either
lessons.summary: Warnings call us from sin. Promises direct us to Christ. God uses both to preserve His people.

sections.title: Distinguish the audience from the elect alone
sections.html: Hebrews addresses a congregation whose members share outward privileges. Its warnings expose the danger of apostasy and are among the means God uses to keep His elect believing. Don’t assume that every person described as sharing covenant blessings must possess the saving union that Scripture says cannot finally be lost.

sections.title: Distinguish weakness from settled rejection
sections.html: A believer who confesses sin and seeks Christ isn’t thereby displaying the hardened rejection of the only sacrifice condemned in Hebrews 10. Remaining sin must be fought, not dismissed. But fear after a fall isn’t proof that forgiveness has become unavailable. Read the warnings alongside the calls to draw near to the merciful High Priest.

sections.title: Ground assurance rightly
sections.html: God’s promises in Christ are the foundation. The Spirit’s work in us and His witness confirm that we belong to Him. Our fruits are imperfect and our perception of them can be troubled. Don’t make a flawless spiritual self-assessment the price of coming to Christ. Equally, don’t use a past profession to shelter a present refusal to repent.

lessons.exercise: What counsel fits a professing believer who is grieved by sin and afraid to approach Christ?
lessons.answer: Call him to confess and forsake sin while directing him to Christ’s sufficiency and welcome. The warning against rejecting Christ must not be used to forbid a repentant sinner from seeking the only Savior it declares indispensable.

lessons.title: Apply the Word without adding human laws
lessons.summary: Faithful application carries the text’s meaning into life while preserving the liberty Christ has given.

sections.title: Move through the right questions
sections.html: Ask what the passage teaches about God, what it required of its first hearers, and what changes or continues in light of Christ. Then state the present duty with its reason. A direct moral command can bind us immediately. A historical instruction to one person may instead reveal a principle whose present application requires judgment.

sections.title: Distinguish duty and prudence
sections.html: God commands generosity, but a particular budgeting method isn’t itself a divine command. He requires attention to His Word, but a chosen morning routine isn’t binding upon every believer. Wise advice can be valuable without being given the force of God’s law. This distinction protects both obedience and a tender conscience.

sections.title: Treat worship with particular care
sections.html: God appoints the elements of public worship. Circumstances common to human meetings are ordered by Christian prudence under Scripture’s general rules. A meeting time isn’t a new element of worship, while an invented religious rite isn’t justified merely because it feels helpful. Read WCF 1.6 and 21.1 together so that the regulative principle neither disappears nor becomes an arbitrary ban on every practical arrangement.

lessons.exercise: How can a teacher recommend a useful practice without wrongly binding the conscience?
lessons.answer: He should identify the biblical duty, explain how the practice may serve it, and distinguish his practical recommendation from God’s binding command. A useful means should not be presented as the only faithful means unless Scripture establishes that requirement.

lessons.title: A study method you can keep using
lessons.summary: Careful reading combines patient work, prayer, and a willingness to be corrected.

sections.title: Write a short account of the passage
sections.html: Read the whole unit, then summarize its main claim in one or two sentences. Mark the words that establish your summary. Identify anything you cannot yet explain. This simple discipline prevents a study from becoming a collection of interesting observations with no account of what the author is saying.

sections.title: Test interpretation and doctrine
sections.html: Consult related passages and a reliable commentary. Distinguish what is explicit, what follows necessarily, and what remains a debated explanation. Compare the confession where the topic is doctrinal, while keeping Scripture as the final authority. If an explanation requires repeatedly making the words say less or more than they appear to say in context, return to the passage.

sections.title: End with a response and an honest limit
sections.html: Name a truth to believe or a duty to practice. Pray in light of it. Keep unresolved questions where you can return to them, and ask a faithful elder when you need help. WLC 157 joins reverence with diligence, meditation, and prayer. Deeper study is not a hunt for novelty. It is a growing ability to receive the same inexhaustibly rich Word with understanding and obedience.

lessons.exercise: Before using a commentary, what should you be able to write about the passage?
lessons.answer: Write its main claim, identify the words and connections that support that claim, and list the genuine questions that remain. A commentary can then test and develop your reading rather than supplying a conclusion you have never examined.

lessons.title: Romans 3 and the righteousness God gives
lessons.summary: Work through the argument that moves from universal guilt to justification through faith in Christ.

sections.title: Read the turn in the argument
sections.html:
Romans 3.19 to 20 closes the preceding account of human guilt. The law stops boasting and gives knowledge of sin rather than a righteous verdict through our obedience. Verse 21 introduces the righteousness of God manifested apart from the law, while immediately stating that the law and prophets bear witness to it. Apart from the law therefore cannot mean contradicted by the Old Testament. Paul distinguishes the ground and means of justification from the scriptural witness that announces it.

The phrase righteousness of God must be understood through what the paragraph says God does for sinners and how He remains righteous in doing it. Don't replace the whole argument with a dictionary definition of righteousness. Its judicial vocabulary, its account of redemption, and the contrast with boasting explain its saving function.

sections.title: Follow the relation of faith, grace, and blood
sections.html:
Verses 22 to 25 describe faith in Jesus Christ, the common guilt of sinners, free justification by grace, and redemption through Christ's blood. These aren't interchangeable causes. Grace identifies the freeness and source of the gift. Christ's accomplished redemption supplies its basis. Faith receives Christ rather than supplying an additional worthiness. Universal guilt makes the same remedy necessary for Jew and Gentile, while the promised benefit is described in relation to believing.

God's setting forth of Christ as a propitiation also answers the question of justice. Earlier divine forbearance wasn't moral indifference to evil. The cross displays God's righteousness in justifying the one who believes. Mercy doesn't succeed by making God's standard unimportant.

sections.title: Let the conclusion test your interpretation
sections.html:
Verses 27 to 31 exclude boasting, deny justification by works, and confess one God who justifies Jews and Gentiles through faith. If your explanation leaves the sinner boasting in a contribution that made God's verdict possible, it hasn't accounted for Paul's conclusion. If it makes faith an excuse to discard God's moral authority, it also misses Paul's final statement that faith establishes the law.

The argument should first settle the ground of our acceptance. Romans 6 will then address the claim that grace permits continued sin. Distinguish those questions without separating the blessings of the one Christ.

lessons.exercise: Explain the distinct roles of grace, Christ’s blood, and faith. Then show how your explanation accounts for the exclusion of boasting.
lessons.answer: Grace is the free source of justification. Christ’s obedience and satisfaction supply its ground. Faith receives and rests upon Him without contributing merit. Boasting is excluded because the righteousness and redemption are His gift rather than our achievement. Good works follow as the fruit of a renewed life, not as an additional ground for the accepting verdict.

lessons.title: Hebrews 10 and the one sufficient offering
lessons.summary: Read the finished sacrifice and the severe warning as parts of one sustained pastoral argument.

sections.title: Identify the inadequacy being contrasted
sections.html:
Hebrews 10.1 to 4 explains why repeated animal sacrifices cannot make worshipers perfect in the sense under discussion. Their repetition and remembrance of sins expose their inability to remove guilt finally. The paragraph isn't saying that every believer under the old administration was unregenerate or unsaved. It addresses what the ceremonial offerings themselves could accomplish. The promise they served was effective through the Christ they anticipated.

The following appeal to Christ's willing obedience identifies the reality to which the ceremonies pointed. Their removal is fulfillment by a sufficient offering, not God's discovery that His earlier revelation was a mistake.

sections.title: Distinguish completion of sacrifice from completion of moral growth
sections.html:
Verses 11 to 18 contrast standing priests who repeat their service with Christ seated after His one offering. His position and the covenant promise of forgiven sins establish the finality of His work. The language of perfecting therefore concerns the sufficient acceptance and access secured by that offering. It must be read with the same book's ongoing calls to endurance and holiness.

A believer's remaining sin doesn't prove that another atonement is required. Neither does the completed atonement make remaining sin harmless. Justification and sanctification need careful distinction precisely because both belong to those Christ saves.

sections.title: Read the warning in relation to the access it protects
sections.html:
Verses 19 to 25 urge the congregation to draw near, hold fast, and encourage one another. The warning in verses 26 to 31 then describes the fearful rejection of the only sacrifice. Its surrounding explanation speaks of trampling the Son and treating covenant blood as unholy. This is more specific than a claim that every sin committed with awareness after conversion permanently bars repentance.

The warning must be heard by the visible congregation, including those whose outward participation may conceal unbelief. God uses the warning to preserve His own people. A grieved sinner should obey the call to draw near through the sufficient High Priest rather than misuse the warning as a reason to refuse Him.

lessons.exercise: How does the argument exclude both repeated atonement and the claim that a believer’s repentance is pointless after a conscious sin?
lessons.answer: The one offering obtains the lasting removal of guilt that animal sacrifices could not provide. The congregation is therefore commanded to approach God through Christ. The warning identifies repudiation of that only refuge, not a command to keep a repentant sinner from seeking it. Its seriousness calls us away from unbelief while the promise directs us to Christ.

lessons.title: Galatians 3 and the law that cannot replace the promise
lessons.summary: Follow Paul’s timeline and covenant reasoning before deciding what he means by the law.

sections.title: Recover the question Paul is answering
sections.html:
Galatians 3 begins by asking whether the Spirit was received through works of law or the hearing of faith. Abraham then supplies the scriptural witness to righteousness through believing. Paul isn't opposing Spirit-produced obedience as such. He is opposing reliance upon law observance as the way to obtain the promised blessing.

The curse passage makes the obstacle plain. The law requires obedience, and sinners have failed. Christ bears the curse so that the blessing comes through faith. A reading that merely reduces the required performance from many commands to a smaller number still hasn't received Paul's remedy.

sections.title: Keep the promise and the later administration in order
sections.html:
Verses 15 to 18 reason from the priority and stability of God's promise. The law given later cannot annul it. Paul identifies the promised seed with Christ, concentrating the fulfillment in the one through whom the blessing reaches His people. The argument doesn't deny Abraham's historical descendants. It explains where the inheritance is finally secured.

When Paul asks why the law was added, his answer concerns its appointed role until the coming of the seed. The law exposes transgression and confines sinners under the need for the promise. Its temporary administrative role mustn't be confused either with an alternative way of eternal salvation or with the abolition of all moral duty.

sections.title: Read the conclusion as incorporation into Christ
sections.html:
Verses 26 to 29 place sonship and inheritance in Christ through faith. The distinctions of Jew and Greek, bond and free, male and female cannot establish superior access to the inheritance. This unity doesn't mean every created distinction or every appointed duty disappears. It answers who shares the blessing as Abraham's seed in Christ.

The chapter therefore protects a single gracious inheritance while explaining a real transition in redemptive history. Covenant unity doesn't erase the coming of Christ, and historical transition doesn't create a different saving gospel.

lessons.exercise: How can the Mosaic administration have a temporary role while the moral law continues to direct a Christian’s life?
lessons.answer: Paul addresses the law’s role within the administration leading to Christ and rejects seeking inheritance through it. The moral duty God reveals is not thereby made evil or obsolete. Christ fulfills the ceremonies and frees His people from the curse while the Spirit teaches the grateful obedience described later in Galatians 5.

lessons.title: Matthew 5 and the righteousness Christ requires
lessons.summary: Read fulfillment and the heart’s obedience together without turning the sermon into another way of justification.

sections.title: Begin with the declaration about fulfillment
sections.html:
Matthew 5.17 to 20 denies destruction of the law and prophets and places their fulfillment in Christ at the center. The phrase law and prophets reaches beyond a bare list of commands to the scriptural witness that anticipates Him. Their enduring truth is secured, not embarrassed, by His coming.

The whole canon explains what fulfillment entails. A fulfilled sacrifice is no longer offered as an unfinished shadow. A moral command isn't emptied of authority because the Savior has obeyed it perfectly. Reading the opening declaration apart from that canonical explanation can make either Mosaic ceremony perpetual or moral obligation disposable.

sections.title: Follow Christ’s exposure of the heart
sections.html:
The following teaching addresses murder and anger, adultery and lust, and other forms of conduct before God. Christ doesn't merely intensify a previously indifferent God into a stricter new deity. He exposes the depth of righteousness already required by the holy law, against readings that protect outward appearance while permitting inward rebellion.

The precise source and scope of the sayings He corrects must be examined individually. Don't presume that every contrast means Moses taught error. Distinguish the command God gave, the misuse or narrowing being opposed, and the authoritative instruction of the Son.

sections.title: Place the required righteousness within the whole Gospel
sections.html:
The sermon commands genuine obedience and exposes a righteousness that cannot be satisfied by religious display. Matthew also presents Jesus as the One who saves His people from their sins and gives His life as a ransom. The demand of the sermon must lead us to repent and receive that Savior, not to invent a way of earning acceptance through superior moral effort.

Those received by grace are then called to obey the same Lord. The Reformed distinction between justification and sanctification preserves the seriousness of the sermon without confusing its commands with the meritorious ground of salvation.

lessons.exercise: Why are both an outward-only obedience and an attempt to earn salvation through deeper obedience inadequate readings?
lessons.answer: The sermon exposes the heart as well as outward conduct, so external conformity is insufficient. Yet the Gospel identifies Christ as the saving Redeemer. The righteousness that justifies is His gift, while the inward obedience He requires is the real fruit of His renewing grace. Neither the command nor the gospel can be erased.

units.label: I.
body: Although the light of nature, and the works of creation and providence, do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom, and power of God, as to leave men inexcusable;^{a} yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God, and of his will, which is necessary unto salvation;^{b }therefore it pleased the Lord, at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that his will unto his Church;^{c} and afterwards, for the better preserving and propagating of the truth, and for the more sure establishment and comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan and of the world, to commit the same wholly unto writing;^{d} which maketh the holy Scripture to be most necessary;^{e} those former ways of God’s revealing his will unto his people being now ceased.^{f}

units.label: II.
body: Under the name of holy Scripture, or the Word of God written, are now contained all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these:
Of the Old Testament

Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. Joshua. Judges. Ruth. I Samuel. II Samuel. I Kings. II Kings. I Chronicles.  | II Chronicles. Ezra. Nehemiah. Esther. Job. Psalms. Proverbs. Ecclesiastes. The Song of Songs. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Lamentations. Ezekiel.  | Daniel. Hosea. Joel. Amos. Obadiah. Jonah. Micah. Nahum. Habakkuk. Zephaniah. Haggai. Zechariah. Malachi.
Of the New Testament

The Gospels according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, John. The Acts of the Apostles. Paul’s Epistles to the Romans. Corinthians I.  | Corinthians II. Galatians. Ephesians. Philippians. Colossians. Thessalonians I. Thessalonians II. To Timothy I. To Timothy II. To Titus. To Philemon.  | The Epistle to the Hebrews. The Epistle of James. The First and Second Epistles of Peter. The First, Second, and Third Epistles of John. The Epistle of Jude. The Revelation.
All which are given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life.^{a}

units.label: III.
body: The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of the Scripture; and therefore are of no authority in the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings.^{a}

units.label: IV.
body: The authority of the holy Scripture, for which it ought to be believed and obeyed, dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself), the Author thereof; and therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God.^{a}

units.label: V.
body: We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church to an high and reverent esteem of the holy Scripture;^{a} and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the doctrine, the majesty of the style, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God), the full discovery it makes of the only way of man’s salvation, the many other incomparable excellencies, and the entire perfection thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence itself to be the Word of God; yet, notwithstanding, our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts.^{b}

units.label: VI.
body: The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man’s salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men.^{a} Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word;^{b} and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed.^{c}

units.label: VII.
body: All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all;^{a} yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed, for salvation, are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them.^{b}

units.label: VIII.
body: The Old Testament in Hebrew (which was the native language of the people of God of old), and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the nations), being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and providence kept pure in all ages, are therefore authentical;^{a} so as in all controversies of religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them.^{b} But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God who have right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded, in the fear of God, to read and search them,^{c} therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every nation unto which they come,^{d} that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner,^{e} and, through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, may have hope.^{f}

units.label: IX.
body: The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly.^{a}

units.label: X.
body: The Supreme Judge, by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.^{a}

sections.title: Of God, and of the Holy Trinity

units.label: I.
body: There is but one only^{a} living and true God,^{b} who is infinite in being and perfection,^{c} a most pure spirit,^{d} invisible,^{e} without body, parts,^{f} or passions,^{g} immutable,^{h} immense,^{i} eternal,^{j}incomprehensible,^{k} almighty,^{l} most wise,^{m} most holy,^{n} most free,^{o} most absolute,^{p} working all things according to the counsel of his own immutable and most righteous will,^{q} for his own glory;^{r} most loving,^{s} gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin;^{t} the rewarder of them that diligently seek him;^{u} and withal most just and terrible in his judgments;^{v} hating all sin,^{w} and who will by no means clear the guilty.^{x}
Exod 34:7; Nahum 1:2-3.

units.label: II.
body: God hath all life,^{a} glory,^{b} goodness,^{c} blessedness,^{d} in and of himself; and is alone in and unto himself all-sufficient, not standing in need of any creatures which he hath made,^{e} nor deriving any glory from them,^{f} but only manifesting his own glory in, by, unto, and upon them: he is the alone fountain of all being, of whom, through whom, and to whom are all things;^{g}and hath most sovereign dominion over them, to do by them, for them, or upon them whatsoever himself pleaseth.^{h} In his sight all things are open and manifest;^{i} his knowledge is infinite, infallible, and independent upon the creature;^{j} so as nothing is to him contingent or uncertain.^{k} He is most holy in all his counsels, in all his works, and in all his commands.^{l} To him is due from angels and men, and every other creature, whatsoever worship, service, or obedience, he is pleased to require of them.^{m}

units.label: III.
body: In the unity of the Godhead there be three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost.^{a} The Father is of none, neither begotten nor proceeding; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father;^{b} the Holy Ghost eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son.^{c}

units.label: I.
body: God from all eternity did, by the most wise and holy counsel of his own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass;^{a} yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin,^{b} nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.^{c}

units.label: II.
body: Although God knows whatsoever may or can come to pass upon all supposed conditions,^{a }yet hath he not decreed anything because he foresaw it as future, or as that which would come to pass upon such conditions.^{b}

units.label: III.
body: By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels^{a} are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others fore-ordained to everlasting death.^{b}

units.label: IV.
body: These angels and men, thus predestinated and fore-ordained, are particularly and unchangeably designed; and their number is so certain and definite that it can not be either increased or diminished.^{a}

units.label: V.
body: Those of mankind that are predestinated unto life, God, before the foundation of the world was laid, according to his eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret counsel and good pleasure of his will, hath chosen in Christ, unto everlasting glory,^{a} out of his mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving him thereunto;^{b} and all to the praise of his glorious grace.^{c}

units.label: VI.
body: As God hath appointed the elect unto glory, so hath he, by the eternal and most free purpose of his will, fore-ordained all the means thereunto.^{a} Wherefore they who are elected, being fallen in Adam, are redeemed by Christ,^{b} are effectually called unto faith in Christ by his Spirit working in due season; are justified, adopted, sanctified,^{c} and kept by his power through faith unto salvation.^{d} Neither are any other redeemed by Christ, effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and saved, but the elect only.^{e}

units.label: VII.
body: The rest of mankind God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy as he pleaseth, for the glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonor and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice.^{a}

units.label: VIII.
body: The doctrine of this high mystery of predestination is to be handled with special prudence and care,^{a} that men attending the will of God revealed in his Word, and yielding obedience thereunto, may, from the certainty of their effectual vocation, be assured of their eternal election.^{b} So shall this doctrine afford matter of praise, reverence, and admiration of God;^{c }and of humility, diligence, and abundant consolation to all that sincerely obey the gospel.^{d}

units.text: The doctrine of this high mystery of predestination is to be handled with special prudence and care,^{a} that men attending the will of God revealed in his Word, and yielding obedience thereunto, may, from the certainty of their effectual vocation, be assured of their eternal election.^{b} So shall this doctrine afford matter of praise, reverence, and admiration of God;^{c }and of humility, diligence, and abundant consolation to all that sincerely obey the gospel.^{d}

units.label: I.
body: It pleased God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost,^{a} for the manifestation of the glory of his eternal power, wisdom, and goodness,^{b} in the beginning, to create or make of nothing the world, and all things therein, whether visible or invisible, in the space of six days, and all very good.^{c}

units.text: It pleased God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost,^{a} for the manifestation of the glory of his eternal power, wisdom, and goodness,^{b} in the beginning, to create or make of nothing the world, and all things therein, whether visible or invisible, in the space of six days, and all very good.^{c}

units.label: II.
body: After God had made all other creatures, he created man, male and female,^{a} with reasonable and immortal souls,^{b} endued with knowledge, righteousness, and true holiness, after his own image,^{c} having the law of God written in their hearts,^{d} and power to fulfil it;^{e} and yet under a possibility of transgressing, being left to the liberty of their own will, which was subject unto change.^{f} Beside this law written in their hearts, they received a command not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil;^{g} which while they kept they were happy in their communion with God, and had dominion over the creatures.^{h}

units.label: I.
body: God, the great Creator of all things, doth uphold,^{a} direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions, and things,^{b} from the greatest even to the least,^{c} by his most wise and holy providence,^{d} according to his infallible fore-knowledgee and the free and immutable counsel of his own will,^{f} to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, goodness, and mercy.^{g}

units.label: II.
body: Although in relation to the foreknowledge and decree of God, the first cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly,^{a} yet by the same providence he ordereth them to fall out, according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently.^{b}
proofs: a. Acts 2:23. • b. Gen 8:22; Exod 21:13 with Deut 19:5; 1 Kings 22:28, 34; Isa 10:6-7; Jer 31:35.

units.label: III.
body: God, in his ordinary providence, maketh use of means,^{a} yet is free to work without,^{b}above,^{c} and against them,^{d} at his pleasure.

units.label: IV.
body: The almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God so far manifest themselves in his providence that it extendeth itself even to the first fall, and all other sins of angels and men,^{a} and that not by a bare permission,^{b} but such as hath joined with it a most wise and powerful bounding,^{c} and otherwise ordering and governing of them, in a manifold dispensation, to his own holy ends;^{d} yet so as the sinfulness thereof proceedeth only from the creature, and not from God; who, being most holy and righteous, neither is nor can be the author or approver of sin.^{e}

units.label: V.
body: The most wise, righteous, and gracious God doth oftentimes leave for a season his own children to manifold temptations and the corruption of their own hearts, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption and deceitfulness of their hearts, that they be humbled;^{a} and to raise them to a more close and constant dependence for their support unto himself, and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for sundry other just and holy ends.^{b}

units.label: VI.
body: As for those wicked and ungodly men whom God, as a righteous judge, for former sins, doth blind and harden,^{a} from them he not only withholdeth his grace, whereby they might have been enlightened in their understandings and wrought upon in their hearts,^{b} but sometimes also withdraweth the gifts which they had,^{c} and exposeth them to such objects as their corruption makes occasion of sin;^{d} and withal, gives them over to their own lusts, the temptations of the world, and the power of Satan;^{e} whereby it comes to pass that they harden themselves, even under those means which God useth for the softening of others.^{f}

units.label: VII.
body: As the providence of God doth, in general, reach to all creatures, so, after a most special manner, it taketh care of his Church, and disposeth all things to the good thereof.^{a}

sections.title: Of the Fall of Man, of Sin, and of the Punishment Thereof

units.label: I.
body: Our first parents, being seduced by the subtlety and temptation of Satan, sinned in eating the forbidden fruit.^{a} This their sin God was pleased, according to his wise and holy counsel, to permit, having purposed to order it to his own glory.^{b}
units.html: Our first parents, being seduced by the subtlety and temptation of Satan, sinned in eating the forbidden fruit.a This their sin God was pleased, according to his wise and holy counsel, to permit, having purposed to order it to his own glory.b
units.text: Our first parents, being seduced by the subtlety and temptation of Satan, sinned in eating the forbidden fruit.^{a} This their sin God was pleased, according to his wise and holy counsel, to permit, having purposed to order it to his own glory.^{b}

units.label: II.
body: By this sin they fell from their original righteousness and communion with God,^{a} and so became dead in sin,^{b} and wholly defiled in all the faculties and parts of soul and body.^{c}
units.html: By this sin they fell from their original righteousness and communion with God,a and so became dead in sin,b and wholly defiled in all the faculties and parts of soul and body.c

units.label: III.
body: They being the root of all mankind, the guilt of this sin was imputed,^{a} and the same death in sin and corrupted nature conveyed to all their posterity descending from them by ordinary generation.^{b}
units.html: They being the root of all mankind, the guilt of this sin was imputed,a and the same death in sin and corrupted nature conveyed to all their posterity descending from them by ordinary generation.b
units.text: They being the root of all mankind, the guilt of this sin was imputed,^{a} and the same death in sin and corrupted nature conveyed to all their posterity descending from them by ordinary generation.^{b}

units.label: IV.
body: From this original corruption, whereby we are utterly indisposed, disabled, and made opposite to all good,^{a} and wholly inclined to all evil,^{b} do proceed all actual transgressions.^{c}
units.html: From this original corruption, whereby we are utterly indisposed, disabled, and made opposite to all good,a and wholly inclined to all evil,b do proceed all actual transgressions.c
units.text: From this original corruption, whereby we are utterly indisposed, disabled, and made opposite to all good,^{a} and wholly inclined to all evil,^{b} do proceed all actual transgressions.^{c}

units.label: V.
body: This corruption of nature, during this life, doth remain in those that are regenerated;^{a} and although it be through Christ pardoned and mortified, yet both itself and all the motions thereof are truly and properly sin.^{b}

units.label: VI.
body: Every sin, both original and actual, being a transgression of the righteous law of God, and contrary thereunto,^{a} doth, in its own nature, bring guilt upon the sinner,^{b} whereby he is bound over to the wrath of Godc and curse of the law,^{d} and so made subject to death,^{e} with all miseries spiritual,^{f} temporal,^{g} and eternal.^{h}
