catechismCourse.answer: The God who is spirit determines acceptable worship. His nature and revealed will govern our approach to Him.

catechismCourse.title: The one living and true God
catechismCourse.teach: There is only one God. Every creature depends upon Him, and no rival shares His divine being. The first duty of faith isn't choosing a favourite deity from several real gods. It is acknowledging the only God and rejecting the idols we have made.
catechismCourse.argument: Isaiah places God's sovereign declaration beside the manufacture of an idol from ordinary wood. The contrast is deliberate. The Maker of all things doesn't receive His existence or authority from human workmanship. Read the whole argument rather than treating the idol passage as mere ridicule.
catechismCourse.guard: An idol can be a false object of worship or a false conception of the true God. A religious name doesn't make an invented god the Lord revealed in Scripture.
catechismCourse.exercise: What makes the idol-maker's actions so unreasonable?
catechismCourse.answer: He depends on created material and then treats part of that material as the source of deliverance.

catechismCourse.title: The Trinity and the divine persons
catechismCourse.teach: The Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are three distinct persons in the one Godhead. Each is fully God. They aren't three shares of deity, and they aren't one person appearing under different names. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son.
catechismCourse.argument: At Christ's baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks from heaven. This shows personal distinction. Read it alongside Matthew 28:19 and Scripture's insistence that God is one. The doctrine follows by holding those truths together.
catechismCourse.guard: The baptism scene alone doesn't state every part of Trinitarian doctrine. Neither eternal generation nor the Spirit's procession describes a beginning or a created, inferior divine person.
catechismCourse.exercise: Which error does the simultaneous activity of the three persons rule out?
catechismCourse.answer: It rules out the claim that Father, Son, and Spirit are merely successive roles of one divine person.

catechismCourse.title: God’s eternal decree
catechismCourse.teach: God's decree is His eternal purpose concerning everything that comes to pass. It rests on His wise and holy will. Election to life is gracious, not a reward for foreseen faith. In passing by others, God remains just, and condemnation is for sin. Grace isn't owed to any sinner.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul repeatedly places salvation within God's purpose in Christ before the foundation of the world. Follow the passage through redemption, the Spirit's sealing, and the praise of God's glory. Election leads to holiness and thanksgiving rather than speculation about a hidden list.
catechismCourse.guard: God isn't the author of sin, and His decree doesn't force innocent people to become unwilling sinners. Don't search the secret decree before receiving Christ as He is offered in the gospel.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Paul identify as a purpose of election in relation to our lives?
catechismCourse.answer: God chose His people to be holy before Him, and their salvation displays the glory of His grace.

catechismCourse.title: Creation and providence carry out God’s decree
catechismCourse.teach: God carries out His eternal purpose through creation and providence. Creation brings creatures into being. Providence preserves and governs them. The distinction matters because the world isn't self-sustaining after its beginning. The Lord continually upholds what He made.
catechismCourse.argument: The heavenly worship grounds God's worthiness in His creation of all things and in His will. Read the living creatures' praise together with the elders' response. Their worship recognizes a Creator whose creatures belong to Him, not an impersonal cause left behind in the distant past.
catechismCourse.guard: An eternal decree doesn't mean that all events happened eternally. God purposes eternally and executes His purpose in time. Our choices and actions are real means within His providence.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does creation give God a claim upon every creature?
catechismCourse.answer: All creatures owe their existence to His will and remain His property, dependent on His preservation.

catechismCourse.title: Creation out of nothing
catechismCourse.teach: God made all things out of nothing by His powerful word, in the space of six days, and all very good. Matter isn't eternal beside Him, and creation isn't part of His own substance. Angels are creatures too, however glorious their powers.
catechismCourse.argument: Trace the repeated divine speech and the order of the creation account. The sun and moon appear as lights appointed by God, not as deities to worship. The passage also prepares for man's calling and the Sabbath. Those features belong to its account of real divine work.
catechismCourse.guard: This companion follows the Standards' six-day confession. The days aren't an excuse to overlook the passage's other teaching about God's sovereignty and creation's goodness. Evil isn't an original ingredient God needed to make a complete world.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does the creation account oppose worship of the heavenly bodies?
catechismCourse.answer: It presents them as things God made and assigned to serve His purposes, not as independent divine powers.

catechismCourse.title: Man created in God’s image
catechismCourse.teach: God made mankind male and female in His image, with knowledge, righteousness, and holiness, and with dominion over the creatures. Man has a true body and a reasonable, immortal soul. Both sexes bear God's image and possess the dignity that comes from His creative act.
catechismCourse.argument: Read the command to rule alongside the blessing and the creation of male and female. Dominion is a commission received from God. It doesn't make man an independent owner who may use God's creatures without regard to His will.
catechismCourse.guard: The image doesn't mean that God has a human body. Sin corrupts man's moral condition, yet fallen people remain human image-bearers. Their dignity doesn't depend on strength, usefulness, or stage of development.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is human dominion a responsibility rather than unlimited permission?
catechismCourse.answer: God delegates it to His image-bearers, who remain accountable to Him for their use of His creation.

catechismCourse.title: God’s preserving and governing providence
catechismCourse.teach: God preserves and governs all His creatures and their actions with perfect holiness, wisdom, and power. He ordinarily works through means, while remaining free to act above or without them. Providence includes His special care for the church and His righteous judgment upon the wicked.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus prepares disciples for persecution and then speaks of sparrows and the hairs of their heads. His point isn't that suffering will disappear. The Father's particular care gives courage when obedience is costly. Read the promise within the command to confess Christ before men.
catechismCourse.guard: God's government of sinful actions doesn't make their evil His moral work. Creatures supply the sinfulness. Nor does providence excuse neglecting ordinary means such as work, medicine, or prudent care.
catechismCourse.exercise: What comfort does Jesus give without promising freedom from persecution?
catechismCourse.answer: The Father knows and governs even the smallest matters, and His disciples are precious to Him.

catechismCourse.title: The covenant of works
catechismCourse.teach: God entered into a covenant of life with Adam, requiring perfect obedience and forbidding the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil on pain of death. Adam's obligation wasn't negotiated between equals. God's condescension gave a creature a covenant promise.
catechismCourse.argument: Observe the generous provision, the calling to work and keep the garden, and the particular prohibition. The threatened death makes the command more than advice about healthy food. Adam stood under a divine arrangement whose breach would bring a judicial consequence.
catechismCourse.guard: The label covenant of works summarizes the arrangement rather than quoting a phrase in Genesis 2. Adam's obedience didn't make God his debtor apart from God's own covenant commitment.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is the threatened death important for understanding Adam's situation?
catechismCourse.answer: It shows that the command belonged to a binding divine arrangement with a penalty for disobedience.

catechismCourse.title: The fall and the freedom of the will
catechismCourse.teach: Our first parents were created upright and able to obey, yet capable of falling. They freely chose disobedience. Their fall wasn't the result of an originally evil nature or a defect in God's command. Through their sin they lost the righteousness in which they had been created.
catechismCourse.argument: Trace the serpent's challenge to God's Word and the woman's changed judgment about the tree. The narrative shows a moral revolt expressed in a real act. The appeal to desire doesn't remove responsibility. God had already made His command known.
catechismCourse.guard: Human freedom doesn't require independence from God's providence. Before the fall man could obey or sin. Fallen man still chooses willingly, but cannot turn himself to saving good without renewing grace.
catechismCourse.exercise: Where does the temptation begin to change the creature's relation to God's Word?
catechismCourse.answer: It invites the creature to sit in judgment on God's command and goodness rather than receive His Word as true.

catechismCourse.title: Sin as want of conformity and transgression
catechismCourse.teach: Sin includes both failing to be what God's law requires and actively breaking what it commands. An inward disposition may be sinful before it produces an outward act. The law reaches love, motives, and desires as well as visible conduct.
catechismCourse.argument: John connects sin with lawlessness while distinguishing the children of God from those who remain under sin's dominion. Read this with his earlier teaching about confession and Christ our advocate in 1 John 1:8-2:2. He isn't teaching that Christians have become sinless.
catechismCourse.guard: Culture, personal preference, and other people's reactions don't determine whether something is sin. Neither should we label as sinful what God's law doesn't forbid. Conscience needs instruction from His Word.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does avoiding a forbidden outward action not necessarily fulfil the commandment?
catechismCourse.answer: God's law also requires inward conformity and positive obedience, which can be absent while outward behaviour looks respectable.

catechismCourse.title: Adam’s first disobedience
catechismCourse.teach: The first sin was eating the forbidden fruit. Its seriousness lay in disobedience to God, not in a naturally poisonous property of the food. The act expressed unbelief and a desire to judge good and evil apart from the Creator's authority.
catechismCourse.argument: Notice the hiding, blame, and divine questioning that follow the eating. The judgments address actual persons and their responsibilities. God doesn't accept the man's appeal to the woman or the woman's appeal to the serpent as an acquittal.
catechismCourse.guard: Recognizing the inward roots of the fall doesn't turn the historical act into a mere symbol. Scripture treats Adam's disobedience as a real event with consequences for the human race.
catechismCourse.exercise: What do the attempts to shift blame reveal about fallen man?
catechismCourse.answer: They show a desire to escape accountability rather than acknowledge sin before the God whose command was clear.

catechismCourse.title: Adam’s representative headship
catechismCourse.teach: Adam represented the human race in the first covenant. His guilt is imputed to those descending from him by ordinary generation, and his corruption is conveyed to them. Our condition involves more than copying a bad example. Christ, conceived by the Holy Ghost, isn't another sinner under Adam's guilt.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul repeatedly contrasts one man's disobedience with the obedience of the one man Jesus Christ. Follow the relation between the representative act and the condition of the many. Death's reign also reaches those who didn't personally repeat Adam's particular transgression.
catechismCourse.guard: The parallel doesn't teach universal salvation. It explains representative headship. Those united to Adam share his condemnation, while those united to Christ receive justification and life.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is Adam's role necessary to Paul's explanation of Christ's saving work?
catechismCourse.answer: Both men act as representative heads, so the consequences of their respective acts extend to those whom they represent.

catechismCourse.title: The estate of sin and misery
catechismCourse.teach: The fall brought mankind into an estate of sin and misery. Sin names our guilt and corruption. Misery includes the loss of communion with God and the consequences of His righteous judgment. Our deepest need isn't merely better surroundings or greater self-confidence.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul describes spiritual death together with active walking in trespasses. Dead sinners aren't inactive people. They live willingly according to a corrupt condition and stand under wrath. The change begins with God's mercy and His making them alive with Christ.
catechismCourse.guard: Spiritual death doesn't mean a person lacks a mind or will. It means he cannot produce saving life from himself. God's grace creates the life from which believing and good works follow.
catechismCourse.exercise: How can Paul describe the same people as dead and actively walking?
catechismCourse.answer: They are active in sin while lacking spiritual life and the ability to bring themselves into saving fellowship with God.

catechismCourse.title: Original sin and actual transgressions
catechismCourse.teach: Original sin includes the guilt of Adam's first sin, the loss of original righteousness, and the corruption of our whole nature. Actual sins flow from this corruption. In believers, remaining sin is forgiven and weakened through Christ, yet is still truly sin.
catechismCourse.argument: David confesses his particular wrongdoing and also traces his need deeper than one outward act. He asks for inward cleansing and a renewed heart. His words about conception describe his own sinful condition, not a claim that marriage or childbirth is inherently sinful.
catechismCourse.guard: Inherited corruption doesn't excuse chosen sins, and admitting chosen sins doesn't explain away our corrupt nature. We need both pardon for guilt and inward renewal by God's Spirit.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does David ask for a clean heart rather than only relief from consequences?
catechismCourse.answer: He recognizes that his wrongdoing arises from a deeper corruption that only God can cleanse and renew.

catechismCourse.title: The misery and punishment of sin
catechismCourse.teach: Sin brings the loss of communion with God, His wrath and curse, the miseries of this life, death, and the pains of hell for ever. Temporal suffering isn't the whole penalty. A sinner's condition before God must be addressed, not merely the painful symptoms of living in a fallen world.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul contrasts service to sin with service to God and then contrasts sin's wages with God's gift. The imagery of wages identifies death as deserved. Eternal life, by contrast, comes through Jesus Christ as a gift, not as the wage of improved conduct.
catechismCourse.guard: Not every particular hardship proves a particular personal sin. Scripture's account of sin's general misery doesn't authorize us to diagnose God's secret purpose in someone else's suffering.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Paul's contrast between wages and gift teach about salvation?
catechismCourse.answer: Death is earned by sin. Eternal life is freely given in Christ and cannot be claimed as our earned payment.

catechismCourse.title: Election and the covenant of grace
catechismCourse.teach: God didn't leave all mankind to perish. Out of His free love He chose a people and provided salvation through a Redeemer. The covenant of grace offers life in Christ and promises the Spirit who brings His people to faith. Its Old and New Testament administrations differ, but its saving substance is one.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul describes Gentiles once alienated from the covenants of promise and now brought near by Christ's blood. Follow the building imagery and the creation of one new man. Christ reconciles believing Jews and Gentiles to God in one body rather than founding two ways of salvation.
catechismCourse.guard: Covenant unity doesn't erase historical changes. Sacrifices and circumcision aren't retained as New Testament ordinances. The same Christ was promised beforehand and is now proclaimed as having come.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Christ's work address both alienation from God and division between peoples?
catechismCourse.answer: His blood reconciles His people to God and brings believing Jews and Gentiles together in one household.

catechismCourse.title: The only Redeemer
catechismCourse.teach: The Lord Jesus Christ is the only Redeemer of God's elect. He is the eternal Son who became man and continues God and man in two distinct natures and one person for ever. A mere creature couldn't bear God's judgment or bring us into lasting fellowship with Him.
catechismCourse.argument: Read Paul's confession of one Mediator within his command to pray for all sorts of people, including rulers. Christ's true humanity makes Him the Mediator who gave Himself a ransom. His unique office rules out other mediators who supposedly supply access to God alongside Him.
catechismCourse.guard: The one Mediator isn't a third being halfway between God and man. He is fully God and truly man. His uniqueness doesn't narrow the church's duty to pray and proclaim the gospel widely.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does the confession of one Mediator support prayer and gospel proclamation?
catechismCourse.answer: All people need the same access to God through Christ, so the church must pray broadly and make Him known.

catechismCourse.title: The incarnation and the two natures
catechismCourse.teach: The Son became man by taking a true body and a reasonable soul, conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the virgin Mary and born of her without sin. He didn't cease to be God or merely appear human. His humanity comes truly from Mary.
catechismCourse.argument: Gabriel identifies the child as Mary's son and as the Son of God. The conception is the Holy Ghost's work. Read the passage without turning the Spirit into a physical father or treating the virgin birth as an ordinary birth given a religious interpretation.
catechismCourse.guard: The divine and human natures remain distinct in one person. Christ's human growth and suffering don't mean His divine nature learned or became weak. His sinlessness doesn't make His humanity incomplete.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does this passage require us to confess about the child's humanity and identity?
catechismCourse.answer: He is truly born of Mary through a miraculous conception and is the holy Son of God, not a merely human religious leader.

catechismCourse.title: Christ the anointed Mediator
catechismCourse.teach: Christ executes the offices of Prophet, Priest, and King in both His humiliation and exaltation. These offices describe the one saving ministry of the one Mediator. He reveals God's will, reconciles us through sacrifice and intercession, and rules and preserves His redeemed people.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of the anointed servant and declares its fulfilment in the hearing of His neighbours. Notice the emphasis on divine appointment and the Spirit's anointing. His mission isn't self-chosen, and the promised deliverance must be understood through His whole ministry.
catechismCourse.guard: Don't divide Christ into separate helpers from whom we select an agreeable office. The Saviour who pardons also teaches and rules. Nor should an earthly minister claim the unique mediatorial office of Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is Christ's anointing relevant to His authority?
catechismCourse.answer: It identifies Him as the Father's appointed and Spirit-equipped Mediator, carrying out God's saving commission.

catechismCourse.title: Christ our Prophet
catechismCourse.teach: Christ reveals God's will for our salvation by His Word and Spirit. He spoke through the prophets before His incarnation and teaches the church through the apostolic Scriptures. His prophetic ministry includes inward illumination, so that His people receive what He has revealed.
catechismCourse.argument: Hebrews begins by comparing God's former speech through the prophets with His climactic speech in His Son. The Son's divine glory and accomplished purification give weight to the command to hear Him. He isn't one religious messenger among many equally sufficient guides.
catechismCourse.guard: The Spirit's illumination opens our understanding of the written Word. It doesn't add a new inspired message or make careless interpretation unnecessary. Christ's teaching must be heard according to the text He has given.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does the opening of Hebrews establish the authority of Christ's revelation?
catechismCourse.answer: God has spoken climactically in the divine Son, who both reveals Him and accomplishes purification for sins.

catechismCourse.title: Christ our Priest
catechismCourse.teach: Christ offered Himself once as a sacrifice to satisfy divine justice and reconcile His people to God. He continually intercedes for them. His intercession rests upon His finished sacrifice, so the believer's access doesn't depend on a fresh offering or a more sympathetic mediator.
catechismCourse.argument: Follow Hebrews' contrast between priests who die and the Son who continues for ever. His ability to save completely is joined to His living intercession. The final verses also contrast His spotless character and once-for-all sacrifice with the repeated offerings of sinful priests.
catechismCourse.guard: The cross isn't merely a display meant to move us to better behaviour. Christ truly bears judgment and makes satisfaction. His intercession doesn't persuade an unwilling Father to begin loving those whom the Father already gave Him.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why doesn't Christ need successors to continue His priestly work?
catechismCourse.answer: He lives for ever and maintains an unchangeable priesthood, interceding on the basis of His sufficient sacrifice.

catechismCourse.title: Christ our King
catechismCourse.teach: Christ subdues us to Himself, rules and defends us, and restrains and conquers His and our enemies. His kingly authority isn't limited to an inward feeling or to the church's voluntary recognition. The risen Mediator possesses all authority and orders all things for His people's salvation.
catechismCourse.argument: The psalm joins royal authority with an enduring priesthood. Read the Lord's invitation to sit at His right hand alongside the promised defeat of enemies. The New Testament identifies this reign with the exalted Christ. His present session isn't inactivity while He waits for a future throne.
catechismCourse.guard: Christ governs His church by His Word through appointed officers. His universal kingship doesn't allow those officers to seize civil authority or invent commands for the conscience.
catechismCourse.exercise: What connection does the psalm make between Christ's present position and His final victory?
catechismCourse.answer: His enthronement carries the certain promise that His enemies will be subdued under His rule.

catechismCourse.title: Christ’s humiliation and obedience
catechismCourse.teach: Christ humbled Himself in His lowly birth and life, obedience under the law, sufferings, cursed death, burial, and continuance under the power of death for a time. He obeyed where we failed and bore the judgment we deserved. His humiliation wasn't a surrender of deity.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul describes the eternal Son's taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death. Trace the subject through the passage. The one who humbles Himself is already in the form of God. Taking humanity is addition of a true nature, not subtraction of divine perfection.
catechismCourse.guard: Christ's continuing under the power of death refers to His burial before the resurrection. It doesn't require a further payment in hell after His finished satisfaction on the cross.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Paul's argument connect Christ's identity with the depth of His humility?
catechismCourse.answer: The one who is truly divine freely takes the servant's condition and obeys even unto the death of the cross.

catechismCourse.title: Christ’s resurrection and exaltation
catechismCourse.teach: Christ rose bodily on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the Father's right hand, and will return to judge the world. His resurrection vindicates His work and secures His people's rising. His exaltation is the triumph of the same incarnate Son who suffered.
catechismCourse.argument: Peter argues from witnessed events and the Psalms to the resurrection and enthronement of Jesus. David's tomb remains, so the promise isn't exhausted by David's experience. Notice how Peter gives a textual reason for identifying the promised Holy One with Christ.
catechismCourse.guard: The Father's right hand names supreme honour and authority. It isn't a claim that the Father has a bodily hand. Christ's humanity remains truly human and located in heaven until His bodily return.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does Peter mention David's tomb while interpreting the psalm?
catechismCourse.answer: David died and his body saw corruption, so the promise points beyond him to the risen Christ.

catechismCourse.title: Redemption purchased and applied
catechismCourse.teach: The Spirit effectually applies the redemption Christ purchased. The work accomplished at the cross and its application to particular sinners must be distinguished without being separated. Everyone for whom Christ purchased redemption will receive its saving benefits in God's appointed time.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul contrasts our former sinful life with God's saving kindness and then locates the change in the Spirit's renewing work through Jesus Christ. Salvation is according to mercy rather than our works of righteousness. The passage joins justification and the hope of inheritance without confusing them.
catechismCourse.guard: Religious sincerity outside Christ isn't another path to salvation. Nor does speaking about the Spirit mean leaving Christ's finished work behind. The Spirit brings us into the benefits of that work.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Paul's account exclude as the cause of our salvation?
catechismCourse.answer: It excludes our own righteous works as the ground and attributes salvation to God's mercy and the Spirit's renewing application.

catechismCourse.title: Union with Christ through faith
catechismCourse.teach: The Spirit works faith in us and thereby unites us to Christ in effectual calling. This union is a real spiritual bond, not a physical mixing of substances. In Christ we receive every saving benefit, and His Spirit makes us living members of His body.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul says that our being in Christ is of God and then identifies Christ as our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. The surrounding argument removes every ground of boasting. Our saving relation to Christ begins with divine grace rather than spiritual superiority.
catechismCourse.guard: Union doesn't make us divine or erase our personal identity. It also doesn't collapse justification into sanctification. Both blessings belong to the same Christ and remain distinct gifts.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does union with Christ leave no room for boasting in ourselves?
catechismCourse.answer: God brings us into Christ, and all the wisdom and righteousness we need for salvation are found in Him.

catechismCourse.title: Effectual calling and regeneration
catechismCourse.teach: In effectual calling the Spirit convinces us of sin and misery, enlightens our minds in Christ's knowledge, and renews our wills, enabling us to embrace Him as freely offered in the gospel. Saving faith follows from renewing grace rather than supplying the condition that causes regeneration.
catechismCourse.argument: Lydia hears apostolic preaching, and the Lord opens her heart to attend to it. Luke joins the outward ministry of the Word with God's inward work. Her response is truly hers, while its saving effectiveness is attributed to the Lord.
catechismCourse.guard: The outward gospel call must go to all. Not everyone who hears it is inwardly renewed. God's effectual work makes unwilling sinners willing without coercing them against their renewed desires.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Lydia's conversion distinguish the preacher's task from God's saving action?
catechismCourse.answer: Paul speaks the Word, while the Lord opens Lydia's heart to receive it. The inward work doesn't render preaching unnecessary.

catechismCourse.title: The benefits of effectual calling
catechismCourse.teach: Those effectually called receive justification, adoption, and sanctification, with the benefits that accompany them. God doesn't give Christ's pardon while withholding every beginning of renewal. Yet a changed life isn't the legal basis on which He declares us righteous.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul's sequence follows God's purpose from foreknowledge to glorification. The repeated subjects show that God doesn't lose some of those He effectually calls along the way. The passage offers certainty in suffering, not a licence to ignore the duties taught elsewhere in the letter.
catechismCourse.guard: A summary sequence doesn't give the precise time interval between every benefit. Nor does its omission of adoption or sanctification make those benefits optional. Read the passage alongside the fuller teaching of Scripture.
catechismCourse.exercise: What grounds the believer's confidence that salvation will reach its appointed end?
catechismCourse.answer: The same God who purposes and calls also justifies and brings His people to glory.

catechismCourse.title: Justification by faith alone
catechismCourse.teach: Justification is God's judicial act of pardoning sin and accepting us as righteous solely for Christ's righteousness imputed to us and received by faith alone. Christ's obedience and satisfaction are the ground. Faith is the receiving instrument, not a replacement righteousness of our own.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul excludes works of the law from justification while locating redemption in Christ's blood. Read his explanation of God's justice. God doesn't simply ignore guilt. He deals with it through the Redeemer, so that His justifying grace is consistent with His righteousness.
catechismCourse.guard: Justification isn't inward moral improvement or a verdict earned by sufficiently strong faith. The justified believer still needs daily forgiveness, but never returns to a state of condemnation.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does faith exclude boasting rather than become a new achievement to boast about?
catechismCourse.answer: Faith receives the righteousness and redemption supplied in Christ instead of presenting our works or faith's quality as merit.

catechismCourse.title: Adoption into God’s family
catechismCourse.teach: God adopts all who are justified into His family for the sake of His only Son. Believers receive His name and fatherly care, access to His throne, and an everlasting inheritance. Adoption changes our standing and privileges without making us sons by nature as Christ is.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul connects the sending of the Son with redemption and the sending of the Spirit into believers' hearts. The movement from bondage to sonship rests on God's action. The believer's cry to the Father is the fruit of this granted relation.
catechismCourse.guard: Fatherly discipline doesn't mean the Father has revoked adoption. Nor does adoption promise an easy earthly life. He trains His children in holiness and brings them through suffering to their inheritance.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Paul distinguish the ground of sonship from the experience of it?
catechismCourse.answer: God sends His Son to redeem and grant adoption, then sends the Spirit who gives the child's response toward the Father.

catechismCourse.title: Sanctification and the remaining conflict
catechismCourse.teach: Sanctification is God's work of renewing the whole person after His image, enabling us increasingly to die to sin and live to righteousness. Sin's dominion is broken through union with Christ, but its presence remains throughout this life. Growth is real, though uneven and contested.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul grounds the command not to let sin reign in the believer's participation in Christ's death and resurrection. He doesn't tell us to create a new spiritual identity by obedience. Because we belong to Christ, we must present ourselves to God and resist sin.
catechismCourse.guard: Progress isn't sinless perfection, and failure isn't permission to surrender. Good works are necessary fruits of grace, never a payment that completes Christ's righteousness or buys continued justification.
catechismCourse.exercise: What order does Paul establish between grace and the command to obey?
catechismCourse.answer: He declares the believer's union with Christ and then commands obedience appropriate to that new life.

catechismCourse.title: Assurance, peace, growth, and perseverance
catechismCourse.teach: Justification, adoption, and sanctification bring peace with God, the comforts of His love, joy in the Holy Ghost, growth in grace, and perseverance to the end. These benefits aren't always felt equally. Peace with God is an objective reconciliation even when a believer's inward peace is weak.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul begins with justification by faith and peace through Christ, then explains hope amid tribulation. Suffering doesn't cancel the believer's accepted standing. God uses it in His work of patient endurance, while His Spirit assures His children of His love.
catechismCourse.guard: Assurance isn't essential to the existence of saving faith, and believers may struggle long before enjoying it fully. Perseverance rests on God's preserving grace, which also moves believers to use His appointed means.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why can a justified person have peace with God while still experiencing severe distress?
catechismCourse.answer: Reconciliation rests on Christ's work, while the felt comfort of that relation can be disturbed without undoing the relation itself.

catechismCourse.title: The believer at death
catechismCourse.teach: At death believers' souls are made perfect in holiness and immediately pass into glory. Their bodies remain united to Christ and rest in their graves until the resurrection. Death is still an enemy, but for those in Christ it no longer carries the curse of condemnation.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul can desire to depart and be with Christ while recognizing that remaining would serve the churches. His hope is personal fellowship with Christ after death. Read this alongside his expectation of bodily resurrection rather than treating disembodied life as the final Christian hope.
catechismCourse.guard: The soul doesn't become unconscious until the last day, and no purgatory is needed to finish paying for sin. Glorification ends the believer's remaining sin without making the believer divine.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Paul's desire to depart differ from despair about the worth of life?
catechismCourse.answer: He desires Christ's presence while still seeing faithful service to others as a meaningful reason to remain.

catechismCourse.title: Resurrection and the final judgment
catechismCourse.teach: At the resurrection believers are raised in glory, openly acknowledged and acquitted in judgment, and made perfectly blessed in the full enjoyment of God for ever. All the dead will rise. The wicked face condemnation and everlasting punishment, while Christ's people enter everlasting life.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul uses the sowing of seed to explain bodily continuity and transformation. Corruption gives way to incorruption, not to the abandonment of the body. His conclusion calls for steadfast labour because resurrection guarantees that service in the Lord isn't vain.
catechismCourse.guard: Spiritual body doesn't mean an immaterial body. It means a body fitted for the Spirit-given life of the age to come. The final public verdict confirms Christ's righteousness received by faith, not a new justification earned by works.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does resurrection hope strengthen ordinary Christian work?
catechismCourse.answer: The Lord who raises His people gives lasting significance to their service, even when present labour seems weak or unnoticed.

catechismCourse.title: The obedience God requires
catechismCourse.teach: God requires obedience to His revealed will. His moral law expresses the duty of a creature toward the holy Creator. It exposes sin and directs the redeemed life. Believers aren't under it as a covenant by which they must earn justification, yet they remain bound to obey it.
catechismCourse.argument: Moses joins fear, love, service, and obedience with the Lord's prior love and mighty deeds. Read the commands about strangers and the vulnerable as part of that same argument. Love for God has definite duties toward those He places beside us.
catechismCourse.guard: The law cannot give a fallen sinner the righteousness needed for acceptance. Neither does the gospel make disobedience harmless. Grace gives pardon and produces a willing obedience.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Moses connect God's gracious dealings with the people's duty?
catechismCourse.answer: God's prior love and deliverance call forth a grateful, wholehearted response expressed in concrete obedience.

catechismCourse.title: The moral law before Sinai
catechismCourse.teach: God first revealed the moral law to man as the rule of obedience in creation. Sinai didn't invent the distinction between good and evil. The written commandments summarize an obligation grounded in man's relation to God, though fallen conscience now judges imperfectly.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul describes Gentiles without Israel's written law who nevertheless show the work of the law in their hearts. Their accusing or excusing thoughts demonstrate moral accountability. This isn't an assertion that conscience provides an uncorrupted, sufficient way of salvation.
catechismCourse.guard: Natural knowledge leaves sinners accountable but cannot replace Scripture. A practice doesn't become good because conscience feels untroubled about it. Conscience itself must be instructed and corrected.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Paul's appeal to conscience establish about people without the written law?
catechismCourse.answer: They remain morally accountable to God, even though they don't possess Israel's written revelation.

catechismCourse.title: The Ten Commandments as a summary
catechismCourse.teach: The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments. Their brevity doesn't limit obedience to ten narrow outward acts. Each command reaches the whole duty it expresses. What God forbids also requires the contrary duty, and what He commands forbids contrary sins.
catechismCourse.argument: Read the commandments as God's covenant address rather than a detached list. Their place after deliverance matters, but their moral authority isn't restricted to Israel's civil order. Jesus and His apostles continue to apply these duties to the heart and life.
catechismCourse.guard: Use the Larger Catechism's rules for interpretation before inventing exceptions or extending commands carelessly. Distinguish moral duties from ceremonial shadows and judicial arrangements whose national form has expired.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why must a prohibition be read with its corresponding positive duty?
catechismCourse.answer: God requires real righteousness, not merely abstention from a particular outward wrong. Forbidding murder also calls us to preserve life.

catechismCourse.title: Love as the sum of the law
catechismCourse.teach: The commandments require love to God with our whole being and love to our neighbour as ourselves. Love sums up the law without replacing its particular commands. God tells us what loving Him and our neighbour entails rather than leaving love to personal definition.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus answers a question about the great commandment by joining the duties toward God and neighbour. The whole law and the prophets hang on these. This presents their unity and purpose, not an exemption from the commands to worship rightly, speak truth, and preserve chastity.
catechismCourse.guard: Affection doesn't justify disobedience. We may sincerely desire another's happiness while approving something God forbids. Biblical love seeks another's good according to God's truth.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why can't we set love against the particular commandments?
catechismCourse.answer: Jesus identifies love as their governing summary. The commands show the concrete shape that rightly ordered love takes.

catechismCourse.title: The lawgiver’s covenant preface
catechismCourse.teach: Before giving the commandments, God identifies Himself as Israel's God and Redeemer. The law comes from the Lord who has already acted to deliver His people. Obedience is owed to Him as Creator and must also answer His covenant mercy.
catechismCourse.argument: Read the mention of Egypt before the first commandment. The people aren't invited to earn a rescue that has not yet occurred. Their deliverer claims their exclusive allegiance. This historical order helps us distinguish redemption from the grateful obedience that follows.
catechismCourse.guard: Israel's outward deliverance didn't mean every Israelite was inwardly regenerate. Nor is the preface a promise that every earthly hardship will end if we keep enough commands.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is the account of deliverance placed before the commandments?
catechismCourse.answer: It identifies the covenant Lord whose gracious rescue supplies a further reason for His people's willing allegiance.

catechismCourse.title: God’s authority and redeeming mercy
catechismCourse.teach: Because the Lord is our God and Redeemer, we are bound to keep His commandments. His authority doesn't depend on our consent. His grace also changes the spirit in which believers obey. We serve the Father who redeemed us, rather than seeking to buy His acceptance.
catechismCourse.argument: Peter calls believers to holiness and then reminds them of the price of redemption. Their reverent conduct rests on the blood of Christ, not on confidence in inherited custom or perishable wealth. Read the command and the saving foundation together.
catechismCourse.guard: Redeeming mercy strengthens the obligation to obey without changing obedience into a second payment for sin. Fear of God is reverent allegiance to our holy Father, not the servile terror of one still condemned in Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: What reason does Peter give for leaving the former manner of life?
catechismCourse.answer: Believers have been redeemed at the cost of Christ's precious blood and now belong to the holy God who called them.

catechismCourse.title: The first commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The first commandment governs whom we worship. The Lord alone is God, so no creature may receive the trust, devotion, or religious honour due to Him. The command addresses the heart's allegiance as well as public acts of worship.
catechismCourse.argument: Read the first commandment before the prohibition of images. The first establishes the true object of worship. The second addresses the worship He authorizes. That distinction helps us see why worship directed toward the true God can still be offered in a forbidden manner.
catechismCourse.guard: A created thing can become an idol without being called a god. Wealth, approval, or personal control can claim the confidence and obedience that belong to the Lord.
catechismCourse.exercise: How do the first and second commandments address different questions?
catechismCourse.answer: The first identifies whom we must worship, while the second governs how the true God is to be worshipped.

catechismCourse.title: Knowing and acknowledging God
catechismCourse.teach: The first commandment requires us to know and acknowledge the only true God as our God and to worship and glorify Him accordingly. Faith receives His self-revelation. Love, fear, hope, and trust must be directed toward Him according to His worth.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus refuses the tempter's offer of the kingdoms and answers with God's command for exclusive worship and service. His refusal joins outward worship with inward allegiance. No promised advantage can make religious compromise a faithful way to fulfil God's calling.
catechismCourse.guard: Knowing facts about God while refusing His authority doesn't fulfil this command. Nor can a vague belief in a higher power replace receiving the Lord as He reveals Himself in Scripture.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why couldn't the offered kingdoms justify the worship Satan demanded?
catechismCourse.answer: No benefit can authorize giving a creature the exclusive worship and service owed to God.

catechismCourse.title: Atheism, idolatry, and practical unbelief
catechismCourse.teach: The first commandment forbids denying the true God, withholding the worship due to Him, or giving it to another. Sin can take the form of explicit unbelief or of living as though God had no claim upon us. Idolatry exchanges the Creator's glory for created substitutes.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul traces false worship to the suppression of known truth. The problem isn't that mankind receives no witness to God. The passage describes a moral refusal to honour Him and a resulting exchange of worship. It explains why idolatry needs repentance, not merely better artistic taste.
catechismCourse.guard: Don't use this doctrine to pretend believers cannot act inconsistently or struggle with fear. Their remaining unbelief needs confession and renewed trust, while their acceptance rests in Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: What exchange lies at the heart of idolatry in Paul's argument?
catechismCourse.answer: People give created things the worship and service that belong to the Creator, whose truth they suppress.

catechismCourse.title: Our worship before God’s face
catechismCourse.teach: The words before me remind us that God sees and is displeased with having any other god. Worship isn't evaluated merely by what other people can observe. A person may approach religious instruction while secretly reserving his deepest allegiance for an idol.
catechismCourse.argument: Ezekiel confronts elders whose idols are established in their hearts. Read the Lord's answer to their outward approach. Their formal act of seeking a prophet doesn't hide their divided allegiance from the God who knows them.
catechismCourse.guard: God's knowledge isn't surveillance that believers must escape. It calls us to honest repentance. Christ's mediation gives access to the God before whom nothing is hidden.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why doesn't an outwardly religious action prove that the heart is rightly directed?
catechismCourse.answer: Someone may seek religious guidance while maintaining inward idols. God judges the allegiance beneath the outward approach.

catechismCourse.title: The second commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The second commandment forbids worshipping God through images or any other way He hasn't appointed. The true God isn't to be represented according to human invention. Right intention cannot authorize a religious practice that contradicts His command.
catechismCourse.argument: Moses reminds Israel that they heard God's voice at Horeb but saw no form. He then forbids making an image. Follow that stated reason. The prohibition isn't limited to an image of a false god, but includes devising a visible form for the Lord who spoke.
catechismCourse.guard: This companion follows the Reformed Presbyterian application against making images of the persons of the Godhead, including portrayals of Christ. The incarnation doesn't give us authority to invent His appearance or use it devotionally.
catechismCourse.exercise: What reason does Moses give for Israel's refusal to make a representation of God?
catechismCourse.answer: God revealed Himself by His voice without showing a form from which they were authorized to make an image.

catechismCourse.title: Receiving and keeping God’s appointed worship
catechismCourse.teach: The second commandment requires receiving, observing, and preserving the religious worship and ordinances God appoints. The church must hear His Word, pray, receive His sacraments, and offer the praise He provides. Faithfulness includes guarding these ordinances from additions that change their nature.
catechismCourse.argument: Luke describes the church continuing in apostolic doctrine, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers. Read these as the fruit of receiving the gospel and being gathered into the church. Their appointed, ordinary character doesn't make them optional or spiritually weak.
catechismCourse.guard: Reformed Presbyterian worship sings the inspired Psalms without instrumental accompaniment. This is our application of the regulative principle. WCF 21.5 names psalm singing, but its wording mustn't be expanded to contain labels or statements it doesn't expressly include.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does the church's steadfast continuation challenge a search for constant religious novelty?
catechismCourse.answer: The apostolic pattern directs believers to persevere in Christ's appointed means rather than replace them when they seem ordinary.

catechismCourse.title: Unauthorized worship and religious images
catechismCourse.teach: The second commandment forbids worship by images and worship not appointed in God's Word. It also forbids corrupting what He has appointed. A practice needn't look irreligious to be disobedient. Humanly devised austerity or ceremony can give an appearance of devotion while obscuring Christ's sufficiency.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul confronts imposed religious regulations and self-chosen worship. Read his argument through the believer's union with Christ. The problem isn't careful obedience to God's commands. It is submitting to human religious requirements as though they supplied the holiness Christ gives.
catechismCourse.guard: Necessary circumstances such as meeting time, language, and seating aren't new elements of worship. They must be arranged prudently under Scripture's general rules, rather than treated as independent sacred ordinances.
catechismCourse.exercise: What distinguishes a necessary circumstance from an invented religious element?
catechismCourse.answer: A circumstance orders an appointed activity in ordinary human life. An invented element adds a religious act claimed as worship without divine warrant.

catechismCourse.title: God’s jealousy and covenant faithfulness
catechismCourse.teach: God strengthens the second commandment by declaring His sovereignty, His propriety in His people, and His zeal for His own worship. His jealousy is holy zeal for His rightful honour, not insecurity. His warnings and promises show that worship has consequences extending beyond one person's private preference.
catechismCourse.argument: Read the warning concerning generations together with the contrast of mercy toward those who love Him. The text addresses covenant households and persistent hatred of God. It doesn't erase individual moral responsibility or make a child guilty merely for being born to a particular parent.
catechismCourse.guard: Family patterns can pass on real corruption and suffering. Yet Ezekiel 18 rejects punishing a righteous child as though he had committed his father's sins. Hold the passages together instead of turning the warning into fatalism.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why should parents take the religious life of their household seriously?
catechismCourse.answer: Their worship and teaching shape succeeding generations, and God's covenant warnings and mercies concern households as well as individuals.

catechismCourse.title: The third commandment
catechismCourse.teach: God's name reveals who He is. The third commandment governs our use of His names, titles, attributes, ordinances, Word, and works. We must speak and act toward Him with the reverence due to the holy God, rather than using sacred things for vanity or gain.
catechismCourse.argument: The command joins a prohibition with the Lord's declaration that He will not acquit its violator. Read the seriousness of that warning. Irreverence isn't made harmless because a culture treats it as casual speech or because no earthly authority notices.
catechismCourse.guard: Taking God's name in vain includes more than profanity. False religious claims, manipulative appeals to divine authority, and careless handling of His Word can also misuse what He has made known.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is misuse of God's name more serious than violating a social convention?
catechismCourse.answer: It dishonours the holy God Himself, who has expressly declared His judgment upon such misuse.

catechismCourse.title: Reverent use of God’s name
catechismCourse.teach: We honour God's name through serious attention to His Word, reverent prayer, truthful confession, and faithful use of His ordinances. This reverence concerns the heart and understanding, not a cultivated religious tone. Familiar words about God still require thoughtful use.
catechismCourse.argument: Ecclesiastes contrasts a readiness to hear with rash speech before God. Its warning about vows shows how religious language binds the speaker. The passage doesn't forbid frequent prayer, but challenges thoughtless speech that assumes God can be approached casually.
catechismCourse.guard: Public prayer needn't be elaborate to be reverent. Nor does a trembling speaker dishonour God by lacking polished language. The issue is sincere, understanding worship offered through Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: What correction does this passage give to the desire to sound impressive before God?
catechismCourse.answer: It directs us to hear humbly and speak thoughtfully, recognizing God's greatness rather than filling the occasion with rash words.

catechismCourse.title: Profaning what God makes known
catechismCourse.teach: The third commandment forbids profaning or abusing anything by which God makes Himself known. This includes twisting Scripture to support sin, invoking God's name deceitfully, and treating His ordinances as tools for status or profit. Outward religious precision cannot excuse inward contempt.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus shows how a religious tradition can make God's command ineffective. The language of a gift dedicated to God had become a means of avoiding duty toward parents. Follow the concrete example before reading His judgment about honouring God with lips while the heart remains far away.
catechismCourse.guard: Not every inherited church practice is a forbidden tradition. The question is whether a practice contradicts God's command or imposes human authority where His Word alone must bind.
catechismCourse.exercise: How can a religious phrase become a means of profaning God's name?
catechismCourse.answer: It can invoke His authority to excuse disobedience, making religious language a cover for refusing His actual command.

catechismCourse.title: God will vindicate His name
catechismCourse.teach: People may escape correction for misusing God's name, but they cannot escape His judgment. He will vindicate His holiness. This warning should make us careful teachers and hearers, knowing that religious office or an approving audience doesn't guarantee His approval.
catechismCourse.argument: Malachi confronts priests who despise God's name while continuing temple worship. Their defective offerings reveal what they think of His worth. The contrast with what they would present to a human governor exposes the contempt hidden inside respectable religious activity.
catechismCourse.guard: The warning isn't a command to invent anxious rituals to make ourselves acceptable. Repent of irreverence and come through Christ, whose sufficient mediation provides the access our defective worship cannot earn.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does Malachi compare offerings to God with gifts to a governor?
catechismCourse.answer: The comparison exposes a willingness to offer God what the worshippers would be ashamed to present to a human authority.

catechismCourse.title: The fourth commandment
catechismCourse.teach: God commands one day in seven to be kept holy to Him. The Sabbath belongs to His moral law and rests upon His pattern in creation. It isn't merely a Jewish civil custom or a day each person may appoint without reference to His command.
catechismCourse.argument: Read the command's reference back to creation. The reason reaches beyond Israel's later ceremonies and national life. The command also includes servants and strangers, showing that those with authority must not preserve their own rest by unnecessarily requiring others to labour.
catechismCourse.guard: The moral duty of a weekly holy day continues while the appointed day changes under the New Testament. Distinguish this from the ceremonial sabbaths that prefigured Christ's work.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does the creation reason explain the continuing importance of this command?
catechismCourse.answer: It grounds the weekly pattern in God's ordering of human life, not only in Israel's temporary national institutions.

catechismCourse.title: A whole day set apart for God
catechismCourse.teach: The fourth commandment requires the keeping holy to God of the time He appoints, especially one whole day in seven. Holiness here means being set apart for His worship and service. The command seeks willing delight in the Lord, not merely cessation of paid employment.
catechismCourse.argument: Isaiah connects turning from ordinary pursuits with honouring the Lord's holy day and delighting in Him. Read the commands as the shape of that honour, not as a mechanism for earning prosperity. God's gift of a holy day makes room for communion with Him.
catechismCourse.guard: The Lord's Day isn't fulfilled by attending one service while treating the rest of the day as ordinary leisure. Necessary and merciful works remain lawful because they accord with God's purpose.
catechismCourse.exercise: What positive purpose gives meaning to Sabbath rest?
catechismCourse.answer: Rest sets apart time for worship and delight in the Lord, rather than functioning as an empty interruption of ordinary work.

catechismCourse.title: The first day as the Christian Sabbath
catechismCourse.teach: From creation until Christ's resurrection God appointed the seventh day. Since the resurrection the first day of the week is the Christian Sabbath, or Lord's Day, to continue to the end of the world. The day honours the risen Saviour and His accomplished work.
catechismCourse.argument: Acts records the disciples gathering to break bread on the first day. Consider this with the resurrection accounts, the first-day collection in 1 Corinthians 16:1-2, and the Lord's Day in Revelation 1:10. The confession's conclusion gathers these passages with the continuing moral command.
catechismCourse.guard: Acts 20 alone isn't a direct sentence commanding the transfer of the day. The doctrinal argument is a good and necessary consequence from Scripture taken together, and should be presented honestly as such.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why should the argument for the Lord's Day use more than one narrative detail?
catechismCourse.answer: It draws together the enduring Sabbath command, Christ's resurrection, and the apostolic first-day pattern rather than resting on a single incidental observation.

catechismCourse.title: Sanctifying the Lord’s Day
catechismCourse.teach: We sanctify the Sabbath by resting from ordinary worldly employment and recreation and spending the day in public and private worship, except for works of necessity and mercy. Preparation helps protect that purpose. Household governors should also make room for those under their care to worship.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus answers an accusation about His disciples by appealing to Scripture and declaring His authority over the Sabbath. The day was made for man's good. His answer corrects human distortions without treating the command as a meaningless burden He simply removes.
catechismCourse.guard: Necessity and mercy aren't loopholes for anything we happen to prefer. Nor should zeal for rest become an excuse to withhold care from someone in need. Christ determines the faithful use of His day.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Christ's lordship protect the Sabbath from both neglect and harsh invention?
catechismCourse.answer: He upholds its God-given purpose and corrects human rules that obstruct the good His command requires.

catechismCourse.title: Sins against the Sabbath
catechismCourse.teach: The fourth commandment forbids neglecting its duties, performing them carelessly, and profaning the day through unnecessary worldly work or recreation. Idleness alone doesn't sanctify a day. The heart can remain occupied with ordinary pursuits even when the body is outwardly at rest.
catechismCourse.argument: Nehemiah confronts trade that makes the holy day function like any other market day. Notice the responsibilities of those governing the community. The passage exposes public and household arrangements that undermine obedience, rather than blaming only isolated consumers.
catechismCourse.guard: Nehemiah's civil actions belonged to his particular office in Israel. The church must teach and exercise its own spiritual discipline without assuming his civil jurisdiction.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does this passage reveal about the effect of shared arrangements on Sabbath keeping?
catechismCourse.answer: Trading practices and the decisions of those in authority can encourage or obstruct the community's obedience to God's command.

catechismCourse.title: Reasons for remembering the Sabbath
catechismCourse.teach: God allows six days for ordinary work, claims the seventh for Himself, gives His own example, and blesses the holy day. Deuteronomy also reminds Israel of deliverance from bondage. The command is supported by His sovereignty and kindness, not arbitrary deprivation.
catechismCourse.argument: Deuteronomy particularly emphasizes rest for servants in connection with Israel's former slavery. Compare Exodus 20, which appeals to creation. The reasons complement one another. Redemption adds a motive for obedience to a duty already grounded in God's ordering of human life.
catechismCourse.guard: Remembering isn't merely recalling which day it is. It involves ordering our work beforehand and receiving the day as God's appointment. Avoid making other people carry avoidable burdens so that our own schedule remains comfortable.
catechismCourse.exercise: How do creation and redemption supply complementary Sabbath reasons?
catechismCourse.answer: Creation establishes the appointed pattern, while redemption teaches the delivered people to honour God and extend rest to those in their care.

catechismCourse.title: The fifth commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The fifth commandment orders our responsibilities within relationships of authority, service, and equality. Father and mother includes parents directly and, by the command's wider moral scope, those God places over us in lawful stations. Their authority is delegated and accountable, never absolute.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul addresses children and parents before turning to servants and masters. Read every address. God gives duties to those who command as well as those who obey, and He reminds earthly masters that they too have a Master in heaven.
catechismCourse.guard: This command cannot justify obeying a sinful order or treating authority as permission to abuse. God's law governs both parties. Proper honour may include seeking lawful protection and correction when authority is misused.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why must the passage's duties for superiors be taught alongside its duties for inferiors?
catechismCourse.answer: Authority is a charge under God, and those who hold it must serve His purposes rather than exploit those entrusted to them.

catechismCourse.title: Honour within our several places
catechismCourse.teach: The fifth commandment requires preserving the honour and performing the duties belonging to each person's place and relation. Inferiors owe lawful respect and obedience. Superiors owe wise care and just government. Equals owe mutual honour rather than rivalry or contempt.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul moves from sober self-assessment to different gifts and then to practical duties within the body. His call to honour others shows that rank or giftedness doesn't remove the obligation to serve. The church's common life requires humility from every member.
catechismCourse.guard: Honour doesn't mean pretending every judgment is correct. Correction can be offered respectfully, and lawful appeals can preserve a relationship's proper order rather than destroy it.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does sober judgment about one's gifts support honouring others?
catechismCourse.answer: It discourages self-exaltation and encourages us to receive others as fellow members whose gifts and needs matter.

catechismCourse.title: Sins against rightly ordered relationships
catechismCourse.teach: The fifth commandment forbids neglecting the honour and duties required in our relationships. Rebellion, contempt, harsh government, and envy among equals all violate its scope. The superior who provokes or exploits others isn't obeying merely because he successfully secures outward compliance.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul places household duties under the Lord's authority and warns that wrongdoing will receive its due without respect of persons. Read this warning alongside the commands. A person's station cannot shield him from God's impartial judgment.
catechismCourse.guard: Submission is always under God's higher command. Distinguishing faithful submission from sinful compliance requires attention to the particular duty and the authority's actual sphere.
catechismCourse.exercise: What prevents an earthly superior from treating his position as immunity from judgment?
catechismCourse.answer: He serves under the Lord, who judges wrongdoing without favouritism and holds every person accountable.

catechismCourse.title: The fifth commandment’s promise
catechismCourse.teach: The promise attached to the fifth commandment teaches God's blessing upon rightly ordered obedience. Long life and prosperity are to be understood so far as they serve His glory and the believer's good. The promise isn't a contract guaranteeing every obedient child a particular lifespan.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul applies the command and promise to children in the New Testament church. This confirms the command's continuing moral use. His next instruction also binds fathers to nurture rather than provoke, preventing a one-sided account of household duty.
catechismCourse.guard: A believer's early death doesn't prove hidden disobedience, and a wicked person's longevity doesn't disprove God's promise. Particular providences must be read under the full counsel of Scripture.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Paul's use of this command establish about Christian obedience?
catechismCourse.answer: The command remains a rule for Christian households, with its promise received under God's wise and sovereign care.

catechismCourse.title: The sixth commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The sixth commandment forbids the unjust taking of human life. Its reach includes the inward anger and contempt from which outward violence grows. Human life belongs to God, and our neighbour's dignity isn't measured by usefulness, strength, or our affection toward him.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus applies the command to anger and insulting contempt and then directs the hearer toward reconciliation. He doesn't contradict Moses by inventing a new moral law. He exposes the heart's guilt beneath a reading satisfied merely to avoid the outward act of murder.
catechismCourse.guard: Not every taking of life has the same moral character. Scripture distinguishes murder from lawful defence and public justice. The command must be applied through those revealed distinctions, not through private permission to retaliate.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Jesus reveal about a merely outward claim to have kept this commandment?
catechismCourse.answer: It can hide anger and contempt that violate the same duty to regard and preserve our neighbour's life.

catechismCourse.title: Preserving our own and our neighbour’s life
catechismCourse.teach: The sixth commandment requires lawful efforts to preserve our own life and the life of others. This includes bodily care, patient speech, relief of distress, and protection from avoidable harm. Mercy seeks a neighbour's actual good instead of merely avoiding personal involvement in violence.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus' parable answers the lawyer's attempt to narrow the category of neighbour. Follow the Samaritan's concrete care and willingness to bear expense. The point isn't that mercy earns eternal life, but that self-justifying restriction of the duty exposes a failure to love.
catechismCourse.guard: Ordinary care and seeking appropriate help are consistent with trusting providence. Care for oneself mustn't become selfish disregard of others, and self-denial mustn't become contempt for the life God entrusted to us.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does the Samaritan demonstrate the positive duty behind the prohibition of murder?
catechismCourse.answer: He actively preserves and restores another's life through practical care, instead of claiming innocence because he didn't cause the injury.

catechismCourse.title: What endangers or destroys life
catechismCourse.teach: The sixth commandment forbids murder and whatever unjustly tends toward destroying life. This includes violent hatred, cruel speech, reckless endangerment, and the unjust destruction of unborn life. Our own lives also belong to God, so despair doesn't grant authority to destroy ourselves.
catechismCourse.argument: James traces the destructive power of speech and confronts the contradiction of blessing God while cursing people made in His likeness. The connection grounds careful speech in our neighbour's relation to God, not merely in avoiding unpleasant social consequences.
catechismCourse.guard: Recognizing the seriousness of harmful thoughts and words doesn't make every angry feeling identical in circumstance or consequence to outward murder. Scripture distinguishes degrees of guilt while condemning the inward root.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does James appeal to God's likeness when warning against cursing people?
catechismCourse.answer: Contempt for a human image-bearer dishonours the God whose likeness that person bears.

catechismCourse.title: The seventh commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The seventh commandment forbids adultery and requires chastity in every condition of life. Marriage is God's covenant union of one man and one woman. Sexual faithfulness concerns desire and imagination as well as outward acts. God's command protects our neighbour rather than treating another person as an object.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus addresses lustful looking before speaking about divorce. His strong language about removing what leads into sin demands decisive repentance, not bodily mutilation. The problem lies in sinful use of our faculties, not in the mere existence of a body or sexual desire.
catechismCourse.guard: The command doesn't make marriage impure or single life incomplete. God requires chastity in both. His law mustn't be adjusted to make a cherished desire lawful.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does Jesus include the direction of the eyes and heart in His explanation?
catechismCourse.answer: The command governs inward sexual allegiance and desire, not only the final outward act of adultery.

catechismCourse.title: Preserving chastity
catechismCourse.teach: The seventh commandment requires preserving our own and our neighbour's chastity in heart, speech, and behaviour. Faithfulness includes modest conduct, honest marital love, and refusing entertainment or relationships that cultivate lust. The positive purpose is a holy use of the life and body God gives.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul locates sexual holiness within God's calling and warns against wronging a brother. Sexual sin isn't merely a private choice without a victim. Read his appeal to the Holy Spirit at the passage's close. Obedience answers the God who gives His Spirit to His people.
catechismCourse.guard: Practical safeguards can help, but they cannot replace inward repentance and faith. Nor does temptation itself prove that a believer must consent to it. Seek the Spirit's strength through the ordinary means of grace.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Paul's reference to wronging another person challenge the idea of purely private sexual sin?
catechismCourse.answer: It shows that impurity violates duties toward neighbours as well as toward God, even when participants describe it as personal freedom.

catechismCourse.title: Impurity in thought, speech, and action
catechismCourse.teach: The seventh commandment forbids unchaste thoughts, words, and actions. Adultery, fornication, pornography, and sexual relations contrary to God's institution of marriage all violate it. Sinful desire isn't made holy by intensity or by receiving social approval.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul calls believers to walk in love after Christ's self-giving and then excludes impurity and corrupt speech. His argument doesn't oppose love to holiness. It identifies the forms of conduct that contradict the love and light belonging to God's children.
catechismCourse.guard: Forgiveness isn't permission to keep cultivating impurity. Yet a believer who falls must be directed to Christ and renewed repentance, not told that Christ's sacrifice is insufficient for this category of sin.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does Paul's pattern show about the relation between love and sexual holiness?
catechismCourse.answer: Christlike love includes refusing impurity and exploitation. Love cannot be used as a name for disobeying God's moral order.

catechismCourse.title: The eighth commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The eighth commandment forbids theft and establishes our duty to respect the lawful goods of others. It reaches dishonest gain and the unjust withholding of what is owed. It also directs us to use our own work and possessions in ways that serve our neighbour.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul moves from stopping theft to honest labour and sharing with those in need. The change is more than avoiding punishment. Grace turns a taker into a worker and giver. Read it within the putting off of the old man and putting on of the new.
catechismCourse.guard: Private property isn't absolute independence from God's claim. Neither may we call every lawful possession theft merely because another person has less. Justice and generosity must both be governed by Scripture.
catechismCourse.exercise: What positive transformation does Paul require beyond ceasing to steal?
catechismCourse.answer: Honest work should provide not only for oneself but also the means to help others in need.

catechismCourse.title: Lawfully furthering another’s estate
catechismCourse.teach: The eighth commandment requires the lawful procuring and furthering of our own and our neighbour's wealth and outward estate. Honest work, fair dealings, faithful stewardship, and generosity belong together. We must also preserve what has been entrusted to our care rather than treating negligence as morally neutral.
catechismCourse.argument: Leviticus places harvest provision for the poor beside prohibitions of theft, fraud, and withheld wages. Read these as distinct duties with a shared concern for justice and neighbour-love. The particulars belonged to Israel's order, while their moral equity continues to instruct us.
catechismCourse.guard: Helping a neighbour's estate doesn't authorize greed or methods God forbids. Charity doesn't cancel the employer's duty to pay justly, and fair payment doesn't cancel the duty of mercy.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why are fair wages and generosity not interchangeable duties?
catechismCourse.answer: Wages are what is owed in justice, while generosity gives freely beyond that debt. One cannot repair theft by renaming a payment as charity.

catechismCourse.title: Theft, fraud, and waste
catechismCourse.teach: The eighth commandment forbids whatever unjustly hinders our own or our neighbour's outward estate. Fraud, withheld wages, dishonest measures, and wasteful mismanagement can violate it without a visible act of taking money from a pocket. Love seeks justice in transactions as well as generosity afterward.
catechismCourse.argument: James confronts wealth accumulated through oppression and unpaid labour. The workers' cry reaches the Lord. Follow the relation between unjust gain and coming judgment. Possession of wealth doesn't establish that its acquisition or use has been lawful.
catechismCourse.guard: Poverty isn't itself proof of virtue, and wealth isn't itself proof of theft. Examine actual duties and conduct. Avoid turning a command against injustice into envy of every unequal outcome.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does retaining unpaid wages fall within the moral concern of this commandment?
catechismCourse.answer: It unjustly keeps another person's lawful due and enriches one party through the deprivation of another.

catechismCourse.title: The ninth commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The ninth commandment forbids false witness and requires truth in our dealings with one another. It protects the truth and the good name of our neighbour, especially in testimony and judgment. A reputation isn't ours to damage merely because a story is interesting or useful to our side.
catechismCourse.argument: Zechariah joins truthful speech, peaceful judgment, and the rejection of false oaths with the Lord's purpose for His people. These duties sustain a just common life. The passage doesn't permit religious enthusiasm to compensate for deceitful dealings.
catechismCourse.guard: Protecting a good name doesn't mean concealing actual wrongdoing from those responsible to address it. Truth may require sober testimony. Distinguish responsible reporting from gossip and the presumption of guilt.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why must truth and just judgment be taught together?
