catechismCourse.answer: Judgment depends on faithful testimony, and truthful speech must serve justice rather than become a weapon of distortion or malice.

catechismCourse.title: Preserving truth and a good name
catechismCourse.teach: The ninth commandment requires maintaining truth and our neighbour's good name as well as our own, especially when bearing witness. We should speak carefully, acknowledge what we don't know, and resist a readiness to believe evil. Love doesn't make careless accusations harmless.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul connects truthful speech with membership in one body. The church's growth in Christ requires speaking truth in love, not using either truth or love as an excuse to abandon the other. Falsehood injures those whose good we are bound to seek.
catechismCourse.guard: A technically accurate statement can still mislead if essential context is deliberately withheld. Preserving a good name isn't flattery. Faithful correction should be proportionate and directed toward the proper good.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does membership in one body strengthen the duty to speak truth?
catechismCourse.answer: Falsehood harms fellow members whose good belongs to our shared life in Christ, while truth serves the body's growth.

catechismCourse.title: Falsehood, slander, and rash judgment
catechismCourse.teach: The ninth commandment forbids anything prejudicial to truth or unjustly injurious to a good name. Lying, slander, malicious insinuation, and accepting a charge without sufficient grounds violate it. Our duty includes the care with which we hear and repeat reports.
catechismCourse.argument: Proverbs warns about the appeal of whispered reports and about answering before hearing. The first account may appear convincing until another examines it. These observations require patient judgment, not a refusal ever to reach a warranted conclusion.
catechismCourse.guard: Being suspicious of everyone isn't discernment. Neither is defending a respected person regardless of evidence. Hear relevant testimony, distinguish established fact from inference, and speak within the limits of what is known.
catechismCourse.exercise: What danger does the proverb about the first account identify?
catechismCourse.answer: A partial presentation can sound complete until it is questioned and compared with relevant evidence from another side.

catechismCourse.title: The tenth commandment
catechismCourse.teach: The tenth commandment forbids coveting what belongs to our neighbour. It reaches the disordered desire beneath outward acts. God's law requires contentment and love even where no other person sees a wrong and no civil court can judge the heart.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul uses the command against coveting to explain how the law exposes sin. The law isn't itself evil because sin seizes its occasion. Read his distinction between the holiness of the commandment and the sinful response it reveals.
catechismCourse.guard: Recognizing inward sin doesn't make every desire unlawful. We may properly seek needed goods or another's good. Coveting resents God's ordering and desires possession in a way contrary to His law.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is this command especially revealing about the inward reach of God's law?
catechismCourse.answer: It directly condemns disordered desire, showing that outward compliance cannot by itself establish righteousness before God.

catechismCourse.title: Contentment and a charitable spirit
catechismCourse.teach: The tenth commandment requires full contentment with our own condition and a right, charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour and all that is his. Contentment rests in God's care. It permits rejoicing in another's good without treating it as a loss of our own worth.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul describes learning contentment in abundance and need through Christ's strength. Read the familiar statement about doing all things in this immediate setting. He speaks about endurance and faithful dependence in changing circumstances, not unlimited personal achievement.
catechismCourse.guard: Contentment doesn't forbid lawful efforts to improve a difficult condition or seek relief from injustice. It forbids a resentful demand that God's goodness must be measured by comparison with someone else's possessions.
catechismCourse.exercise: What does the context teach about Paul's confidence in Christ's strength?
catechismCourse.answer: Christ enables him to remain faithful in both want and abundance, rather than guaranteeing every desired earthly outcome.

catechismCourse.title: Discontent, envy, and inordinate desire
catechismCourse.teach: The tenth commandment forbids discontent with our estate, envy or grief at our neighbour's good, and inordinate desires for what is his. Such desires can drive disputes long before they produce theft or adultery. We must bring the desire itself under God's judgment.
catechismCourse.argument: James traces quarrels to desires at war within people and exposes prayers directed toward indulging those desires. The remedy includes submission to God and humbling oneself before Him. His promise of grace opposes pride rather than approving its demands.
catechismCourse.guard: A desire for relief from suffering isn't automatically coveting. Examine whether the desire submits to God's will and respects the neighbour's good, rather than treating every painful longing as the same sin.
catechismCourse.exercise: How can even prayer become entangled with covetousness?
catechismCourse.answer: We can ask God to serve disordered desires instead of seeking His will and the good He commands.

catechismCourse.title: Our inability to keep the law perfectly
catechismCourse.teach: No mere man since the fall can perfectly keep God's commandments in this life. We break them daily in thought, word, and deed. Christ alone is sinless. Regeneration begins true obedience without removing all corruption, and glorification brings the freedom from sin for which believers long.
catechismCourse.argument: James includes himself among those who offend in many things and particularly warns teachers about speech. This calls for humility and careful conduct. It doesn't make the command to govern the tongue meaningless or excuse a deliberate refusal to repent.
catechismCourse.guard: Imperfect obedience can still be sincere and accepted through Christ. Its defects prevent it from earning justification. We obey from a received salvation, while confessing the sin that remains even in our best works.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why should our inability to obey perfectly produce neither self-righteousness nor surrender?
catechismCourse.answer: It destroys confidence in our merit while directing us to Christ's pardon and the Spirit's strength for real, though imperfect, obedience.

catechismCourse.title: Degrees and aggravations of sin
catechismCourse.teach: All sin is hateful to God, but sins aren't equally heinous. Their nature and circumstances can aggravate guilt. Greater knowledge, entrusted responsibility, deliberate malice, and harm to others can make an offence more serious. The law's reach doesn't erase these distinctions.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus tells Pilate that another bears greater sin, even while affirming that Pilate's authority is received from above. The comparison recognizes degrees of guilt without excusing the lesser wrong. Read the dialogue within the actual decisions each person makes.
catechismCourse.guard: Degrees of sin don't create a category of harmless disobedience. Nor may we use another's greater guilt to avoid confessing our own. Every sin needs the mercy found in Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Christ's comparison establish degrees of guilt without acquitting Pilate?
catechismCourse.answer: He identifies a greater sin while still treating Pilate as an accountable ruler making a morally serious decision.

catechismCourse.title: What every sin deserves
catechismCourse.teach: Every sin deserves God's wrath and curse in this life and that which is to come. The holiness of the lawgiver gives sin its seriousness. No sin is so small that it deserves pardon as a debt, yet no sin is beyond pardon for those who truly repent through Christ.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul explains the curse upon everyone who fails to continue in all that the law requires, and then declares Christ's bearing of that curse for His people. Follow the movement from the law's demand to redemption. Our hope is a curse borne by the Redeemer, not a lowered standard.
catechismCourse.guard: Christians must distinguish what their sin deserves from the condemnation Christ has removed. The justified are under fatherly discipline, not a renewed judicial curse that makes Christ's satisfaction incomplete.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why doesn't the gospel solve our problem by reducing God's requirement?
catechismCourse.answer: It supplies redemption through Christ's bearing the curse, preserving the law's holiness while delivering His people from condemnation.

catechismCourse.title: Escaping God’s wrath through Christ
catechismCourse.teach: God requires faith in Jesus Christ, repentance unto life, and diligent use of the outward means by which Christ communicates redemption. Faith and repentance are His gifts and our real duties. The means are His appointed way of nourishing us, not a payment added to Christ's work.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul describes his ministry in terms of repentance toward God and faith toward the Lord Jesus Christ. Read this beside his readiness to suffer for the gospel of grace. The apostolic message joins a free Saviour with a genuine command to turn and believe.
catechismCourse.guard: Using the means doesn't justify a person who refuses Christ. Nor should a troubled sinner wait until repentance feels sufficiently deep before coming to Him. Come to the Saviour who grants both pardon and renewal.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why must repentance and faith be taught together without making either a meritorious work?
catechismCourse.answer: Both are necessary responses produced by grace, while Christ alone supplies the righteousness and satisfaction on which salvation rests.

catechismCourse.title: Saving faith in Jesus Christ
catechismCourse.teach: Saving faith receives and rests upon Jesus Christ alone for salvation as He is offered in the gospel. It includes knowledge and assent, but goes beyond merely agreeing that Christian claims are true. Faith personally relies on the promised Saviour rather than on works, religious standing, or the strength of one's believing.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus connects coming to Him with believing in Him and promises not to cast out those who come. Read the promise alongside the Father's giving and the Son's preserving work. Divine sovereignty strengthens the gospel promise rather than placing a secret qualification in front of the sinner.
catechismCourse.guard: Faith can be weak and assailed while still truly resting on Christ. Its saving value lies in its object. Assurance that I believe isn't the same thing as the direct act of receiving Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: Where should a person look when anxious that his faith is too weak to save?
catechismCourse.answer: He should look to the Christ who receives those who come, rather than turn faith's strength into a substitute saviour.

catechismCourse.title: Repentance unto life
catechismCourse.teach: Repentance unto life is a saving grace by which a sinner, seeing sin's evil and receiving God's mercy in Christ, grieves for and hates sin, turns to God, and purposes new obedience. It concerns particular sins as well as the corrupt heart from which they come.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul distinguishes godly sorrow from the sorrow of the world by their source and fruit. Read the concrete changes he describes. Genuine repentance isn't measured only by emotional intensity, but by an earnest turning from the wrong toward faithful obedience.
catechismCourse.guard: Repentance doesn't make satisfaction for sin or earn pardon. Tears without turning aren't its fulfilment, but returning struggles don't automatically prove that every earlier confession was false. Continue coming to Christ and forsaking the sin.
catechismCourse.exercise: What distinguishes godly sorrow from merely regretting painful consequences?
catechismCourse.answer: Godly sorrow recognizes sin before God and issues in a changed response, rather than simply wanting the discomfort removed.

catechismCourse.title: The ordinary means of grace
catechismCourse.teach: Christ ordinarily communicates the benefits of redemption through His ordinances, especially the Word, sacraments, and prayer. Their efficacy comes from His Spirit and blessing. They aren't human techniques for producing spiritual results on demand, nor dispensable accessories to private faith.
catechismCourse.argument: Luke describes baptized believers continuing in apostolic teaching and prayers within the gathered church. Their fellowship and generosity grow from that shared life. Read the ordinary pattern after the extraordinary events of Pentecost rather than making the unusual event the required pattern for every later gathering.
catechismCourse.guard: Private reading and prayer don't replace the public ministry Christ appoints. Nor does attendance work automatically. Receive the means with faith, seeking the Lord who uses them.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why should believers continue in ordinary ordinances instead of waiting for extraordinary experiences?
catechismCourse.answer: Christ appoints these means for His church's ongoing nourishment and promises His blessing through them.

catechismCourse.title: The Word made effectual by the Spirit
catechismCourse.teach: The Spirit makes the reading, and especially the preaching, of the Word an effectual means of convincing and converting sinners and building believers in holiness and comfort. The text's authority is already divine. The Spirit's inward work gives saving reception of what is truly revealed.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul contrasts reliance on rhetorical display with the demonstration of the Spirit's power, then explains spiritual reception of God's truth. He doesn't praise careless speech or oppose sound reasoning. He denies that human skill can produce the saving knowledge God gives.
catechismCourse.guard: A hearer's conversion doesn't make a passage inspired, and failure to believe doesn't remove its authority. Preachers must faithfully explain Scripture and depend on God rather than attempt to manufacture conviction.
catechismCourse.exercise: What distinction should a preacher maintain between faithful explanation and saving effectiveness?
catechismCourse.answer: He is responsible to preach the Word truly, while only God's Spirit can make that Word savingly received.

catechismCourse.title: Reading and hearing with faith
catechismCourse.teach: We should attend to the Word with diligence, preparation, and prayer, receive it with faith and love, lay it up in our hearts, and practise it in our lives. Understanding a difficult passage may take patient study. Reverence isn't a substitute for careful reading, and careful reading isn't a substitute for obedience.
catechismCourse.argument: James contrasts hearing alone with doing the Word and uses a mirror to expose forgetful attention. The Word must be received meekly because it addresses us, not merely other people's errors. Read the examples of bridled speech and practical care as applications of that reception.
catechismCourse.guard: Application must grow from the passage's actual meaning. A moving personal thought isn't necessarily what the text teaches. Test your summary against the paragraph and distinguish what it states from a possible implication.
catechismCourse.exercise: What makes the mirror illustration an appropriate warning for Bible readers?
catechismCourse.answer: A person can recognize something true momentarily and then leave unchanged, failing to retain and act on what the Word reveals.

catechismCourse.title: The Spirit’s efficacy in the sacraments
catechismCourse.teach: The sacraments become effectual means of salvation through Christ's blessing and the working of His Spirit in those who receive them by faith. Neither the rite itself nor the minister's personal holiness contains an independent saving power. The Lord gives what the signs signify according to His promise.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul distinguishes the servants who plant and water from God who gives the increase. This passage addresses ministry generally rather than defining a sacrament. Its principle helps explain why outward administration and inward spiritual fruit must be distinguished without despising appointed means.
catechismCourse.guard: A sacrament isn't an empty illustration simply because it doesn't work automatically. Nor does an unbelieving recipient receive Christ savingly merely by handling the outward sign. The Spirit joins faithful reception with the promised benefit.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why can the church value a minister's service without treating him as the source of grace?
catechismCourse.answer: God uses appointed servants while retaining the power to give spiritual life and growth Himself.

catechismCourse.title: Sign, seal, and sacramental union
catechismCourse.teach: A sacrament is a holy ordinance instituted by Christ in which sensible signs represent, seal, and apply Christ and the benefits of the new covenant to believers. The sign and the thing signified remain distinct, yet have a real sacramental relation established by God's institution.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul calls Abraham's circumcision a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith he already possessed. The order matters to his argument against making circumcision the cause of justification. The seal confirms God's promise rather than certifying that every recipient is inwardly regenerate.
catechismCourse.guard: Scripture can name the sign by the benefit it signifies. That sacramental language mustn't be forced into the claim that water itself regenerates or that bread changes into Christ's bodily substance.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does Abraham's example show that a sacramental sign isn't the meritorious cause of justification?
catechismCourse.answer: He was counted righteous through faith before receiving circumcision, which then served as its covenant sign and seal.

catechismCourse.title: The two New Testament sacraments
catechismCourse.teach: Christ instituted baptism and the Lord's Supper as the New Testament sacraments. Baptism is administered once as the sign of admission into the visible church. The Supper is received repeatedly for spiritual nourishment. Both declare the same Christ, though their signs, uses, and proper recipients differ.
catechismCourse.argument: The risen Lord commissions His church to make disciples, baptize, and teach under His universal authority. Read this institution alongside His command concerning the Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. The church administers ordinances received from Him rather than inventing further sacraments.
catechismCourse.guard: The number of sacraments isn't determined by how moving a ceremony feels. Marriage, ordination, and other lawful actions mustn't be made additional sacraments of the New Testament.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why must sacramental practice begin with Christ's institution rather than church creativity?
catechismCourse.answer: A sacrament carries His covenant promise and authority, which no merely human ceremony can supply for itself.

catechismCourse.title: Baptism as a covenant sign and seal
catechismCourse.teach: Baptism is washing with water in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. It signifies and seals ingrafting into Christ, participation in the covenant of grace, and engagement to be the Lord's. Its benefits must be received through the Spirit's work, not assumed from the outward washing alone.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul appeals to baptism's meaning while explaining the believer's union with Christ's death and resurrection. His purpose is to rule out continuing under sin's dominion. He isn't teaching that everyone who receives water necessarily possesses the inward reality, regardless of faith.
catechismCourse.guard: Baptism's efficacy isn't tied to the moment of administration. Dipping isn't necessary, and pouring or sprinkling is lawful. A valid baptism is administered once, not repeated whenever a believer's assurance weakens.
catechismCourse.exercise: How should a baptized believer use baptism's meaning in the battle against sin?
catechismCourse.answer: He should remember his belonging to Christ and live in the reality baptism signifies, rather than treat grace as permission to remain under sin's rule.

catechismCourse.title: Believers and their children
catechismCourse.teach: Baptism is administered to those outside the visible church who profess faith in Christ and obedience to Him, and also to the infants of one or both believing parents. This follows the covenant inclusion of believers' children, while preserving the distinction between visible membership and inward regeneration.
catechismCourse.argument: Peter addresses hearers with the promise for them and their children and for those afar off whom the Lord calls. Read this with Genesis 17:7-14 and the New Testament household accounts. The infant-baptism argument rests on covenant continuity and the church's membership, not on one verse describing an infant's baptism.
catechismCourse.guard: Baptized children need the new birth and must be taught to repent and believe. Covenant membership isn't a substitute for saving union with Christ, yet neither is it an empty status without privileges and obligations.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why should infant baptism never be taught as a guarantee of regeneration?
catechismCourse.answer: The outward sign and visible membership are distinct from the Spirit's inward work, which God grants according to His promise and purpose.

catechismCourse.title: Feeding upon Christ in the Supper
catechismCourse.teach: In the Lord's Supper, by giving and receiving bread and wine according to Christ's appointment, His death is shown forth and worthy receivers truly partake of His body and blood by faith for spiritual nourishment. His presence is real and spiritual, not a change of the elements into His bodily substance.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul calls the cup and bread a communion in Christ's blood and body and draws a consequence for fellowship with idols. The ordinance is more than recalling an absent teacher. It expresses and strengthens participation in Christ and the unity of those who belong to Him.
catechismCourse.guard: The Supper doesn't repeat Christ's sacrifice. The bread and wine remain what they are. Unbelieving recipients take the outward elements without savingly feeding upon Christ and may receive them to judgment.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does Paul connect participation in the Supper with refusing idolatrous fellowship?
catechismCourse.answer: Communion with Christ lays an exclusive claim upon His people and cannot be combined with religious participation that denies that allegiance.

catechismCourse.title: Preparing for the Lord’s Table
catechismCourse.teach: Worthy receiving calls for self-examination concerning knowledge, faith, repentance, love, and new obedience. Worthiness doesn't mean personal merit or sinlessness. We discern the Lord's body and come as needy believers to the Saviour who supplies our nourishment.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul rebukes a divided congregation whose conduct at the meal contradicts its meaning. Read the warning about judgment within those concrete abuses. Examination should lead to a faithful participation that honours Christ and His body, not to indifference about other members.
catechismCourse.guard: A doubting believer who sincerely seeks Christ and grieves over sin isn't to be treated as a wilful unbeliever. The ignorant or scandalous may be kept from the Table by the church's lawful oversight. Seek the elders' help where preparation or admission is in question.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does self-examination differ from trying to prove oneself sinless before coming?
catechismCourse.answer: It tests whether we discern Christ and turn to Him in faith and repentance, rather than requiring a righteousness of our own.

catechismCourse.title: Prayer through the Mediator
catechismCourse.teach: Prayer offers our desires to God for things agreeable to His will, in Christ's name, with confession of sins and thankful acknowledgement of mercies. We address God alone. The Holy Spirit helps our weakness, and Christ's mediation gives the access we cannot earn by eloquence or intensity.
catechismCourse.argument: Hebrews grounds the invitation to come to the throne of grace in our great High Priest's identity and sympathy. Boldness is confidence in Him, not casualness toward God. The promised mercy and grace meet needy people who draw near through Christ.
catechismCourse.guard: Praying in Christ's name isn't a formula that guarantees a desired outcome. It means approaching on His authority and merits, asking under His will. The Spirit's help doesn't excuse thoughtlessness or disregard for Scripture.
catechismCourse.exercise: What gives a weak believer confidence to pray when his words feel inadequate?
catechismCourse.answer: His access rests on Christ's sufficient priesthood and the invitation of God's grace, not on the quality of his performance.

catechismCourse.title: The rule and pattern of prayer
catechismCourse.teach: The whole Word directs prayer, and the Lord's Prayer gives a special pattern. Its petitions order our concerns around God's glory and our true needs. It may be used as a prayer with understanding and as a model that guides other words offered to God.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus places this pattern after warnings against performing for an audience and trusting empty repetition. Read those warnings with the prayer itself. A short, familiar prayer can be offered sincerely, while a spontaneous one can still become a performance.
catechismCourse.guard: The pattern isn't a charm, and using its exact words isn't wrong. Understanding and faith matter. Neither a memorized form nor spontaneous language is acceptable apart from a heart approaching God through Christ.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does the context correct confidence in either impressive public language or sheer repetition?
catechismCourse.answer: The Father knows His children's needs, so prayer must seek Him sincerely rather than depend on display or quantity of words.

catechismCourse.title: Our Father in heaven
catechismCourse.teach: The preface to the Lord's Prayer teaches us to draw near with holy reverence and confidence, as children to a Father able and ready to help. The word our also teaches us to pray with and for others. Heavenly majesty and fatherly kindness belong together.
catechismCourse.argument: Paul joins adoption, the Spirit's witness, and the child's cry to the Father with sharing Christ's sufferings and inheritance. Read the family language through union with Christ. The confidence of Christian prayer rests on granted sonship rather than a universal saving fatherhood apart from Him.
catechismCourse.guard: God's being in heaven doesn't mean He is absent from earth or limited to a place. The expression directs us to His exalted majesty and power while inviting trust in His fatherly care.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why should the preface produce both reverence and confidence?
catechismCourse.answer: We address the sovereign God who has received us as His children through Christ and is able to supply what is good.

catechismCourse.title: Hallowed be thy name
catechismCourse.teach: The first petition asks that God enable us and others to glorify Him in all by which He makes Himself known, and that He order all things to His own glory. His name is already holy. We ask that His holiness be known, honoured, and vindicated among His creatures.
catechismCourse.argument: Ezekiel connects the vindication of God's name with cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit's renewing work. His concern for His glory doesn't exclude mercy toward His people. It explains a salvation in which they have no ground for boasting in their own worth.
catechismCourse.guard: Seeking God's honour isn't permission to neglect a neighbour's need. The same God is honoured when His people reflect His truth and mercy. This petition also calls us to repent of bringing reproach upon His name.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does this petition ask for a change among creatures rather than an increase in God's holiness?
catechismCourse.answer: God is perfectly holy already. We ask that His holiness be rightly acknowledged and displayed in His dealings and our response.

catechismCourse.title: Thy kingdom come
catechismCourse.teach: The second petition asks that Satan's kingdom be destroyed, Christ's kingdom of grace advanced, ourselves and others brought into it and kept in it, and the kingdom of glory hastened. We pray for the gospel's spread and the church's faithful growth under the reigning Christ.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus' compassion for shepherdless people leads Him to command prayer for workers in the harvest. The kingdom comes through His saving work and the appointed ministry of His Word. Prayer for its advance includes concern for real people and faithful labourers.
catechismCourse.guard: The petition isn't a promise of uninterrupted earthly triumph or a mandate to identify a political party with Christ's kingdom. It includes the final consummation that only His return will bring.
catechismCourse.exercise: What practical concern should accompany prayer for the kingdom's advance?
catechismCourse.answer: We should seek the spread of the gospel through faithful workers and the gathering and shepherding of people under Christ.

catechismCourse.title: Thy will be done
catechismCourse.teach: The third petition asks God by His grace to make us able and willing to know, obey, and submit to His will as the angels do in heaven. We ask for inward obedience, not mere outward conformity. We also submit to His providential ordering when we cannot explain it.
catechismCourse.argument: The psalm calls the angels and heavenly hosts to bless the Lord as those who do His commandments. Their prompt service supplies the comparison in the prayer. Read it as a model of obedience to God's revealed command, not a demand to discover His secret decree.
catechismCourse.guard: Submission to providence doesn't require approving sin that God permits. We may oppose wrong and seek lawful relief while trusting His government. Our duty is found in His revealed will.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why must we distinguish God's revealed commands from His secret purpose when praying this petition?
catechismCourse.answer: We are responsible to obey what He reveals, while trusting the purpose He hasn't disclosed rather than trying to uncover it.

catechismCourse.title: Our daily bread
catechismCourse.teach: The fourth petition asks for a competent portion of the good things of this life as God's free gift, and for His blessing with them. Bread represents our lawful bodily needs. Daily dependence teaches gratitude, contentment, and concern for others who share those needs.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus' teaching about food, clothing, and the Father's care belongs with the call to seek His kingdom first. He doesn't deny bodily need or make responsible work faithless. He directs anxious people away from treating provision as a burden outside their Father's knowledge.
catechismCourse.guard: This petition doesn't guarantee wealth or forbid storing supplies prudently. We must use lawful means and ask that what we receive serve our good. Possession without God's blessing cannot satisfy the heart.
catechismCourse.exercise: What makes asking for daily bread different from demanding prosperity?
catechismCourse.answer: It seeks sufficient provision under the Father's wise care, with His blessing and in submission to His kingdom's priorities.

catechismCourse.title: Forgive us our debts
catechismCourse.teach: The fifth petition asks that God freely pardon all our sins for Christ's sake. We are encouraged to ask as those whom grace has made willing to forgive others. Believers need daily confession and fatherly pardon, while their justified standing remains grounded in Christ's completed work.
catechismCourse.argument: The parable contrasts an immense forgiven debt with the servant's refusal to show mercy. Its warning exposes the contradiction of seeking pardon while cherishing an unforgiving spirit. The servant's cruelty isn't presented as a minor defect in an otherwise sound claim upon mercy.
catechismCourse.guard: Forgiving others doesn't earn God's forgiveness or require pretending wrong never happened. It is compatible with truthful testimony, lawful justice, and appropriate boundaries. Reconciliation also involves repentance and the actual circumstances.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why is readiness to forgive evidence of grace rather than its purchase price?
catechismCourse.answer: It reflects mercy received from God and a changed heart, rather than supplying satisfaction for the guilt only Christ can remove.

catechismCourse.title: Deliver us from evil
catechismCourse.teach: The sixth petition asks that God keep us from being tempted to sin or support and deliver us when we are tempted. We confess our weakness and dependence. The request includes rescue from Satan, the world's snares, and the corrupt desires remaining within us.
catechismCourse.argument: Jesus directs the disciples to watch and pray in the hour of trial. Their willingness doesn't remove their weakness. Read their sleep and His obedience together. Our confidence cannot rest in present good intentions or in a claim that we would never fall as others have.
catechismCourse.guard: God may test His children, but He never entices anyone to evil. Prayer for preservation must accompany watchfulness and use of lawful safeguards. Refusing those means while demanding protection is presumption.
catechismCourse.exercise: Why does a willing spirit still need watchfulness and prayer?
catechismCourse.answer: Human weakness remains, so sincere intentions must depend on God's preserving help rather than become confidence in ourselves.

catechismCourse.title: The kingdom, power, glory, and Amen
catechismCourse.teach: The conclusion of the Lord's Prayer teaches us to take encouragement from God alone and to praise Him by ascribing the kingdom, power, and glory to Him for ever. Amen expresses our desire and assurance that He hears. The prayer ends where it began, with the sufficiency and honour of God.
catechismCourse.argument: David's prayer acknowledges that all things come from God and asks Him to preserve the people's willing hearts. Divine sovereignty doesn't silence petition. Because God owns and rules all, His people ask Him for what they cannot secure in their own strength.
catechismCourse.guard: Amen isn't a magical ending or a promise that every requested detail must occur exactly as we imagine. It expresses sincere agreement and confidence that our Father hears and answers according to His wise will.
catechismCourse.exercise: How does praise of God's sovereignty strengthen prayer rather than make it pointless?
catechismCourse.answer: The God who rules and supplies all things is able to give what we ask, and He appoints prayer as a means of seeking His help.

doctrineSupplements.title: Free will in man’s four states
paragraphs: The will is a real faculty by which a person chooses willingly. Its moral condition changes through the history of creation, fall, redemption, and glory. Freedom never means independence from God, and moral inability doesn't mean that sinners are physically forced to choose what they hate.

In innocence, Adam had power to do what pleased God but could fall. In the fallen estate, man willingly serves sin and cannot convert himself or prepare himself for conversion by his own strength. In the estate of grace, God frees the will from bondage to sin and enables spiritual good, though remaining corruption brings real conflict. In glory, the will is perfectly and unchangeably free to good alone.

Paul's slavery imagery describes a change of mastery that produces a change of life. The redeemed act willingly, yet their freedom is the fruit of deliverance. Read his commands to present our members to righteousness as duties made possible by that deliverance, not as the means by which an enslaved sinner first purchases it.

The holy freedom of heaven corrects the claim that real freedom must always include the ability to sin. The glorified saints won't be less human because they cannot fall away. Their perfected wills will delight without corruption in the God they know.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: Why is the glorified believer's inability to sin compatible with perfect freedom?
doctrineSupplements.answer: Freedom is perfected in willing, uncorrupted obedience to God, rather than in the perpetual possibility of choosing evil.

doctrineSupplements.title: Assurance without presumption
paragraphs: Saving faith receives Christ. Assurance is the believer's well-grounded persuasion that he belongs to Christ and will be saved. The two must be distinguished. A believer may genuinely rest in Christ while struggling to recognize the evidences of grace in his own life.

The Confession grounds assurance in the truth of God's promises, inward evidence of the graces to which those promises belong, and the Spirit's witness of adoption. No private revelation is needed. The promises are primary, and the Spirit trains us to recognize His work through the Word rather than through an untested inward voice.

John joins Christ's advocacy for sinners with the evidential place of obedience. Read both parts. Christ is the ground of acceptance, while walking in His commandments gives evidence of knowing Him. John doesn't make perfect performance the condition of having an advocate, and he doesn't allow a profession of faith to excuse settled disobedience.

Serious sin and neglected means can wound assurance. Spiritual darkness doesn't by itself prove that grace has ended. Repent, return to the promises, and seek pastoral help. Don't demand an immediate level of emotional confidence as the price of approaching the Saviour.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: How can we examine the fruits of faith without making those fruits the ground of justification?
doctrineSupplements.answer: Treat them as evidence of the Spirit's work while resting acceptance before God solely on Christ's righteousness.

doctrineSupplements.title: Lawful oaths and vows
paragraphs: A lawful oath solemnly calls God to witness the truth of what we affirm or promise and to judge falsehood. A vow is a solemn promise made to God. Both belong to religious worship and require truth, understanding, and reverence. They aren't devices for making ordinary dishonesty acceptable.

Hebrews appeals to God's oath as gracious confirmation of His unchangeable promise. Its account of an oath's confirmatory purpose shows that solemn swearing isn't inherently evil. Christ's prohibition of rash and evasive swearing in Matthew 5 must be read with this teaching, rather than used to cancel every lawful oath.

We must swear only by God's name, only about what is true or intended in good faith, and in the plain sense of the words. A lawful oath can be required by a lawful authority. Mental reservations that deliberately defeat the words' meaning are deceit, not clever escape.

A vow cannot bind us to sin, prevent a commanded duty, or promise what God hasn't enabled us to perform. Monastic vows of perpetual single life, professed poverty, and unconditional obedience to a religious order aren't a higher state of perfection. God's commands, rather than religious invention, determine our duty.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: Why can't a promise to do something sinful become binding merely because God's name was invoked?
doctrineSupplements.answer: God's authority cannot authorize disobedience to His own law. The sinful promise itself calls for repentance, not performance.

doctrineSupplements.title: Marriage and divorce
paragraphs: Marriage is God's covenant union of one man and one woman, ordained for their mutual help, the legitimate increase of mankind and the church, and the prevention of uncleanness. Both parties must be able to give a lawful consent. Christians are commanded to marry in the Lord, not to enter a union that disregards the faith.

Jesus answers a divorce controversy by returning to creation and God's joining of husband and wife. The appeal makes marriage more than a private arrangement dissolved whenever affection declines. His treatment of Moses' concession also requires distinguishing regulation in a fallen society from God's original institution.

The Confession identifies adultery and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied by church or civil authority as sufficient grounds for dissolving marriage. Such matters require a public and orderly process rather than private self-acquittal. A difficult marriage doesn't itself supply a biblical ground for divorce, and every case requires truthful attention to the facts.

Teaching covenant permanence must never authorize violence, coercion, or concealment of wrongdoing. Immediate protection and lawful intervention can be necessary while marital obligations and any ground for dissolution are carefully considered. The church must uphold God's law toward both spouses and provide wise pastoral care rather than slogans.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: Why does Christ return to creation instead of allowing the controversy to be settled by personal preference?
doctrineSupplements.answer: God instituted marriage and gives its binding character. Fallen desires and later concessions cannot redefine the union He created.

doctrineSupplements.title: Christ’s church and its membership
paragraphs: The invisible church is the whole number of the elect united to Christ. The visible church consists of those throughout the world who profess the true religion, together with their children. These are two ways of considering Christ's church, not two unrelated peoples with different saviours.

Christ alone is the church's Head. He gives the ministry, oracles, and ordinances of God for gathering and perfecting the saints. Paul connects His gifts with the body's growth in truth and love. Belonging to Christ therefore calls believers into an ordered common life rather than permanent independence from His gathered people.

Visible membership brings real privileges and obligations, but doesn't guarantee regeneration. Churches also differ in purity and may err. Test their teaching and worship by Scripture while refusing the idea that personal disagreement gives a right to despise every lawful authority or abandon Christian fellowship.

Read the historical judgments of WCF 25 in their own words, including its rejection of any rival universal head of the church. This companion retains the source's original text. Those claims must be examined and explained from Scripture rather than silently edited or used as a substitute for judging particular teaching truthfully.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: Why don't imperfect churches make the visible church unnecessary?
doctrineSupplements.answer: Christ Himself gives His public ministry and ordinances for His people's growth, even while calling actual churches to correction and greater faithfulness.

doctrineSupplements.title: Presbyterian government, discipline, and councils
paragraphs: Christ appoints government in His church in the hands of church officers, distinct from the civil magistrate. The keys of the kingdom concern the ministry of the Word and the exercise of spiritual discipline. Ministers and ruling elders serve under Christ rather than becoming lords of the conscience.

Ministers labour in the Word and doctrine as well as ruling. Ruling elders share in the church's government. Deacons are appointed for service and care of outward needs, not to replace the ministry of Word or the elders' rule. These distinct offices must be exercised according to the scriptural qualifications, rather than distributed merely for status.

Acts 15 shows a doctrinal controversy brought before apostles and elders, considered with testimony and Scripture, and answered for the churches' peace. The apostolic setting is unique, but the connected deliberation supports church government wider than an isolated congregation. Scripture supplies the rule for the conclusion.

Church censures aim to reclaim offenders, deter sin, preserve the church's purity, and vindicate Christ's honour. Their severity should fit the offence and the person's response. The church mustn't confuse restoration with ignoring unrepentant scandal, nor confuse discipline with punishment undertaken for personal revenge.

Synods and councils ministerially determine controversies and settle matters of order under God's Word. Their authority is real but fallible. No council becomes an infallible rule of faith. Civil questions belong to their proper sphere, and a church court mustn't take upon itself the ordinary business of civil government.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: How can a council's decision carry authority while remaining open to correction?
doctrineSupplements.answer: Its authority is ministerial under Scripture. It binds according to God's Word and can be corrected where it departs from that rule.

doctrineSupplements.title: The communion of saints
paragraphs: All saints united to Christ share fellowship with Him in His graces, sufferings, death, resurrection, and glory. United to one another in love, they share in each other's gifts and have duties contributing to mutual good. This communion begins with Christ's gift before becoming our obligation.

Paul's body illustration joins real diversity with mutual dependence. An apparently weak member cannot be dismissed as unnecessary, and an honoured member cannot claim independence. The Spirit places members within a body whose shared suffering and joy contradict both pride and neglect.

Christian communion includes worship, spiritual service, and relief in outward things according to ability and need. It should extend as God gives opportunity to those in every place who call upon the Lord Jesus. Ordinary church membership is a central expression of this duty, not its entire boundary.

This fellowship doesn't make believers partakers of Christ's divine substance or equal with Him. Nor does it abolish lawful property or erase responsibility for one's household. Shared life calls for willing, wise generosity under God's law, rather than either isolated self-sufficiency or a coerced erasure of all distinctions.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: How does Paul's body illustration correct both superiority and withdrawal?
doctrineSupplements.answer: Every member receives a place and gifts from God and needs the others, so neither despising another nor claiming independence fits the body.

doctrineSupplements.title: Christ’s kingship and civil authority
paragraphs: Civil government is ordained by God for His glory and the public good. Its office concerns justice and protection within a lawful civil sphere. Rulers remain accountable to God's moral law and to the universal authority of Christ. Christian obedience includes lawful honour, tribute, and prayer for those in authority.

Paul grounds the magistrate's office in God's appointment and describes the sword's public function against wrongdoing. The text doesn't identify every act of a ruler as righteous. An office can be divinely ordained while an officeholder sins in its use. God's command remains higher than a human command.

The source's unrevised WCF 23.3 assigns the magistrate duties toward the preservation of true religion while denying him the ministry of Word and sacrament or the keys of the kingdom. This isn't religious neutrality. Church and state have distinct offices, but neither is morally independent of God.

The church uses spiritual means and mustn't usurp the sword. The magistrate cannot make doctrine true by decree or administer church censures. Particular public-policy applications require careful moral judgment and mustn't be presented as though every preferred policy were expressly stated in the Confession.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: How does divine appointment of an office differ from divine approval of everything its holder does?
doctrineSupplements.answer: God establishes the office's lawful purpose while judging rulers who exceed or misuse their delegated authority.

doctrineSupplements.title: The free offer and the warrant to believe
paragraphs: The gospel freely offers Jesus Christ to sinners and commands all who hear to repent and believe. The warrant to come is God's revealed invitation and command, not prior knowledge of election or an inward discovery of special worthiness. Christ receives every sinner who truly comes to Him.

Isaiah's invitation addresses those with no purchase price and calls the wicked to forsake his way. The free invitation and the command to turn belong together. Grace supplies what the hearer cannot buy, while refusing to leave sin unchallenged.

The Father's election and Christ's definite redemption don't restrict the outward offer to a class we can identify beforehand. God brings His elect to faith through that proclaimed gospel. Ministers must make the promise known without inventing hidden conditions that keep troubled sinners from Christ.

The offer doesn't mean that every hearer is already forgiven or that repentance is unnecessary. Neither should a convicted sinner delay coming until he has produced enough sorrow. Come empty-handed to Christ, receiving Him as Saviour and Lord.
doctrineSupplements.exercise: What gives an anxious hearer the right and duty to come to Christ now?
doctrineSupplements.answer: God's revealed invitation and command, together with Christ's promise to receive those who come, supply the warrant without access to the secret decree.
